Section 4 · The Normal Heart

Exercise Physiology, Cardioprotection and Prevention

Most coronary disease comes from three habits — poor diet, physical inactivity and smoking — and Dr. Qazi’s argument was that exercise should be prescribed like a drug, because each step up in fitness lowers mortality about as much as a cardiac medicine does. This section covers how the circulation responds to exercise, why that protects the heart, how cardiac rehabilitation works, and the diets with outcome data behind them.

Abbreviations used in this section CVD cardiovascular disease · CAD coronary artery disease · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · HR heart rate · SV stroke volume · CO cardiac output · SBP / DBP systolic / diastolic blood pressure · VO₂ oxygen uptake · VO₂max / VO₂peak maximal / symptom-limited peak oxygen uptake · MET metabolic equivalent (resting energy use, about 3.5 mL of oxygen per kg per minute) · CR cardiac rehabilitation · MI myocardial infarction · STEMI ST-elevation myocardial infarction · ECG electrocardiogram · ACE angiotensin-converting enzyme · ACC/AHA American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association · ACS acute coronary syndrome · CABG coronary artery bypass graft · PCI percutaneous coronary intervention (a stent) · PAD peripheral artery disease · HF heart failure · HFrEF heart failure with reduced ejection fraction · LVAD left ventricular assist device · RPE rating of perceived exertion (Borg scale, 6–20) · FITT frequency, intensity, time, type · DASH Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension · HDL / LDL high- / low-density lipoprotein · CRP C-reactive protein · NO nitric oxide · METs metabolic equivalents

Why exercise protects the heart ★ HY

  • Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide.
  • An estimated 75–90% of coronary disease is explained by modifiable risk factors: poor diet, physical inactivity and cigarette smoking.
  • Physical inactivity is an independent risk factor, linked to about 12% of all deaths in the United States.
  • Regular moderate activity lowers all-cause mortality by about 25% in patients with coronary disease and by 20–30% in the general population.
Protective effectHow
Anti-inflammatoryLower C-reactive protein
AntithromboticLess platelet aggregation, more fibrinolysis
AntiarrhythmicBetter autonomic balance: more vagal tone, less sympathetic activity
AntiatherogenicBetter endothelial function from higher flow and shear stress, which raises nitric oxide production
Risk factorsLower total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides · higher HDL · lower blood pressure · better insulin sensitivity · weight loss
Anti-ischemicBetter myocardial perfusion, a higher ischemic threshold, ischemic preconditioning
PsychologicalLess depression and stress, more social support
🎙️ From the recording: what she stressed
  • Too much of a good thing: inflammatory markers are actually high straight after a marathon, and ultra-endurance runners commonly develop atrial fibrillation. The protection belongs to regular, moderate exercise.
  • The lipid change she sees most in clinic is a clear rise in HDL when sedentary patients start exercising.
  • In a trial of depressed patients on one antidepressant, adding regular exercise worked about as well as adding a second antidepressant.

The cardiorespiratory response to exercise ★ HY

TermMeaning
Age-predicted maximal heart rate220 minus age (give or take 10–15 beats)
Heart-rate reservePeak heart rate minus resting heart rate
VO₂max versus VO₂peakOxygen use at true maximal effort versus at the point symptoms stop the test; VO₂peak is lower in most sedentary adults
METThe energy of resting metabolism, 1 MET ≈ 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min
MET-hoursIntensity × time × frequency — walking at 3 METs for 1 hour on 3 days is 9 MET-hours a week

Heart rate

rises linearly, then plateaus

Climbs in a straight line with workload, and at any steady submaximal load levels off within 2–3 minutes. The maximum is about 220 minus age.

Stroke volume

rises early, then flattens

Rises along a curve and is nearly maximal by about 50% of VO₂max. After that, cardiac output rises mainly through heart rate.

Oxygen extraction

about three-fold

Working muscle pulls about three times as much oxygen out of each litre of blood at peak as at rest. Muscle’s share of cardiac output goes from 15–20% at rest to 85–90%.

Blood pressure

systolic up, diastolic flat

Systolic pressure rises about 8–12 mm Hg per MET, to roughly 190 in men and 170 in women at peak. Diastolic pressure stays the same or falls slightly.

🧠 Why diastolic pressure stays flat — and how cardiac output keeps rising
  • Arterioles in working muscle, skin and heart dilate, so total peripheral resistance falls sharply. The extra output flows through those open beds instead of raising diastolic pressure. Flow to the brain stays constant; flow to the gut and kidneys falls.
  • Dr. Morganelli’s point: a high output is only possible if venous return keeps up. Sympathetic tone stiffens the veins, which pushes blood out of the venous reservoir and raises the pressure driving it back to the heart (Section 5).
  • Board add-on The Fick principle ties it together: oxygen uptake equals cardiac output times the arterial–venous oxygen difference, and exercise raises both.
  • Board add-on On an exercise test, a fall in systolic pressure as the workload rises suggests severe ischemia or left ventricular dysfunction.
🛋️

Deconditioned

  • High resting heart rate.
  • The rate shoots up as soon as the treadmill starts and stays high long after stopping.
🏃

Conditioned (a marathoner)

  • Slow resting heart rate.
  • The rate stays low for much of the test and drops back to baseline quickly afterward.

VO₂peak is measured by cardiopulmonary exercise testing, mostly in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction to judge transplant candidacy — a falling VO₂peak means the patient is getting closer to transplant.

Fitness, METs and mortality

  • Cardiorespiratory fitness is a powerful independent predictor of mortality in cardiovascular disease.
  • In coronary disease, each 1-MET increase in exercise capacity lowers mortality by 8–35% — comparable to statins, beta-blockers, low-dose aspirin and ACE inhibitors after a heart attack. A meta-analysis of 33 studies gave a relative risk of 0.87 per MET.
  • Men who went from unfit to fit over about five years roughly halved their mortality. Getting fit later still counts.
  • The least-fit, highest-risk patients (below about 5 METs) should be referred to structured cardiac rehabilitation.
Class of recommendation2019 ACC/AHA primary prevention — physical activity
ICounsel adults at every visit to be physically active
IAt least 150 minutes a week of moderate or 75 minutes a week of vigorous aerobic activity, or a combination
IIaIf they cannot reach that, some moderate or vigorous activity still helps
IIbCutting sedentary time may be reasonable

Dr. Qazi asked the class to find ways to talk about exercise without the patient feeling fat-shamed — patients often hear it as a comment on their weight.

Cardiac rehabilitation: who, when and the phases ★ HY

Cardiac rehabilitation is the secondary-prevention tier of the prevention pyramid. Its core parts are assessment, exercise training, activity counselling, nutrition counselling, management of weight, blood pressure, lipids and diabetes, tobacco cessation, and psychosocial care.

  1. Phase I — inpatient. Physical therapy and education straight after the event or procedure. Dr. Qazi: now mostly meaningless, because a STEMI gets emergency PCI and goes home in a day or two, so patients go straight to phase II.
  2. Phase II — outpatient and supervised. 36 sessions, usually three a week, ECG-monitored, over 8–12 weeks, in a staffed facility. Continuous ECG monitoring is its defining feature. Medicare pays for the 36 sessions.
  3. Phases III and IV — maintenance. Independent, unmonitored continuation of what was learned in phase II. Not covered by insurance — “like an expensive gym membership.”
IndicationClass
Acute coronary syndrome in the past 12 monthsI
After CABG or PCII
Chronic stable anginaI
Peripheral artery disease (walking programme is first-line for claudication)I
Chronic heart failureIIa — Medicare covers it only with an ejection fraction of 35% or less
Valve repair or replacement, LVAD, heart or heart–lung transplantListed

When to start

timing

1–2 weeks after discharge for a non-surgical event; 2–6 weeks after CABG or other major surgery (at least 4 weeks after a sternotomy in practice).

The intake

before the first session

History, examination and a symptom-limited exercise test to set fitness and maximal heart rate and watch for ischemia or arrhythmia — on the patient’s usual medications, so the prescription matches how they will exercise.

AHA risk classes

A to D

A apparently healthy · B stable disease, low risk · C moderate-to-high risk during exercise · D unstable, so restrict activity. Most rehab patients are B or C.

Underused

only 30–40% enrol

Older patients, women, minorities, the uninsured and those with depression miss out most. The strongest lever you control is the strength of the physician’s endorsement — put “rehab referral done?” in your post-MI template.

EvidenceWhoResult
Meta-analysis of 47 trialsAfter MI, CABG or PCI, or with anginaTotal mortality down 13%, cardiovascular mortality down 26%; fewer admissions, less angina and depression
HF-ACTIONHeart failure with reduced ejection fractionThe seminal heart-failure rehab trial: 11% fewer deaths or hospitalizations, 15% fewer cardiovascular deaths or heart-failure admissions, better quality of life
REHAB-HFFrail older adults after a heart-failure admissionA low-intensity programme (strength, balance, mobility, endurance) improved physical function, quality of life and mood

Writing the exercise prescription

FITTPrescription
FrequencyAt least 3 times a week, preferably most days
Intensity40–80% of heart-rate reserve or of VO₂ reserve · 65–80% of peak heart rate · RPE 11–16
Time5–10 minutes warm-up, 30–60 minutes aerobic, 5–10 minutes cool-down
TypeWalking, jogging, cycling, rowing, elliptical — plus resistance, flexibility, and balance work in older patients
  • The threshold intensity that improves fitness in heart disease is about 45% of oxygen-uptake reserve, roughly 70% of peak heart rate; progress toward 50–80%.
  • If the patient gets angina, set the target heart rate about 10 beats below the ischemic threshold — the rate at which angina appeared on the exercise test.
  • Board add-on The heart-rate-reserve (Karvonen) method: target = resting rate + chosen percentage × (peak rate − resting rate).
  • Dr. Qazi’s practical sweet spot is about 65–70% of maximal heart rate. Resistance training is never wrong and is the strongest defence against frailty.

Diet and lifestyle in primary prevention

The 2019 ACC/AHA primary-prevention guideline is team-based and accounts for social determinants of health: assess ASCVD risk, keep blood pressure below 130/80, reach 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, use aspirin only in select high-risk patients, treat type 2 diabetes with diet, exercise and metformin first, stop tobacco — and eat well.

ClassNutrition recommendation
IEmphasize vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, whole grains and fish
IIaReplace saturated fat with mono- and polyunsaturated fat
IIaLess dietary cholesterol and sodium
IIaMinimize processed meat, refined carbohydrate and sweetened drinks
III: harmAvoid trans fats
🫒

Mediterranean diet — PREDIMED

  • Daily grains, fruit, vegetables, legumes, nuts and olive oil; fish and poultry a few times a week; red meat a few times a month.
  • PREDIMED (7,447 high-risk adults): adding extra-virgin olive oil or nuts cut heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death by about 30% (hazard ratio 0.70) compared with a low-fat diet. Re-analysed in 2018; the benefit held.
  • The only diet with randomized-trial evidence of fewer cardiovascular events.
🧂

Sodium and DASH

  • Higher sodium intake: stroke up 24%, fatal coronary disease up 32%. Cutting sodium lowers systolic pressure by about 3.4 mm Hg.
  • DASH-Sodium: the DASH diet lowers systolic pressure at every sodium level, and lowering sodium lowers it further — the effects add up.
  • Target below 2,400 mg of sodium a day, with further benefit below 1,500 mg.
🎙️ From the recording: diets in practice
  • Eggs are fine. Only a small share of dietary cholesterol shows up in the blood; the real culprits are saturated fat and refined carbohydrate.
  • Mediterranean in practice: plenty of carbohydrate as long as it is complex; fat mainly from olive oil or nuts; protein mainly from seafood.
  • Ornish and Esselstyn (fully plant-based, no oils) showed plaque regression in small series but are almost impossible to sustain.

Q: During a treadmill test a healthy 50-year-old goes from 3 to 9 METs. Predict what happens to his systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Answer

Systolic pressure rises about 8–12 mm Hg per MET, so roughly 50–70 mm Hg over 6 METs. Diastolic pressure stays the same or falls slightly, because arterioles in working muscle dilate and total peripheral resistance drops.

Q: At about what fraction of VO₂max does stroke volume plateau, and what drives cardiac output higher after that?

Answer

About 50% of VO₂max. After that, cardiac output rises mainly through heart rate.

Q: Describe phase II cardiac rehabilitation, and say when a patient can start after an uncomplicated stent for unstable angina and after bypass surgery.

Answer

Outpatient, supervised, individualized exercise and risk-factor work: 36 sessions, about three a week, ECG-monitored, over 8–12 weeks. Start 1–2 weeks after discharge for the stent and 2–6 weeks after bypass surgery.

Q: Which cardiac rehabilitation indication is class IIa rather than class I?

Answer

Chronic heart failure. Acute coronary syndrome within 12 months, bypass or stent, stable angina and peripheral artery disease are all class I.

Q: On the intake exercise test, angina appears at a heart rate of 120. Where should the training heart rate be set?

Answer

About 10 beats below the ischemic threshold, so roughly 110 beats per minute.

Q: Which diet has randomized-trial evidence of fewer cardiovascular events, and what was the effect size?

Answer

The Mediterranean diet, in PREDIMED: about 30% fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths (hazard ratio 0.70) with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts.

Supporting sectionSource: CV Pharm Basic Sciences Review (Scully) · Cardiac Physiology Review (Morganelli)

Section 5 · The Normal Heart

Control of the Circulation: Receptors, Signals, Pressure and Flow

No study-guide objective names this material, but every drug and every compensation later in the block depends on it. Dr. Scully’s framing: every cardiovascular drug works by turning one physiologic dial, and boards ask “what changes in the body when this drug is given?” Dr. Morganelli added the pieces he does not usually teach in year one — venous return and the Guyton curves — because you need them for IV fluids and heart failure.

Abbreviations used in this section ANS autonomic nervous system · NE / Epi / ACh norepinephrine / epinephrine / acetylcholine · α1, α2, β1, β2 adrenergic receptor subtypes · M2 / M3 muscarinic receptor subtypes · NN neuronal nicotinic receptor · Gq / Gi / Gs the three G-protein pathways · cAMP / cGMP cyclic AMP / cyclic GMP · PKA / PKG protein kinase A / G · MLCK myosin light-chain kinase · NO nitric oxide · PDE3 / PDE5 phosphodiesterase 3 / 5 · SA / AV node sinoatrial / atrioventricular node · If the “funny” pacemaker current · MAP mean arterial pressure · CO cardiac output · TPR / SVR total peripheral / systemic vascular resistance (the same thing) · HR / SV heart rate / stroke volume · VR venous return · Pmsf mean systemic filling pressure · Pra / CVP right atrial / central venous pressure · RAAS renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system · ACE angiotensin-converting enzyme · ADH antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) · ANP atrial natriuretic peptide · JG cells juxtaglomerular cells (the kidney’s renin-releasing cells) · MAO / COMT monoamine oxidase / catechol-O-methyltransferase (the enzymes that break down catecholamines) · ECG electrocardiogram · PR interval the ECG time from atrial to ventricular depolarization · HF heart failure · CV cardiovascular · DAG diacylglycerol · IP3 inositol trisphosphate · IV intravenous

The autonomic receptors of the heart and vessels ★ HY

ReceptorWhereWhat it doesG protein
α1Vascular smooth muscle (also the pupil dilator)Contraction — vasoconstriction, so resistance risesGq
α2Presynaptic nerve terminals · brainstemInhibits transmitter release and lowers sympathetic outflow — the brakeGi
β1Heart · JG cells of the kidneyFaster rate, stronger contraction, faster conduction · more reninGs
β2Bronchi · vessels of skeletal muscleBronchodilation · vasodilationGs
M2SA and AV nodesSlower rate and slower AV conductionGi
M3Smooth muscle (pupillary constrictor), glandsContraction, secretionGq
NNEvery autonomic ganglion, sympathetic and parasympathetic, plus the adrenal medullaDepolarizes the postganglionic neuronIon channel
  • Sympathetic “fight or flight” uses norepinephrine from nerve endings and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla.
  • Because β1 sits on the JG cells, β1 stimulation raises renin and beta-blockers lower it.
  • The peripheral vessels have no parasympathetic supply. Their tone comes only from sympathetic α1 signalling, kept “a little on” like a dimmer switch so there is always room to dial it back.
  • Nicotine looks like “both” — a racing heart and a busy gut — because NN receptors sit in both branches’ ganglia. That is also why nicotine toxicity is unpredictable.
  • Muscarinic receptors are cholinergic receptors: a muscarinic effect is produced by cholinergic drugs and blocked by atropine.

G-protein signalling: odd Gq, even Gi, betas are Gs

🪝 The rule and the exception

For muscarinic and alpha receptors, odd numbers are Gq and even numbers are Gi: M1, M3 and α1 use Gq; M2 and α2 use Gi. “Betas are BS” — every beta receptor breaks the rule and uses Gs.

PathwayReceptorsCascadeResult
GqM1, M3, α1Phospholipase C splits a membrane lipid into IP3 (releases stored calcium) and DAG (activates protein kinase C)Smooth muscle contraction
GiM2, α2Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP falls; the βγ subunit also blocks presynaptic calcium entrySlower heart (M2) · less transmitter release (α2)
GsAll βActivates adenylyl cyclase, so cAMP rises and PKA is switched onHeart: faster and stronger · smooth muscle: relaxation
🫀

In the heart: one enzyme, two hands on it

  • β1 (Gs) and M2 (Gi) both act on adenylyl cyclase.
  • More cAMP lets PKA phosphorylate the L-type calcium channel and phospholamban, giving faster, stronger beats.
  • The net heart rate is the integrated cAMP signal.
🩸

In vascular smooth muscle: calcium is the currency

  • Contract: α1 and Gq raise calcium, which switches MLCK on.
  • Relax through cAMP: β2 and Gs activate PKA, which inhibits MLCK.
  • Relax through cGMP: nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase; cGMP and PKG switch on myosin light-chain phosphatase. This is how nitrates work.

Pacemaker and fast-response action potentials ★ HY

Dr. Morganelli: “You’ll see this on the boards, I guarantee it.” These are the currents the antiarrhythmic drugs target (Section 10), and the waves you read on the ECG (Section 6).

  • The conduction path: SA node, both atria, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres, ventricles.
  • The atria are electrically insulated from the ventricles; the only way through is the AV node, which delays the impulse about 0.1 s so the ventricles can finish filling.
  • Conduction is fastest in the Purkinje fibres (about 4 m/s) and slowest in the AV node (about 0.05 m/s).
  • The atria have a short plateau because they add only the last of the filling; the ventricles, especially the left, have a long one.
⏱️

Pacemaker (slow-response) — SA and AV node

  • Phase 4: the funny current, a slow inward sodium current that drifts the cell up from about −60 mV. Its slope sets the heart rate. It is “funny” because hyperpolarization switches it on.
  • Phase 0: the upstroke is calcium through L-type channels, at a threshold near −40 mV.
  • Phase 3: potassium out.
  • No true resting potential.
💪

Fast-response — atria, ventricles, Purkinje

  • Phase 0: fast sodium channels open.
  • Phase 1: a brief potassium current out — the notch.
  • Phase 2 (plateau): calcium in, balanced by potassium out. This calcium is the trigger for contraction.
  • Phase 3: potassium out.
  • Phase 4: stable resting potential near −90 mV.
🔑 The three ions Dr. Scully asked about in class

Myocyte upstroke is sodium. Nodal upstroke is calcium. Repolarization in both is potassium. So a calcium channel blocker slows the SA node and AV conduction (a longer PR interval) but spares the myocyte upstroke.

InputTransmitter and receptorEffect on the pacemakerResult
SympatheticNE on β1More funny current and calcium current, so a steeper phase 4Faster rate, faster conduction, stronger contraction
Parasympathetic (vagus)ACh on M2Less funny and calcium current (flatter phase 4) and more potassium conductance, so the cell starts further from thresholdSlower rate, slower AV conduction
  • With no autonomic input at all — a transplanted, denervated heart — the rate is about 100 per minute. Resting vagal tone normally holds it lower.
  • Overdrive suppression: the fastest SA cells reach threshold first and suppress slower backup pacemakers.
  • Absolute (effective) refractory period: from phase 0 to the middle of phase 3, while the sodium channels are inactivated. It prevents summation and tetany and guarantees time to fill.
  • Relative refractory period: the end of phase 3, when a stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire the cell. A premature beat landing here can start an arrhythmia.

MAP = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance ★ HY

🔑 The equation with three exclamation marks on the slide

MAP = CO × TPR. The body adjusts cardiac output and resistance to hold MAP where it is — MAP itself is the dependent variable. When one tissue dilates to get more flow, total resistance falls, so cardiac output must rise to hold the pressure. If resistance halves during exercise, output has to double.

DialTurned up byTurned down by
Heart rateAntimuscarinics · β agonists and catecholamines · PDE3 inhibitorsMuscarinic agonists · beta-blockers · calcium channel blockers
Preload — venous toneSympathetic toneNitric oxide (nitrates, nitroprusside)
Preload — blood volumeThirst, fluidsDiuretics · RAAS blockade
ContractilitySympathetic tone and catecholamines on β1Beta-blockers · calcium channel blockers
Resistanceα1 nerves · circulating catecholamines · angiotensin II · calcium channelsα1 blockers · central α2 agonists · nitric oxide · RAAS blockers · calcium channel blockers
  • The ANS is the fast responder; the kidney’s sodium and water handling is the long-term answer. The kidney’s role is so large that hypertension can be transplanted with a kidney.
  • Angiotensin II acts on the adrenal cortex (aldosterone), the proximal tubule (more sodium reabsorption), the efferent arteriole (maintains filtration), the hypothalamus (thirst and ADH) and the heart (remodelling).
  • ACE is also kininase II, the enzyme that breaks down bradykinin — the reason ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema (Section 29).
  • In heart failure, lowering afterload means the failing ventricle can eject a larger stroke volume for the same contractility. These same dials give the mortality benefits in Section 18.

Flow, resistance and Poiseuille’s law

  • Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. For the whole circulation the driving pressure is MAP, since venous pressure is close to zero.
  • Continuity: flow = cross-sectional area × velocity. Where the total area is largest, velocity is lowest — so the capillary network has the slowest flow in the body (about 0.03 cm/s), which gives time for exchange. The trap: a single capillary is tiny, but the question is about the whole network.
  • Poiseuille: resistance = 8 × viscosity × length ÷ (π × radius⁴). Radius dominates: double it and flow rises 16-fold; halve it and flow falls to one-sixteenth.
  • Viscosity is mostly hematocrit — it rises with dehydration, polycythemia and blood doping.
  • Series resistances add, so adding one raises the total. Parallel resistances add as reciprocals, so adding a branch lowers the total — which is why a capillary bed offers little resistance even though each capillary is very resistant. Dr. Morganelli saw a board question that made you calculate one.
  • Laminar flow is silent and efficient. Turbulent flow loses energy and makes noise — murmurs and bruits (Section 3).

Venous return, mean systemic filling pressure and the Guyton curves

New this year, and needed for IV fluids and for treating heart failure.

  • About 70% of the blood sits in the veins — a reservoir that can be mobilized in hemorrhage and shock. Veins are highly compliant: they accept whatever volume they are given.
  • Venous return = (peripheral venous pressure − right atrial pressure) ÷ venous resistance. The gradient is only about 8 mm Hg to 0, so small changes in either pressure swing venous return a lot. Right atrial pressure (measured clinically as CVP) opposes return.
  • Mean systemic filling pressure is the pressure throughout the circulation when flow stops — about 7–8 mm Hg. It is the main upstream push for venous return.
  • Dr. Morganelli’s view on the chicken-and-egg question: the energy comes from the heart, so cardiac output drives venous return — and at steady state the two are equal.
🛏️

Unstressed volume

  • Blood that fills the veins up to the point their walls start to stretch — about 70% of venous volume at rest.
  • Makes no pressure. Like the first air pumped into a flat air mattress.
🎈

Stressed volume

  • Blood above the unstressed volume. It stretches the walls, makes pressure, and is the volume that flows.
  • It sets the mean systemic filling pressure. It depends on total blood volume and on how stiff the veins are.
ScenarioStressed volumeFilling pressure − atrial pressureVenous return
NormalAbout 30% of venous volume8 − 0Normal
Transfusion or fluid load↑ (mostly stressed)12 − 1↑, and the kidneys then excrete the excess
More venous tone (sympathetic)↑ — stiffer veins shift blood from unstressed to stressed10 − 1↑ — how venous return keeps up with output in exercise
Hemorrhage↓ (both volumes fall)Falls↓
Nitrates plus sildenafil↓↓ — veins suddenly far more compliantCollapses↓↓, and blood pressure crashes — never combine them
📉

The vascular function curve

  • Right atrial pressure plotted against cardiac output, with a pump setting the flow.
  • When output is zero, atrial pressure equals the mean systemic filling pressure (about 8) — the y-intercept.
  • As output rises, atrial pressure falls, widening the gradient for return. Below about 0 the vena cava collapses and output cannot rise further.
  • More volume or stiffer veins shift the curve right; hemorrhage or more compliant veins shift it left.
📈

The cardiac function curve and Guyton’s crossing

  • Starling’s curve with heart rate built in: output rises as right atrial pressure rises.
  • Better contractility moves it up and left; failure moves it down and right.
  • Where the two curves cross is the steady state, where output equals venous return — normally about 5 L/min at an atrial pressure near 2.
⚠️ Heart failure read off the curves
  • Weaker contractility drops the cardiac curve, so the crossing slides to a lower output at a higher atrial pressure.
  • Blood shifts to the venous side (jugular distension, edema) and leaves the arterial side (low blood pressure, poor perfusion).
  • Low pressure triggers sympathetic tone and fluid retention, which shift the vascular curve right: output is partly restored, but at an even higher venous pressure.
  • A badly failing heart can be Starling-insensitive: extra fluid only raises venous pressures. Dr. Morganelli’s class question — the most accurate statement about IV fluid in decompensated heart failure is that fluid can make the patient worse.

Regulating MAP: the reflexes and the heart-failure paradox ★ HY

SystemSpeedSensor and triggerMain effect
High-pressure baroreflexSecondsStretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus nerve)Sympathetic and vagal output to heart rate, contractility, resistance and venous tone
Low-pressure (volume) reflexLongerStretch receptors in the atria and venae cavae, triggered by high venous pressureDiuresis: less renal sympathetic tone, less ADH, more ANP — plus the Bainbridge reflex (heart rate rises)
ADH (vasopressin)LongerHigh plasma osmolality; low baroreceptor firingWater reabsorption without sodium (plus vasoconstriction at high doses)
RAASSlow onset, can last indefinitelyLow renal perfusion, low sodium at the macula densa, β1 on the JG cellsAngiotensin II constricts arterioles; aldosterone retains sodium and water
  • Baroreflex: a fall in pressure means less stretch and less firing, so sympathetic output rises and vagal output falls — heart rate, contractility, resistance and venous tone all rise until firing returns to normal. In heart disease this reflex can stay switched on indefinitely.
  • Hypovolemic shock shows both speeds: the sympathetic response acts in seconds; RAAS, ADH and fluid shifts rebuild volume over hours to days.
⚠️ Two direction slips in the recording
  • Renin: the recording says the macula densa cells “stop making renin.” The slide is right — less sodium reaching the macula densa increases renin release from the JG cells.
  • ADH: the recording says baroreceptors “increase their firing” to raise ADH. It is falling pressure, less baroreceptor firing, more ADH.
🎯 The heart-failure paradox — “you just have to know this”

In heart failure the venous pressures are high, so the volume reflex tries to get rid of salt and water. At the same time the arterial side is underfilled, so the pressure-defending systems — the baroreflex, RAAS and ADH — switch on. The pressure-defending systems win, so the patient retains salt and water and becomes more congested. Normal physiology leads you into a dead end here; you have to know the clinical outcome.

His last class question: a woman with a dilated cardiomyopathy, ejection fraction 30%, low blood pressure, edema, low urine output, a low serum sodium and a very low urine sodium. The low serum sodium is dilutional hyponatremia — aldosterone holds on to sodium (hence the low urine sodium) while ADH retains water on top of it, out of proportion to the salt.

The four reflex questions from class

QuestionWhat happensAnswer
IV phenylephrineα1 constriction raises resistance and pressure; the baroreceptors fire more; vagal output on M2 slows the SA nodeReflex bradycardia, blocked by atropine
What ends norepinephrine’s signal?Mainly reuptake by the norepinephrine transporter (about 70%); MAO and COMT clear the restHigh synaptic NE acts on presynaptic α2 (Gi) to cut further release — the brake clonidine and methyldopa use
M2 antagonist, then IV norepinephrineNE hits α1, α2 and β1 but not β2. Alone it gives pressure up, heart rate down (reflex). With M2 blocked, the reflex cannot actHeart rate up and pressure up

Q: A drug selectively activates β1 receptors. Besides tachycardia, what happens to plasma renin, and why?

Answer

Renin rises, because β1 receptors on the juxtaglomerular cells stimulate renin release. Beta-blockers lower renin for the same reason.

Q: A drug blocks the funny current in SA-node cells. What happens to the phase 4 slope and the heart rate?

Answer

Phase 4 flattens, so the cell takes longer to reach threshold and the heart rate slows. Board add-on Ivabradine works this way.

Q: Arteriolar radius falls by half with nothing else changing. What happens to flow through that bed?

Answer

Resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, so it rises 16-fold and flow falls to one-sixteenth.

Q: On a vascular function curve, what does the y-intercept represent, and what happens to it after a large hemorrhage?

Answer

It is the mean systemic filling pressure — the right atrial pressure when output is zero. Hemorrhage lowers the stressed volume, so the filling pressure falls, the curve shifts left, and the maximum cardiac output falls.

Q: A patient receives a rapid 2-litre saline infusion and her heart rate rises. Which reflex is this, and what else do the same receptors do?

Answer

The Bainbridge reflex: atrial stretch raises the heart rate. The same low-pressure receptors also lower renal sympathetic activity, lower ADH and raise atrial natriuretic peptide, so the kidneys excrete salt and water.

Q: A patient is given an M2 antagonist and then IV norepinephrine. What happens to heart rate and blood pressure?

Answer

Both rise. Norepinephrine alone raises pressure and slows the heart through the baroreflex. With M2 blocked, the reflex bradycardia cannot happen, so the direct β1 tachycardia shows through.

Section 6 · The ECG & Arrhythmias

Reading the ECG: Rate, Rhythm, Waves, Intervals and Axis

Dr. Qazi reads an electrocardiogram in about half a second, but only because she has read hundreds of thousands of them with the same system. That is the real lesson of this lecture: you get there by looking at every tracing the same way every single time, so that nothing is missed. Your first solo reading will take a long time, and that is expected — even experienced emergency physicians call cardiology to ask about a tracing.

Abbreviations used in this section ECG / EKG electrocardiogram (the same thing) · SA node sinoatrial node · AV node atrioventricular node · P wave atrial depolarization · QRS ventricular depolarization · T wave ventricular repolarization · PR interval start of P to start of QRS · QT / QTc QT interval / QT corrected for heart rate · bpm beats per minute · ms milliseconds · mm millimetres · aVR, aVL, aVF the augmented limb leads (right arm, left arm, foot) · V1–V6 the precordial (chest) leads · LVH / RVH left / right ventricular hypertrophy · LBBB / RBBB left / right bundle branch block · LAFB / LPFB left anterior / posterior fascicular block · MI myocardial infarction · AF atrial fibrillation · MAT multifocal atrial tachycardia · WAP wandering atrial pacemaker · VT ventricular tachycardia · ST ST segment (between the QRS and the T wave)

The reading order, and why you never deviate from it ★ HY

Every tracing gets the same seven steps in the same order. The payoff is that an abnormality you were not looking for still gets found, because you walked past it on the way to something else.

  1. Rate. Count the QRS complexes on the rhythm strip and multiply by six. Tachycardia is 100 or more, bradycardia is under 60.
  2. Rhythm. First ask whether it is regular. If it is regular, is it sinus, using the five criteria below? If it is irregular, which of the five irregular rhythms is it?
  3. Axis. Look at the QRS in lead I and in aVF, with lead II as a back-up. Decide left, right or normal, and then ask why.
  4. Intervals. The PR interval first (is there AV block?), then the QRS duration (is there a bundle branch block?), then the QT and corrected QT (is there torsades risk?).
  5. Chamber enlargement. The P waves in leads II and V1 tell you about the atria. Voltage plus axis tells you about the left ventricle. R-wave progression plus axis tells you about the right ventricle.
  6. Ischemia, injury and infarction. ST elevation means transmural injury, ST depression means subendocardial injury, and Q waves mean dead myocardium. Then ask which territory.
  7. Say it in one sentence. For example: “Sinus bradycardia, rate 42, normal axis, 2:1 atrioventricular block.”
🎙️ From the recording — and from the electrophysiologist too

“Look at it the same way every single time.”

The Maine Medical Center electrophysiologist who gave the second electrocardiogram lecture adds two rules to the same list:

  • An electrocardiogram is always read together with the clinical history — his “Love Island” rule is that alone, it gets voted off the island.
  • Each tracing is worth ten points, and about eight are for the clinical big picture (sinus rhythm? heart block? bundle branch block? ventricular tachycardia? normal?). Only about two are for fine detail such as left atrial enlargement.
  • The American Board of Internal Medicine agrees: report the findings that are definite and that matter for management, because reading a tracing is “not an exercise in identifying minutiae.”

The paper, the waves and the leads

The tracing is a drawing of the heart’s electricity, and each wave is one step of conduction: the SA node fires, the atria depolarize (the P wave), the impulse pauses in the AV node (the PR segment), it runs through the bundle of His and the bundle branches into the Purkinje fibres, the ventricles depolarize (the QRS), and the ventricles repolarize (the T wave). The SA node sets the pace for one reason only — it is the fastest pacemaker in the heart.

MeasureFrom → toNormalWhat a long one means
Small box—0.04 s (40 ms)Standard paper speed is 25 mm/s
Big boxFive small boxes0.20 s (200 ms)Five big boxes make one second
The whole tracing—10 secondsAbout 2.5 s shown per lead, with a full 10-second rhythm strip along the bottom
PR intervalStart of P to start of QRS120–200 ms = up to one big boxDelayed conduction through the AV node: think atrioventricular block (Section 8)
QRS durationStart to end of QRS< 120 ms = under three small boxesA bundle branch block, or an impulse that started in the ventricle (Sections 7 and 8)
QT / corrected QTStart of QRS to end of TCorrected QT < 450 ms men, < 460 ms womenRisk of torsades de pointes, which rises sharply over 500 ms
🔑 Naming the QRS, because every later criterion uses it

Q is the first negative deflection. R is the first positive deflection. S is the negative deflection that comes after an R. A second R is written R′ and said “R-prime.” Capital letters mean big waves and lower-case letters mean small ones, so “rSR′” describes a small initial positive, a deep negative, and then a second positive. You will not always see a Q or an S, and that is normal.

The leads. Ten electrodes give twelve views. Six are limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF) looking at the frontal plane, and six are chest leads (V1 through V6) looking at the horizontal plane. The long strip across the bottom of the printout is the full ten-second rhythm strip, and it is almost always lead II.

Step 1 — Rate

🔑 Dr. Qazi’s method, which works whether or not the rhythm is regular

Count every QRS on the rhythm strip and multiply by six, because a standard twelve-lead tracing is ten seconds long. If you are holding a six-second monitor strip instead, multiply by ten. That is the whole method.

  • Tachycardia is 100 or more, normal is 60 to 99, and bradycardia is under 60. A sinus rhythm running at 110 must be called sinus tachycardia, not simply sinus rhythm.
  • The machine’s printed rate is correct roughly 90% of the time. Artifact and patient movement fool it, so check it yourself.
  • Board add-on For a regular rhythm you can also count big boxes between two R waves and run down the sequence 300 · 150 · 100 · 75 · 60 · 50, or divide 1500 by the number of small boxes. This shortcut only works when the rhythm is regular.

Step 2 — Rhythm: regular or irregular? ★ HY

Ask the regularity question first, because it splits the whole problem in half.

🧠 If it is regular, is it sinus? All five must be true
  1. The R–R intervals are regular. March the QRS complexes out with calipers.
  2. The P–P intervals are regular. This one matters enormously once you get to heart block.
  3. The PR interval is constant from beat to beat.
  4. There is a P wave for every QRS, which the first three criteria have effectively proven.
  5. The P wave is upright in lead II, which tells you the impulse started in the SA node. In V1 a normal P wave is biphasic, like one cycle of a sine wave.

If it is irregular, there are five things it can be

RhythmWhat you seePicture
Atrial fibrillation No P waves at all, an irregularly irregular R–R with no pattern to it, and an undulating baseline. This is the arrhythmia you will meet most often — roughly 90% of the rhythm problems in adult cardiology. Covered in Section 9.
Sinus arrhythmia Normal sinus P waves, with the rate speeding and slowing with respiration. Common in young people and entirely normal.
Second-degree atrioventricular block Dropped beats — a P wave with no QRS after it — make the rhythm look irregular, though there may be a repeating pattern. Covered in Section 8.
Wandering atrial pacemaker Several atrial foci take turns, so you see three or more different P-wave shapes, at a rate under 100.
Multifocal atrial tachycardia Exactly the same picture, but at a rate of 100 or more. Board add-on Classically a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
🪝 Wandering atrial pacemaker and multifocal atrial tachycardia are one diagnosis with a speed limit

Both need three or more P-wave morphologies with an irregular rhythm. The only difference is the rate: under 100 makes it a wandering atrial pacemaker, 100 or over makes it multifocal atrial tachycardia. If an examiner gives you one and then changes the rate, they are asking for the other name.

Atrial flutter, which Dr. Qazi called “highly tested”

  • Look for flutter waves in a sawtooth pattern, seen best in the inferior leads II, III and aVF.
  • Conduction may be at a fixed ratio of flutter waves to QRS complexes, such as 4:1, which makes the rhythm regular, or at a variable ratio, which makes it irregular. So flutter can land in either half of your regular-versus-irregular split.
  • The circuits differ, and this is worth holding on to: typical flutter circles in the right atrium around the cavotricuspid isthmus, whereas atrial fibrillation starts around the pulmonary veins in the left atrium. Section 8 uses this to explain why each one is ablated differently.

Step 3 — Axis, in two seconds, and then “why?” ★ HY

Dr. Qazi’s practical view is that the axis matters chiefly as a criterion for other diagnoses rather than as a finding in its own right. So skip the quadrant arithmetic and simply look at whether the QRS is mostly up or mostly down in lead I and in aVF.

AxisLead IaVFMemory hook
NormalUpUp“Two thumbs up”
LeftUpDownThe peaks point away from each other
RightDownUpThe peaks point toward each other
  • If aVF sits on the isoelectric line and you cannot call it, use lead II instead, with the same pattern: positive for normal, negative for left, positive for right. Dr. Qazi says that gets you to the right answer about 95% of the time.
  • Board add-on In degrees, a normal axis runs from about −30° to +90°.

Having named the axis, the useful work is asking what caused it. There is a short list on each side.

⬅️

Left axis — four causes

  • Left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Left bundle branch block
  • Left anterior fascicular block
  • An old inferior myocardial infarction, because the Q waves in II, III and aVF make aVF negative
➡️

Right axis — three causes

  • Right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Left posterior fascicular block
  • An old lateral myocardial infarction, with Q waves in I and aVL
  • Lung disease also shifts the axis rightward, but it does not change how you read the tracing
⚠️ The classic wrong answer on axis

Right bundle branch block has a normal axis. So if you see a right bundle branch block and right axis deviation, the right answer is not “right bundle branch block” — it is right bundle branch block plus left posterior fascicular block. The same logic runs the other way for the fascicular blocks generally, which are covered in Section 7: a fascicular block is a left or right axis with no other explanation, in a tracing whose QRS is still narrow.

Putting the first three steps together

Once you can call rate, rhythm and axis, you can already produce a usable one-line read on most tracings, and you have narrowed what the intervals and the ST segments could possibly mean. Sections 7 and 8 take over from here: Section 7 reads the tracing for structural and metabolic disease, and Section 8 reads it for arrhythmia and block.

🩺 A reminder from the second lecture: read the patient too

Before you commit to a reading, add the questions the electrophysiologist asks at the bedside:

  • Was the patient symptomatic at the time of the tracing? That question alone separates pericarditis from a heart attack.
  • Is the patient stable? That decides treatment before the diagnosis is final.
  • Is there an old tracing to compare with? Knowing that a wide QRS was already there last year changes everything.
  • If the tracing is full of noise, check the leads and repeat it — garbage in, garbage out — because the machine will still print a confident diagnosis on top of artifact.

Q: A standard twelve-lead tracing shows seven QRS complexes on the rhythm strip. What is the rate, and what do you call it?

Answer

Seven times six is 42 beats per minute, so this is bradycardia. The multiplication works because a standard twelve-lead tracing runs for ten seconds.

Q: List the five criteria that must all be met before you can call a rhythm sinus.

Answer

Regular R–R intervals, regular P–P intervals, a constant PR interval, a P wave for every QRS, and an upright P wave in lead II. The last one is the criterion that actually proves the impulse came from the sinoatrial node.

Q: An irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 118 beats per minute has three different P-wave shapes. Name it. What would you call the same tracing at 82 beats per minute?

Answer

Multifocal atrial tachycardia at 118. At 82 the identical picture is called a wandering atrial pacemaker. The rate of 100 is the only dividing line.

Q: The QRS is positive in lead I and negative in aVF. The QRS is narrow, there is no voltage evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy, and there are no Q waves in II, III or aVF. What is the diagnosis?

Answer

Left anterior fascicular block. This is a left axis with every other cause excluded: the narrow QRS rules out a left bundle branch block, the voltages rule out hypertrophy, and the absence of inferior Q waves rules out an old inferior infarction.

Q: A patient’s tracing shows a wide QRS with an rSR′ pattern in V1 and V2, and the axis is clearly rightward. Why is “right bundle branch block” an incomplete answer?

Answer

Because an isolated right bundle branch block leaves the axis normal. The right axis needs its own explanation, and the usual one here is an added left posterior fascicular block.

Q: A monitor strip six seconds long shows nine QRS complexes. What is the rate?

Answer

90 beats per minute. A six-second strip is multiplied by ten rather than six. Getting the strip length right is the only way the method can go wrong.

LO 34LO 35LO 38LO 41LO 42Source: ECG Basics (Qazi) · ECG II (Maine Med electrophysiology)

Section 7 · The ECG & Arrhythmias

The ECG of Disease: Hypertrophy, Bundle Branch Block, Ischemia and Electrolytes

Section 6 gave you the reading order. This section is what you find when you use it on a sick heart. Four families of finding live here: a chamber that has grown, a conduction pathway that has broken, a coronary artery that has closed, and an electrolyte that has drifted. Each one changes a specific part of the tracing, and each one has a short list of criteria worth memorising outright.

Abbreviations used in this section ECG electrocardiogram · LAE / RAE left / right atrial enlargement · LVH / RVH left / right ventricular hypertrophy · BBB bundle branch block · LBBB / RBBB left / right bundle branch block · LAFB / LPFB left anterior / posterior fascicular block · WPW Wolff–Parkinson–White · TWI T-wave inversion · ST elevation / ST depression the ST segment above / below baseline · MI myocardial infarction · STEMI ST-elevation myocardial infarction · NSTEMI non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction · RCA right coronary artery · LAD left anterior descending artery · LCx left circumflex artery · PDA posterior descending artery · QTc QT interval corrected for heart rate · VT ventricular tachycardia · K / Mg potassium / magnesium · mm millimetres (one small box is 1 mm tall) · COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease · HCM hypertrophic cardiomyopathy · QRS the ventricular depolarisation complex on the ECG · PR PR interval (atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation) · CV cardiovascular

Atrial enlargement: look at the P wave in leads II and V1

The P wave is the right atrium depolarizing first and the left atrium second, so the two atria each own one half of it. Lead II looks at the P wave along its length and lead V1 looks at it end-on, which is why you need both.

FindingLead IILead V1ContextPicture
Normal Upright and narrow Biphasic, like one cycle of a sine wave The right half then the left half
Left atrial enlargement Still upright but wider. Board add-on Over 120 ms, often notched — “P mitrale” Mostly negative, with a large terminal negative portion Common with ageing and a stiff left ventricle, and in athletes
Right atrial enlargement Tall and peaked. Board add-on Over 2.5 mm — “P pulmonale” Mostly positive, with a large initial positive portion In a child, think congenital heart disease
🪝 Which half of the P wave grew?

The right atrium makes the first half of the P wave and the left atrium makes the second. So right atrial enlargement makes the P taller (a bigger first half piles onto the second), and left atrial enlargement makes it wider (a bigger second half stretches it out). In V1, the lead sees the right atrium coming toward it and the left atrium going away, which is why right atrial enlargement makes V1 mostly positive and left atrial enlargement makes it mostly negative.

Left ventricular hypertrophy ★ HY

This one earns its place clinically as well as on an exam. New heart failure with left ventricular hypertrophy on the tracing starts a whole work-up. Hypertrophy also produces T-wave inversion and ST depression — the so-called strain pattern — which is easy to mistake for ischemia.

CriterionRuleNote
Left axisRequiredThe forces are pulled leftward by the extra muscle
R wave in aVL> 11 mmThe most specific criterion
S in V1 or V2, plus R in V5 or V6≥ 35 mmThe most sensitive criterion (Sokolow–Lyon)

Call left ventricular hypertrophy when you have the left axis plus either voltage criterion, or both.

R-wave progression and right ventricular hypertrophy

  • Normal progression: V1 shows a small r wave with a deep S, the R grows as you move across the chest, the transition where R equals S falls at V3 or V4, and V5 and V6 show a tall R with a small s.
  • Right ventricular hypertrophy is a right axis together with a reversed progression: a tall R already in V1, getting smaller as you move toward V6. It is rare in adults, so think congenital disease when you see it.
  • Board add-on A tall R in V1 is not only hypertrophy. It also appears in right bundle branch block, in a posterior infarction and in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Poor R-wave progression appears after an anteroseptal infarction, and in left ventricular hypertrophy, left bundle branch block and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Wide QRS: bundle branch and fascicular blocks ★ HY

A normal QRS is under 120 ms, or three small boxes. When it is wide, the first thought is a bundle branch block: conduction delayed somewhere below the bundle of His. Picture the anatomy — the bundle of His divides into a right bundle and a left bundle, and the left bundle then splits into an anterior and a posterior fascicle.

BlockCriteriaPicture
Left bundle branch block
  • QRS ≥ 120 ms
  • Left axis (required, per the lecture)
  • V1 to V3 negative — an rS pattern or simply mostly negative, essentially always
  • I, aVL, V5 and V6 positive — a broad R wave, sometimes notched at its peak
Right bundle branch block
  • QRS ≥ 120 ms
  • Normal axis
  • rSR′ “rabbit ears” in V1 and V2, or at least mostly positive complexes there
  • Slurred S waves in I, aVL, V5 and V6
Left anterior fascicular block
common on its own		 A left axis with no other explanation: no hypertrophy, no left bundle branch block, a normal QRS width, and no inferior Q waves.
Left posterior fascicular block
rare alone		 A right axis with no other explanation: no right ventricular hypertrophy, no old lateral infarction. Usually met as part of right bundle branch block plus left posterior fascicular block.
🪝 WiLLiaM and MaRRoW Board add-on

Look at the shape of the complex in V1 and in V6. Left bundle branch block makes a W in V1 and an M in V6 — WiLLiaM. Right bundle branch block makes an M in V1 and a W in V6 — MaRRoW. The capital letters in each word tell you which bundle it is.

🧠 The difference between a bundle and a fascicle, on the tracing

A bundle branch block makes the QRS wide, because a whole ventricle has to be depolarized cell by cell. A fascicular block leaves the QRS normal, because the other fascicle still delivers the impulse to the left ventricle quickly — it just arrives from an unusual direction, which shifts the axis. So the question “is the QRS wide?” sorts the two groups before you look at anything else.

Board add-on One more wide-QRS pattern belongs here by sight: a short PR interval with a slurred upstroke on the QRS, called a delta wave. That is pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, the setting for Wolff–Parkinson–White, and it is worked through properly in Section 8.

The QT interval and what lengthens it ★ HY

Bazett’s formula corrects the QT for rate: the corrected QT equals the measured QT divided by the square root of the R–R interval in seconds. Normal is under 450 ms in men and 460 ms in women, and you worry above 500 ms.

  • The eyeball test. Mark the halfway point between two R waves. If the T wave has finished before that halfway mark, the QT is normal about 90% of the time. If it reaches or passes the mark, calculate it properly.
  • Why it matters: a long QT sets up polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, which is torsades de pointes — a twisting ribbon of complexes whose amplitude waxes and wanes. The mechanism, early afterdepolarizations during a prolonged repolarization, is in Section 10.
  • A wide QRS from a bundle branch block lengthens the QT by itself, so account for that before calling the repolarization abnormal.
CauseWhat the lecture emphasised
Class III antiarrhythmic drugsDofetilide is the only drug Dr. Qazi has personally seen cause torsades. Sotalol does it when the electrolytes are off. Amiodarone prolongs the QT but she has never seen torsades from it.
ElectrolytesLow magnesium and low potassium. High potassium prolongs everything instead — a wide QRS and a long PR.
Other drugsFluoroquinolones and other antibiotics, every antidepressant, antipsychotics, antiemetics, antifungals and antiretrovirals. The list keeps growing, so check the medication list and the electrolytes before you prescribe. Dr. Qazi lost a patient to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia after a newly started fluoroquinolone.
Congenital long QT syndromeThe young athlete who collapses. The twelve-lead tracing is the key first test — although the commonest cause of sudden death on the field is still hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Section 8 has the genetics.

Electrolytes on the tracing ★ HY

⬆️

High potassium

  • Tall, narrow, peaked T waves — the earliest change.
  • As it worsens, every interval widens: the PR lengthens, the QRS broadens, and eventually the P wave flattens and disappears.
  • A severely hyperkalemic tracing can end up looking like a sine wave.
⬇️

Low potassium

  • Flattened T waves with a prominent U wave following them.
  • The U wave merges with the T, so the QT (really a QU) looks long — which is exactly the torsades risk.
  • Low magnesium does the same thing, and the two usually travel together.

Ischemia, injury and infarction — Dr. Qazi’s “favourite part” ★ HY

Two questions do all the work: which finding is it, and which territory is it in. Get the coronary anatomy straight first and the territory question answers itself.

ArteryCourseSuppliesLeads
Right coronary artery, giving the posterior descending arteryDown the anterior atrioventricular groove, then the posterior descending artery in the inferior interventricular groove. Right-dominant in about 80% of people.The inferior wall and the inferior third of the septumII, III, aVF
Left circumflex arteryPosterior atrioventricular groove and the obtuse marginal branches. Gives the posterior descending artery in about 20% — left dominance.The inferolateral, or “posterior”, wallNo direct leads, so you look for reciprocal changes in V1 to V3
Left anterior descending artery — the “widowmaker”Anterior interventricular groove, with septal perforators and diagonals. Feeds more than 40% of the left ventricle.The anterior wall, the upper two thirds of the septum, and the anterolateral wallV1–V3 anteroseptal · V4–V6 anterior · I, aVL anterolateral

The three findings, and what each one means

FindingWhat it meansWhat you doPicture
ST elevation Transmural injury — a STEMI. Usually plaque rupture with 100% occlusion. Needs at least 1 mm of elevation in two or more contiguous leads, forming an anatomic pattern. Open the artery now — the catheterisation laboratory, or thrombolytics then transfer. “Time is muscle.”
ST depression Subendocardial injury — an NSTEMI. Rupture narrowing the artery to 70–90%, with some flow continuing. At least 1 mm below baseline, and often diffuse rather than confined to one territory. Stabilise first; this is not an indication for emergent revascularisation.
Q waves Dead myocardium — an old infarction. At least one small box wide and deep, in an anatomic pattern. The infarct is complete, usually by 12 to 24 hours. Nothing acute. Note it, and remember a Q wave is normal only in lead III.
T-wave inversion Non-specific. Ischemia, electrolytes, metabolic disturbance. In Dr. Qazi’s words, she does not know what an inverted T wave means without the context. Interpret it with the history and the rest of the tracing, never alone.
🧠 Reciprocal changes confirm a STEMI

ST elevation in one territory together with ST depression in the opposite leads is an electrical mirror image, and it confirms the diagnosis. The classic pairing is inferior ST elevation in II, III and aVF with ST depression in aVL and the anterior leads. When you are not sure whether an ST segment is really elevated, go looking for the mirror.

🔑 How a STEMI evolves over time Board add-on
  • The sequence: hyperacute T waves first (broad, tall and symmetric, the earliest sign of occlusion), then ST elevation, then Q waves with T-wave inversion as the ST segment returns toward baseline.
  • V2 and V3 thresholds are higher than elsewhere: at least 2 mm in men 40 and over, 2.5 mm in men under 40, and 1.5 mm in women.
  • A posterior infarction is read from the front as ST depression with a tall R wave and an upright T wave in V1 to V3 — the mirror image again.
  • A known left bundle branch block or a paced rhythm makes ischemia very hard to read.
🩺 Two mimics to keep off your differential by accident
  • Pericarditis also raises the ST segments, but everywhere rather than in one coronary territory, and it adds PR-segment depression (Section 23).
  • Early repolarization raises the J point in young people and is usually a normal variant. It comes from a larger transient outward potassium current in the epicardium than in the endocardium, which creates a voltage gradient early in repolarization.
  • Neither should be called a heart attack, and in both the history settles it.

Q: The axis is left. The S wave in V2 measures 22 mm and the R in V5 measures 18 mm. The R in aVL is 13 mm. What is the diagnosis, and which criterion here is the most specific?

Answer

Left ventricular hypertrophy. Both voltage criteria are met: 22 plus 18 is 40, which clears the 35 mm Sokolow–Lyon threshold, and the R in aVL is over 11 mm. The R in aVL above 11 mm is the more specific of the two; the precordial sum is the more sensitive.

Q: A tracing shows a QRS of 150 ms, a left axis, deeply negative complexes in V1 to V3 and a broad notched R wave in I, aVL and V6. What is it?

Answer

Left bundle branch block. Every criterion is present: a wide QRS, a left axis, negative V1 to V3, and a broad positive complex laterally. The W in V1 and M in V6 is the WiLLiaM half of the mnemonic.

Q: A patient has ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with ST depression in I and aVL. Which artery is occluded, and what does the ST depression add?

Answer

The right coronary artery, producing an inferior STEMI. The depression in I and aVL is a reciprocal change — the electrical mirror image — and it confirms that the elevation is real. In about 20% of people the circumflex is dominant and causes the same picture.

Q: There are Q waves in II, III and aVF, but the ST segments are flat. What does this mean, and what else does it explain about the tracing?

Answer

An old, completed inferior infarction — dead myocardium rather than acute injury. It also explains a left axis, because those inferior Q waves make aVF negative.

Q: A dialysis patient misses two sessions. The tracing shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves and a QRS that has widened since last month. What is happening, and what would the opposite electrolyte abnormality look like?

Answer

Hyperkalemia. Peaked T waves come first, then every interval widens as it worsens. Hypokalemia does the reverse of the T wave: it flattens the T and brings out a U wave, which makes the QT look long and carries torsades risk.

Q: A patient is on dofetilide for atrial fibrillation and is started on ondansetron for nausea. Potassium is 3.1 and magnesium is low. What rhythm are you worried about, and why?

Answer

Torsades de pointes. Two QT-prolonging drugs are stacked on top of each other and both of the electrolytes that protect repolarization are low. Dofetilide was the one drug Dr. Qazi named as having actually caused torsades in her own practice.

Q: A tall R wave appears in V1. Give three explanations other than right ventricular hypertrophy.

Answer

Right bundle branch block (the R′ of the rabbit ears), a posterior myocardial infarction (the mirror image of a posterior Q wave), and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The axis and the QRS width separate them.

LO 29LO 30LO 39LO 40LO 42LO 43LO 44LO 45LO 46LO 47LO 48Source: ECG II (Maine Med electrophysiology) · ECG Basics (Qazi)

Section 8 · The ECG & Arrhythmias

Arrhythmias and Heart Block: Lethal Versus Non-Lethal

Eleven study-guide objectives point at this section, which tells you how much of the exam lives here. Two questions sort nearly every fast rhythm in the lecture: is the QRS narrow or wide, and is the rhythm regular or irregular. Two more decide what you do about it: is the patient stable, and what does the history say. Everything below hangs on those four.

Abbreviations used in this section ECG electrocardiogram · SVT supraventricular tachycardia · PSVT paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia · AVNRT atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia · AVRT atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia, which uses an accessory pathway · JET junctional ectopic tachycardia · AT atrial tachycardia · AF atrial fibrillation · AFL atrial flutter · VT / VF ventricular tachycardia / fibrillation · WCT wide-complex tachycardia · BBB / LBBB / RBBB bundle branch block, left / right · aberrancy a supraventricular beat conducted with a bundle-branch pattern · AV node atrioventricular node · AV dissociation atria and ventricles firing independently · AV block atrioventricular block · CHB complete heart block · EAD / DAD early / delayed afterdepolarization · WPW Wolff–Parkinson–White · LQTS long QT syndrome · QTc QT corrected for heart rate · TdP torsades de pointes · ARVC arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy · HCM hypertrophic cardiomyopathy · CCB calcium channel blocker · EP study electrophysiology study · IV intravenous · TIA transient ischemic attack · MI myocardial infarction · AED automated external defibrillator · ACLS advanced cardiac life support · QRS the ventricular depolarisation complex on the ECG · PR PR interval (atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation) · ST ST segment (between the QRS and the T wave) · RS RS complex (an R wave followed by an S wave)

How arrhythmias start: three mechanisms

The electrophysiologist’s framing was that you never get away from the action potential. Every arrhythmia in this section is one of three failures, and knowing which one you are looking at tells you which drug class is going to help (Section 10).

MechanismWhat goes wrongClassic examples
Automaticity, enhanced or abnormalA focus fires too fast, or fires somewhere it should not. A problem of phase 3 and phase 4.Atrial tachycardia from an irritable focus; junctional ectopic tachycardia
Triggered activitySmall depolarizations during or just after repolarization reach threshold and trigger a whole new action potential.Early afterdepolarizations cause torsades in long QT; delayed afterdepolarizations cause ischemic ventricular arrhythmias and digoxin toxicity
Re-entry — the most common, and the usual mechanism of supraventricular tachycardiaA short circuit between two pathways with different conduction speeds and different refractory periods.AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter, ventricular tachycardia around a scar
🔑 Re-entry in four steps — worth being able to draw

Picture a pathway that divides into two limbs. The slow path conducts slowly but recovers quickly (a short refractory period). The fast path conducts quickly but recovers slowly (a long refractory period).

  1. A normal beat travels down both limbs and meets itself at the bottom. Nothing happens.
  2. A premature beat arrives while the fast path is still refractory, so it is blocked there and goes down the slow path only. This is unidirectional block.
  3. By the time it reaches the bottom, the fast path has recovered, so the impulse turns around and runs back up it.
  4. It re-enters the slow path and the circuit keeps spinning. Each lap throws off a new impulse, which overdrives the sinoatrial node.

That is why a premature beat starts the tachycardia when a normal beat does not: only a premature beat finds one limb still refractory.

🩺 “What else is going on?” — the setting that permits an arrhythmia

An arrhythmia almost never arrives out of nowhere, and examiners know it. Look for ischemia or an old infarct scar (examiners love an arrhythmia paired with a myocardial infarction), electrolyte disturbance in potassium or magnesium, drug-induced proarrhythmia — digoxin causes a whole host of arrhythmias and remains a test-writer favourite even though it is used less now — and autonomic tone, which changes the QT, the heart-rate variability and the conduction velocities themselves.

Atrioventricular block: measure the same three things every time ★ HY

A normal PR interval is 200 ms or less, which is one big box. A long PR means slowed conduction through the atrioventricular node. Dr. Qazi’s rule for every block is to measure the P–P interval, the R–R interval and the PR interval, in that order, and let the pattern name itself.

BlockP–PR–RPRThe keyPicture
First degreeRegularRegularLong (over 200 ms) but constant Every P wave conducts. It is simply slow.
Second degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach)RegularIrregularLengthens progressively, then a QRS is dropped The PR after the dropped beat is shorter than the PR before it — far easier to spot than the gradual lengthening itself. Benign.
Second degree, Mobitz IIRegularIrregularConstant A P wave suddenly fails to conduct, often in a repeating pattern such as every third beat. High grade — this one needs a pacemaker.
Third degree (complete)RegularRegularAll over the place Atrioventricular dissociation: the P waves and the QRS complexes each march out on their own schedule, with the atrial rate usually faster than the ventricular one.
🧠 In every atrioventricular block, the P–P interval is constant

That is the sanity check. The sinus node is doing its job perfectly in all four blocks — the failure is downstream. If the P waves do not march out, you are looking at something other than heart block, and you should go back to the rhythm step in Section 6.

⚠️ 2:1 atrioventricular block — the trick tracing
  • When every other P wave is blocked, there are never two conducted P waves in a row, so you have nothing to compare and you cannot tell Mobitz I from Mobitz II. Call it “2:1 atrioventricular block” and let the history decide.
  • An asymptomatic 25-year-old is probably Mobitz I and benign. An 80-year-old with syncope or exhaustion is treated as Mobitz II and gets a pacemaker. A young patient with syncope should raise congenital heart block — ask about the family history.
  • Tip: look for the hidden P wave sitting inside the T wave — it looks exactly like the other P waves once you find it.

Narrow-complex tachycardias: the supraventricular family

🎯 The sentence to carry out of this lecture

“Supraventricular tachycardia is a category, not a diagnosis.”

Fast, narrow and arising above the ventricles is a family. Naming the member matters because the treatment differs.

RhythmWhere it livesWhat to knowPicture
Sinus tachycardiaSinoatrial node The most common supraventricular tachycardia. Always ask why — it is a response, not a disease.
AVNRT — atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardiaA slow and a fast pathway inside the atrioventricular node The second most common arrhythmia by this lecturer’s count. The P wave is hidden inside the QRS, so a regular narrow tachycardia with no visible P wave is the tip-off.
AVRT — atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardiaThe atrioventricular node plus an accessory pathway the patient was born with Orthodromic runs down the node and up the pathway, giving a narrow QRS. Antidromic runs down the pathway, giving a wide one. This is the Wolff–Parkinson–White circuit, below.
Atrial tachycardiaOne irritable atrial focus The shape of the P wave depends on where in the atrium the focus sits.
Atrial flutterA circuit in the right atrium Covered in full below, and the anticoagulation question is in Section 9.
Atrial fibrillationMany wavelets, triggered from the pulmonary veins The most common arrhythmia overall. Section 9.
🔑 Why typical AVNRT has no visible P wave

A premature beat goes down the slow pathway and back up the fast one. Coming up the fast pathway, it reaches the atria at almost exactly the moment it is also reaching the ventricles, so the atria and ventricles depolarize together and the P wave is buried inside the QRS. That single mechanical fact is why “regular, narrow, no P wave” is such a reliable clue.

Breaking a regular supraventricular tachycardia, step by step

  1. Is the patient stable? If not, stop here: sedate well and perform synchronised cardioversion. The lecturer’s view on energy is “go big or go home,” because being shocked is brutal and you do not want to repeat it; guidelines list 50 to 100 joules.
  2. Vagal manoeuvres first if the patient is stable with a good blood pressure. Valsalva (having the patient try to blow the plunger out of a syringe is easier to explain than “bear down”), cold water, tilting, or carotid sinus massage.
  3. Adenosine, 6 mg by rapid push with an immediate flush, then 12 mg if there is no response in a minute or two.
  4. If that fails and the patient is still stable: an intravenous beta-blocker, diltiazem or verapamil — all of which slow the atrioventricular node.
  5. If that fails: synchronised cardioversion.
  6. Long term: an electrophysiology study with catheter ablation is a class I recommendation for suitable patients, done from the groin, modifying the slow pathway. Otherwise, medical therapy with nodal blockers. Flecainide or propafenone only if there is no structural heart disease. Many young patients choose pills first and come back for ablation after two or three years of emergency visits.
🩺 Carotid sinus massage, done safely

Pressure on the carotid sinus triggers a parasympathetic reflex that slows conduction through the atrioventricular node and can break AVNRT. The technique is to listen to both carotids first, then press firmly for 10 to 20 seconds with the electrocardiogram, heart rate and blood pressure monitored.

Absolute contraindications: recent myocardial infarction; stroke or transient ischemic attack within the last three months; carotid artery occlusion; a history of ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation; a previous bad reaction to the manoeuvre. Relative: a carotid bruit — image the carotids first, because stenosis or atheroma risks occluding the other side or embolising plaque.

⚠️ A slip in the recording: sinus, not body

The recording refers to the “carotid body” having parasympathetic tone. The manoeuvre actually works on the carotid sinus baroreceptors, with cranial nerve IX carrying the afferent signal and the vagus the efferent. The carotid body is a chemoreceptor, sensing oxygen and carbon dioxide. Section 5 has the reflex in full.

AdenosineDetail
Dose6 mg rapid bolus with a flush, then 12 mg if no response in one to two minutes. Half-life under 5 seconds, so it does not accumulate — which is also why it must be pushed hard and flushed, to reach the heart as a concentrated bolus.
What you should seeA few seconds of profound slowing. As it wears off at around 30 seconds you often see a Wenckebach-like pattern: the PR lengthens, a beat drops, and then sinus rhythm returns.
Adverse effectsFacial flushing, chest pain, a sense of impending doom, hypotension, a few seconds of asystole, bronchospasm, occasionally non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. Warn the patient — they feel it.
Do not useA heart transplant — the denervated heart is supersensitive and may have prolonged asystole. Wolff–Parkinson–White — it can trigger atrial fibrillation that degenerates to ventricular fibrillation. Caution in severe reactive airway disease and in ischemic heart disease.

Atrial flutter

  • Negative sawtooth flutter waves in II, III and aVF, and positive in V1. That combination defines typical, counterclockwise flutter.
  • The circuit is a macro-re-entry loop running counterclockwise around the tricuspid valve, climbing the muscular septum, and it depends on the cavotricuspid isthmus — the strip of tissue between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus.
  • Why the waves point that way: an electrode records current coming toward it as positive. The wavefront climbs the thick septum away from the feet, so the inferior leads see it going away and record it as negative. It climbs toward V1, high on the right chest, so V1 records it as positive.
  • Why flutter often runs faster than fibrillation. In flutter the atria fire at an organised 250–300, and the node settles into a 2:1 ratio, locking the ventricle at about 150. In fibrillation the atria fire chaotically at 360–450 or more, bombarding the node, which conducts irregularly at roughly 120 to 150 and is easier to slow with drugs. Days of flutter at a fixed 150 produce a tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.
  • Long term: catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus, usually offered after even a single episode because the rate runs so high. The lecturer’s image is a traffic circle with a Jersey barrier dropped into it. Warn the patient that ablation does not prevent atrial fibrillation — about half of flutter patients develop it within roughly two years.
🔑 Adenosine in flutter is diagnostic, not therapeutic

When a fast narrow tachycardia has its P waves hidden and you cannot tell flutter from AVNRT, adenosine blocks the atrioventricular node for a few seconds and unmasks the sawtooth flutter waves underneath. It will not stop the flutter, because the circuit does not use the atrioventricular node. It does stop AVNRT, which does. So the response to adenosine itself tells you which rhythm you had.

Wide-complex tachycardia: ventricular tachycardia versus supraventricular tachycardia ★ HY

Why ventricular tachycardia is wide:

  • A normal beat rides the His–Purkinje superhighway, so both ventricles activate at once and the QRS is under 120 ms.
  • Ventricular tachycardia starts in the ventricular muscle itself — a focus, or a circuit around a scar — so it skips the conduction system and creeps cell to cell, giving a QRS of 120 ms or more that looks slurred and, in the lecturer’s word, ugly.
  • The catch: a supraventricular rhythm conducted through a bundle branch block is also travelling cell to cell for part of the ventricle, so it is also wide.
⚠️ The rule that is “constantly on the test”

If it is wide and you cannot tell, assume ventricular tachycardia, treat it as ventricular tachycardia, and work it out afterwards. If the patient is unstable, sedate and cardiovert. In the lecturer’s words, nobody will ever mark you wrong for treating a supraventricular tachycardia with left bundle branch block as ventricular tachycardia — but the reverse mistake kills people. Having a baseline tracing, so you know whether the bundle branch block was already there, helps enormously.

🫀

The clinical setting favours ventricular tachycardia

  • Organic heart disease — an ejection fraction of 20% against a normal of 55 to 65%, or an old infarct scar.
  • Potassium disturbance, with low potassium the worse one for ventricular irritability.
  • Hypoxia from infarction or lung disease, and acidosis.
  • Valve disease, including mitral valve prolapse.
  • Drugs: digoxin toxicity, antiarrhythmics, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants, caffeine, alcohol, nicotine.
  • It does occur in structurally normal hearts, where it behaves more like a supraventricular tachycardia — but if you do not know the history, treat it as life-threatening.
📐

Findings on the tracing that favour it

  • Atrioventricular dissociation — P waves marching at their own rate straight through the tachycardia. Present in 25 to 33% of cases.
  • Capture or fusion beats — a sinus impulse sneaks through between ventricular beats and briefly captures the normal conduction, giving one narrow beat, or a hybrid. Only about 5% of cases, but almost diagnostic.
  • Negative precordial concordance — every QRS negative from V1 through V6, meaning activation starts at the apex and moves away from all the chest leads. Virtually diagnostic.
  • Positive concordance — all upright V1 to V6, an origin at the base. Strongly suggestive, though an accessory pathway can do it too.
  • A “northwest” axis, pointing up toward the right shoulder, so that aVR is strikingly positive.
  • A very wide QRS, over 140 ms with a right bundle shape or over 160 ms with a left bundle shape.

The lecturer’s advice for now is to concentrate on capture and fusion beats and on atrioventricular dissociation and leave the rest for your clinical years.

🧠 The initial deflection tells you which pathway was used
  • A supraventricular rhythm with a bundle branch block starts on the normal conduction system, so the first part of the QRS is sharp and fast and only the later part slurs. Ventricular tachycardia is slow and slurred from the very first millisecond.
  • Ventricular tachycardia can be irregular at onset — about 70% become regular by the twentieth beat — so regularity does not rule it out.
  • It can conduct backwards to the atria, so look at any P waves carefully before calling them dissociated.
🔑 The Brugada stepwise approach (1991), validated on 554 wide tachycardias

Work the steps in order. The first “yes” diagnoses ventricular tachycardia and you stop.
