  1. Is there an absence of any RS complex in all the precordial leads?
  2. Is the longest R-to-S interval over 100 ms? Measure from the onset of the R wave to the nadir, the deepest point, of the S wave in any precordial lead.
  3. Is there atrioventricular dissociation?
  4. Do the classical morphology criteria in V1 and V6 fit?

The lecturer said explicitly that he does not expect you to know Wellens’ detailed morphology table, nor would it be tested — it is for your clinical years.

Wolff–Parkinson–White ★ HY

The lecturer flagged this as “highly tested, and life-threatening in a young person.” An accessory pathway — the bundle of Kent — connects atrium to ventricle directly, bypassing the atrioventricular node.

🚧

The atrioventricular node is a toll booth

  • In the lecturer’s description, “the most passive-aggressive structure you will ever see”: the faster the atria fire, the more it slows conduction down.
  • It will usually pass about 150 to 160 beats per minute at most, perhaps 200 in someone aged 18 to 25.
  • This is a protective property, and it is the thing an accessory pathway takes away.
🏎️

The accessory pathway has no toll booth

  • It conducts everything it receives, as fast as it receives it.
  • In atrial fibrillation, blocking the node simply sends more impulses down the pathway instead, so the ventricular rate climbs, and very fast rates degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.
  • That is the entire reason for the management rule below.
  • On the resting tracing: bypassing the node removes the isoelectric PR segment, giving a short PR. Early ventricular activation creeps cell to cell, giving a slurred upstroke — the delta wave — and a wider QRS.
  • Pattern versus syndrome. Pattern is pre-excitation on the tracing with no symptoms, present in 0.15 to 0.25% of people and in 0.55% of first-degree relatives; it can be intermittent or disappear with age. Syndrome is the pattern plus an arrhythmia. In an aviation study of 22,500 people, the pattern was present in 0.25% and only 1.8% of those had an arrhythmia.
  • Of the arrhythmias in the syndrome, roughly 80% are AVRT, 15 to 30% atrial fibrillation and about 5% flutter. Sudden death risk is 0–0.39% and is especially low in the asymptomatic. Multiple pathways, found in up to 13%, mark higher risk.
  • Who gets studied: symptomatic patients with palpitations or lightheadedness get an electrophysiology study to measure how fast the pathway conducts. Asymptomatic patients can be watched with a yearly tracing and taught the warning symptoms.
  • Associations: most patients have structurally normal hearts. When there is congenital disease it tends to be right-sided, and Ebstein anomaly — the tricuspid valve displaced down into the right ventricle — is the lesion most strongly tied to Wolff–Parkinson–White. Mitral valve prolapse goes with left-sided pathways, and familial cases with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
⚠️ No nodal blockers in Wolff–Parkinson–White — the one thing to know

No adenosine, no calcium channel blockers, no beta-blockers, and no vagal manoeuvres. Every one of those slows the node and pushes more conduction down the accessory pathway. This reverses the usual supraventricular tachycardia algorithm, which is exactly why it is tested so often.

What you do instead: when in doubt, sedate and cardiovert. The drug of choice is procainamide, given at 30 mg/min up to a maximum of 17 mg/kg, then 2 to 4 mg/min for maintenance. Stop the infusion when the arrhythmia is suppressed, if the patient becomes hypotensive, or if the QRS widens by 50% or more. Watch for hypotension, QRS widening and torsades.

Long QT and the genetic arrhythmia syndromes

The case that opens this part of the lecture is a 24-year-old runner who “went down with a seizure.” The tracing showed torsades de pointes at about 300 per minute, with the axis twisting around a point so the amplitude waxed and waned. The seizure was cerebral hypoperfusion — patients in cardiac arrest often convulse. After an automated external defibrillator shock, the sinus tracing showed a QT of roughly 600 ms.

  • Congenital long QT syndrome affects about 1 in 5,000 and is mostly autosomal dominant. More than fifteen genes are known; types 1 through 3 account for 85 to 90%. Most are potassium-channel defects affecting phases 2 and 3, which lengthen the action potential, allow early afterdepolarizations, and set off torsades.
  • It presents with recurrent syncope — in the lecturer’s words, “they just go down,” not subtle — and with sudden cardiac death.
  • The Schwartz score combines the tracing, the clinical history and the family history: 1 point is low probability, 2 to 3 intermediate, and 4 or more high.
  • Board add-on Acute torsades is treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate, with cardioversion if the patient is unstable. Correct the potassium and magnesium and stop every QT-prolonging drug.
ConditionKey ideaPicture
Long QT syndromePotassium or sodium channel defects lengthen repolarization, allowing early afterdepolarizations and torsades.
Short QT syndromeAn abnormally short QT predisposing to atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation.
Wolff–Parkinson–WhiteAn accessory pathway allowing pre-excited atrial fibrillation to degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.
Brugada syndromeMostly affects the right ventricular outflow tract; coved ST elevation in V1 and V2.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathyFibro-fatty replacement of the right ventricular wall.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathyThe most common of these, and the commonest cause of sudden death on the playing field. Section 19.

Palpitations and syncope: what the work-up has to exclude

Two of the objectives for this section are phrased as excluding a dysrhythmia or heart block in a patient with palpitations or syncope. Put the pieces above into an order.

  1. A twelve-lead tracing in sinus rhythm. It is the cheapest test in medicine — the lecturer’s line was that nothing for twenty dollars gives you more information. Look specifically for a delta wave (Wolff–Parkinson–White), a long QT, the coved ST elevation of Brugada, voltage criteria suggesting hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Q waves from an old infarction, and the PR interval and QRS width for conduction disease.
  2. A rhythm strip during symptoms, which is what ambulatory monitoring and wearables are for. A wearable flags atrial fibrillation from irregularity of the R–R interval, so frequent premature beats can fool it, and an irregular report always needs visual confirmation.
  3. Ask about the setting. Syncope with exertion or with emotional stress in a young person points to the genetic syndromes above and to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Syncope with no prodrome at any age is more worrying than syncope with a long warning.
  4. Check the reversible contributors: potassium and magnesium, thyroid function, the medication list for anything that prolongs the QT, and alcohol or stimulant use.
  5. Family history of sudden death under 30, or of unexplained drowning or car accidents.
🧠 Lethal versus non-lethal, in one view

Immediately lethal: ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, which need defibrillation; torsades, which needs magnesium and often a shock; and pre-excited atrial fibrillation, because of what it can become.

Potentially lethal, by what it leads to: Mobitz II and complete heart block can progress to asystole and need a pacemaker; sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia can degenerate into fibrillation; atrial fibrillation and flutter cause stroke and, left fast, a tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.

Generally non-lethal: sinus arrhythmia, first-degree block, Mobitz I, a wandering atrial pacemaker, and AVNRT, which is miserable but rarely dangerous in a structurally normal heart.

Q: The P–P interval is regular and the R–R interval is regular, but the PR interval changes from beat to beat. The atrial rate is 80 and the ventricular rate is 36. What is the diagnosis?

Answer

Third-degree, or complete, atrioventricular block. Both chambers are marching out regularly but on independent schedules — atrioventricular dissociation — which is why the PR interval is meaningless here.

Q: Why does it matter whether a second-degree block is Mobitz I or Mobitz II, and what single feature is easiest to find on the strip?

Answer

Mobitz I is benign; Mobitz II is high grade and needs a pacemaker. The easiest feature is that in Mobitz I the PR interval after the dropped beat is shorter than the PR before it, which is much easier to see than the gradual lengthening. In Mobitz II the PR is constant throughout.

Q: A stable 30-year-old has a narrow regular tachycardia at 180 with no visible P waves. Vagal manoeuvres fail. What is the next step, at what dose, and what should the monitor show as it wears off?

Answer

Adenosine 6 mg by rapid intravenous push with a flush, repeated at 12 mg if needed. As it wears off you should see transient atrioventricular block — the PR lengthening and then a dropped beat — before sinus rhythm returns. The underlying rhythm is almost certainly typical AVNRT, where the P wave is buried in the QRS.

Q: Adenosine is given for a narrow tachycardia. It does not terminate the rhythm, but regular sawtooth waves appear during a few seconds of block. What does that tell you?

Answer

That the rhythm does not depend on the atrioventricular node: it is atrial flutter. Adenosine was diagnostic rather than therapeutic. Definitive therapy is cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, and the patient is anticoagulated exactly as for atrial fibrillation.

Q: During a wide regular tachycardia at 160, one narrow complex appears that looks like the patient’s normal beats. What is it, and what does it prove?

Answer

A capture beat: a sinus impulse got through the atrioventricular node while the ventricular circuit happened to be resetting. It proves the atria and ventricles are running independently — atrioventricular dissociation — and therefore that this is ventricular tachycardia.

Q: A 22-year-old has an irregular, very fast, wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS width varies from beat to beat. The blood pressure is stable. Which drugs are contraindicated, and what do you give?

Answer

This is pre-excited atrial fibrillation in Wolff–Parkinson–White. Contraindicated: adenosine, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and vagal manoeuvres — all of them divert conduction down the accessory pathway. Give procainamide, or sedate and cardiovert. Cardiovert immediately if the patient becomes unstable.

Q: A 19-year-old faints while swimming. The corrected QT is 520 ms and an uncle died suddenly at 25. What is the diagnosis, what is the mechanism of the fatal rhythm, and what should she avoid?

Answer

Congenital long QT syndrome, usually an autosomal dominant potassium-channel defect. A prolonged phase 2 to 3 allows early afterdepolarizations, which trigger torsades de pointes. She should avoid QT-prolonging drugs — antiemetics, antifungals, antidepressants, fluoroquinolones — and keep her potassium and magnesium normal.

Q: A stable 70-year-old with a prior myocardial infarction and an ejection fraction of 25% has a wide regular tachycardia. The QRS is negative in every lead from V1 to V6. What is the rhythm, and why?

Answer

Ventricular tachycardia. Negative precordial concordance is virtually diagnostic, and the clinical setting fits perfectly: scar from an old infarct plus a low ejection fraction is the classic substrate for re-entrant ventricular tachycardia.

LO 30LO 31Source: ECG II (Maine Med electrophysiology) · Antiarrhythmic Pharmacology (Scully)

Section 9 · The ECG & Arrhythmias

Atrial Fibrillation: Risk Stratification and Management

The electrophysiologist gave this topic its own warning: “You will not escape atrial fibrillation.” It is the most common arrhythmia in the United States and in the world, and it turns up in surgery, in primary care, in obstetrics and in the intensive care unit. Two dangers drive everything you do about it — stroke and heart failure — and the management sequence below is built around them.

Abbreviations used in this section AF atrial fibrillation · AFL atrial flutter · ECG electrocardiogram · R–R interval the gap between successive R waves · RVR rapid ventricular response · CHA₂DS₂-VASc the stroke-risk score: Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age 75 or over (2 points), Diabetes, Stroke or transient ischemic attack (2 points), Vascular disease, Age 65–74, Sex category female · CHA₂DS₂-VA the same score without the female-sex point · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant · TIA transient ischemic attack · MI myocardial infarction · HF heart failure · TSH thyroid-stimulating hormone · PE pulmonary embolism · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · ICU intensive care unit · CAD coronary artery disease · OSA obstructive sleep apnea · AFFIRM the trial comparing rate with rhythm control · EP study electrophysiology study · QRS the ventricular depolarisation complex on the ECG · ST ST segment (between the QRS and the T wave) · QT QT interval (ventricular depolarisation plus repolarisation)

Recognising it

  • Irregularly irregular R–R intervals, with no pattern you can predict.
  • No P waves and no isoelectric baseline — and the practical version of that, from the lecture, is that no two “P waves” look the same.
  • A variable ventricular rate, which may be fast or slow.
  • The QRS is usually narrow, unless there is a pre-existing bundle branch block, an accessory pathway, or rate-related aberrancy.
  • Fibrillatory waves are described as fine (under 0.5 mm) or coarse (over 0.5 mm). Coarse ones can mimic P waves and cause a misdiagnosis.
  • The lecturer’s reassurance about exams: irregular plus clean narrow complexes is almost always atrial fibrillation, and you will not be handed a strange atypical tracing.

The definitions — know the first three for the wards

TermDefinition
ParoxysmalIntermittent, and it terminates within 7 days.
PersistentContinuous for more than 7 days and requiring an intervention — a drug, cardioversion or a procedure. It stays “persistent” even if later treatment converts it to a paroxysmal pattern.
Long-standing persistentContinuous for more than 12 months.
PermanentPatient and clinician have jointly decided to stop trying to restore sinus rhythm. This is a treatment decision, not a disease state.
First detectedThe first documentation of atrial fibrillation, whatever symptoms came before.
SubclinicalFound on a device or a wearable in someone with no symptoms and no previous tracing showing it. Not automatically treated — it depends on the risk factors.
Atrial high-rate episodesDevice-detected events above a programmed rate. They need visual confirmation before you act on them.
AF burdenHow much atrial fibrillation there is: frequency multiplied by duration, or the percentage of monitored time spent in it.

An episode currently counts as atrial fibrillation at 30 seconds or longer. The lecturer expects that cut-off to be replaced by a burden-based definition within about two years, which is worth knowing if a question seems to turn on the number.

Why there is no complete cure: two different diseases wearing one name

🧑

The young patient

  • Triggered activity from the pulmonary veins, which are richly supplied with autonomic nerve tissue.
  • Here atrial fibrillation behaves like a nervous-system or genetic disease — long QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome can both cause it.
  • Ablation works by electrically isolating those veins, which the lecturer describes as wrapping them in electrical tape.
👴

The older patient

  • Hypertension, diabetes and valve disease remodel the atrium into a maze of scar with altered autonomic supply.
  • Impulses get lost in it and find many ways out, so there is no single circuit to destroy.
  • After a hundred thousand or more beats a day for decades, ablation cannot cure all of it.

Triggers and causes

  • Hypertension — years of high afterload cause left ventricular hypertrophy, the atria then pump against a stiff ventricle, distend and scar. Ischemic heart disease.
  • Valve disease, especially mitral stenosis or regurgitation.
  • Electrolytes — low potassium or magnesium after a heavy night, a viral illness or poor fluid intake. This cause is reversible, so look for it.
  • Acute infection. Thyrotoxicosis, which gives rapid atrial fibrillation with a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone, is often reversible and is rate-controlled with a beta-blocker while the thyroid is treated.
  • Alcohol, the third-ranked risk factor: a direct myocardial toxin with autonomic effects on top. Board add-on Atrial fibrillation after a binge is called “holiday heart.” Sympathomimetic drugs.
  • Pulmonary embolism (it distends the right ventricle and then the right atrium), pericardial disease, acid–base disturbance, pre-excitation, cardiomyopathy, obesity, diabetes and sleep apnea.
⚠️ Two pairings examiners love

Atrial fibrillation together with ST elevation, which is rare in real life but common on tests, and atrial fibrillation together with thyrotoxicosis. If a vignette gives you new atrial fibrillation plus tremor, weight loss and heat intolerance, the thyroid is the answer and the beta-blocker is the treatment.

🔑 It is not mainly palpitations

Fatigue and shortness of breath are the most common symptoms — heart-failure-type complaints, typically “I cannot climb a flight of stairs any more.” Only about 50 to 60% of patients feel palpitations at all. A vignette describing new exertional breathlessness in an older patient with an irregular pulse is describing atrial fibrillation, not just deconditioning.

Acute management, step by step

  1. Diagnose it. Irregular R–R intervals, and P waves that do not match each other.
  2. Ask how long it has been going on. One hour versus two weeks changes everything that follows, particularly whether you can cardiovert safely.
  3. Assess anticoagulation with the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, which is moving toward CHA₂DS₂-VA.
  4. Choose rate or rhythm control. Acutely this is usually rate control first.
  5. Treat the underlying cause. Is the potassium 2? Is the thyroid off? Is there an infection? Fixing the cause may fix the rhythm.

Stroke risk and the anticoagulation decision ★ HY

LetterRisk factorPoints
CCongestive heart failure1
HHypertension1
A₂Age 75 or over2
DDiabetes1
S₂Prior stroke, transient ischemic attack or thromboembolism2
VVascular disease — prior myocardial infarction, peripheral arterial disease, aortic plaque1
AAge 65 to 741
ScFemale sex — dropped in CHA₂DS₂-VA1
  • The lecture rule: a score of 2 or more usually means a blood thinner.
  • Female sex is a risk modifier, not a strong independent risk factor, which is why the next guideline drops the point and renames the score CHA₂DS₂-VA.
  • A young person in atrial fibrillation for a couple of hours with no risk factors can be rate-controlled, or sedated and cardioverted, with no long-term anticoagulation.
  • Longer term, the decision rests on the risk factors, the duration, and whether you are planning to cardiovert. A direct oral anticoagulant is now the usual choice over warfarin.
⚠️ Test trap: “it is only flutter”

Atrial flutter gets exactly the same anticoagulation as atrial fibrillation, scored with the same CHA₂DS₂-VASc risk profile. This is a class 1 guideline recommendation. The two rhythms are usually, in the lecturer’s word, “a family” — the same atria tend to produce flutter, fibrillation, premature atrial beats and focal firing at different times.

Rate control versus rhythm control

  • The AFFIRM trial in the late 1990s found rate control and rhythm control broadly equivalent, and that answer shaped practice for years.
  • Today rhythm control is favoured long term for most symptomatic patients and for those with reduced heart function. Rate control remains reasonable in older patients with many other illnesses.
  • Rate control drugs act on the atrioventricular node: beta-blockers (class II) and verapamil or diltiazem (class IV), with digoxin as an additional option. Rhythm control drugs act on the atrial muscle: class I sodium-channel blockers and class III potassium-channel blockers. Section 10 works through all of them.
  • Long term, treat the whole patient and not just the rhythm. The pillars are stroke risk, optimising every modifiable risk factor, and symptom management. The risk-factor list is heart failure, exercise, arterial hypertension, diabetes, tobacco, obesity, ethanol and sleep — treating these alone can cut the number of episodes substantially.
🩺 Why atrial fibrillation hurts sick patients so much

Up to 15% of medical intensive care patients are in atrial fibrillation, and it hurts them in two ways:

  • Losing the atrial kick costs preload — the electrophysiologist quotes about 15% of ventricular filling.
  • A fast rate shortens filling time on top of that. A stiff ventricle, from sepsis or hypertrophy, is especially preload-dependent and suffers most.
  • A persistently high rate also produces a tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.
  • As the lecturer put it, atrial fibrillation “comes out at your worst” — with a cold, a pneumonia or an appendicitis — and the high sympathetic tone of being ill makes the rate hard to control.
⚠️ Where the sources disagree on the atrial kick

The electrophysiologist quotes the atrial kick as about 15% of ventricular filling. Dr. Morganelli’s physiology lecture (Section 1) puts it at about 10% at rest, and Dr. Qazi quoted 20 to 25%. All three are making the same point — the contribution is modest at rest but matters a great deal when the ventricle is stiff or the rate is fast. If an exam forces a number, the usual board answer is 10 to 30% depending on ventricular compliance.

Q: A 72-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes is found to be in atrial fibrillation. What is her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, and what follows from it?

Answer

Age 65 to 74 gives 1, hypertension 1, diabetes 1 and female sex 1, for a total of 4 (or 3 using CHA₂DS₂-VA, which drops the sex point). A score of 2 or more means anticoagulate, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant.

Q: One patient’s atrial fibrillation stopped on its own after 5 days. Another’s ran continuously for 3 weeks and needed cardioversion. Classify each.

Answer

The first is paroxysmal — it ended within 7 days. The second is persistent — longer than 7 days and it required an intervention. The second patient stays classified as persistent even if drugs later keep the episodes short.

Q: A 34-year-old presents with new atrial fibrillation at 140, a tremor, weight loss and a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone. What is the trigger, and what is the first-line rate control?

Answer

Thyrotoxicosis, which is a reversible cause. Rate-control with a beta-blocker while the thyroid disease itself is treated; the rhythm often resolves with it.

Q: What is the most common presenting symptom of atrial fibrillation?

Answer

Fatigue and shortness of breath, not palpitations — only about half of patients notice palpitations at all.

Q: A patient with typical atrial flutter and a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 3 is about to be discharged. The intern says anticoagulation is not needed because it is flutter and not fibrillation. Is that right?

Answer

No. Flutter carries the same stroke risk and the same anticoagulation recommendation as atrial fibrillation, using the identical score. This is a class 1 recommendation and a favourite trap.

Q: A 45-year-old is brought in after a weekend of heavy drinking with palpitations and an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm. He has no other medical history. What is the likely diagnosis, what is the eponym, and does he need long-term anticoagulation?

Answer

Atrial fibrillation triggered by alcohol — “holiday heart.” His CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 0, so he does not need long-term anticoagulation. Rate control or cardioversion for the episode, plus checking and replacing potassium and magnesium, and counselling about alcohol.

LO 32LO 94Source: Pharmacology of Cardiac Rhythm (Scully) · Golan ch. 28 · ECG II

Section 10 · The ECG & Arrhythmias

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

Unlike the other cardiology pharmacology lectures, this one is new material rather than a refresher, and Dr. Scully builds the whole thing on a single skill: knowing which ion carries each phase of the action potential, separately in nodal tissue and in myocytes. Once you have that, every class tells you its own story — which tissue it targets, what it does to the action potential, what it is indicated for, and what goes wrong with it.

Abbreviations used in this section AP action potential · SA / AV node sinoatrial / atrioventricular node · Na⁺ / K⁺ / Ca²⁺ sodium / potassium / calcium · If the “funny” pacemaker current · IKr the rapid component of the delayed-rectifier potassium current · ERP effective refractory period · AF / AFL atrial fibrillation / flutter · PSVT paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia · VT / VF ventricular tachycardia / fibrillation · PVC premature ventricular contraction · TdP torsades de pointes · QT / QRS / PR the electrocardiogram intervals · CCB calcium channel blocker · DHP dihydropyridine, the “-dipine” drugs · MI myocardial infarction · EF ejection fraction · CrCl creatinine clearance · PFT / TFT / LFT pulmonary / thyroid / liver function tests · NAPA N-acetylprocainamide · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · CNS central nervous system · CYP450 the cytochrome P450 liver enzymes · NCX the sodium–calcium exchanger · SR sarcoplasmic reticulum · Fab antibody fragment · AChE acetylcholinesterase · BBB blood–brain barrier · WPW Wolff–Parkinson–White · ST ST segment (between the QRS and the T wave) · AMP adenosine monophosphate · ATPase adenosine triphosphatase · ECG electrocardiogram

The organising idea: rate drugs hit the node, rhythm drugs hit the muscle ★ HY

⏱️

Rate control targets nodal tissue

  • The tissue with automaticity: the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.
  • The nodal upstroke is carried by calcium, and the rate is set by sympathetic tone.
  • So: class II (beta-blockers) and class IV (verapamil, diltiazem). Digoxin and adenosine also slow the node.
🎼

Rhythm control targets myocytes

  • Atrial and ventricular muscle.
  • Either the sodium upstroke of phase 0, or the potassium repolarization that ends the plateau.
  • So: class I (sodium-channel blockers) and class III (potassium-channel blockers).

Dr. Scully’s practical version: when you hear someone say “we are going to try a rate approach for this patient’s atrial fibrillation,” they mean a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker. “Rhythm control” means a class I or class III drug.

The action potentials you have to be able to draw

PhaseSA nodal cellVentricular myocyte
4Slow diastolic depolarization, driven by the inward funny current, carried mainly by sodiumResting membrane potential, held steady by inward and outward currents in balance
0Upstroke carried by inward calcium through voltage-gated channelsRapid depolarization carried by inward sodium through fast channels
1—The early notch: sodium channels inactivate and potassium leaves through the transient outward current
2—The plateau: inward calcium balanced against outward potassium
3Repolarization by outward potassiumRapid repolarization: the calcium current falls and the outward potassium current rises
🔑 The three facts the whole lecture rests on
  • Phase 0 is calcium in nodal cells and sodium in myocytes. Potassium repolarizes both. That single sentence explains why calcium channel blockers act on the node and sodium-channel blockers act on muscle.
  • Only the myocyte has a plateau, and it is a calcium plateau. It prolongs contraction to get a good squeeze for ejection.
  • The pacemaker cell has automaticity because of the funny current, carried by sodium. It is “funny” because hyperpolarization, not depolarization, is what opens it.
🧠 How autonomic tone sets the rate — both limbs meet at one enzyme

Sympathetic stimulation acts at β1 receptors through Gs, raising adenylyl cyclase activity and cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A. That phosphorylates the calcium channels and phospholamban, giving a steeper phase 4, faster conduction and a stronger contraction. Parasympathetic stimulation acts at M2 receptors through Gi, lowering cyclic AMP, leaving the cell more hyperpolarized with a flatter phase 4 and a slower rate. Both converge on adenylyl cyclase, and therefore on protein kinase A.

Anything that makes phase 4 steeper, makes the threshold more negative, or leaves the resting potential less negative will speed the heart up. Raise the threshold without changing the slope and the drift simply takes longer to get there, so the rate falls. The fastest pacemaker always wins: sinoatrial node 60 to 100, atrioventricular node and bundle of His 40 to 60, Purkinje fibres 20 to 40.

The Vaughan Williams classification ★ HY

ClassBlocksMain tissueApproachAction-potential changeECG change
I (A, B, C)Fast sodium channelsMyocytes, with a little nodal effectRhythmSlows the phase 0 slope. IA also prolongs the duration.Wider QRS; IA also lengthens the QT
IIBeta-adrenergic receptorsNodalRateFlattens phase 4; prolongs repolarization at the atrioventricular nodeLonger PR
IIIRepolarizing potassium channelsMyocytesRhythmLonger phases 2 and 3, so a longer effective refractory periodLonger QT
IVL-type calcium channels (the non-dihydropyridines)NodalRateSlows the phase 0 and phase 4 slopes in the nodeLonger PR
⚠️ The goal, and the catch

The aim is to restore and maintain normal sinus rhythm without causing proarrhythmia. Dr. Scully’s warning is blunt: “They are all proarrhythmic at the right dose.” These drugs are also not cleanly selective, and several act in more than one class — sotalol and amiodarone most obviously.

Class I — sodium-channel blockers

All class I drugs block the fast sodium channel that carries phase 0 in myocytes, so the upstroke and the conduction velocity both slow. In nodal tissue they also raise the threshold slightly and flatten phase 4, but that effect is minor, which is why class I counts as a rhythm drug. Some of them also block potassium channels, and that is where the three subclasses part company.

🔑 Use-dependent block, and why it matters for ischemic tissue

Sodium channels cycle through resting, open and inactivated states. Class I drugs bind with high affinity to the open and inactivated states, which makes the block use-dependent: the faster the tissue fires, the more block builds up. That is also why they work preferentially on ischemic tissue, which cannot hold its membrane potential, fires more often, and therefore keeps its channels in the bindable states.

🚕

Upstroke slowing: the “salty CAB driver”

  • From the biggest effect on phase 0 to the smallest: C > A > B.
  • Or, in increasing order, the salty cheeseburger with Bacon And Cheese: B < A < C.
🐻

Repolarization: Goldilocks

  • IA is too long — it prolongs repolarization.
  • IB is too short — it shortens it.
  • IC is just right — no change.
  • Prolonged repolarization means a prolonged refractory period, which means torsades risk for IA, just like class III.
🧠 Why a long refractory period causes torsades

If repolarization is too slow, the voltage-gated sodium channels recover from inactivation before the membrane has dropped back below threshold. They fire again, and the membrane oscillates. Those oscillations are early afterdepolarizations — triggered activity — and repeated ones become torsades de pointes. This is the shared mechanism behind class IA and class III toxicity.

Class IA — quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide

DrugWhat to knowAdverse effects and warnings
Quinidine
the IA prototype, oral		 Blocks sodium channels in the open state and potassium channels as well, so conduction velocity falls and the effective refractory period lengthens — together, less re-entry. Torsades de pointes. Cinchonism — reduced hearing, tinnitus, blurred vision and delirium, named after the cinchona bark it comes from. Anticholinergic effects, nausea, diarrhea, headache. Contraindicated with QT prolongation and in myasthenia gravis. Monitor potassium: hypokalemia both reduces efficacy and worsens the QT prolongation.
Procainamide
intravenous or oral		 Supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias. Used to reduce re-entrant arrhythmia in acute myocardial infarction with low cardiac output, and it is the drug of choice in Wolff–Parkinson–White with atrial fibrillation (Section 8). Acetylated in the liver to the active metabolite NAPA, then cleared renally. The same profile as quinidine, plus drug-induced lupus with chronic use — a malar butterfly rash and arthralgias. Board add-on More likely in slow acetylators. Importantly, it does not alter digoxin levels.
Disopyramide Similar to quinidine. Fewer gastrointestinal effects but more profound anticholinergic effects. Board add-on It is negatively inotropic and can worsen heart failure.
⚠️ Quinidine raises digoxin levels — a stated board favourite

Quinidine displaces digoxin from plasma proteins and reduces its renal clearance, so free digoxin rises. Drug bound to plasma protein is generally inactive, because the effect tracks the free drug — displace it and you have effectively given a bigger dose. Quinidine’s effects on potassium change digoxin’s pharmacodynamics on top of that. Dr. Scully said outright that drug interactions with digoxin are a board favourite. Board add-on The memory hook for the subclass is “the QUEEN PROofreads DISsertations” — Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide.

Class IB — lidocaine and mexiletine

  • They block sodium channels in the open and inactivated states but dissociate rapidly, so the block is mild and washes off between beats in healthy tissue.
  • The result is an almost preferential effect on damaged myocardium, with little effect on normal muscle — ischemic tissue fires more often and holds its channels in the bindable states.
  • Lidocaine is intravenous, and is also the local anesthetic. It is second-line emergency therapy for ventricular arrhythmias; in stable patients it is reserved for troublesome premature ventricular contractions or ventricular tachyarrhythmias. Its adverse effects are central nervous system effects — confusion, dizziness, seizures, because it blocks central sodium channels too — plus methemoglobinemia and tremor. Adjust the dose for hepatic function.
  • Mexiletine is the oral relative, used for chronic ventricular arrhythmias. Board add-on Phenytoin also has class IB activity.
  • Board add-on The hook: class IB is Best after a myocardial infarction; class IC is Contraindicated. Class IB drugs also treat digitalis-induced arrhythmias.

Class IC — flecainide and propafenone

  • Marked slowing of the phase 0 upstroke — the biggest effect of the three subclasses — with repolarization unchanged. They suppress premature ventricular contractions.
  • They widen the QRS, and more so with exertion. The QRS is ventricular depolarization, so a flatter upstroke makes it take longer, and use-dependence means faster rates produce more block.
  • Flecainide is indicated for sustained ventricular tachycardia and for prevention of atrial fibrillation in a structurally normal heart. Adverse effects: new or worsening arrhythmia, sinus-node dysfunction, markedly reduced conduction velocity, and central effects including blurred vision, headache and ataxia.
  • Propafenone is its partner. Board add-on It also has weak beta-blocking activity.
⚠️ The vignette clue for class IC

A prior myocardial infarction, scar, heart failure or any structural disease in the history means avoid class IC — these drugs are proarrhythmic in ischemic and structural heart disease. Dr. Scully’s phrasing was that paying attention to the context clues in your vignettes can keep you from causing an arrhythmia. Board add-on The CAST trial showed higher mortality with class IC drugs after myocardial infarction.

🩺 How a class IC drug produces a tracing that looks like ventricular tachycardia

A case from the arrhythmia lecture: a 42-year-old athlete with known atrial flutter “on meds” arrives with a regular wide-complex rhythm at 250, and the machine reads it as ventricular tachycardia. What actually happened is that the class IC drug slowed the flutter circuit enough that the atrioventricular node could now conduct it 1:1, while use-dependent sodium block widened the QRS further at that rate. The giveaway is that the QRS onset deflects rapidly, and the history is flutter on an antiarrhythmic.

Always give an atrioventricular nodal blocker alongside a class IC drug — that is how this is prevented.

Class II — beta-blockers

  • They block sympathetic input to the pacing regions, giving a flatter phase 4 because the funny-current drift slows, and they prolong repolarization at the atrioventricular node.
  • A longer nodal refractory period reduces re-entry: an aberrant impulse arriving at a node that is still refractory simply stops.
  • Indications: supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias, especially those triggered by sympathetic activation — exercise, emotional stress, test-taking, public speaking. Also stable exertional angina, mortality reduction after myocardial infarction, and hypertension (though not first-line there).
GenerationDrugsWhat distinguishes them
First — non-selective (β1 and β2)Propranolol, nadolol, pindolol, timololNot for asthmatics: albuterol needs β2, and blocking β2 causes bronchoconstriction.
Second — β1-selectiveAtenolol, metoprolol, esmololLess β2 risk. Esmolol has a very short half-life — it washes in and washes out — which suits a hemodynamically unstable patient. In practice it is limited by the volume of fluid needed to run it.
Third — extra cardiovascular effectsCarvedilol and labetalol also block α1; nebivolol stimulates endothelial nitric oxide productionVasodilating as well as rate-slowing.
🔑 Two answers Dr. Scully flagged as the “nitty-gritty” questions
  • Which beta-blocker for a patient with a prolonged QT? Propranolol, because it does not prolong repolarization.
  • When is a beta-blocker first-line for hypertension? In pregnancy, where the answer is labetalol. Lowering cardiac output would normally trigger the baroreceptor reflex, clamping down peripheral vessels including those perfusing the placenta. Labetalol’s α1 blockade prevents that compensatory vasoconstriction, so placental perfusion is protected.
MechanismAdverse effectWho gets it
β2 antagonism causing smooth-muscle spasmBronchospasm, vasospasm, cold extremities, impotenceThe non-selective first generation
An exaggerated therapeutic effectNegative inotropy, heart block, symptomatic bradycardiaAll of them
Central nervous system penetrationInsomnia, depression, vivid nightmaresThe lipophilic drugs: propranolol, betaxolol, metoprolol

Board add-on Beta-blockers mask hypoglycemia in diabetics by blunting the tachycardia and tremor. Taper them — abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and acute coronary syndrome. Avoid them in pheochromocytoma or cocaine use before alpha-blockade, because of unopposed alpha stimulation. And be careful combining them with verapamil or diltiazem, which risks heart block.

Class III — potassium-channel blockers

They block the repolarizing potassium currents, so phase 2 and phase 3 both lengthen and the effective refractory period grows. Potassium flows out against the calcium coming in during the plateau; when the calcium channels close, potassium finishes the job. Dr. Scully said explicitly that you will not be examined on the distinction between the delayed and rapid delayed-rectifier subtypes — the effect on the action potential is the same.

⚠️ The class III risk: a long QT becomes torsades

The plateau is the distance between depolarization and repolarization, so prolonging it prolongs the QT. Torsades occurs in about 2% of patients on ibutilide and 1–3% on dofetilide. In Dr. Scully’s words, that seems like a low number — it is 2 in 100 people. That is why these drugs are not started as outpatient medications.

Contraindications: any concurrent QT-prolonging drug, congenital long QT syndrome, and any other class I or class III drug at the same time. Which class I subclass also prolongs repolarization? IA — the Goldilocks porridge that was too long.

DrugMechanismIndicationWhat sets it apart
Ibutilide
intravenous		Inhibits the delayed-rectifier potassium current and enhances the slow inward sodium currentTermination of atrial fibrillation and flutter — chemical conversion, the alternative to electrical cardioversionTerminates only. Atrioventricular block, prolonged QT, torsades in about 2%.
Dofetilide
oral		Inhibits the rapid component of the delayed-rectifier potassium currentConversion of atrial fibrillation and flutter and maintenance of sinus rhythm afterwardsNo negative inotropy, so it is usable with a depressed ejection fraction. Renally excreted — dose by creatinine clearance.
Sotalol
mixed class II and III		Beta-blockade plus potassium-channel blockSevere ventricular arrhythmias, especially in patients who cannot tolerate amiodarone; preventing recurrent atrial fibrillation or flutterAdverse effects of both classes: fatigue and bradycardia from class II, torsades from class III. Can you draw it? A flatter phase 4 in the node plus a longer plateau in the myocyte.

Amiodarone — “it does all the things”

Amiodarone has class I, II, III and IV activity, given intravenously or orally. It was once used for everything, then abandoned as its adverse effects emerged, and it is now back on “every algorithm and every protocol” because the monitoring is understood. Indications: unstable ventricular tachycardia, recurrent ventricular fibrillation, supraventricular arrhythmias, and off-label prevention of recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and flutter. Contraindications: second- and third-degree heart block, symptomatic bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a prolonged QT, which it may worsen.

SystemAdverse effectMonitoringPicture
CardiovascularReduced nodal function, reduced contractility, hypotensionElectrocardiogram
PulmonaryPneumonitis progressing to pulmonary fibrosis — the toxicity that killsBaseline and annual pulmonary function tests
ThyroidHypo- or hyperthyroidismBaseline and annual thyroid function tests
HepaticRaised liver enzymesLiver function tests
NeurologicalPeripheral neuropathy, headache, ataxia, tremor—
EyeCorneal microdeposits, usually harmless and often found at a routine eye examinationRegular eye examinations
SkinPhotosensitivity and blue-grey discoloration—
  • A student asked whether these come from a single dose. No: the cardiovascular effects can appear acutely, but the other organ toxicities require long-term use.
  • Board add-on Amiodarone is about 37% iodine by weight — hence the thyroid effects. It inhibits CYP450, raising warfarin, digoxin and simvastatin levels, and it is lipophilic with a half-life of weeks.
  • Despite prolonging the QT, its torsades risk is low, and it has almost no negative inotropy, so it is safe in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.

Class IV — verapamil and diltiazem

🩸

Dihydropyridines — the “-dipines”

  • Arterial vasodilators, lowering systemic vascular resistance.
  • They act better at the peripheral vasculature than at the heart, which is why they are not antiarrhythmics.
🫀

Non-dihydropyridines

  • Negative inotropes and chronotropes: less contractility, slower rate, slower conduction.
  • Verapamil is the best at nodal tissue; diltiazem does both jobs, each less effectively.
  • They act preferentially on pacemaker tissue, which depends on calcium for its upstroke. Blocking L-type channels slows the upstroke in the atrioventricular node and therefore slows conduction, keeping the node refractory so ectopic signals cannot get through.
  • Indications: re-entrant paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia where the atrioventricular node is part of the circuit; atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, for rate control; hypertension; and ischemic heart disease including vasospastic angina.
  • Caution in conduction-system disease — both drugs can worsen existing sinoatrial and atrioventricular node abnormalities.
  • Adverse effects: bradycardia, atrioventricular block, heart failure; hypotension; edema with diltiazem; constipation with verapamil.
⚠️ Intravenous verapamil plus a beta-blocker is contraindicated

The combination can cause irreversible electromechanical dissociation — drug-induced heart failure in which there is electrical activity with no effective contraction. Separately, the non-dihydropyridines raise plasma digoxin by competing for its renal excretion.

Outside the classes

Adenosine — “have you tried turning it off and on again?”

  • Mechanism: adenosine binds the P1 purinergic receptor, a G-protein coupled receptor, working through Gi/o; the βγ subunit opens potassium channels, which hyperpolarizes sinoatrial, atrial and atrioventricular nodal cells. The result is a big pause — brief asystole or severe bradycardia — after which the underlying rhythm takes back over.
  • Indication: conversion of narrow-complex paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, very commonly pre-hospital and in the emergency department, and highly effective.
  • Try no drug first: vagal manoeuvres — Valsalva (asking the patient to blow the plunger out of a syringe is an easier instruction than “bear down”), cold water, carotid sinus massage, tilting.
  • Give it like a hand grenade: 6 mg all at once with an immediate saline flush. It is fast on and fast off, so it has to reach the heart at high concentration.
  • What the patient feels: a sense of impending doom, like being kicked in the chest, with flushing, headache and chest pain. Warn them.
  • Bronchoconstriction can last up to 30 minutes in asthma — that was the clue in Dr. Scully’s hockey-player case, where the resistance on the bag-valve mask rose after the drug was given.
  • Board add-on Theophylline and caffeine block adenosine receptors, so larger doses are needed. Avoid it in pre-excitation and in asthma. It is also used diagnostically, to unmask flutter waves (Section 8).
  • It fixes re-entry, not sinus tachycardia. As the lecturer put it, if the patient is tachycardic because she needs 15 litres of fluid, adenosine will not help.

Digoxin

🔑 The mechanism, in one chain

Digoxin blocks the sodium–potassium ATPase, so intracellular sodium rises. The sodium–calcium exchanger can then no longer extrude calcium, and may even run backwards. Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium stores grow, calcium-induced calcium release is bigger, and contractility rises. That is the inotropic effect, and it is why digoxin appears in heart failure (Section 18).

Separately, it has a direct antiarrhythmic effect on the conduction system — less atrioventricular nodal automaticity, a longer nodal refractory period and slower conduction — plus autonomic effects: reduced sympathetic outflow, sensitised baroreceptors and increased vagal tone. Indications: heart failure, and rate control in atrial fibrillation and flutter.

⚠️ Potassium is the key to everything about digoxin
  • Hypokalemia increases the digoxin effect and causes toxicity. Low extracellular potassium phosphorylates the pump, which raises digoxin’s binding affinity.
  • Hyperkalemia reduces its clinical effect, because potassium competes with digoxin at the pump.
  • Signs of toxicity? Check the serum potassium first. In Dr. Scully’s words, we do not have to give an antidote if all we have to do is fix their potassium.
  • It has a narrow therapeutic index, so dose it with kidney function and potassium in mind.
TypeInteractionWhy
PharmacodynamicBeta-blockers and calcium channel blockersAdditive slowing of the node and reduction of contractility
PharmacodynamicPotassium-wasting diuretics — loop and thiazideHypokalemia increases digoxin binding, causing toxicity
PharmacokineticErythromycin, or any oral antibioticIt kills the gut bacteria that metabolise digoxin before absorption, so more drug is absorbed than the dose assumed
PharmacokineticQuinidineDisplaces it from plasma proteins and reduces renal clearance
PharmacokineticVerapamil and diltiazemCompete for renal excretion
  • Toxicity on the tracing: down-sloping, scooped ST depression — the “reverse check” — plus arrhythmias.
  • Eyes: yellow-green halos around lights (xanthopsia), altered colour vision, blurred vision. Art historians suspect Van Gogh had digitalis toxicity — he was reportedly treated with foxglove for “dropsy,” the old word for heart-failure edema.
  • Other: anorexia and nausea, agitation.
  • Treatment: normalise the potassium, and give digoxin immune Fab, which binds digoxin one to one. It can itself cause heart failure or anaphylaxis.
  • Board add-on An acute digoxin overdose causes hyperkalemia, because the pumps are blocked — even though chronic hypokalemia is what predisposes to toxicity. Hyperkalemia in poisoning is an indication for Fab. Typical toxic rhythms are premature ventricular contractions, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, and atrial tachycardia with atrioventricular block.

Atropine

  • A non-selective muscarinic antagonist that crosses the blood–brain barrier, so its effects go well beyond the heart.
  • Cardiac indications: symptomatic bradycardia and atrioventricular block. It blocks vagal M2 input, so the rate rises. The relevant rhythms are sinus bradycardia, first-degree block, second-degree Mobitz I and II, and complete heart block.
  • First-line for symptomatic bradycardia is atropine; second-line is the catecholamines, the sympathetic amines. Dr. Scully said he would not ask “here is an indication, what is the drug?” except for bradycardia — so this pairing is worth knowing cold.
  • A paradox worth knowing: at low doses atropine can briefly slow the heart before the expected tachycardia. The slide explains this as M1 blockade showing itself before M2 blockade.
🩺 The anticholinergic toxidrome, and the right antidote

Mad as a hatter (confusion and delirium) · dry as a bone (dry mucosa, no sweating) · blind as a bat (blurred vision, cycloplegia) · red as a beet (flushed skin) · hot as a hare (hyperthermia).

  • Physostigmine is the answer: an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that lets acetylcholine build up and compete atropine off the receptors, and it crosses the blood–brain barrier, so it reverses the central signs as well.
  • Pyridostigmine is the wrong answer here — it does not cross into the central nervous system, so it misses the delirium.
  • Pralidoxime is for organophosphate poisoning, which is cholinergic excess, the opposite problem.
