🎯 What Dr. Scully said he would and would not ask

He will not ask “here is an indication, name the drug” — except for bradycardia, where the answer is atropine first and then the catecholamines. His slide notes also make the broader point that treating an arrhythmia goes beyond antiarrhythmic drugs: atrial fibrillation also needs anticoagulation and cardiovascular risk reduction (Section 9).

Q: Which ion carries phase 0 in a sinoatrial nodal cell, and which carries it in a ventricular myocyte? Why does that distinction organise this whole lecture?

Answer

Calcium through L-type channels in the node; sodium through fast channels in the myocyte. Potassium repolarizes both. That is precisely why calcium channel blockers act on the node (rate control) and sodium-channel blockers act on muscle (rhythm control).

Q: A patient on quinidine reports ringing in the ears, blurred vision and confusion. Name the syndrome. Which class IA drug would have avoided the separate problem of raising digoxin levels?

Answer

Cinchonism — reduced hearing, tinnitus, blurred vision and delirium. Procainamide does not alter digoxin levels, though it brings its own problem of drug-induced lupus with chronic use.

Q: Why does lidocaine suppress ventricular ectopy arising from ischemic tissue while barely affecting healthy myocardium?

Answer

It binds sodium channels in their open and inactivated states and dissociates rapidly. Ischemic, depolarized tissue fires often and holds its channels in those bindable states, so the block accumulates there. In normal tissue the drug washes off between beats.

Q: A patient with a prior myocardial infarction and a reduced ejection fraction develops recurrent atrial fibrillation. Is flecainide a reasonable choice?

Answer

No. Class IC drugs are proarrhythmic in ischemic and structural heart disease. Flecainide is for preventing atrial fibrillation in a structurally normal heart. The hook is “IB is Best after a myocardial infarction, IC is Contraindicated.”

Q: A patient on flecainide for atrial flutter arrives with a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 250. What has happened, and how could it have been prevented?

Answer

1:1 atrial flutter with use-dependent QRS widening. Flecainide slowed the flutter circuit enough for the atrioventricular node to conduct every beat, and the faster rate produced more sodium-channel block, widening the QRS further. Prevent it by always giving an atrioventricular nodal blocker alongside a class IC drug.

Q: Which beta-blocker would you choose for a patient who already has a prolonged QT, and why? And which for hypertension in pregnancy?

Answer

Propranolol for the long QT, because it does not prolong repolarization. Labetalol in pregnancy, because its α1 blockade prevents the baroreflex vasoconstriction that would otherwise reduce placental perfusion.

Q: What distinguishes dofetilide from ibutilide, and why can dofetilide be used in a patient with a reduced ejection fraction?

Answer

Dofetilide also maintains sinus rhythm after conversion, whereas ibutilide only terminates the arrhythmia. It is usable with a low ejection fraction because it has no negative inotropic effect. Both are started in hospital because of a 1 to 3% risk of torsades.

Q: A patient on long-term amiodarone develops a dry cough, dyspnea and bilateral reticular opacities. Name the toxicity and the monitoring that should have been in place.

Answer

Amiodarone pulmonary fibrosis, the toxicity that kills. Baseline and annual pulmonary function tests, alongside thyroid function, liver function and regular eye examinations.

Q: A patient on digoxin is started on furosemide, and a week later reports yellow halos and nausea. What is the first laboratory value to check, and why?

Answer

Serum potassium. The loop diuretic has caused hypokalemia, and potassium competes with digoxin at the sodium–potassium ATPase, so low potassium increases digoxin binding and precipitates toxicity. Fixing the potassium may be all that is needed.

Q: A patient on metoprolol is given intravenous verapamil for supraventricular tachycardia and becomes profoundly hypotensive with no effective contraction. Explain.

Answer

Intravenous verapamil combined with a beta-blocker can cause irreversible electromechanical dissociation. The combination is contraindicated.

Q: A 24-year-old hockey player collapses with a rapid regular narrow-complex rhythm at 192 with no P waves. He is given a drug and the bag-valve mask becomes noticeably harder to squeeze. What was the rhythm, what was the drug, and what confirms it?

Answer

Narrow, regular, no P wave, very fast — paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia from re-entry. The drug was adenosine, acting at the P1 receptor through Gi/o to open potassium channels and hyperpolarize nodal tissue, producing transient atrioventricular block that breaks the circuit. The confirming clue is the transient bronchoconstriction — the stiff bag.

Q: After repeated doses of atropine a patient is febrile, flushed, dry, delirious and has dilated pupils. Which antidote, and why that one rather than the alternatives?

Answer

Physostigmine, because it is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and so reverses the central delirium as well as the peripheral signs. Pyridostigmine does not enter the central nervous system; pralidoxime treats organophosphate poisoning, which is the opposite problem.

LO 83LO 84LO 85Source: Vascular Pathology (Gardner) · CV Pharm Basic Sciences Review (Scully)

Section 11 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Arteriosclerosis Versus Atherosclerosis

Dr. Gardner framed the whole vascular lecture as ordinary cell pathology happening inside a high-pressure plumbing system. Injury, inflammation and repair are the same processes you met in general pathology; the pressure is what turns a small lesion into a heart attack forty years later. This section sorts out the two “annoying words”, then follows a plaque from the first injured endothelial cell to the event that kills.

Abbreviations used in this section EC endothelial cell · SMC smooth muscle cell · IEL internal elastic lamina · LDL low-density lipoprotein · ox-LDL oxidized LDL · HDL high-density lipoprotein · NO nitric oxide · PDGF platelet-derived growth factor · FGF fibroblast growth factor · ECM extracellular matrix · CRP C-reactive protein · vWF von Willebrand factor · FMD fibromuscular dysplasia · MI myocardial infarction · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · CV cardiovascular · H&E hematoxylin and eosin stain · ECG electrocardiogram

Two annoying words

🔑 The umbrella and the subset

Arteriosclerosis means any hardening of the arteries — it is the umbrella term. Atherosclerosis is the one kind caused by an atheroma, the lipid-filled plaque in the intima. Every case of atherosclerosis is arteriosclerosis; most arteriosclerosis is not atherosclerosis.

The arteriosclerosis subtypes

Learn these by which layer is affected and who gets it. The pictures are worth more than the words here, because the exam shows you the slide.

SubtypeWhat happens in the wallWhere, and whoConsequencePicture
Hyaline arteriolosclerosisA pink, glassy, homogeneous wall. Plasma proteins leak across injured endothelium and smooth muscle cells add extra matrix.Small arteries and arterioles. Benign (long-standing) hypertension, diabetes, ageing.A narrow lumen; in the kidney this is nephrosclerosis.
Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosisConcentric “onion-skin” layers of smooth muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane, sometimes with fibrinoid necrosis.Malignant hypertension; pre-eclampsia.The lumen is obliterated; in the kidney, necrotizing arteriolitis.
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosisCalcium in the media, along the internal elastic lamina.Ageing. Visible on a plain X-ray as “pipe-stem” or tram-track arteries.Usually asymptomatic, because the lumen is spared. The stiff vessel tears easily with trauma. Board add-on It makes leg arteries non-compressible, so the ankle–brachial index reads falsely high.
Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasiaProgressive thickening of the intima after chronic immune or mechanical injury — the stereotyped injury response running on.After stents and balloon angioplasty; transplanted organs and vascular grafts.A common cause of graft failure and restenosis.
AtherosclerosisAn intimal plaque made of cells, matrix, lipid and calcium.Large and medium arteries.About 40% of global mortality, through heart attack, stroke and peripheral vascular disease.
⚠️ Two look-alike names

Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia is acquired, after a stent, a balloon or a graft. Fibromuscular dysplasia is a rare, largely inherited condition in which segments of the arterial wall are replaced by connective tissue, giving a “string of beads” angiogram and aneurysms at several sites. Board add-on Fibromuscular dysplasia classically affects the renal arteries of young women and causes secondary hypertension (Section 28).

The response to vascular injury

Everything in this section starts with the endothelium, so it is worth being clear about what a healthy one does.

  • Intact endothelium means no clot, no inflammation and a relaxed vessel. It makes prostacyclin, thrombomodulin, heparin-like molecules and plasminogen activator, and it dilates the vessel with nitric oxide.
  • Damaged or “activated” endothelium flips the switch: clotting, leak, inflammation and constriction. Atherosclerosis, hypertension, vasculitis and thrombosis are all versions of that one switch.
  • Strip the endothelium off and collagen is exposed, so platelets bind immediately (through von Willebrand factor) and clotting starts.
  • On the lab sheet, endothelial dysfunction shows up as prolonged clotting times, a raised D-dimer and a raised CRP.
  • Diseases with major endothelial dysfunction: diabetes, which is ultimately a microvascular disease, hypertension, heart and kidney failure, inflammatory bowel disease, stroke and atherosclerosis.

Cellular and mechanical consequences of injury

  1. Mechanical: flow. Turbulent flow at branch points and ostia stresses the endothelium, while smooth laminar flow protects it. That is why plaques sit at branch points, and why they are patchy, not circumferential.
  2. Mechanical: pressure. Hypertension damages the endothelium directly and, over years, lifts it off and lets plasma proteins pile up underneath (the hyaline change above).
  3. Cellular: the stereotyped response. Any injury that strips the endothelium, or reaches the media, makes smooth muscle cells migrate across the internal elastic lamina into the intima, proliferate and lay down matrix. The result is intimal thickening.
  4. The long-run direction is stenosis. Intimal thickening partly resolves, but the tendency is toward a narrower lumen. In large vessels, repeated injury is atherosclerosis.

How a plaque progresses, and its natural history ★ HY

The lecture’s model is response to injury: atherosclerosis is an aberrant, chronic wound-healing reaction in the intima.

  1. Endothelial injury. Hyperlipidemia (LDL is directly toxic to endothelium), hypertension and turbulent flow, smoking, glycation in diabetes, and viruses that “nick” the endothelium.
  2. LDL enters the intima and is oxidized. The injured endothelium releases cytokines and puts out adhesion molecules.
  3. Monocytes enter and become macrophages, which eat the oxidized LDL and become foam cells. Collections of foam cells are the fatty streak.
  4. Platelets adhere and release growth factors such as platelet-derived growth factor.
  5. Smooth muscle cells migrate in from the media and proliferate, with more matrix and T cells, building fibrous tissue. This makes the fibrofatty atheroma.
  6. Lipid accumulates, cells die and calcium is deposited, forming a necrotic core that is often visible on X-ray.

Anatomy of the plaque

  • Everything sits inside the intima, inside the internal elastic lamina. The media may thin underneath it, but the plaque is intimal.
  • From the lumen down: endothelium, then the fibrous cap (smooth muscle cells, macrophages, foam cells, collagen), then the necrotic core (cell debris, foam cells, calcium and cholesterol crystals, which dissolve during processing and leave clefts on histology).
  • The four components in one line: cells, matrix, lipid and calcium.

Where plaques form

In the order the lecture gave them, which is also the First Aid order: abdominal aorta (and iliacs), coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, internal carotids, circle of Willis. Board add-on First Aid’s hook is “a copy cat named Willis”.

Thin cap versus thick cap: the natural history

💥

Thin-cap plaque (vulnerable)

  • A big lipid core under a thin cap, with many macrophages.
  • Prone to rupture and hemorrhage into the plaque, which exposes the thrombogenic core.
  • Sudden thrombosis of the vessel: myocardial infarction and sudden cardiac death.
  • Board add-on Often not the tightest stenosis before it ruptures.
🧱

Thick-cap or fibrocalcific plaque (stable)

  • More collagen, more calcium.
  • Chronic injury, surface erosion and calcification make it grow slowly.
  • A critical stenosis that limits flow on exertion: stable angina (Section 12).

The outcomes of a plaque

  • Thrombosis on the surface, occluding the vessel.
  • Hemorrhage into the plaque, causing sudden instability or occlusion.
  • Rupture with embolism downstream. Board add-on Cholesterol emboli after angiography give livedo reticularis, blue toes and acute kidney injury with palpable pulses.
  • Ongoing inflammatory remodelling that weakens the wall into an aneurysm, which can rupture or dissect (Section 32).
  • The summary sentence the lecture wants: myocardial infarction, stroke and peripheral vascular disease are all consequences of atherosclerosis.
🩺 “Atherosclerotic cardiovascular death in one slide”

The left main coronary artery at autopsy: lipid, foam cells and cholesterol clefts under a thin cap; hemorrhage into the plaque breaks through into the lumen; thrombus occludes the artery; fatal infarction. In Dr. Gardner’s words, forty years of slow injury, then a sudden event. Board add-on Fatty streaks are already present in the aortas of teenagers.

Risk factors and epidemiology

Hyperlipidemia

the main driver

LDL is directly toxic to the endothelium and is the raw material of the foam cell.

Smoking

initial injury

A major contributor to the first endothelial injury.

Hypertension

injury

Pressure and turbulent flow damage the endothelium.

Diabetes

injury

High glucose glycates endothelial surface proteins.

Age, male sex, family history

fixed

Family history roughly means inherited lipid handling and clotting responses. Board add-on Postmenopausal status is a fixed risk factor too.

  • Risk factors multiply rather than add. At age 55, stacking high systolic pressure, high cholesterol, low HDL, diabetes, smoking and LVH on the ECG takes the 10-year cardiovascular risk past 50%.
  • Online calculators show that a typical person’s 10-year cardiovascular risk is about the same as their 10-year cancer risk.
  • Atherosclerosis rarely travels alone: it co-exists with hypertension, ischemic heart disease and heart failure. That is why Dr. Scully pairs it with the lipid drugs (Section 31) and the antiplatelet drugs, which stop clot forming on a ruptured plaque.

Q: An 80-year-old has an incidental plain film showing “tram-track” calcification of both femoral arteries. His pulses are normal and he has no claudication. What is the lesion, and why is he asymptomatic?

Answer

Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis. The calcium sits in the media, so the lumen is not narrowed. It is a consequence of ageing and is usually harmless.

Q: A kidney biopsy from a patient with a blood pressure of 230/140, headache and papilledema shows arterioles with concentric, laminated wall thickening and fibrinoid necrosis. Name the lesion. How would the arterioles of a patient with 20 years of well-controlled diabetes differ?

Answer

Hyperplastic (“onion-skin”) arteriolosclerosis, the lesion of malignant hypertension. The diabetic patient would show hyaline arteriolosclerosis: a homogeneous, glassy pink wall from leaked plasma protein, without the layers.

Q: Six months after a coronary stent, a patient’s angina returns. Angiography shows the stented segment has narrowed again. What process is responsible?

Answer

Fibromuscular intimal hyperplasia — the stereotyped response to injury. The stent damaged the wall, smooth muscle cells migrated from the media into the intima, proliferated and laid down matrix, and the lumen narrowed.

Q: Which cell becomes a foam cell, what does it eat, and in which layer of the artery does the whole atheroma — necrotic core included — sit?

Answer

A macrophage, derived from a monocyte, that has ingested oxidized LDL. The atheroma sits in the intima, inside the internal elastic lamina.

Q: Why do atherosclerotic plaques cluster at branch points and ostia rather than along straight segments?

Answer

Turbulent flow there activates and injures the endothelium — faster turnover, apoptosis and a rough surface — whereas laminar flow keeps the endothelium in its quiet, protective state.

Q: A 52-year-old man dies suddenly. At autopsy, the left anterior descending artery has a plaque narrowing it by only 50%, with a large lipid core, a thin fibrous cap that has torn, and occlusive thrombus on top. A second plaque elsewhere narrows a vessel by 85% but has a thick collagenous cap. Which plaque killed him, and what was the other one more likely to cause?

Answer

The thin-cap (vulnerable) plaque: it ruptured, exposed its thrombogenic core and caused occlusive thrombosis. The thick-cap fibrocalcific plaque is a stable critical stenosis, which typically causes exertional (stable) angina. Degree of stenosis does not predict which plaque ruptures.

LO 16LO 17LO 18LO 100Source: Application Session 1 (Watkins) · Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Ischemic Heart Disease Pharmacology (Scully)

Section 12 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Stable Ischemic Heart Disease Versus Acute Coronary Syndrome

Dr. Watkins opened the chest-pain case with a warning: “If you do not consider coronary artery disease you will never diagnose it.” His second rule was “Listen to the patient and they will tell you the diagnosis.” This section follows his 72-year-old patient from eight weeks of exertional chest pressure to a non-ST-elevation infarction, and uses her to separate the stable from the acute.

Abbreviations used in this section CAD coronary artery disease · SIHD stable ischemic heart disease · ACS acute coronary syndrome · UA unstable angina · NSTEMI / STEMI non-ST-elevation / ST-elevation myocardial infarction · NSTE-ACS non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome · MI myocardial infarction · MINOCA myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries · ECG electrocardiogram · hs-cTn high-sensitivity cardiac troponin · ETT exercise treadmill test · MPI myocardial perfusion imaging · CCTA coronary computed tomography angiography · CAC coronary artery calcium score · TTE transthoracic echocardiogram · LBBB left bundle branch block · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · PCI percutaneous coronary intervention (a stent) · CABG coronary artery bypass grafting · GRACE Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events risk score · LVEF left ventricular ejection fraction · NTG nitroglycerin · ED emergency department · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · PREVENT the American Heart Association’s risk equations · FH familial hypercholesterolemia · RCA / LAD right coronary / left anterior descending artery · PR PR interval (atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation) · ACE angiotensin-converting enzyme · INOCA ischemia with no obstructive coronary arteries · P2Y12 the platelet ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor · IV intravenous

Stable angina, unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI ★ HY

All four sit on one spectrum of oxygen supply versus demand. The difference between them is what the plaque is doing: sitting still, cracking with a partial clot, or cracking with a complete one.

SyndromeWhat the artery is doingPainTroponinECGPicture
Stable anginaA fixed stenosis, usually 70% or more. Supply cannot rise to meet demand.Exertional, predictable, minutes, relieved by restNormalUsually normal at rest; ST depression during exertion
Unstable (crescendo) anginaA vulnerable plaque has ruptured with a non-occlusive thrombusLonger, more frequent, lower threshold, or new at restNormal on a standard assayST depression or T-wave inversion, or normal
NSTEMIRupture with a partially occlusive thrombus, 70–90% narrowing with some flow. Subendocardial infarct.At rest, persistentRaisedST depression, T-wave inversion, or nothing specific
STEMIRupture with a completely occlusive thrombus. Transmural infarct.At rest, persistent, severeRaised, peaks far higherST elevation in a territory, later Q waves
Vasospastic (variant, Prinzmetal) anginaSpasm of coronary smooth muscle, no plaque neededAt rest, night to early morning, young patientsNormalTransient ST elevation only during the attack

Pictures: Scully lecture slide 7 (artery strips); AMBOSS (infarct schemas, board add-on).

  • Acute coronary syndrome means unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI. It is the stable-to-acute jump: acute myocardial infarction is thrombosis in a coronary artery, usually from plaque rupture.
  • As stable angina progresses toward unstable angina, duration and frequency rise and the exertional threshold falls. That trend is the warning.
  • Board add-on With high-sensitivity troponin, most patients once labelled unstable angina turn out to have a small troponin rise and are now called NSTEMI. UWorld calls unstable angina “largely obsolete” as a diagnosis, but it remains on exams as rest angina with a normal troponin.
  • MINOCA and INOCA — infarction or ischemia without obstructive coronary disease — account for about 10–15% of infarcts. The core problem is microvascular and endothelial dysfunction (diabetic small-vessel disease, genetic failure of small-vessel relaxation); associations are hypertension, aortic stenosis and anemia.
  • Chronic ischemic heart disease is progressive loss of myocytes from many small, silent, healed infarcts — common in diabetics who do not feel the pain.

Why angina appears with exertion first: coronary flow reserve

  • Resting coronary flow stays normal until a stenosis reaches about 80–90%.
  • Maximal (stress) flow begins to fall at about 50% stenosis.
  • So stable angina shows up on exertion first, and a stress test unmasks a lesion that the resting ECG misses.
  • The myocardium is perfused in diastole, so a fast heart rate shortens supply time as it raises demand (Section 1).

Not every infarct is a ruptured plaque

New name (2023)Old nameTriggerWho
Primary MIType 1Plaque rupture or erosion with thrombus; spontaneous coronary dissectionYounger, male; smoking, dyslipidemia, prior MI. Higher in-hospital death.
Secondary MIType 2Supply–demand mismatch: sepsis, shock, tachycardia, severe hypertension, anemiaOlder, female; heart failure, atrial fibrillation, valve, kidney or liver disease. Lower peak troponin; poor long-term outlook.
Procedural MITypes 4–5Complications of PCI or cardiac surgery—

Both types can show ST changes and a troponin rise. With an ongoing acute coronary syndrome the initial treatment is the same; a type 2 infarct is then managed by fixing the underlying problem rather than as a thrombotic occlusion.

Chest pain: the approach from history and exam ★ HY

Always ask about quality, location, onset, duration, what relieves it and associated symptoms, and add Dr. Watkins’s question: “Can you make the chest pain occur?” Angina is predictable and inducible; random pain is not.

FeaturePoints toward ischemiaPoints away
QualityDull pressure, squeezing, heaviness, tightnessSharp, stabbing, tearing
LocationSubsternal, radiating to neck, jaw, arm or backPinpoint (a fingertip-sized spot) or migratory
DurationMinutesSeconds, or hours on end
OnsetExertion or emotional stressNo clear trigger
PatternPredictable; the patient can induce itRandom
ResolutionOver minutes with restSeconds, or not at all
  • Sharp pain worse on inspiration and lying flat suggests pericarditis. Sudden ripping pain to the back suggests an acute aortic syndrome. Relief with nitroglycerin is not diagnostic of ischemia.
  • Women are persistently under-diagnosed — a lower index of suspicion before menopause, and a tendency to attribute pain elsewhere. Women, people with diabetes and the elderly more often describe left- or right-sided, stabbing, throat or abdominal discomfort. Diabetic neuropathy can make infarcts silent.
  • Coronary disease presents about 10 years later in women; smoking roughly 6× the infarct risk in women versus 3× in men, and diabetes is a more potent risk factor in women (Section 37).
  • Only about 30% of chest pain is cardiac (Dr. Scully), so keep the differential wide.

The exam and the risk factors

  • Examine for vascular disease elsewhere and for heart failure: full and equal pulses, bruits, heart sounds (listen for an S3), edema, and the skin for xanthomas.
  • Risk factors: smoking, family history (especially onset under 60), lipids, diabetes, hypertension; also stress, alcohol, drugs and adherence.
  • Tendon xanthoma and corneal arcus before 45 are highly specific for familial hypercholesterolemia; xanthelasma has low specificity (Section 30).

The differential that matters Board add-on

MimicWhat separates it from an acute coronary syndrome
Aortic dissectionTearing pain to the back, a blood-pressure difference of more than 20 mm Hg between the arms, a wide mediastinum. Never give an anticoagulant until it is excluded (Section 32).
Pulmonary embolismHypoxemia with clear lungs; a mild troponin rise from right-ventricular strain.
Acute pericarditisPositional, pleuritic, better sitting forward; diffuse ST elevation with PR depression (Section 23).
MyocarditisGradual onset; troponin that stays at a plateau rather than rising and falling.
Vasospastic anginaBrief (under about 15 minutes), self-limited, at rest, in a young smoker; transient ST elevation.
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathyA postmenopausal woman after an emotional or physical stressor; apical ballooning on echo, clean coronaries.

The ECG in each

The tracing is worked through in full in Section 7 (territories, reciprocal change, STEMI evolution, posterior infarction). The points this section needs:

  • Everyone with chest pain gets a 12-lead ECG. Look for ST elevation, LBBB, Q waves, ST depression and T-wave changes. Pathologic Q waves suggest a prior infarct.
  • Stable angina: usually a normal resting tracing — Dr. Watkins’s patient had a completely normal one.
  • NSTEMI: ST depression in about a third of patients; deep T-wave inversions (3 mm or more) are more common but less specific. The leads do not localise the infarct well.
  • STEMI: new ST elevation at the J point in two or more contiguous leads, more than 1 mm (higher thresholds in V2–V3). Board add-on STEMI equivalents: a new LBBB with a convincing story, ST elevation in aVR with diffuse depression (left main), and ST depression in V1–V3 (posterior).

Stress testing and catheterization

Step 1: estimate the pre-test probability

  • The CAD Consortium calculator uses age, sex and symptom type, then adds risk factors, and can add the coronary calcium score, which raises specificity (a calcium score of 0 makes obstructive disease much less likely).
  • His 72-year-old patient came out at about 40–50%: intermediate risk.
  • The Pooled Cohort (ASCVD) and PREVENT calculators are for prevention in people without symptoms; they are not the right tool once someone has chest pain.

Step 2: choose the test

  • Any suspicion of an acute coronary syndrome means the ACS pathway, not outpatient testing.
  • Able to exercise with an interpretable resting ECG: low-to-intermediate likelihood, a plain exercise ECG; intermediate-to-high, exercise with imaging (echo or perfusion) or CCTA.
  • Uninterpretable resting ECG (LBBB, paced rhythm, digoxin, LVH with strain): exercise with imaging.
  • Unable to exercise: pharmacologic stress echo or perfusion imaging, or CCTA.
  • His choice for her was a stress echocardiogram: more sensitive and specific than a plain treadmill test, especially in women.
  • Stress testing during active ischemia is contraindicated.

Step 3: catheterization — how fast?

SituationFeaturesTiming
STEMIST elevation meeting criteriaPrimary PCI, door-to-balloon under 90 minutes. Board add-on If PCI is not available, fibrinolysis (alteplase), ideally within 30 minutes of arrival.
NSTE-ACS, very high riskHemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock, refractory pain, life-threatening arrhythmia or arrest, a mechanical complication, acute heart failure, recurrent dynamic ST changesImmediate, under 2 hours
NSTE-ACS, high riskNSTEMI by troponin, dynamic ST–T changes, GRACE over 140Early, under 24 hours
NSTE-ACS, intermediate riskDiabetes or renal insufficiency, LVEF under 40% or heart failure, early post-infarct angina, prior PCI or CABG, GRACE 109–140Under 72 hours

Her angiogram showed a 90% ruptured plaque in the right coronary artery with thrombus, treated with two drug-eluting stents. Board add-on Bypass surgery is preferred over stenting for left main disease, three-vessel disease, and two-vessel disease involving the LAD in a diabetic.

Medical management side by side

Stable ischemic heart diseaseAcute coronary syndrome
WhereThe officeAn ambulance to the emergency department — never by car
First stepsTreat the blood pressure; as-needed sublingual nitroglycerin; lipids and thyroid tests; arrange a stress test; teach the red flags (prolonged, severe or rest pain means call 911)In the office while waiting: aspirin, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, monitoring. In the ED: repeat ECG, serial troponin, bedside echo, IV nitroglycerin, heparin bolus, clopidogrel load
AntianginalBeta-blocker first line, nitrates second; calcium channel blockers; ranolazine if refractory (Section 16)Beta-blocker unless shock, bradycardia or decompensated heart failure; nitrates unless hypotension or right-ventricular infarct
AntithromboticAspirin (single antiplatelet)Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor) plus an anticoagulant
LipidsStatinHigh-intensity statin straight away
RevascularisationIf symptoms persist despite medicines, or high-risk anatomyTimed by risk, as in the table above
🔑 Optimal medical therapy saves lives

The four classes are antiplatelet + statin + ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker + beta-blocker. In long-term follow-up, patients on none, one or two of them had about 20% ten-year mortality, against about 13% on three or four.

🎯 Troponin belongs in the emergency department

“I would never order a troponin in the outpatient setting. If you think about ordering a troponin, that patient should be in an emergency room.” — Dr. Qazi

Dr. Watkins made the same point: troponin is for a suspected acute coronary syndrome, measured serially, in the ED. And waiting for insurance pre-approval for an admission in an acute coronary syndrome would, in his word, be “malpractice.”

Q: A 72-year-old woman has 8 weeks of chest pressure walking up a steep hill with her dog, radiating to her jaw, lasting minutes and easing with rest. It is not getting worse. Her resting ECG is normal and she can walk on a treadmill. What is the working diagnosis, and what test comes next?

Answer

Stable ischemic heart disease at intermediate pre-test probability — typical features, new but not progressive, so not an acute coronary syndrome. Next is an exercise stress echocardiogram, which is more sensitive and specific than a plain treadmill test, especially in women. Treat her blood pressure and give as-needed sublingual nitroglycerin meanwhile.

Q: A week later the same patient tells you that over 4 days her pain has come more often and lasted up to 45 minutes, and last night she had 4 hours of pain at rest. Her ECG shows new inferolateral ST depression. Her husband offers to drive her to the hospital. What do you do?

Answer

Treat it as a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome. Cancel the stress test (contraindicated in active ischemia), give aspirin, nitroglycerin, oxygen if she is hypoxic, and monitoring in the office, and send her by ambulance — no patient with ACS symptoms is ever transferred by car.

Q: An NSTEMI patient becomes hypotensive and confused in the emergency department, with cool extremities. How soon should catheterization happen?

Answer

Immediately — within 2 hours. Cardiogenic shock is a very-high-risk feature. An uncomplicated NSTEMI by troponin alone would be early invasive, within 24 hours.

Q: An 84-year-old woman with septic shock and a heart rate of 140 has a troponin rise and diffuse ST depression. Angiography a year ago showed mild fixed disease. What kind of infarction is this?

Answer

A secondary (type 2) infarction: supply–demand mismatch from sepsis, hypotension and tachycardia, not plaque rupture. Treat the sepsis; she is not managed as a thrombotic occlusion.

Q: At what degree of stenosis does maximal coronary flow start to fall, and at what degree does resting flow fall? Why does this explain the clinical picture of stable angina?

Answer

Maximal flow falls from about 50%; resting flow is preserved until about 80–90%. So a moderate stenosis causes symptoms only when demand rises, on exertion, and the resting ECG is normal — which is why you need a stress test to find it.

Q: A patient’s chest pain is sharp, worse when lying flat and on deep breaths, and better sitting forward. A second patient has sudden ripping pain through to the back and a 30 mm Hg difference in arm pressures. What does each suggest?

Answer

The first is acute pericarditis — non-ischemic, positional, pleuritic pain. The second is an acute aortic dissection, which must be excluded before any anticoagulant or thrombolytic is given.

LO 23LO 24Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Application Sessions 1 & 2 (Watkins, Segal, Qazi)

Section 13 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Cardiac Biomarkers: Troponin, BNP and NT-proBNP

Two blood tests answer two different questions. Troponin asks “are heart muscle cells dying right now?” The natriuretic peptides ask “is the heart wall being stretched?” Most exam traps come from forgetting which question a test answers, or from the things that push each test up or down without heart disease.

Abbreviations used in this section cTn cardiac troponin · TnI / TnT / TnC troponin I / T / C · hs-cTn high-sensitivity cardiac troponin · CK-MB creatine kinase, MB (heart) fraction · ANP atrial natriuretic peptide · BNP B-type (brain) natriuretic peptide · NT-proBNP N-terminal pro-BNP, the inactive fragment · NPV / PPV negative / positive predictive value · ARNI angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (sacubitril/valsartan) · cGMP cyclic guanosine monophosphate · MI myocardial infarction · STEMI / NSTEMI ST-elevation / non-ST-elevation MI · ACS acute coronary syndrome · PE pulmonary embolism · CKD chronic kidney disease · HF heart failure · COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease · ED emergency department · URL upper reference limit · ECG electrocardiogram

Troponin: physiology, timing, sensitivity and specificity ★ HY

Where it comes from

  • The troponin complex sits on the thin filament with tropomyosin. TnC binds calcium, TnI inhibits actin–myosin binding at rest, TnT anchors the complex to tropomyosin (Section 1 has the contraction mechanics).
  • The cardiac isoforms of TnI and TnT differ from skeletal muscle ones, which is what makes the test heart-specific.
  • Dying myocytes release troponin, and the size of the rise tracks the amount of injury. STEMIs peak far higher than NSTEMIs.

Timing

MarkerRisesPeaksBack to normalUse
High-sensitivity troponin1–3 h (within about an hour of injury)12–24 h7–10 daysThe gold standard for diagnosing infarction
Standard troponin Board add-on4–8 h12–24 h7–10 daysOlder assays; the “rises at 4 hours” number in First Aid
CK-MB4–6 hAbout 24 h2–3 daysHistorical. Its only remaining niche is re-infarction within a few days, because troponin is still up from the first event

How it is used

  • Myocardial injury means a troponin above the 99th percentile of the upper reference limit. Acute injury means a rise and/or fall on serial values.
  • With high-sensitivity assays most patients are ruled in or out on the first value; equivocal ones are repeated at 1 or 3 hours, and the rate of change is diagnostic. Dr. Watkins’s patient went from 50 to 325 in four hours.
  • Infarction = acute injury plus a clinical picture of ischemia (symptoms, ECG changes, a new wall-motion abnormality).
  • Troponin is an emergency-department test. If you are worried enough to order one in the office, the patient belongs in the ED.

Sensitivity, specificity and weaknesses

  • More sensitive and more specific than CK-MB for myocardial necrosis — very specific for heart muscle, but not specific for infarction.
  • It rises with any myocyte injury. The lecture’s list: a marathon, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis and chronic heart failure — without the steep rise or the high peak of an infarct.
  • Board add-on Others: sepsis and type 2 (supply–demand) infarction, tachyarrhythmias, takotsubo cardiomyopathy, cardioversion or cardiac contusion, stroke, and chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance gives a chronically raised, flat level).
  • It cannot detect injury in the first hour or so, and a single value says nothing about direction — hence serial testing.
  • A flat, mildly raised troponin that does not change on repeat means chronic injury or a secondary (type 2) event, not plaque rupture — the cocaine heart-failure case in Application Session 2.

BNP versus NT-proBNP: physiology and limitations ★ HY

Physiology

  • Ventricular myocytes respond to wall stretch — volume or pressure overload — by making pro-BNP, which is cleaved into two pieces in equal amounts: active BNP (32 amino acids) and inert NT-proBNP (76 amino acids).
  • Board add-on Its sibling ANP comes from the atria in response to atrial stretch. Both act through cGMP.
  • What BNP does: vasodilation, natriuresis and diuresis (it dilates the afferent arteriole and raises the glomerular filtration rate), and it suppresses renin, aldosterone and sympathetic tone. It is the body’s counter-regulator to the renin–angiotensin system in heart failure — a fight it eventually loses (Section 17).
  • BNP is cleared by neprilysin and by natriuretic-peptide clearance receptors. NT-proBNP is cleared mainly by the kidney, which is why it lasts longer.

How it is used

  • Diagnostic and prognostic in acute and chronic heart failure. Its strength is the negative predictive value: in a breathless patient, a low level makes heart failure very unlikely.
  • That makes it the tiebreaker between heart failure and pneumonia or a COPD exacerbation.
  • BNP also carries prognostic value in asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.

Limitations

ProblemEffectWhy
Sacubitril (ARNI)BNP rises as a drug effect; NT-proBNP is unaffectedSacubitril inhibits neprilysin, which degrades BNP. Follow NT-proBNP in patients on sacubitril/valsartan.
Kidney diseaseBoth rise; NT-proBNP rises moreNT-proBNP is renally cleared
AgeLevels rise with ageHence the age-specific NT-proBNP rule-in cut-offs
Obesity Board add-onFalsely low — a normal value does not exclude heart failureIncreased clearance by adipose tissue
Other causes of stretch Board add-onRaised without left heart failureAtrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and right ventricular strain, pulmonary hypertension, sepsis, acute coronary syndrome
Flash pulmonary edema or pericardial constriction Board add-onCan be lower than expectedNot enough time to synthesise it, or the ventricle cannot stretch

Head-to-head comparison

Troponin (high-sensitivity)BNPNT-proBNP
The question it answersAre myocytes dying?Is the ventricle stretched?Is the ventricle stretched?
SourceSarcomere of injured cardiomyocytesVentricular myocytesVentricular myocytes (same molecule, other half)
BiologyStructural proteinActive hormone, 32 amino acidsInert fragment, 76 amino acids
Half-lifeElevated 7–10 daysAbout 20 min1–2 h
Rule outUndetectable or below the 99th percentile, with no change on repeat≤ 100 pg/mL≤ 300 pg/mL
Rule inRise and/or fall above the 99th percentile> 400 pg/mLAge-specific: under 50, > 450 · 50–75, > 900 · over 75, > 1,800
Main useDiagnose MI, especially NSTEMI (in STEMI the ECG decides)Diagnose and follow heart failureDiagnose and follow heart failure; use on an ARNI
SacubitrilNo effectRaised (neprilysin blocked)No effect
Kidney diseaseChronically raised, flatRaisedRaised more

🧠 Telling them apart in one line

Troponin is a crime-scene marker — it leaks out of cells that have already been damaged. BNP is a stress signal — a hormone the stretched ventricle chooses to secrete. NT-proBNP is BNP’s receipt: made in the same amount, does nothing, and hangs around longer.

Q: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is switched from enalapril to sacubitril/valsartan. Three months later he feels much better, but his BNP has risen. Which test should you follow instead, and why?

Answer

NT-proBNP. Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that degrades BNP, so BNP rises as a drug effect. NT-proBNP is an inert fragment that neprilysin does not clear, so it still reflects wall stretch.

Q: A healthy 35-year-old runner has a mildly raised troponin the morning after a marathon. How does his troponin curve differ from that of an infarction?

Answer

It is a low, flat, short-lived bump with no steep rise and no high peak. Serial testing showing the rate of change separates it from an infarction, along with the absence of an ischemic story or ECG changes.

Q: A patient had an NSTEMI 4 days ago. Today he has new chest pain and ST changes. His troponin is still elevated from the first event. Which marker is classically used to diagnose re-infarction, and why?

Answer

CK-MB, because it returns to normal in 2–3 days while troponin stays up for 7–10 days. A new CK-MB rise points to a new event. (In practice a fresh rise on serial high-sensitivity troponin is now used.)

Q: A 68-year-old with a body-mass index of 44 presents with dyspnea, orthopnea and leg edema. Her BNP is 60 pg/mL. Does this rule out heart failure?

Answer

No. Natriuretic peptides are falsely low in obesity because adipose tissue clears them faster. With a convincing clinical picture, get an echocardiogram rather than relying on the number.

Q: Which natriuretic peptide is biologically active, which has the longer half-life, and which rises more in chronic kidney disease?

Answer

BNP is active (vasodilation, natriuresis, renin suppression). NT-proBNP has the longer half-life (1–2 hours versus about 20 minutes) and rises more in kidney disease, because it is cleared by the kidney.

LO 20Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner)

Section 14 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Myocardial Infarction: the Morphology and Histology Timeline

Dr. Gardner’s “infarct clock” is the most reliably tested table in cardiac pathology. Learn it as a story rather than a grid: the muscle dies, neutrophils arrive, macrophages clean up, granulation tissue fills the hole, and collagen scars it. Each stage has a look under the microscope, a look to the naked eye and — this is the clinical payoff — a complication that belongs to it (Section 15).

Abbreviations used in this section MI myocardial infarction · EM electron microscope · H&E hematoxylin and eosin stain · LV left ventricle · LAD left anterior descending artery · STEMI / NSTEMI ST-elevation / non-ST-elevation MI · PCI percutaneous coronary intervention · ROS reactive oxygen species · TTC triphenyltetrazolium chloride, the stain used to show fresh infarcts at autopsy

Gross and microscopic changes over time ★ HY

TimeGrossLight microscopePicture
0 – ½ h
reversible		NoneNone. Only the electron microscope shows anything: myofibril relaxation, glycogen loss, mitochondrial swelling.
½ – 4 h
irreversible from here		NoneUsually none; some wavy fibres at the border. (Electron microscope: sarcolemmal disruption, mitochondrial densities.)
4 – 12 hOccasional dark mottlingEarly coagulative necrosis, edema, hemorrhage.
12 – 24 hDark mottlingOngoing coagulative necrosis; pyknotic nuclei; hypereosinophilic myocytes; marginal contraction band necrosis; the first neutrophils.
1 – 3 daysMottling with a yellow-tan centreLoss of nuclei and striations; a brisk neutrophil infiltrate.
3 – 7 daysHyperemic border, central yellow-tan softeningDead fibres and dying neutrophils disintegrate; macrophages begin at the border.
7 – 10 daysMaximally yellow-tan and soft, with depressed red-tan marginsWell-developed phagocytosis; granulation tissue at the margins.
10 – 14 daysRed-grey depressed bordersEstablished granulation tissue with new vessels and early collagen.
2 – 8 weeksGrey-white scar, advancing from the border to the coreMore collagen, fewer cells.
> 2 monthsScarring completeDense collagenous scar.

Pictures: Gardner lecture, slide 63 — about 1 day (wavy fibres), 3 days (neutrophils), 7 days (macrophages), 10 days (granulation tissue on trichrome, collagen in blue) and 60 days (scar).

⚠️ The sources put the wavy fibres in different hours

The lecture slide puts wavy fibres at ½–4 hours, at the border. First Aid says 0–4 hours; the UWorld library table says 4–12 hours. Everyone agrees on what matters: wavy fibres are the first light-microscope change, seen within the first day, before neutrophils. Dr. Gardner also admitted the 0–½ hour electron-microscope changes would be hard to call blind.

🔑 The four anchors to memorise
  • Day 1 — coagulative necrosis begins; wavy fibres; looks normal or dark to the eye. Board add-on This is the window when ventricular arrhythmia kills.
  • Days 1–3 — neutrophils. Board add-on First Aid ties the early fibrinous pericarditis to this window.
  • Days 3–10 — macrophages, yellow and soft. The rupture window.
  • Weeks to months — granulation tissue, then scar. The true-aneurysm window.
⚠️ Why the timeline matters clinically

The wall is softest at about 3–7 days. Neutrophils and macrophages have digested the dead muscle, and collagen has not arrived yet. That is the rupture window for the free wall, the septum and the papillary muscle (Section 15).

What it looks like to the naked eye

  • Transmural versus subendocardial. A completely occluded artery kills the full wall thickness (the STEMI pattern). A partial or transient occlusion kills only the inner third, the subendocardium, which is the last zone the coronary blood reaches and is under the highest wall stress (the NSTEMI pattern).
  • Board add-on A very fresh infarct can be shown at autopsy with TTC stain: living muscle stains dark red-brown, the infarct stays pale because it has lost its dehydrogenase enzymes.

Reperfusion injury

Opening the artery saves muscle, but the returning blood does some damage of its own.

  • When flow returns to damaged myocytes, calcium floods in and the myofibrils hypercontract. Under the microscope that gives contraction band necrosis: dense, hypereosinophilic transverse bands across the myocytes.
  • Board add-on Returning oxygen also generates free radicals (reactive oxygen species), and the returning blood leaks through damaged capillaries, so a reperfused infarct is often hemorrhagic.
  • Contraction bands also appear at the margins of an unreperfused infarct at 12–24 hours, but a diffuse band of contraction necrosis after a stent or thrombolysis is the reperfusion picture.

Q: A man dies 2 days after a large anterior myocardial infarction. What will the infarct look like grossly and under the microscope?

Answer

Grossly, mottled with a yellow-tan centre. Microscopically, coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclei and striations and a brisk neutrophil infiltrate — the 1–3 day window.

Q: A patient gets a stent 3 hours after an LAD occlusion. A biopsy of the territory shows hypereosinophilic myocytes crossed by dense transverse bands. What is this, and what caused it?

Answer

Contraction band necrosis from reperfusion injury. Calcium floods into damaged myocytes when flow returns, and the myofibrils hypercontract.

Q: An autopsy shows an infarct whose border is filled with loose connective tissue containing many small new blood vessels, fibroblasts and a little early collagen. How old is it?

Answer

About 10–14 days — established granulation tissue with new vessels and early collagen. Macrophages dominate before that (3–10 days) and dense scar after about 2 months.

Q: Why is the left ventricular free wall most likely to rupture about 3–7 days after an infarct, rather than on day 1 or at week 3?

Answer

At 3–7 days neutrophils and macrophages have digested the dead muscle but collagen has not yet been laid down, so the wall is at its softest. On day 1 the necrotic muscle still holds its shape; by week 3 granulation tissue and collagen are reinforcing it.

Q: A 60-year-old diabetic woman has progressive heart failure but has never reported chest pain. Autopsy shows many patchy grey-white scars throughout the left ventricle. Name the entity.

Answer

Chronic ischemic heart disease from multiple silent, healed infarcts; her diabetic neuropathy blunted the pain. Grey-white scar means each infarct was more than about two months old.

LO 19Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Application Session 1 (Watkins)

Section 15 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Complications After STEMI

Three days after leaving hospital with a right coronary stent, Dr. Watkins’s patient walked into the office breathless, unable to lie flat, with a heart rate of 130 and a new holosystolic murmur with a thrill. His teaching point: sudden dyspnea plus a new murmur after an infarct is a mechanical complication until proven otherwise, and the two critical tests are the ECG and the echocardiogram. This section sorts every complication by when it happens, because the timing usually gives the answer.

Abbreviations used in this section MI myocardial infarction · STEMI / NSTEMI ST-elevation / non-ST-elevation MI · LV / RV left / right ventricle · RA / PA right atrium / pulmonary artery · LAD left anterior descending artery · LCx left circumflex artery · RCA right coronary artery · PDA posterior descending artery · VF / VT ventricular fibrillation / tachycardia · NSVT non-sustained VT · AF atrial fibrillation · AV atrioventricular · VSR / VSD ventricular septal rupture / defect · MR mitral regurgitation · PEA pulseless electrical activity · CHF congestive heart failure · JVD jugular venous distension · ECG electrocardiogram · ICU intensive care unit · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · AKI acute kidney injury · ARDS acute respiratory distress syndrome · CPR cardiopulmonary resuscitation · IABP intra-aortic balloon pump · PR PR interval (atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation) · V4R right-sided chest lead V4 · SA sinoatrial · IV intravenous

Non-mechanical complications

ComplicationWhenDetail
ArrhythmiaEarly — first 24–48 h, but any timeVF, VT and NSVT, supraventricular tachycardias, AF. The strongest reason to keep infarct patients in hospital on a monitor. Board add-on Ventricular arrhythmia is the commonest cause of death in the first day, often before the patient reaches hospital.
Bradycardia and heart blockEarlyInferior (RCA) infarcts: the RCA supplies the SA node in about 60% and the AV node in about 90%. A septal (LAD) infarct can cause right bundle branch block, because septal branches feed the right bundle.
Contractile failure, cardiogenic shockFirst 24 h onwardShock in about 10%, typically when ≥ 40% of the LV is infarcted. Moderate CHF is common.
Right ventricular infarctWith an inferior MIRight heart failure: hypotension, JVD and clear lungs. Board add-on The RV is preload-dependent: give IV fluids, and avoid nitrates, diuretics and opioids. Confirm with right-sided leads (ST elevation in V4R).
Recurrent ischemiaAny timeStent thrombosis (usually presents with chest pain and new ST elevation), untreated coronary disease.
Early (peri-infarction) pericarditis2–3 daysFibrinous, over a transmural infarct. Pleuritic pain and a friction rub. Usually self-limited.
Dressler syndrome (post-cardiac injury)> 2 weeks, to monthsAutoimmune: cardiac antigens released by the injury provoke antibodies and immune-complex pericarditis. Fever, pleuritic pain, rub, effusion. Board add-on Treated with aspirin or an NSAID plus colchicine.
Mural thrombus, embolismDays to weeksDamaged endocardium and an akinetic segment let clot form in the LV, which can embolise: stroke, limb or gut ischemia.
Chamber dilationWeeks to monthsLoss of muscle and remodelling; leads to chronic heart failure (Section 17).
Non-anginal chest pain from anxietyAny timeCommon — but a diagnosis of exclusion.

Mechanical complications ★ HY

Necrotic muscle “blows out”, giving sudden, severe heart failure, respiratory failure and shock. They follow transmural (STEMI) infarcts almost exclusively, and are commoner with a first infarct, single-vessel disease, late or no reperfusion, older age and female sex.

ComplicationArtery and riskWhenPresentationThe clinching findingPicture
Papillary muscle ruptureInferior MI (RCA); older, hypertensive80% within 7 days of an inferior STEMIAcute hypotension and flash pulmonary edemaA new apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla (acute MR). Posteromedial muscle 3× more often: it has a single supply from the PDA, the anterolateral one has two (LAD and LCx).
Ventricular septal ruptureOlder, female; large ST deviation. LAD (apical septum) or RCA (basal septum)3–5 daysAcute heart failure (less severe than papillary rupture) and hypotension; often chest painA harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border with a thrill. Left-to-right shunt, so an oxygen step-up from RA to PA on a right-heart catheter.
Free-wall ruptureAge over 70, female, anterior MI (LAD); no prior infarctTwo peaks: early (24 h) and 3–5 daysSudden chest pain, often after coughing or straining; tamponade, shock, sudden death (> 50% mortality)PEA — the monitor shows a rhythm but there is no pulse; about 95% predictive. Muffled heart sounds, JVD, no murmur.
Pseudoaneurysm Board add-onAnterior or inferolateral3–14 daysOften silent; may cause chest pain, murmur or embolismA contained free-wall rupture: the wall is pericardium and clot only, with a narrow neck. High risk of rupture, so emergency surgery.
True ventricular aneurysmLarge anterior (LAD) STEMIWeeks to monthsHeart failure, refractory angina, VT, mural thrombus and embolismA thin, scarred wall that bulges outward in systole (dyskinesia). Board add-on Persistent ST elevation and deep Q waves weeks after the MI. Rarely ruptures.
⚠️ Where the sources disagree on mechanical complications
  • Free-wall rupture timing. Dr. Gardner gives 3–7 days (the soft-wall window); Dr. Watkins gives two peaks, 24 hours and 3–5 days; First Aid says 5–14 days; UWorld says half within 5 days and the rest up to 2 weeks. For an exam: first week to two weeks, peaking around days 3–7.
  • The papillary-rupture murmur. The case slide describes a holosystolic apical murmur to the axilla. UWorld points out that acute MR is often only early systolic, and silent in up to half of cases, because left atrial and ventricular pressures equalise quickly. A flash pulmonary edema with no murmur after an inferior MI can still be papillary rupture.

Timing tells you the complication ★ HY

WindowWhat the infarct looks like (Section 14)What goes wrong
0–24 hoursCoagulative necrosis beginningVentricular arrhythmia and sudden death, bradycardia and AV block, acute heart failure, cardiogenic shock
1–3 daysNeutrophilsEarly fibrinous pericarditis
3–14 daysMacrophages, the softest wallRuptures: papillary muscle (acute MR), septum (left-to-right shunt), free wall (tamponade), pseudoaneurysm
2 weeks to monthsGranulation tissue, then scarTrue aneurysm, mural thrombus, Dressler syndrome, chronic heart failure
🧠 Matching pairs

Pair each rupture with its artery and its sound. Inferior infarct, apical murmur to the axilla: papillary muscle. Septal rupture, sternal-border murmur with a thrill and an oxygen step-up. Anterior infarct, no murmur, muffled sounds and PEA: free wall.

Labs, ECG and management of each

ComplicationKey testManagement
Ventricular arrhythmiaMonitor; check potassium and magnesiumDefibrillation for VF or pulseless VT; correct electrolytes; reperfusion (Section 8)
Bradycardia / AV blockECG: inferior ST elevation with sinus bradycardia or blockAtropine, then pacing if needed (Section 10)
Cardiogenic shockEcho: global or large regional dysfunction, no mechanical lesionImmediate revascularisation, inotropes, mechanical support Board add-on
RV infarctRight-sided ECG (V4R)IV fluids; avoid nitrates and diuretics Board add-on
Papillary muscle ruptureEcho: flail leaflet, severe MRStabilise (afterload reduction, often an IABP Board add-on), then surgery, which cuts mortality to about 30%
Septal ruptureEcho with Doppler; oxygen step-up RA → PAICU, stabilisation, surgical repair
Free-wall ruptureEcho: pericardial effusion with tamponadePericardiocentesis as a bridge; emergency surgery — mostly fatal
True aneurysmECG: persistent ST elevation with Q waves; echo: thin dyskinetic wallHeart-failure treatment; anticoagulate if there is mural thrombus; surgery for refractory failure or VT Board add-on
Early pericarditis / DresslerECG: diffuse ST elevation with PR depression; echo for effusionAspirin (high dose) ± colchicine Board add-on
🩺 After an infarct, the other organs suffer too

Low flow everywhere causes ischemia–reperfusion injury and systemic inflammation: acute kidney injury (in about 40% of patients who survive CPR), acute liver injury with raised enzymes (“shock liver”), and acute lung injury or ARDS. Overall mortality after an infarct is about 30% in the first year, then about 3% a year.

Q: Four days after an anterior MI, a patient becomes hypotensive with a new harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border and a palpable thrill. A pulmonary artery catheter shows oxygen saturation of 62% in the right atrium and 80% in the pulmonary artery. Diagnosis?

Answer

Ventricular septal rupture. Oxygenated blood shunting left to right causes the oxygen step-up. Papillary muscle rupture would give an apical murmur radiating to the axilla with no step-up.

Q: An elderly woman, 4 days after her first, large anterior STEMI, coughs, has sudden chest pain and loses her pulse while the monitor still shows sinus rhythm. What happened?

Answer

Left ventricular free-wall rupture causing hemopericardium and tamponade, presenting as pulseless electrical activity. Day 4 is the soft-wall window.

Q: Three days after an inferior STEMI, a man develops sudden severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum and hypotension. A soft murmur is heard at the apex. Which structure has failed, and why that one?

Answer

The posteromedial papillary muscle has ruptured, causing acute mitral regurgitation and flash pulmonary edema. It is supplied only by the posterior descending artery (usually from the RCA), whereas the anterolateral muscle has a double supply.

Q: An inferior-wall STEMI patient’s heart rate falls to 38. Which artery is occluded, and why is the rate slow?

Answer

The right coronary artery, which supplies the SA node in about 60% and the AV node in about 90% of people. Ischemia causes sinus bradycardia or AV block. Treat with atropine, then pacing.

Q: Five weeks after an MI, a patient has fever, pleuritic chest pain that eases sitting forward, and a friction rub. What is it, and what is the mechanism? How would the same symptoms on day 2 differ in cause?

Answer

Dressler syndrome (post-cardiac injury syndrome): an autoimmune pericarditis in which antibodies to cardiac antigens released by the infarct form immune complexes in the pericardium. On day 2 the same picture is early fibrinous pericarditis — direct inflammation over a transmural infarct, not autoimmunity.

Q: Two months after a large anterior MI, a patient has worsening heart failure. His ECG still shows ST elevation and deep Q waves in V1–V4. Echo shows a thin segment that bulges outward during systole. Diagnosis, and what two other complications does it carry?

Answer

A true left ventricular aneurysm — a scarred, dyskinetic wall. It also causes mural thrombus with embolism and ventricular tachycardia from re-entry around the scar. Unlike a pseudoaneurysm, it rarely ruptures.

Q: After an inferior STEMI, a patient is hypotensive with distended neck veins but clear lungs. Nitroglycerin is given and the blood pressure falls further. What has been missed, and what should be given instead?

Answer

A right ventricular infarct. The failing right ventricle depends on preload, so nitrates (and diuretics, and opioids) drop its output. Give IV fluids, and confirm with ST elevation in the right-sided lead V4R.

LO 16LO 17Source: Ischemic Heart Disease Pharmacology (Scully) · Application Session 1 (Watkins)

Section 16 · Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Ischemic Heart Disease Pharmacology

Dr. Scully’s organising sentence: “We could increase supply of oxygen, or we could decrease demand — and one tends to be much easier than the other.” Plaque and endothelial dysfunction make supply hard to raise, so nearly every antianginal works by lowering demand — heart rate, contractility, preload or afterload. For each drug he wants the name, indication, mechanism, adverse effects, contraindications and interactions, applied to two cases: stable and vasospastic angina.

Abbreviations used in this section O₂ oxygen · HR heart rate · BP blood pressure · NO nitric oxide · sGC soluble guanylyl cyclase · cGMP cyclic guanosine monophosphate · PKG protein kinase G · ALDH2 mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 · PDE5 phosphodiesterase-5 · NTG nitroglycerin · SL sublingual · ISDN / ISMN isosorbide dinitrate / isosorbide-5-mononitrate · EDV end-diastolic volume · CCB calcium channel blocker · DHP dihydropyridine (the “-dipines”) · ISA intrinsic sympathomimetic activity · AV atrioventricular · HCN hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channel · NCX sodium–calcium exchanger · CYP3A4 cytochrome P450 3A4 · ACh acetylcholine · ACS acute coronary syndrome · STEMI / NSTEMI ST-elevation / non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction · PCI percutaneous coronary intervention · CABG coronary artery bypass grafting · ACEi / ARB ACE inhibitor / angiotensin receptor blocker · MRA mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · HOCM hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy · RV right ventricle · LV left ventricle · QT QT interval (ventricular depolarisation plus repolarisation) · P2Y12 the platelet ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor · ADP adenosine diphosphate · CNS central nervous system · COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease · COX cyclooxygenase · ECG electrocardiogram · IV intravenous

The treatment map

🏃

Stable (exertional) angina

  • Abort an attack: sublingual nitroglycerin.
  • Prevent: a beta-blocker (the best monotherapy), ± a calcium channel blocker or a long-acting nitrate.
  • Still refractory: ranolazine.
🌙

Vasospastic (variant, Prinzmetal) angina

  • Abort: sublingual nitroglycerin.
  • Prevent: a calcium channel blocker (a dihydropyridine or diltiazem) ± a nitrate.
  • No beta-blockers.
🛡️

Risk reduction for everyone

  • Antiplatelet therapy.
  • A statin (Section 31).
  • Smoking cessation.
  • Control of hypertension and diabetes.

Nitrates, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and ranolazine

Nitrates — nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, isosorbide-5-mononitrate

  1. Bioactivation. The organic nitrate is converted to nitric oxide by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH2).
  2. Signalling. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raising cGMP, which activates protein kinase G and relaxes smooth muscle.
  3. Where. Mostly the venous capacitance vessels.
  4. Result. Lower preload, smaller end-diastolic volume, less wall stress, less oxygen demand. A small rise in supply from dilating epicardial arteries “isn’t the major driving force.”
  • Pharmacogenetics: ALDH2 polymorphisms, common in people of East Asian descent, reduce bioactivation, so nitrates work less well.
  • Adverse effects: the vasodilator trio of flushing, hypotension and headache, plus reflex tachycardia. Board add-on Methemoglobinemia; reflux from a relaxed lower esophageal sphincter.
  • Contraindication: low blood pressure.
  • Tolerance: long-acting nitrates lose effect with continuous use, so prescribe a nitrate-free interval, usually overnight (take the patch off at night). The “Monday morning headache” of munitions workers was tolerance lost over the weekend.
FormUseOnset / duration Board add-onNote
Nitroglycerin, sublingual or sprayAbort an acute attack2–5 min / 15–30 minBypasses first-pass metabolism
Transdermal nitroglycerinProphylaxisAbout 30 min / 8–14 hRemove overnight
Isosorbide dinitrate (oral)ProphylaxisAbout 1 h / 4–6 hLow oral bioavailability
Isosorbide-5-mononitrate (oral)Long-term prophylaxis — often the drug of choice30–45 min / 6–24 hThe exception: high oral bioavailability, no first-pass loss

Long-acting nitrates are not first-line as monotherapy.

Beta-blockers — the best monotherapy for exertional angina

  • Mechanism: block β1, lowering heart rate and contractility (and wall tension and blood pressure), so oxygen demand falls. A slower rate also lengthens diastole, the time when the coronaries fill.
  • Dosing: titrate to a resting heart rate of about 50 while limiting the peak exertional rate (the lecture’s figure).
  • Adverse effects: fatigue, bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm with non-selective drugs.
  • Contraindications: vasospastic angina; IV verapamil at the same time; cardiogenic shock; asthma or COPD is a relative contraindication.
  • Board add-on Avoid beta-blockers with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (pindolol, acebutolol): partial agonism raises demand.

Calcium channel blockers

  • Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine): arterial dilation lowers afterload, so the ventricle needs less work for the same output; they also dilate coronaries. Adverse effects: peripheral edema, flushing, reflex tachycardia. Board add-on Avoid short-acting nifedipine, whose reflex tachycardia can worsen ischemia.
  • Non-dihydropyridines (verapamil, diltiazem): lower afterload and directly lower heart rate and contractility. Adverse effects: bradycardia, AV block, constipation (verapamil), worsening of a low ejection fraction. Avoid in severe aortic stenosis and HOCM, and with a beta-blocker IV.
  • In vasospastic angina the calcium channel blocker is the preventive drug, and CCB plus nitrate is an effective pair.

Why a beta-blocker and a nitrate work so well together Board add-on

Beta-blockerNitrateTogether
Heart rate↓↑ (reflex)Unchanged or slightly ↓
Contractility↓↑ (reflex)Unchanged
End-diastolic volumeUnchanged or ↑↓Unchanged or slightly ↓
Ejection time↑↓Unchanged
Oxygen demand↓↓↓↓

Each drug cancels the other’s unwanted effect: the beta-blocker stops the nitrate’s reflex tachycardia, and the nitrate stops the beta-blocker’s rise in end-diastolic volume.

Ranolazine — for refractory angina

  • The problem it fixes: ischemic myocytes have an increased late-phase sodium current. Sodium loads the cell, the sodium–calcium exchanger brings in calcium, and calcium overload raises diastolic wall stress, which raises oxygen demand.
  • Mechanism: blocks the late sodium current, so less calcium overload and less diastolic wall stress.
  • It does not change heart rate or blood pressure Board add-on — useful when those are already low.
  • In the trials, women (XX) benefited more than men (XY).
  • Adverse effects: dose-dependent QT prolongation, dizziness, constipation. Board add-on A CYP3A4 substrate: avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and other QT-prolonging drugs. Contraindicated in cirrhosis.
⚠️ A slide mix-up: ivabradine versus ranolazine

One Application Session 1 slide gives ivabradine’s mechanism as “inhibits the late sodium current.” That is ranolazine. Ivabradine blocks the funny current (If) through HCN channels in the sinus node, slowing the heart without changing contractility; its signature side effect is luminous visual phenomena. The heart-failure lecture gives the correct mechanism (Section 18).

Vasospastic angina: the board favourite

  • The patient: a 34-year-old with chest pain that wakes him from sleep, no pain on exertion, worse exercise tolerance in the morning, and a normal ECG between attacks. Board add-on Smoking, cocaine, amphetamines and triptans are triggers.
  • Diagnostic criteria: nitrate-responsive rest angina, especially night to early morning; hyperventilation can precipitate it; transient ischemic ECG changes (ST elevation or depression, new U waves) only during an attack; documented spasm on angiography; calcium channel blockers, but not beta-blockers, suppress it.
  • Provocation testing: hyperventilation, ergot or intracoronary acetylcholine. Acetylcholine contracts coronary smooth muscle through M3 receptors — “M1s in the CNS, M2s in the heart, M3s everywhere else.” Board add-on In healthy vessels acetylcholine acts on endothelial M3 receptors to release nitric oxide and dilate; with endothelial dysfunction the direct smooth-muscle contraction wins.
  • Why no beta-blocker: blocking β2-mediated dilation leaves unopposed α vasoconstriction, which makes spasm worse. The lecturer noted this has been contested recently but is “still ingrained in the literature and the recommendations.”

The acute coronary syndrome drug bundle

Dr. Scully deliberately left acute coronary syndromes to the clinical lectures and to the antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs from Heme. The bundle below combines Dr. Watkins’s case with the board version.

DrugWhyHold or avoid when
Aspirin, chewed, straight awayIrreversible COX-1 inhibition: less thromboxane A2, less platelet aggregation on the ruptured plaque. Board add-on The single drug that most reduces early mortality.True aspirin allergy (use a P2Y12 inhibitor)
P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel load in the case; prasugrel, ticagrelor)Blocks ADP-induced platelet activation. With aspirin it makes dual antiplatelet therapy, continued for 12 months. Board add-onBoard add-on Often held in NSTEMI until the angiogram, in case bypass surgery is needed (it must be stopped about 5 days before CABG)
Anticoagulant (heparin bolus in the case; enoxaparin, bivalirudin)Limits thrombus extensionSuspected aortic dissection; active bleeding
Nitroglycerin, sublingual then IVRelieves pain; lowers preloadHypotension, RV infarct, PDE5 inhibitor in the last 24–48 h, severe aortic stenosis
Beta-blocker (oral metoprolol)Lowers demand and arrhythmia risk; may limit infarct sizeCardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, bradycardia or heart block, cocaine-induced chest pain
High-intensity statin (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin)Stabilises plaque; reduces recurrence Board add-on—
OxygenOnly if hypoxic (the case says “O₂ as needed”)Normal saturation — no benefit
ReperfusionSTEMI: PCI within 90 minutes; fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable. NSTEMI: angiography timed by risk (Section 12)Fibrinolysis: prior hemorrhagic stroke, active bleeding, suspected dissection Board add-on

On discharge, continued indefinitely Board add-on: aspirin, a beta-blocker, a high-intensity statin and an ACE inhibitor or ARB (to limit remodelling), plus the P2Y12 inhibitor for a year, and an MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) if the ejection fraction stays low. This is the “optimal medical therapy” of Section 12.

Q: A 34-year-old man wakes with chest pain several nights a month and has poor exercise tolerance in the mornings only. His ECG and troponins are normal between episodes. What do you prescribe to stop an attack, what to prevent one, and what must you avoid?

Answer

Vasospastic angina. Abort with sublingual nitroglycerin; prevent with a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine or diltiazem). Avoid beta-blockers, which leave unopposed α vasoconstriction and worsen spasm.

Q: A man taking sublingual nitroglycerin for angina asks his doctor for sildenafil. What is the danger, and what is the mechanism?

Answer

Severe, refractory hypotension. Nitrates raise cGMP through nitric oxide and guanylyl cyclase; PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown, so smooth-muscle relaxation is amplified.

Q: A patient wears a 24-hour nitroglycerin patch and finds it stops working after a week. What has happened, and what is the fix?

Answer

Nitrate tolerance. Prescribe a nitrate-free interval — take the patch off overnight.

Q: Why do nitrates relieve exertional angina mainly by acting on veins, and why does adding a beta-blocker make them work better?

Answer

Venodilation lowers preload, so end-diastolic volume, wall stress and oxygen demand all fall; the coronary effect is minor because ischemic arterioles are already maximally dilated. The fall in blood pressure triggers a baroreflex tachycardia through sympathetic β1 outflow, which the beta-blocker prevents.

Q: A patient with refractory angina, a resting heart rate of 52 and a blood pressure of 98/60 is already on a beta-blocker and a nitrate. Which antianginal can be added without lowering either number further, and what must be checked first?

Answer

Ranolazine, which blocks the late sodium current and does not change heart rate or blood pressure. Check the QT interval and the medication list for other QT-prolonging drugs and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.

Q: A patient with stable angina also has hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Which antianginal class should be avoided, and why?

Answer

Nitrates (and dihydropyridine vasodilators). Lowering preload shrinks the left ventricular cavity and worsens the dynamic outflow obstruction. A beta-blocker is the right choice here.

Q: A patient with an acute inferior STEMI has a heart rate of 48 and a blood pressure of 82/50. Which two drugs from the standard bundle should be held?

Answer

The beta-blocker (bradycardia and hypotension) and nitroglycerin (hypotension, and a likely right ventricular infarct with an inferior STEMI). Aspirin, the P2Y12 inhibitor, the anticoagulant and the statin still go ahead, along with emergency PCI.
