Section 17 · Heart Failure & the Myocardium

Heart Failure: Reduced Versus Preserved Ejection Fraction

Congestive heart failure is the point at which the heart cannot meet the body’s metabolic demands. Dr. Gardner put its prognosis bluntly: about 50% five-year survival, comparable to many cancers. Dr. Segal closed the case session with the four questions this section is built around: Is this heart failure, and what type? Is the patient congested? Is perfusion adequate? Which treatments help now and later?

Abbreviations used in this section HF heart failure · CHF congestive heart failure · HFrEF heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (systolic) · HFpEF heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (diastolic) · HFmrEF / HFimpEF mildly reduced / improved ejection fraction · EF / LVEF (left ventricular) ejection fraction · LV / RV / LA left ventricle / right ventricle / left atrium · EDV / ESV end-diastolic / end-systolic volume · ESPVR / EDPVR end-systolic / end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship · CO cardiac output · SVR systemic vascular resistance · JVP / JVD jugular venous pressure / distension · HJR hepatojugular reflux · PND paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea · DOE dyspnea on exertion · S3 / S4 third / fourth heart sound · NYHA New York Heart Association · ACC/AHA American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association · RAAS renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system · AT II angiotensin II · BNP / NT-proBNP B-type natriuretic peptide / its N-terminal fragment · ANP atrial natriuretic peptide · PASP pulmonary artery systolic pressure · E/e′ echo ratio estimating filling pressure · AF atrial fibrillation · CKD chronic kidney disease · COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease · OSA obstructive sleep apnea · MI myocardial infarction · NO nitric oxide · AV arteriovenous · CXR chest X-ray · TTE transthoracic echocardiogram · ICU intensive care unit · BMI body mass index · ED emergency department · GLP-1 glucagon-like peptide-1 · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · SGLT2 sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 · ECG electrocardiogram · IV intravenous

The pathophysiology of each ★ HY

How overload becomes failure

  1. Three common causes, two kinds of overload. Hypertension gives pressure overload; valve disease gives pressure overload (stenosis) or volume overload (regurgitation); myocardial infarction gives regional dysfunction with volume overload.
  2. More cardiac work raises wall stress and stretches the myocytes.
  3. Hypertrophy and/or dilation. Protein synthesis rises, immediate-early genes and the fetal gene programme switch on.
  4. Fibroblasts proliferate and lay down fibrosis, and the existing blood supply cannot keep up with the bigger muscle.
  5. Dysfunction: systolic or diastolic failure, arrhythmias (poor vascularity, interrupted conduction) and neurohumoral activation.
OverloadSarcomeres addedShapeExample
PressureIn parallelConcentric: thick wall, normal or small cavity, high relative wall thicknessHypertension, aortic stenosis
VolumeIn seriesEccentric: dilated cavity, normal wall, low relative wall thicknessAortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, after MI

HFrEF versus HFpEF: the mechanics

💔

HFrEF — a pumping problem

  • Contractility falls: the ESPVR slope drops. Usually from myocyte loss in ischemic heart disease, and/or high afterload.
  • Less is ejected, so blood is left behind: ESV rises, then EDV rises and the ventricle dilates.
  • A smaller stroke volume out of a bigger EDV means the EF falls.
  • The Starling curve shifts down and to the right.
🧱

HFpEF — a filling problem

  • Compliance falls (fibrosis, hypertrophy), or relaxation is slow: the EDPVR steepens.
  • Less EDV at a higher end-diastolic pressure, which backs up into the lungs.
  • Stroke volume falls because EDV falls, but contractility is intact, so the EF is preserved.
  • Now thought to be about as common as HFrEF, and under-explored and under-treated.
⚠️ A recording slip to ignore

The physiology recording ends the HFpEF explanation with “so in this case you would see a reduced ejection fraction.” The slide is right: in HFpEF the stroke volume is reduced but the ejection fraction is preserved, because contractility is unchanged.

HFrEF versus HFpEF: the tissue and the patient

FeatureHFrEF (systolic)HFpEF (diastolic, “stiff”)
EF≤ 40%≥ 50%, with evidence of raised filling pressures
Typical patientYounger man after an MIOlder woman with obesity, hypertension, diabetes, CKD, AF
Risk factorsObesity, hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, male, volume overload, myocarditis, MIObesity, hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, female, COPD, age, anemia, inflammation, liver disease, sleep apnea, gout, cancer
HypertrophyEccentric; rounded heart, more LV massConcentric; bigger left atrium
Myocyte deathPresentAbsent
Endothelial dysfunctionA late featureEarly and prominent — much less nitric oxide
FibrosisPerivascular, interstitial and replacementMarked perivascular (impairs oxygen exchange) and interstitial; more collagen cross-linking
TitinFlexible isoform; aggregation and cleavage, so stiffness is normal or lowerShift to the stiff N2B isoform and phosphorylation changes: more stiffness
Extra heart soundS3 (volume overload)S4 (atrium pushing into a stiff ventricle)
How patients dieMostly cardiovascular deathMore often non-cardiovascular

The neurohumoral spiral: why the failing heart gets worse

  1. Falling cardiac function lowers arterial pressure, and the baroreceptor reflex fires.
  2. Sympathetic outflow rises: α-mediated vasoconstriction and tachycardia.
  3. β1 on the juxtaglomerular cells releases renin, angiotensin II rises and vasoconstricts: more afterload.
  4. Angiotensin II releases aldosterone: sodium and water retention, volume expansion, more preload.
  5. More afterload and more preload raise oxygen demand and worsen the failure. In Dr. Scully’s words, “some of our compensations end up making this condition worse.”
  • Why the natriuretic peptides do not rescue it: chronically dilated atria and ventricles become resistant to their own natriuretic peptide, so the kidney keeps reabsorbing sodium despite volume overload (Section 13 has BNP).
  • That is why every mortality-reducing drug in Section 18 cuts a link in this chain.

Left- versus right-sided signs and symptoms

🫁

Left heart failure — “short of breath”

  • Usually from MI or hypertension.
  • Backward: blood backs up into the lungs — dyspnea, DOE, orthopnea, PND, crackles, pulmonary edema.
  • Forward: poor organ perfusion — fatigue, cool extremities, low urine output.
  • Board add-on Orthopnea: lying flat shifts blood from the legs to the chest. PND: overnight reabsorption of edema adds venous return. “Heart-failure cells” are hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages.
🦶

Right heart failure — “swollen ankles”

  • The most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure.
  • Venous back-up: raised JVP, a positive hepatojugular reflux, peripheral edema, ascites, effusions, splenomegaly.
  • Congestive hepatomegaly, the “nutmeg liver”, which can progress to cardiac cirrhosis.
  • Isolated right failure: an RV infarct, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale (lung disease such as COPD), tricuspid disease, primary RV cardiomyopathy.

Dr. Segal’s caveat: the clean right/left split is for boards. In clinic the signs are usually mixed, because one side failing eventually drags the other down.

Other ways of classifying heart failure

AxisOne endOther end
Acute / chronicAcute = new (de novo)Chronic, or an acute decompensation of chronic failure
By EFHFrEF ≤ 40% · HFimpEF previously ≤ 40%, now > 40%HFmrEF 41–49% · HFpEF ≥ 50% (both with raised filling pressures)
OutputHigh-output: high demand — thyrotoxicosis, an AV fistula for dialysis, severe obesity, Board add-on anemia, wet beriberi. High CO, low SVR.Low-output: pump failure, high SVR, low CO (cardiogenic shock)
Symptoms: NYHA classI: no limitation · II: slight (ordinary activity causes symptoms)III: marked (less than ordinary activity) · IV: symptoms at rest

Dr. Qazi: in practice cardiologists use the NYHA class together with the ACC/AHA stage (A–D), and “that’s enough to classify the patient.” Board add-on Stage A is at risk with no structural disease, B is structural disease without symptoms, C is symptomatic, D is refractory.

The acutely decompensated patient: wet or dry, warm or cold

  • Wet and warm is the commonest: diurese, on the ward. Wet and cold is cardiogenic shock: ICU, inotropes plus diuretics.
  • Dr. Qazi: “Get the patient back on the Starling curve.” Reduce preload first (diurese), then work on afterload.
  • Never start a beta-blocker while decompensated — it is a negative inotrope (Section 18).

What alcohol and cocaine do

  • Alcohol causes a dilated cardiomyopathy: indirectly through sympathetic and RAAS activation and hypertension, directly through oxidative stress, fibrosis and impaired excitation–contraction coupling. Malnourished drinkers can also have thiamine deficiency, “wet” beriberi — a high-output failure.
  • Cocaine blocks noradrenaline reuptake. In a patient on a β1-selective blocker such as metoprolol, the β effects are blunted but α vasoconstriction is unopposed, so afterload rises — “the one thing you don’t want to increase in heart failure.” Carvedilol and labetalol block both.

Labs and diagnostics

Build the differential first

  • Dyspnea in buckets: cardiac (coronary disease, heart failure, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, valves, pericardium), pulmonary (COPD, asthma, pneumonia, embolism, interstitial disease), anemia, neuromuscular, and anxiety — but rule out the serious things first.
  • Edema by Starling forces: raised capillary hydrostatic pressure (heart failure, venous insufficiency, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers) versus low oncotic pressure (cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition). “Pitting edema is nothing more than salt and water trapped in the interstitium.”

The exam

  • JVP = height above the sternal angle plus 5 cm. A resting heart rate of 90 is a worry: often sympathetically driven.
  • S4 = a non-compliant ventricle. S3: physiologic in the young, but in heart-failure patients a marker of volume overload (Dr. Qazi).
  • The Mallampati score doubles as an OSA screen — and sleep apnea worsens heart failure.

Targeted labs — not a net

TestWhy
Complete blood countExclude anemia
Metabolic panelSodium, potassium, kidney and liver function, glucose — baselines before the drugs
Thyroid-stimulating hormoneExclude thyroid disease
Hemoglobin A1cBaseline, and drug choice (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists)
Iron studiesIron deficiency is common in heart failure; IV iron is now part of care
High-sensitivity troponinExclude myocardial injury (in the ED, not the office)
BNP or NT-proBNPDiagnostic and prognostic — rule-out values 100 and 300 pg/mL (Section 13)

Imaging and the ECG

  • Echocardiogram: chamber sizes, EF, hypertrophy pattern, valves, and diastolic function graded 1–3. Grade 1 usually means a normal left atrial pressure (and is normal for age in the elderly); grade 2 means a raised left atrial pressure.
  • ECG: ischemia, Q waves, LVH (“11 and 35” — Section 7), AF, bundle branch block.
  • Chest X-ray: Kerley B lines (short horizontal lines at the bases from fluid in the interlobular septa, “very characteristic of heart failure”), cephalization, a wide vascular pedicle, cardiomegaly, pleural effusions.
  • The H₂FPEF score estimates the probability of HFpEF: Heavy (BMI over 30) 2, Hypertensive (2 or more drugs) 1, atrial Fibrillation 3, Pulmonary hypertension (PASP over 35) 1, Elder (over 60) 1, Filling pressure (E/e′ over 9) 1. Dr. Segal’s patient scored 5 — over 80% probability.

Pathology: gross and microscopic

OrganGrossMicroscopic
Heart, pressure overloadMassively thick LV wall, normal RV, small cavity (concentric)Huge myocytes with enlarged “boxcar” nuclei; interstitial and perivascular fibrosis
Heart, volume overload or after MIDilated, heavy heart; wall normal or thin (eccentric)Hypertrophied myocytes, replacement fibrosis and scar
Lungs (left failure)Heavy, wet lungs; pleural effusionsAlveolar edema; hemosiderin-laden macrophages (“heart-failure cells”) Board add-on

Q: A 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and obesity has 3 weeks of exertional dyspnea, orthopnea and ankle swelling. JVP is 7 cm, there are basal crackles, an S4 and no S3. Echo shows an EF of 65%, concentric hypertrophy and grade II diastolic dysfunction. Diagnosis and mechanism?

Answer

Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Impaired relaxation of a concentrically hypertrophied, stiff ventricle: a filling problem with a raised end-diastolic pressure. Grade II diastolic dysfunction implies a raised left atrial pressure; the S4 is the atrium hitting the stiff ventricle.

Q: A patient’s end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship is much steeper than normal while the end-systolic line is unchanged. What type of failure is this, and what happens to stroke volume and ejection fraction?

Answer

HFpEF. A stiff ventricle fills less, so EDV and stroke volume fall, but with contractility unchanged the EF is preserved.

Q: At autopsy, a liver has a mottled red-and-tan cut surface. What is the most likely cardiac cause, what does it usually come from, and what can it progress to?

Answer

Right heart failure, which is usually secondary to left heart failure. Chronic passive congestion gives the nutmeg liver, which can progress to cardiac cirrhosis.

Q: A hemodialysis patient with a large upper-arm fistula has dyspnea, edema, a wide pulse pressure, a raised cardiac output and a low systemic vascular resistance. What kind of heart failure is this?

Answer

High-output heart failure from the AV shunt: high demand, high cardiac output, low resistance. Thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia and wet beriberi do the same.

Q: A patient with HFrEF has cool, mottled extremities, confusion, a rising creatinine, a JVP of 16 cm and crackles. Which hemodynamic profile is this, and where should he be treated?

Answer

Wet and cold — cardiogenic shock. ICU, with inotropes plus decongestion (diuretics, vasodilators, ultrafiltration).

Q: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF on metoprolol has used crack cocaine and now has worsening pulmonary edema with a high blood pressure. Which receptor effect explains the deterioration?

Answer

Unopposed α1 vasoconstriction. Cocaine floods the synapse with noradrenaline; the β1-selective blocker leaves the α receptors free, so afterload rises. Carvedilol or labetalol, which block α too, avoid this.

Q: A patient has bilateral pitting ankle edema, an albumin of 1.9 g/dL and 4+ proteinuria, with a normal JVP and no orthopnea. Which Starling force is deranged?

Answer

Low plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome) — not the raised capillary hydrostatic pressure of heart failure, which would come with a high JVP.

Section 18 · Heart Failure & the Myocardium

Heart Failure Pharmacology

Dr. Scully’s frame for the whole lecture: the damage in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is irreversible, so every drug either helps the patient live longer or helps them feel better. Know which is which. The four drugs that lower mortality, started together and fast, cut cardiovascular death or hospitalisation by roughly two-thirds; Dr. Segal’s summary was that patients on all four live on average about five years longer.

Classes that lower mortality versus classes that only relieve symptoms ★ HY

⏳

Reduce mortality — the four pillars

  • ARNI (or ACEi, or ARB)
  • Beta-blocker — carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol
  • MRA — spironolactone, eplerenone
  • SGLT2 inhibitor — dapagliflozin, empagliflozin (HFrEF and HFpEF)
  • Board add-on Hydralazine plus isosorbide dinitrate in self-identified Black patients with NYHA III–IV symptoms already on full therapy (the A-HeFT trial)
🩹

Symptomatic relief only

  • Diuretics (furosemide) — relieve congestion
  • Digoxin
  • Venodilators (nitrates) and vasodilators (hydralazine, nitroprusside)
  • Aquaretics (tolvaptan)
  • Inotropes: sympathomimetic amines (dobutamine) and PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone)
PillarHow it helpsMortality reductionHospitalisation reduction
ACEi / ARB, then ARNILess angiotensin II, less myocyte growth and collagen; the ARNI adds natriuretic peptides (more cGMP)17%; switching to ARNI a further 28%31%; ARNI switch 21%
Beta-blockerLess sympathetic drive, antioxidant, longer coronary filling, better oxygen balance35%41%
MRALess myocyte growth and fibrosis, anti-inflammatory, less sympathetic activation30%35%
SGLT2 inhibitorBetter myocardial energetics, less fibrosis and oxidative stress, natriuresis, better endothelial function17%31%

Together they drive reverse remodelling: smaller LV volumes and mass, a higher EF, lower filling pressures. The hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation falls from 0.84 (ACEi plus beta-blocker) to 0.36 (all four). The summary slide’s numbers: relative risk reduction 73%, number needed to treat 3.9, median survival extended 7–11 years.

How each HFrEF drug works

ARNI — sacubitril/valsartan (first-line renin–angiotensin drug)

  • Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, a neutral endopeptidase, so natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and substance P accumulate: natriuresis, diuresis and vasodilation. Valsartan blocks AT1.
  • Preferred order: ARNI over ACEi, ACEi over ARB.
  • Adverse effects: hypotension (SBP falls 5–7), orthostasis, hyperkalemia. Boxed warning: fetal toxicity — anything targeting the renin–angiotensin system is contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • It raises measured BNP, so follow NT-proBNP (Section 13).
  • Board add-on Stop an ACE inhibitor 36 hours before starting an ARNI, and never combine them: two sources of bradykinin cause angioedema.

ACE inhibitor (enalapril) or ARB

  • Less angiotensin II, so less vasoconstriction (afterload) and less aldosterone (a small diuretic effect — a little preload too).
  • Adverse effects: hyperkalemia (less aldosterone means less ENaC-driven potassium secretion), cough and angioedema with ACE inhibitors (bradykinin), hypotension, teratogenic. Never two renin–angiotensin drugs together.

Beta-blockers

  • Lower heart rate and contractility, so less oxygen demand; blunt the chronic sympathetic drive that remodels the heart.
  • Only the evidence-based three: metoprolol succinate (the once-daily form, not tartrate), carvedilol, bisoprolol.
  • Carvedilol also blocks α1, lowering afterload — more output from the contractility the patient has.
  • Start only when the patient is compensated, near euvolemic; never newly in acute decompensation. A warm patient already on one usually continues it.

MRA — spironolactone, eplerenone

  • Block the aldosterone receptor: less ENaC, less sodium reabsorption and potassium wasting; anti-fibrotic.
  • Spironolactone is not selective: it blocks androgen receptors too, giving gynecomastia, impotence and abnormal menses. Eplerenone is the selective alternative (twice daily, costlier). Finerenone is a non-steroidal MRA entering HFpEF practice.
  • Hyperkalemia is the danger with every MRA, especially with an ARNI or ACE inhibitor. Board add-on Avoid if potassium is over 5.0 or eGFR under 30.

SGLT2 inhibitors — dapagliflozin, empagliflozin

  • Block the sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 in the proximal tubule. The heart-failure benefit has little to do with glucose (they lower A1c by only about 0.5%): they are natriuretic and diuretic.
  • More sodium and chloride at the macula densa triggers tubuloglomerular feedback, constricting the afferent arteriole and lowering intraglomerular pressure — renal and cardiovascular protection. Dr. Scully adds anti-inflammatory and anti-remodelling effects “we don’t truly understand.”
  • The one class for both HFrEF and HFpEF, with or without diabetes. For decades the only class I drugs for HFpEF were loop diuretics.
  • Adverse effects: genital and urinary infections, volume depletion, back pain, renal impairment, and gangrene of the perineum — counsel every patient. Board add-on That is Fournier gangrene; also euglycemic DKA.
  • Re-check diuretic doses when starting one, to avoid hypovolemia.

The other drugs

DrugMechanismUseSignature adverse effect
Furosemide (loop)Blocks NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, which reabsorbs about 25–30% of filtered sodiumCongestion; a robust initial diuresisLow K, Na, Ca, Mg; hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; dose-dependent ototoxicity
Ethacrynic acidA non-sulfonamide loop diureticThe board answer for a sulfa allergyOtotoxicity

IvabradineBlocks the funny current (If) through HCN channels in the SA nodeSinus rate still high on a maximal beta-blocker; slows rate without changing contractility or BPLuminous visual phenomena, bradycardia

⚠️ Two slide errors

Vericiguat is labelled a soluble guanylate cyclase “inhibitor” on one slide; it is a stimulator, as the same slide’s “restores NO pathway” implies. And one Application Session 1 slide gives ivabradine ranolazine’s mechanism; ivabradine blocks the funny current (Section 16).

Diuretics: why the loop stops working

  • The braking phenomenon (tolerance). The distal convoluted tubule hypertrophies and grabs more of the sodium that escapes the loop. Furosemide (“Lasix lasts six” hours) causes natriuresis for about 6 hours, then the kidney reabsorbs avidly for the next 18. That is why loops are not used alone for chronic hypertension.
  • The fix is sequential nephron blockade: add a thiazide.
  • Why both waste potassium: more sodium reaches the principal cell, ENaC takes it up alone, the lumen goes negative, and potassium (through ROMK) and hydrogen ion are secreted — a hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Why loops lose calcium and magnesium: in the thick ascending limb, potassium recycling through ROMK makes a lumen-positive potential that drives calcium and magnesium between cells. Block NKCC2 and the potential disappears.
⚠️ A recording slip

The recording places the potassium-for-hydrogen swap in “beta-intercalated cells.” It is the α-intercalated cells that secrete hydrogen ion; β-intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate.

Inotropes and pressors for the hypotensive patient

DrugReceptorsEffect in heart failure
Dobutamineβ1 — a racemic mixture whose α-agonist and α-antagonist enantiomers cancelClean inotropy; top of most algorithms
Milrinone, inamrinonePDE3 inhibitors — no receptorcAMP persists, same PKA endpoint. Board add-on An “inodilator”: watch for hypotension and arrhythmia
Norepinephrineα1 + β1, no β2Raises contractility but α1 raises afterload, and the baroreflex gives reflex bradycardia
Epinephrineβ1, β2, α, dose-dependentInotropy with wider systemic effects
DopamineD1, then β1, then α1 as the dose risesWatch the dose: too high and α vasoconstriction appears

How an inotrope adds force: β1 stimulation activates Gs and adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP. Protein kinase A then phosphorylates the L-type calcium channel and phospholamban (freeing SERCA), so more calcium is available each beat. Give an inotrope first to a hypotensive, adequately filled patient; add a vasopressor only for persistent shock, accepting that it buys perfusion “at the cost of” afterload.

Reading drug effects on the Frank–Starling curve

MoveWhat happenedThe patient
A → BContractile failure: down onto a flatter curveLow-output symptoms
B → CUntreated, preload rises over timeCongestion: edema, dyspnea
C → D → EInotrope (dobutamine, digoxin): a higher curve, then preload fallsBetter output, then less congestion
C → FAfterload reduction (ACE inhibitor): a higher curve plus a small preload dropMore output, less congestion
C → GPreload reduction (furosemide): down the same curve, no rise in outputCongestion relieved; fatigue and cool extremities remain
🎯 The exam skill

“You’re going to have to pick PV loops. What happens a beat later if you change this? What shift happens if you give this drug?” — Dr. Scully

Know what each drug does to preload, afterload or contractility, then pick the matching shift.

The stepwise chronic regimen

First: the decompensated patient

  1. Airway, oxygen, monitoring: pulse oximetry, supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support, cardiac monitor, IV access, sit them up.
  2. Decongest — reduce preload first: IV loop diuretic (± a thiazide), strict intake and output, daily weights, sodium restriction, watch electrolytes and kidneys.
  3. Early vasodilator therapy for afterload once breathing improves.
  4. Hypotensive? Check volume, then an inotrope (dobutamine, milrinone) if SBP is under about 85 with shock signs and adequate filling; a vasopressor only as a temporising measure.

Then: getting onto all four pillars

  1. Diurese to near euvolemia.
  2. Afterload reduction, typically starting an ARNI (alternative: hydralazine plus a long-acting nitrate).
  3. Beta-blocker once compensated.
  4. SGLT2 inhibitor and MRA at low doses — start all four before up-titrating any single drug.
  5. Start in hospital (Dr. Qazi: follow-up is too unreliable to wait), teach the patient and their main support person with a nurse educator, follow up within 7–10 days, then titrate over 4–6 weeks checking kidney function, potassium and NT-proBNP.
  6. Secondary: digoxin, hydralazine plus nitrate, ivabradine, vericiguat. Diuretics as needed for symptoms throughout.

And for HFpEF

  • Everyone: a diuretic for congestion and an SGLT2 inhibitor unless contraindicated (pregnancy, type 1 diabetes, volume depletion, recurrent genitourinary infection) — “the first drug with real HFpEF benefit.”
  • Some: a GLP-1 agonist if the BMI is 30 or more; an MRA if potassium and kidney function allow.
  • Not first-line in HFpEF: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and ARNI (reserved for selected patients with an EF of 50–60%).
  • Lifestyle: DASH or Mediterranean diet, no fluid restriction unless hyponatremic, cardiac rehabilitation (30 minutes of moderate walking cuts mortality about 16%), weight loss, treat sleep apnea.
⚖️ Race and the renin–angiotensin drugs

Heart failure was one of the first conditions in which avoiding renin–angiotensin drugs in Black patients was debunked. The old recommendation has been disproven repeatedly and removed from risk calculators, and race-agnostic prescribing closes outcome disparities. Hydralazine plus nitrate (A-HeFT) is an add-on, not a replacement.

Adverse effects and monitoring

DrugWatch forMonitor
ARNIHypotension, hyperkalemia, angioedema (never with an ACEi; 36-hour washout), fetal toxicityBP, potassium, creatinine; follow NT-proBNP not BNP
ACEi / ARBHyperkalemia, cough and angioedema (ACEi), creatinine rise, teratogenicityPotassium and creatinine
Beta-blockerBradycardia, hypotension, fatigue; worsening if started while decompensatedHeart rate, BP, volume status
SpironolactoneHyperkalemia; gynecomastia, impotence, menstrual changePotassium and creatinine, especially with an ACEi or ARNI
SGLT2 inhibitorGenital and urinary infection, Fournier gangrene, volume depletion, euglycemic DKAVolume status; adjust the diuretic
Loop diureticHypo-K, -Na, -Ca, -Mg, alkalosis, ototoxicity, gout, digoxin toxicity via low KElectrolytes, magnesium, kidney function, weight
NitroprussideCyanide toxicity, hypotensionLactate and acid–base on prolonged infusion
🔑 Potassium in a combined regimen

Enalapril (or an ARNI) and spironolactone both raise potassium; furosemide lowers it. The net is unpredictable, so monitor potassium and renal function, and remember all of them lower blood pressure.

Q: Which HFrEF drug classes reduce mortality, and which relieve symptoms only?

Answer

Mortality: ARNI/ACEi/ARB, beta-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors. Symptoms only: diuretics, digoxin, veno- and vasodilators, aquaretics, dobutamine and milrinone.

Q: Sacubitril inhibits which enzyme, which three substances accumulate, and what must be done before starting it in a patient on enalapril?

Answer

Neprilysin, so natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and substance P accumulate. Stop the enalapril at least 36 hours beforehand, because ACE inhibitor plus neprilysin inhibitor stacks bradykinin and causes angioedema.

Q: A man on spironolactone for HFrEF develops tender breast enlargement. Why, and what is the alternative?

Answer

Spironolactone is non-selective and blocks androgen receptors. Switch to eplerenone, the selective MRA.

Q: A congested patient needs a loop diuretic but reports an anaphylactic sulfonamide allergy. What is the board answer, and what adverse effect does it share with furosemide?

Answer

Ethacrynic acid, the non-sulfonamide loop diuretic. Like furosemide it causes dose-dependent ototoxicity.

Q: Furosemide relieves a congested patient’s dyspnea, but the fatigue and cool extremities remain. Explain using the Frank–Starling curve, and say what would help.

Answer

Preload reduction slides the patient down the same curve: the end-diastolic pressure falls, but cardiac output does not rise. Moving onto a higher curve needs afterload reduction (ACE inhibitor, ARNI, hydralazine) or an inotrope.

Q: A patient on a prolonged infusion of a drug that raises cGMP develops a rising lactate and an anion-gap metabolic acidosis, then dies of an arrhythmia. Which drug, and why does it dilate arterioles when nitroglycerin mainly dilates veins?

Answer

Sodium nitroprusside, with cyanide toxicity — cyanide sits at the core of its structure. It releases nitric oxide spontaneously, so it acts on arterioles and veins alike; nitroglycerin needs enzymatic bioactivation, which happens mainly on the venous side.

Q: A diabetic HFrEF patient on empagliflozin reports perineal pain, redness and swelling. What is the concern? And by which renal mechanism does this drug lower intraglomerular pressure?

Answer

Fournier gangrene (necrotising infection of the perineum) — see the patient immediately. The pressure effect is tubuloglomerular feedback: more sodium and chloride at the macula densa constricts the afferent arteriole.

Q: Dobutamine binds α receptors, yet acts clinically as a pure β1 agonist. Why? And why does norepinephrine raise contractility yet often slow the heart?

Answer

Dobutamine is a racemic mixture: one enantiomer is an α agonist, the other an α antagonist, so the α effects cancel. Norepinephrine’s α1 vasoconstriction (with no β2 dilation) raises blood pressure, and the baroreflex increases vagal tone: reflex bradycardia.

LO 61LO 62Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Pediatric Cardiology · ECG II (genetic arrhythmias)

Section 19 · Heart Failure & the Myocardium

The Cardiomyopathies

A cardiomyopathy is a disease of the heart muscle itself. Dr. Gardner sorted them by shape — dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive — and by what the shape does: a dilated heart cannot pump (systolic failure), a hypertrophic or restrictive heart cannot fill (diastolic failure). Learn each one as a shape, a cause list, an echo picture, a slide and a treatment.

Abbreviations used in this section DCM dilated cardiomyopathy · HCM / HOCM hypertrophic (obstructive) cardiomyopathy · RCM restrictive cardiomyopathy · ARVC arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy · LV / RV / LA left ventricle / right ventricle / left atrium · LVEF / EF (left ventricular) ejection fraction · LVOT left ventricular outflow tract · SAM systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve · MYH7 β-myosin heavy chain gene · MYBPC3 myosin-binding protein C gene · TTN titin gene · TnI / TnT troponin I / T · ICD implantable cardioverter-defibrillator · AED automated external defibrillator · VT / VF ventricular tachycardia / fibrillation · AF atrial fibrillation · ECG electrocardiogram · CXR chest X-ray · MRI magnetic resonance imaging · GDMT guideline-directed medical therapy (Section 18) · CCB calcium channel blocker · AD autosomal dominant · QRS the ventricular depolarisation complex on the ECG · ST ST segment (between the QRS and the T wave) · LVAD left ventricular assist device · HFrEF heart failure with reduced ejection fraction

Dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive and arrhythmogenic compared ★ HY

TypeLVEF and mechanismCausesSecondary look-alikesPicture
Dilated — “kind of a catch-all”; Board add-on about 90% of cases< 40%. Low contractility: systolic dysfunction. Eccentric hypertrophy.Genetic (20–50%: cytoskeleton, mitochondria; Board add-on TTN most often); alcohol; peripartum; myocarditis (Coxsackie B, Chagas); hemochromatosis; chronic anemia; anthracyclines (doxorubicin); sarcoidosis; idiopathic. Board add-on Cocaine, thyrotoxicosis, wet beriberi.Ischemic heart disease, valvular, hypertensive, congenital
Hypertrophic — 1 in 50050–80%. Low compliance: diastolic dysfunction. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy.Genetic (sarcomere proteins, autosomal dominant); Friedreich ataxia; storage diseases; infants of diabetic mothersHypertensive heart disease; aortic stenosis
Restrictive45–90%. Low compliance: diastolic; the muscle sometimes cannot relax.Amyloidosis; radiation fibrosis; idiopathic. Board add-on Sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Löffler endocarditis, endocardial fibroelastosis.Constrictive pericarditis
Arrhythmogenic right ventricularRV failure and ventricular arrhythmiaInherited; fibro-fatty replacement of the right ventricle. Board add-on Desmosome genes; an epsilon wave after the QRS in V1–V3.—

Pictures: Robbins & Cotran Atlas and Gardner lecture (dilated, hypertrophic, amyloid); AMBOSS (arrhythmogenic, board add-on).

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death in young athletes

  • Genetics: autosomal dominant, males more than females; sarcomere mutations — MYBPC3, MYH7 (β-myosin heavy chain), troponin I and T.
  • Two problems at once: the thick wall limits diastolic filling, and the hypertrophied septum interferes with mitral closure, so some blood regurgitates to the left atrium. In HOCM the septal bulge plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet obstructs the outflow tract.
  • Exam: a harsh crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur that gets louder with Valsalva (anything that shrinks the ventricle) and softer with squatting or handgrip — worked through in Section 3. Board add-on An S4.
  • The hypertrophy usually does not appear until early adolescence, so screen first-degree relatives repeatedly.
  • How it kills: VT or VF, probably from transient hypoxia in scarred, thick muscle. HCM is the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes — about 36% of 1,435 cases, ahead of coronary artery anomalies (17%). Basketball is the sport most often involved.
  • Sudden-death risk markers: family history of sudden death, unexplained syncope, severe LV hypertrophy, non-sustained VT, an abnormal blood-pressure response to exercise, outflow obstruction, fibrosis on MRI.
🩺 The championship-game case

A 16-year-old soccer player had three months of palpitations and dizziness after sprints that he told no one about, then a non-contact collapse. The AED read VT and needed two shocks. ECG: sinus rhythm with LV hypertrophy. Bedside echo: a massively thickened septum. “AEDs are life-saving and should be around everywhere, especially at sporting events” — HCM mortality has fallen from 3–6% to about 1% because of them.

Other cardiomyopathies worth knowing Board add-on

  • Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy: a postmenopausal woman after an emotional or physical stressor, chest pain, ST changes and a modest troponin rise, with apical ballooning and clean coronaries. Probably a catecholamine surge. Recovers over weeks (Section 37 lists it among the causes that cluster in women).
  • Peripartum cardiomyopathy: dilated, in the last month of pregnancy or the months after delivery.
  • Chagas disease: a dilated cardiomyopathy with right bundle branch block decades after Trypanosoma cruzi infection, now considered endemic to the United States (Section 23).

Echocardiogram findings

TypeEchoECG and other clues
DilatedDilated ventricles (all four chambers often), thin walls, global hypokinesis, EF under 40%, functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, sometimes mural thrombusBoard add-on S3, a systolic regurgitant murmur, a “balloon” heart on CXR
HypertrophicA thick LV, most pronounced in the septum (asymmetric), small cavity, normal or high EF; in HOCM, SAM and an LVOT gradient that rises with ValsalvaECG: LV hypertrophy, often deep septal Q waves
RestrictiveBig atria, normal-sized stiff ventricles, normal or near-normal EF, severe diastolic dysfunction. Board add-on In amyloid, thick walls with a speckled, “sparkling” myocardiumBoard add-on Low-voltage ECG despite a thick myocardium — the amyloid clue
Arrhythmogenic RVDilated, thin, poorly moving right ventricle; MRI shows fatty infiltrationVT of left bundle branch block morphology; Board add-on epsilon waves

Morphology and histology

TypeGrossMicroscopic
DilatedHeavy heart, big thin-walled ventricles; mural thrombiNon-specific: hypertrophied and attenuated myocytes, interstitial fibrosis. In hemochromatosis, iron in the myocytes on Prussian blue
HypertrophicAsymmetric septal hypertrophy, small banana-shaped cavity, a fibrous plaque on the outflow tract where the mitral leaflet strikesMyofibre disarray — hugely hypertrophied myocytes in a swirling, branching pattern; interstitial and replacement fibrosis; thickened septal vessels
Restrictive (amyloid)Firm, rubbery, waxy myocardium; big atriaPink extracellular deposits; under polarized light, birefringence. Board add-on Apple-green birefringence on Congo red
Arrhythmogenic RVThin RV wallFibro-fatty replacement of RV myocytes
🍺 A historical aside the lecturer said is not on the exam

“Cobalt-beer cardiomyopathy”: in 1964–66, cobalt salts added to canned beer to stabilise the foam caused a specific cardiomyopathy in heavy drinkers.

Management

TypeTreatment
DilatedTreat it as HFrEF: the four pillars, diuretics for congestion, an ICD for low EF, transplant or an LVAD at the end (Section 18). Remove the cause: stop alcohol, limit anthracycline doses, treat iron overload. Board add-on Anticoagulate for AF or mural thrombus.
Hypertrophic“Do less” — stop strenuous and competitive exercise. Septal reduction by surgical myectomy or alcohol ablation of septal vessels. An ICD is essential in high-risk patients. Board add-on Beta-blockers or a non-dihydropyridine CCB to slow the rate and lengthen filling; mavacamten if refractory. Avoid anything that lowers preload or afterload — diuretics, nitrates, dihydropyridine vasodilators, dehydration.
RestrictiveTreat the cause (for transthyretin amyloid, specific stabilising drugs; for hemochromatosis, phlebotomy or chelation); cautious diuresis. Board add-on
Arrhythmogenic RVAvoid endurance exercise; beta-blockers; ICD. Board add-on

Q: A 17-year-old collapses and dies during a basketball game. His father died suddenly at 35. At autopsy there is asymmetric septal hypertrophy. What will histology show, which gene family is mutated, and how is it inherited?

Answer

Myofibre disarray of hypertrophied myocytes. Sarcomere genes — β-myosin heavy chain (MYH7), myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3), troponins. Autosomal dominant. This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the commonest cause of sudden death in young athletes.

Q: A woman treated for breast cancer with doxorubicin develops dyspnea two years later. Echo shows a dilated left ventricle with an EF of 25%. Classify the cardiomyopathy, and how is the risk limited?

Answer

Dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic dysfunction from anthracycline cardiotoxicity, which is dose-dependent — hence lifetime dose limits.

Q: Which cardiomyopathy pattern does cardiac amyloidosis produce, what is its pericardial mimic, and what ECG finding is the giveaway?

Answer

Restrictive — diastolic dysfunction with a preserved EF and big atria. The mimic is constrictive pericarditis. The ECG clue is low voltage despite a thick myocardium.

Q: A patient with known HCM becomes lightheaded after being started on a diuretic and a nitrate for “heart failure.” His systolic murmur is louder. Why, and what should he be on instead?

Answer

Lowering preload shrinks the ventricle, bringing the septum and mitral leaflet closer and worsening the outflow obstruction. Stop both; use a beta-blocker (or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) to slow the rate and lengthen filling.

Q: Why might a 9-year-old who carries his family’s HCM mutation have a normal echocardiogram?

Answer

The hypertrophy usually does not appear until early adolescence. First-degree relatives need repeated screening through the teenage years.

Q: A young cyclist has exertional palpitations and a VT with left bundle branch block morphology. MRI shows a thin, poorly contracting right ventricle infiltrated by fat. Diagnosis?

Answer

Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — inherited fibro-fatty replacement of the right ventricle. Stop endurance sport; ICD for high risk.

LO 63Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Cardiothoracic Surgery (McGrath)

Section 20 · Heart Failure & the Myocardium

Heart Tumors

Dr. Gardner’s subtitle for this topic was “only one is common.” That one is the left atrial myxoma — benign, on a stalk, and dangerous because of where it sits. The surgeon’s contribution is the reassuring part: take out the whole stalk with a cuff of septum, and it does not come back.

Myxoma, rhabdomyoma and metastases

TumourWho and whereHow it presentsHistology
MyxomaThe most common primary cardiac tumour, usually in the left atrium, on a stalk attached at the fossa ovalis. IL-6 release causes fevers, weight loss and a high ESR. Rhabdomyoma Board add-onThe most common primary cardiac tumour in children, usually in the ventricles; associated with tuberous sclerosisOften found on fetal or neonatal echo; outflow obstruction or arrhythmia; many regressA hamartoma; “spider cells” (glycogen-filled myocytes)

Sarcomas, mesotheliomaPrimary malignant cardiac tumours are vanishingly rare. Mesothelioma involves the pericardium in about 1% (asbestos)Constriction or effusion—
⚠️ “Most common” depends on the question

Both lecturers call myxoma the most common cardiac tumour. First Aid adds the distinction exams use: the most common primary tumour in adults is the myxoma, in children the rhabdomyoma, and the most common cardiac tumour overall is a metastasis. Read which one the question is asking.

🩺 Dr. McGrath’s case

A 68-year-old woman with dyspnea and a TIA; head CT negative. Transthoracic echo found a 3 cm left atrial myxoma and no coronary disease. It was resected through the right atrium together with its attachment at the fossa ovalis, and the septum patched with pericardium.

Management and long-term survival

  • Diagnosis: echocardiography (transesophageal for detail). Board add-on Cardiac MRI characterises the mass.
  • Treatment: surgical resection, promptly, because of the risk of embolism and of sudden obstruction.
  • It does not recur if you resect the whole stalk plus a piece of atrial septum, patching the septal hole with pericardium.
  • Long-term survival after complete resection is excellent — it is benign, “a tumour, not a cancer.” Board add-on Recurrence is rare (a few percent), higher in familial forms such as the Carney complex (multiple myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation, endocrine tumours), so those patients get serial echoes.
  • Metastatic disease is managed by draining the effusion (needle pericardiocentesis or a surgical subxiphoid pericardial window) and treating the primary; the outlook is that of the cancer. Surgeons may help remove a renal cell carcinoma thrombus extending up the IVC.

Q: A 50-year-old woman has weight loss, intermittent fevers, a high ESR, and dizziness that comes on when she lies down. Echo shows a pedunculated left atrial mass. Diagnosis, and which cytokine explains the systemic symptoms?

Answer

Left atrial myxoma, causing positional ball-valve obstruction of the mitral orifice. IL-6 release causes the constitutional symptoms.

Q: A woman has episodic dyspnea and near-fainting that change with position, and a TIA. Echo shows a mobile mass on a stalk attached to the fossa ovalis. How do you prevent recurrence after surgery?

Answer

Resect the whole stalk plus a cuff of atrial septum, and patch the septum. Done completely, a myxoma does not recur.

Q: A newborn with seizures and hypopigmented skin patches has several intramural masses in both ventricles on echo. What are they, and what is the associated condition?

Answer

Cardiac rhabdomyomas — the most common primary cardiac tumour in children — associated with tuberous sclerosis. Many regress on their own.

Q: A patient with metastatic lung cancer develops hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. How do cardiac metastases usually present, and what is the immediate treatment?

Answer

Through the pericardium, as a bloody effusion with tamponade. Drain it: pericardiocentesis, or a surgical subxiphoid pericardial window for recurrence.

LO 55LO 56LO 57LO 58Source: Endocarditis, Myocarditis & Pericarditis (Infectious Disease) · Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Pediatric Cardiology · Cardiothoracic Surgery

Section 21 · Infection & Inflammation

Infective Endocarditis: Epidemiology, Pathogenesis and Organisms

Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endocardial surface — mostly the native or prosthetic valves, but also septal defects, shunts and intravascular devices. It is non-contagious and, untreated, almost invariably fatal. Dr. Gardner’s summary: it is “easily missed, and usually easy to treat.” The microbiology is the core of the lecture: which organism, which patient, which valve.

Abbreviations used in this section IE infective endocarditis · IDU / PWID injection drug use / people who inject drugs · CIED cardiac implantable electronic device (pacemaker, ICD) · ICD implantable cardioverter-defibrillator · MRSA / MSSA methicillin-resistant / -sensitive Staphylococcus aureus · CoNS coagulase-negative staphylococci · GPC gram-positive cocci · GNR gram-negative rods · HACEK Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella · NBTE non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis · RHD rheumatic heart disease · MVP mitral valve prolapse · VSD / PDA ventricular septal defect / patent ductus arteriosus · PVE prosthetic valve endocarditis · IBD inflammatory bowel disease · PCR polymerase chain reaction · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · CNS central nervous system · WBC white blood cells · CHF congestive heart failure · HCV / HBV hepatitis C / B virus · CV cardiovascular · GI gastrointestinal · GU genitourinary · ID infectious disease · IgG immunoglobulin G · CT computed tomography · IV intravenous

Epidemiology and risk factors

Acute versus subacute — “not used anymore,” still used everywhere

FeatureAcuteSubacute
CourseFulminant, abruptIndolent
Fever and signsHigh fever, systemic toxicity, high WBCLow-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss
ValveCan attack a normal valveA previously damaged valve (historically rheumatic)
Organisms“Professional” pathogens: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenesLess virulent, often normal flora: viridans streptococci, enterococci
Death if untreatedUnder 6 weeks, from catastrophic heart failure6 weeks to months, from CHF
Empiric antibioticsBroad — think MRSAMore targeted

The formal modern scheme is etiology-based, but clinicians, UpToDate and the 2023 Duke criteria still use acute versus subacute as a bedside read of speed and virulence. “Don’t correct your attending.”

The numbers

  • Incidence in the US about 1–3 per 100,000 (lecture; the outline says 3–7), rising slightly — the highest among Western countries.
  • Mortality 15–20% in hospital, up to 40% at one year. About half eventually need valve surgery.
  • The flip of the antibiotic era: acute disease was about 20% and subacute 75%; now in industrialised countries about 75% is acute, mostly S. aureus.

Who gets it

Risk factorDetail
Age and sexMore than half are over 50; rare in children unless there is a congenital defect. Men more than women (3:1 to 9:1), except under 35.
Poor dentition, recent dental workChronic gum disease and intermittent bacteremia. The riskiest procedures manipulate the gingiva, the oral mucosa or the periapical region. Even toothbrushing seeds the blood (0–26%); a dental extraction does so in 18–85%.
Structural heart diseasePresent in 75%. Children: VSD, bicuspid aortic valve, PDA, coarctation.
Valve diseaseRheumatic heart disease was the historic number one (now about 9% in the US). It has been replaced by MVP with regurgitation (about 30%) and aortic stenosis or regurgitation.
DevicesPacemakers and ICDs: about 23% of cases, skin flora carried in at placement
Injection drug useRight-sided disease — see below
Chronic hemodialysisAbout 300 per 100,000 — “huge”
OthersPrior IE (2–8% recur), prosthetic valves, cardiac surgery (nosocomial), immunosuppression, poorly controlled diabetes
💉 Why injection drug use is so strong a risk (a USMLE favourite)
  • Younger patients (20–30), men more than women.
  • Many injections a day with skin contamination, contaminated diluents and shared needles; saliva as a diluent brings in mouth flora.
  • More likely to be colonised with S. aureus, so S. aureus is the most common organism in people who inject drugs.
  • Particulates such as talc damage the tricuspid and pulmonic endothelium, and injected bacteria reach the right heart first.

Pathogenesis and lesions by organ

Normal endocardium resists bacteria. You need two things: an endocardial injury and a bacteremia.

  1. Endocardial injury. A congenital defect, turbulent flow (high to low velocity), a leaky valve, catheter trauma, or injected talc.
  2. A sterile platelet–fibrin nidus forms on the exposed collagen — a “sterile vegetation” (non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis). No bugs yet.
  3. Transient bacteremia from any traumatised colonised mucosa: dental work, toothbrushing, GI, urinary or obstetric procedures. Usually cleared.
  4. Bacteria stick to the nidus and colonise it; more platelets and fibrin are laid down, and antibodies form immune complexes.
  5. Biofilm and vegetation: a sheath of fibrin, leukocytes, red cells, platelets and up to 109 bacteria per gram.
🧠 Why endocarditis is so hard to cure — biofilm

The best endocarditis pathogens, S. aureus and S. epidermidis, make biofilm. Biofilm bacteria are about 500× more antibiotic-resistant: drugs and antibodies penetrate poorly, and the bacteria slow or stop growing — while most antibiotics need actively growing bacteria. That is why treatment must be bactericidal and long (Section 22).

What the vegetation does — three ways

🩸

Seeding

  • Continuous, low-level bacteremia that seeds distant sites — osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, abscesses. S. aureus infects anything it touches.
💥

Destruction

  • Cytokines, proteases and bacteria destroy the valve: perforation, chordal rupture, ring abscess, aneurysm. New regurgitation and heart failure; heart block if an abscess reaches the conduction system.
🎯

Emboli

  • Friable vegetations break off as septic emboli: stroke, cerebral hemorrhage, brain abscess, mycotic aneurysm, infarcts of the spleen and kidney.
OrganLesionMechanism
HeartVegetations, perforated cusps, ring abscess, heart block; pericarditis (spread from the mitral valve) and myocarditis (contiguous spread)Direct invasion
BrainEmbolic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, brain abscess, meningitis, mycotic aneurysmSeptic emboli
KidneyWedge-shaped infarcts and abscesses; immune-complex glomerulonephritis (hematuria, casts)Emboli; immune complexes
SpleenSplenomegaly (about 40%), infarcts, abscessSystemic infection; emboli
LungRight-sided disease: septic pulmonary emboli (cavitating nodules). Left-sided disease: pulmonary edema, effusionEmboli; heart failure
Skin, eyes, nailsPetechiae, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions; Osler nodes, Roth spots (Section 22)Emboli; immune complexes
Bones and jointsOsteomyelitis, septic arthritisMetastatic infection

Endocarditis can also present as severe sepsis or septic shock, especially with toxin-producing organisms (S. aureus, S. pyogenes). And because the presentation ranges so widely, clinicians often chase the consequence — a “renal problem,” a stroke — instead of the source.

Left- versus right-sided endocarditis ★ HY

Left-sidedRight-sided
ShareAbout 90%. Mitral 28–45% (most common), aortic 5–36%About 10%. Tricuspid 90%, pulmonic 10%. Tricuspid is only 0–6% overall but about 60% in IDU
WhoOlder; structural or valve disease; prosthetic valves; dental sourceIDU, intracardiac devices, central lines, dialysis, immunosuppression, congenital disease
OrganismsS. aureus, viridans streptococci, enterococci, CoNS on prosthesesS. aureus 70–80%; streptococci and enterococci about 25%
MurmurHolosystolic (mitral regurgitation) or diastolic (aortic regurgitation)Often no murmur; a holosystolic tricuspid murmur when present
Emboli go toSystemic circulation: brain, spleen, kidney, skinLungs: septic pulmonary emboli in about 75% — dyspnea, cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic pain
CourseDepends on the organismSlower; mimics other disease; co-infection with HCV or HBV common
SurgeryReplacement often neededIf needed, try to repair the tricuspid valve first (Dr. McGrath)
⚠️ The IDU valve on boards versus in the pediatric case

The classic board answer for a person who injects drugs is the tricuspid valve with S. aureus. The pediatric lecture’s homeless 17-year-old had a vegetation on the mitral valve. Both happen; for a question, tricuspid plus septic pulmonary emboli is the expected pattern.

Organism and setting ★ HY

Staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci cause 80–90%. Viruses: no conclusive evidence.

OrganismShareClassic settingClue
Staphylococcus aureus31%Most common; acute; normal, prosthetic and right-sided valves; IDU; survival under 70%Gram-positive cocci, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive — sometimes all a question gives you
Viridans streptococci17%Subacute; a damaged valve; a dental sourceα-hemolytic; a group, not a species — “there is no Streptococcus viridans”. Board add-on Dextran helps them stick to the fibrin–platelet nidus
Coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis)11%Prosthetic valves (about 40% of prosthetic-valve IE), devices, lines; nosocomial; mostly methicillin-resistantThe most common bacterium on skin; biofilm
Enterococci (E. faecalis)11%Nosocomial — urinary catheters, IV lines, GU procedures; damaged valves—
S. gallolyticus (bovis group)7%Colon cancer or IBD — “I’m giving you the answer to a board question”Board add-on Order a colonoscopy
HACEK2%Slow-growing oral and GI gram-negatives on damaged valves — rare but over-testedHaemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella
Gram-negative rods (non-HACEK)2%Elderly with silent urinary infections; health-care contactE. coli, Klebsiella
Anaerobes2–16%Odontogenic — periodontitis, abscess; mostly prosthetic valvesMortality 21–43%
Fungi (Candida, Aspergillus)2%Immunocompromised; IV linesLarge, bulky vegetations that embolise; survival under 50%; usually needs surgery

Culture-negative endocarditis

  • The most common reason is antibiotics given before blood cultures, which mask ordinary staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. So always draw three sets first.
  • The organisms that will not grow on agar: Coxiella burnetii (Q fever — farm animals, needs cell culture) and Bartonella (henselae from cats, quintana in homeless people with body lice — very slow). Also Chlamydophila, Tropheryma whipplei, Legionella, Mycoplasma, Brucella.
  • HACEK organisms grow slowly and were once a classic culture-negative cause; modern systems usually grow them. Board add-on
  • PCR has cut the culture-negative rate and shown that Coxiella and Bartonella are the commonest. Serology counts too: a Coxiella phase I IgG over 1:800 is a Duke major criterion.
  • About 25% of endocarditis is now polymicrobial.

Q: A patient develops high fever, rigors and rapidly worsening heart failure over 10 days on a previously normal valve. Which organism tops the differential, and how broad should empiric therapy be?

Answer

Acute endocarditis from Staphylococcus aureus, a “professional pathogen” that attacks normal valves. Empiric therapy must be broad, covering MRSA.

Q: A febrile man who injects heroin has cough, hemoptysis and multiple peripheral cavitating nodules on chest CT, but no murmur. Diagnosis, valve and organism?

Answer

Right-sided (tricuspid) endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli, most likely S. aureus. Right-sided disease often has no audible murmur.

Q: A 68-year-old with iron-deficiency anemia has endocarditis, and blood cultures grow a non-enterococcal group D streptococcus. What else must you investigate?

Answer

Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis) endocarditis is associated with colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease — get a colonoscopy.

Q: Three months after an aortic valve replacement, a patient develops subacute endocarditis. Most likely organism, and its key virulence factor?

Answer

Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative), introduced from the skin and protected by biofilm on the prosthetic material.

Q: A shepherd with fevers has echo-proven vegetations but three negative blood cultures. A second patient, homeless with body lice, has the same picture. Likely organisms, and how is the first confirmed?

Answer

The shepherd: Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), confirmed by PCR or a phase I IgG over 1:800, which is a Duke major criterion. The homeless patient: Bartonella quintana. Both are culture-negative causes.

Q: Why does endocarditis need both a damaged endothelium and a bacteremia, and why does a dentist ask about heart disease?

Answer

Normal endocardium resists bacteria; injury exposes collagen, on which a sterile platelet–fibrin nidus forms for bacteria to stick to. A dental extraction throws a large bolus of mouth bacteria, including viridans streptococci, into the blood — so patients with high-risk valve disease get prophylactic antibiotics.

Section 22 · Infection & Inflammation

Infective Endocarditis: Diagnosis and Management

The infectious-disease lecturer called the clinical picture “a mess”: anything from rapidly progressive to indolent, so the diagnosis is often delayed. The way through is the same every time — suspect it in anyone with a typical organism in the blood plus a risk factor, draw three sets of cultures before any antibiotic, image the valves, and score it with the 2023 Duke criteria. Treatment is long, bactericidal and often surgical.

Abbreviations used in this section IE infective endocarditis · TTE / TOE transthoracic / transesophageal echocardiography · CT computed tomography · FDG-PET/CT fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/CT · CIED cardiac implantable electronic device · HOCM hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy · RF rheumatoid factor · ESR / CRP erythrocyte sedimentation rate / C-reactive protein · IgG immunoglobulin G · PCR polymerase chain reaction · MSSA / MRSA methicillin-sensitive / -resistant S. aureus · PCN penicillin · GNR gram-negative rods · HACEK the five slow-growing gram-negatives (Section 21) · PBP penicillin-binding protein · MR / AR / TR mitral / aortic / tricuspid regurgitation · IDU injection drug use · IV intravenous · PR PR interval (atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation) · ID infectious disease · CYP450 cytochrome P450 · DNA deoxyribonucleic acid

Clinical presentation and exam signs

Fever

about 90%

With chills, anorexia, night sweats, myalgia, arthralgia. Common but not diagnostic.

New or changed murmur

about 85%

Holosystolic (mitral regurgitation), diastolic (aortic regurgitation), or holosystolic tricuspid — often absent in right-sided disease.

Splenomegaly, petechiae

about 40% each

Petechiae on the conjunctiva, palate and limbs, more with S. aureus.

Presenting complication

common

Heart failure, stroke, a “renal problem”, back pain from vertebral osteomyelitis.

The peripheral signs ★ HY

SignWhat it looks likeMechanismPicture
PetechiaePinpoint hemorrhages — conjunctiva, palate, extremitiesMicro-emboli break capillaries
Splinter hemorrhagesNon-blanching red-brown linear streaks under the nailsEmboli — capillary hemorrhage
Janeway lesionsPainless, flat hemorrhagic plaques on the palms and solesSeptic emboli forming dermal micro-abscesses; S. aureus
Osler nodesPainful, raised nodules on the finger and toe padsImmune complexes
Roth spotsRetinal hemorrhages with pale centresImmune complexes
ClubbingBulbous fingertips — under 10%Platelet-derived growth factors
GlomerulonephritisHematuria, red-cell casts, proteinuriaImmune complexes

Pictures: ID lecture deck. Osler nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots each occur in under 10% — the lecturer called them the “question-writer” signs.

🧠 Immune complex or embolus?

Immune complexes: Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis, a positive rheumatoid factor. Emboli: Janeway lesions, splinters, petechiae, organ infarcts. Board add-on “Osler = Ouch”, and FROM JANE: Fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed hemorrhage, Emboli.

Blood cultures, echo and the diagnostic criteria ★ HY

Laboratory findings — mostly non-specific

  • Blood cultures: the bacteremia is continuous but low-level (under 100 organisms per mL), so draw three separate sets, before antibiotics.
  • Blood: anemia (of chronic disease), thrombocytopenia in 15–20%, raised ESR and CRP, hypergammaglobulinemia, and a positive rheumatoid factor in 50–60% — an antibody against the Fc portion of IgG, made in response to circulating immune complexes.
  • Urine: proteinuria, hematuria, pyuria, casts, bacteriuria.
  • A full dental evaluation is recommended — a clue to viridans streptococci or anaerobes.
⚠️ A disagreement on the white count

The lecturer said leukopenia is “not usually seen in IE”; the course outline lists it among the hematology findings. For an exam, a high white count fits acute disease and anemia fits subacute disease; leukopenia is not a typical clue.

The imaging ladder

TestSensitivityBest for
TTEabout 65%The cheap first look: vegetations, abscess, new regurgitation
TOEabout 95%When the TTE is negative but suspicion is high; vegetation size (embolic risk); perforation; prosthetic valves
Cardiac CT—Perivalvular abscess
FDG-PET/CT—Inflammation around prosthetic valves and device leads

The 2023 Duke criteria

TierCriterion
Major — microbiologicA typical organism in 2 or more separate blood-culture sets · an occasional or rare organism in 3 or more · positive PCR for Coxiella, Bartonella or T. whipplei · Coxiella phase I IgG over 1:800 · Bartonella IgG over 1:800
Major — imagingEcho or cardiac CT: vegetation, leaflet perforation or aneurysm, abscess, pseudoaneurysm, fistula · new significant regurgitation (worsening of old is not enough) · new partial prosthetic dehiscence · abnormal FDG-PET activity on a valve or device (3 months or more after implant)
Major — surgicalEndocarditis seen at cardiac surgery
MinorPredisposition (prior IE, prosthetic valve or repair, congenital disease, more than mild regurgitation or stenosis, a device, HOCM, injection drug use) · fever ≥ 38.0 °C · vascular (emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, abscess, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial or conjunctival hemorrhage, Janeway lesions) · immunologic (positive RF, Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis) · microbiology not meeting major · imaging (PET under 3 months) · a new regurgitant murmur when no echo is available
ResultRequires
DefinitePathology (organism or histology in a vegetation, valve, device or embolus) — or clinically 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor
Possible1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor
RejectedA firm alternative diagnosis; resolution with under 4 days of antibiotics; no endocarditis at surgery or autopsy after 4 days or fewer of antibiotics; criteria not met
🧠 Definite = “2 · 1 + 3 · 5”

Two majors, one major plus three minors, or five minors. Possible is “1 + 1, or 3.” The 2023 version is the most sensitive and works best for left-sided disease.

The full work-up of a vignette

  1. Suspect it: a typical organism in the blood (staphylococci, streptococci, enterococci), or fever plus a murmur, plus a risk factor (IDU, a prosthetic valve, recent dental work, dialysis, immunosuppression).
  2. Look for the peripheral signs and the complication that brought them in.
  3. Three blood-culture sets before antibiotics; basic labs, urinalysis, rheumatoid factor.
  4. Stable? Wait for the cultures. Acutely ill? Draw the three sets, then start empiric antibiotics immediately.
  5. TTE first, then TOE if negative with high suspicion, or for a prosthetic valve; CT for abscess, PET for prosthetics.
  6. Score it with Duke.
  7. Narrow to targeted therapy once the organism is known, and decide on surgery.
  8. Find the source: dental evaluation; colonoscopy for S. gallolyticus; remove infected lines or devices.

Antibiotic regimens and their mechanisms ★ HY

Principles

  • Aggressive — the response is slow because of biofilm and ongoing emboli.
  • Bactericidal, not bacteriostatic — the drug itself must kill the organisms already inside the vegetation, where host defences cannot reach.
  • Long — usually 4–6 weeks IV.
  • Empiric: cover MRSA and MSSA (including S. epidermidis), streptococci and enterococci with vancomycin plus cefepime or ceftriaxone.

Targeted therapy (the course handout)

OrganismRegimenDuration
S. aureus, methicillin-sensitiveNafcillin or oxacillin (or flucloxacillin)Handout says “3–5 days” — almost certainly a typo; standard is about 6 weeks Board add-on
S. aureus, methicillin-resistantVancomycin + rifampin6 weeks
S. epidermidis (mostly resistant)Vancomycin + rifampinMore than 6 weeks
Viridans streptococci, penicillin-sensitivePenicillin G or ceftriaxone4 weeks
Viridans streptococci, penicillin-resistantPenicillin G + gentamicin, or vancomycin4 weeks
Enterococci, penicillin-sensitivePenicillin G + gentamicin, or ceftriaxone + gentamicin, or vancomycin4 weeks
Enterococci, penicillin-resistantGentamicin + ampicillin–sulbactam, or vancomycin6 weeks
Gram-negative rods (enteric)Gentamicin + cefepime, or meropenem6–8 weeks
PseudomonasTobramycin + cefepime, or meropenem6–8 weeks
HACEKCeftriaxone or ciprofloxacin4 weeks
CandidaCaspofungin or liposomal amphotericin B, then fluconazole or voriconazole6–8 weeks, then lifelong suppression
AspergillusLiposomal amphotericin B + voriconazole, then voriconazole6 weeks, then lifelong
Coxiella burnetiiA quinolone + doxycycline—
BartonellaDoxycycline + rifampin (corrected in class — not gentamicin)—

How the drugs work Board add-on

The lecture gives the regimens; the mechanisms (objective 60) come from First Aid’s antimicrobial pages.

DrugClassMechanismKills or inhibits?Watch for
Penicillin G, ampicillinβ-lactamBinds penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking of the cell wallBactericidalHypersensitivity; destroyed by β-lactamase
Nafcillin, oxacillinPenicillinase-resistant penicillinSame, but a bulky side chain resists β-lactamase — for MSSABactericidalInterstitial nephritis; useless against MRSA (altered PBP)
Ceftriaxone (3rd generation), cefepime (4th)Cephalosporinβ-lactam: inhibits cell-wall cross-linking. Cefepime adds Pseudomonas coverBactericidalEnterococci are intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins alone
VancomycinGlycopeptideBinds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell-wall precursors, blocking their incorporationBactericidal (except against enterococci)Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, vancomycin infusion reaction (flushing) — slow the infusion
Gentamicin, tobramycinAminoglycosideBinds the 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNABactericidalNephrotoxicity, ototoxicity; needs oxygen to enter, so useless against anaerobes
RifampinRifamycinInhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; penetrates biofilm — why it is added for prosthetic materialBactericidalResistance if used alone; red-orange body fluids; CYP450 inducer
DoxycyclineTetracyclineBinds the 30S subunit, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA attachmentBacteriostaticPhotosensitivity; teeth discoloration in children
MeropenemCarbapenemβ-lactam resistant to most β-lactamasesBactericidalSeizures at high dose
🧠 Synergy: why gentamicin is paired with a cell-wall drug for enterococci

Penicillin or ampicillin alone only inhibits enterococci. Damaging the cell wall lets the aminoglycoside get in to its ribosomal target, and together they are bactericidal — which endocarditis requires. Board add-on

Surgical indications

About half of patients eventually need valve surgery, usually replacement. Surgery also drains exudate and removes splenic or renal abscesses. Board add-on The main indications:

  • Heart failure from valve destruction (the commonest indication).
  • Uncontrolled infection: a perivalvular abscess, new heart block, a fistula, or bacteremia persisting despite appropriate antibiotics.
  • Difficult organisms: fungi, highly resistant organisms; S. aureus on a prosthetic valve.
  • Prevention of embolism: a large vegetation (over 10 mm) with embolic events.
  • Prosthetic-valve dehiscence or relapse after a full course.
🩺 Dr. McGrath’s cases
  • A 34-year-old woman who injected heroin had tricuspid endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli. The vegetation did not clear on antibiotics, so the surgeon did a radical tricuspid repair plus 6 weeks of IV antibiotics — repair first on the right side. She relapsed twice (aortic, then gram-negative), ending in a bioprosthetic replacement.
  • A 38-year-old with an old rheumatic mitral repair developed prosthetic-valve endocarditis two weeks after dental work without antibiotic cover, and needed a redo mitral replacement.
🔑 Who gets antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work Board add-on

Only the highest-risk hearts: a prosthetic valve or prosthetic repair material, prior endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic, or within 6 months of repair, or with a residual defect), and a transplanted heart with valve disease. Only for procedures that manipulate gingiva or the periapical region or perforate the mucosa. The usual drug is amoxicillin before the procedure. Mitral valve prolapse or a bicuspid valve alone does not qualify.

Q: An acutely ill patient with suspected endocarditis is in the emergency department. What must happen before the first antibiotic dose, and what is the empiric regimen?

Answer

Draw three separate blood-culture sets — antibiotics before cultures are the commonest cause of culture-negative endocarditis — then start vancomycin plus cefepime (or ceftriaxone) to cover MRSA, MSSA, coagulase-negative staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci.

Q: A patient has a fever of 38.6 °C, known mitral valve prolapse with regurgitation, and Osler nodes. Blood cultures and echo are pending. How many Duke criteria are met, and what is the category so far? What would make it definite?

Answer

Three minor (predisposition, fever, an immunologic phenomenon), so possible endocarditis. One major criterion — a typical organism in two culture sets, or a vegetation on echo — would make it definite (1 major + 3 minor).

Q: The transthoracic echo shows no vegetation in a patient with a high suspicion of endocarditis. What is the next imaging step, and why?

Answer

A transesophageal echo — about 95% sensitive against about 65% for the transthoracic study — which also sizes the vegetation to estimate embolic risk.

Q: Three weeks after dental work, a man with old rheumatic mitral disease has low-grade fevers, painful nodules on his finger pads and retinal hemorrhages with pale centres. Organism, mechanism of the skin and eye findings, and the usual drug?

Answer

Subacute endocarditis from viridans streptococci on a damaged valve. Osler nodes and Roth spots are immune-complex deposits. If penicillin-sensitive: penicillin G or ceftriaxone for 4 weeks.

Q: Why are bactericidal drugs required for endocarditis, and why is gentamicin added to ampicillin for enterococcal disease?

Answer

The dense, poorly perfused vegetation and biofilm protect the organisms from host defences, so the drug must kill them; suppression lets them regrow. Ampicillin alone only inhibits enterococci; its cell-wall damage lets gentamicin reach the 30S ribosome, and the pair is synergistically bactericidal.

Q: A patient with MRSA prosthetic-valve endocarditis is on vancomycin. Which drug is added, what is its mechanism, and why is it chosen here?

Answer

Rifampin, which inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material; it is never used alone because resistance develops fast. (Vancomycin works by binding D-Ala-D-Ala.)

Q: On day 10 of appropriate antibiotics for S. aureus aortic-valve endocarditis, a patient’s PR interval lengthens and then he develops complete heart block. What has happened, and what does it mean for management?

Answer

A perivalvular (aortic ring) abscess has extended into the conduction system. This is uncontrolled infection — an indication for surgery. Confirm the abscess on TOE or cardiac CT.

Section 23 · Infection & Inflammation

Myocarditis and Pericarditis

The second half of the infection lecture was, in the lecturer’s words, a “fairly brief” pass — “Myo and Peri, sounds like a sixties singing group that didn’t make it.” The exam task is to tell the three layers apart: the endocardium (bacteria, valves, emboli), the myocardium (mostly viruses, heart failure and arrhythmia in a young person) and the pericardium (that distinctive pain, a rub and diffuse ST elevation).
