Pictures: ID lecture deck (vegetations); Robbins & Cotran Atlas (viral myocarditis); Gardner lecture slide 84 (fibrinous pericarditis).

Myocarditis: signs, symptoms and causes

Inflammation of the myocardium — infectious, immune-mediated or toxic — damaging the myocytes, the conduction system, autonomic nerves and interstitium. It is often unsuspected: about 4% of unrelated autopsies show it, and more in young sudden deaths.

Four mechanisms of damage

  1. Direct cell damage by the agent itself (mostly viruses).
  2. Cytokines and cell-mediated immunity — a general immune response, such as a cytokine storm.
  3. Antigen-specific cytotoxicity — a focused immune attack on one microbial antigen.
  4. Toxin cytotoxicity — the best example is diphtheria.

The causes

CategoryAgents
Viruses (the main cause)Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 — the most common in current adult data. Coxsackie B — the classic answer from the 1960s–90s, mostly children; older board questions still use it. Adenovirus, which shares the coxsackie–adenovirus receptor on myocytes. Less often CMV, EBV, influenza, RSV, HIV, SARS-CoV-2
Bacterial toxinsCorynebacterium diphtheriae toxin — historically the main way diphtheria killed children, more than the pseudomembrane; Clostridium perfringens
SpirochetesBorrelia burgdorferi (Lyme) — about 10% develop conduction disease (heart block)
Spread from endocarditisContiguous extension or septic emboli
ParasitesTrypanosoma cruzi (Chagas), Toxoplasma (cat owners), Plasmodium; trichinosis
Fungi (immunocompromised)Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Candida, Coccidioides
Immune-mediated (Gardner)Post-viral; post-streptococcal (rheumatic fever); SLE; drug hypersensitivity (methyldopa, sulfonamides); transplant rejection; immune checkpoint inhibitors
UnknownSarcoidosis; giant cell myocarditis

Many cases are idiopathic and simply assumed viral, so the true share is unknown. COVID-19: myocarditis after infection is about 1 in 5,000; after vaccination about 1 in 15,000–50,000, with a very benign course.

🩺 Chagas disease — called out because its epidemiology is changing
  • Trypanosoma cruzi enters through the feces of the triatomine (“kissing”) bug. After a transient acute phase, amastigotes lodge in heart muscle and in the nerves of the gut.
  • Decades later about 20% develop cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia and sudden death, or megacolon and megaesophagus.
  • Endemic to South America and now considered endemic to the US. Think of it in late middle age with unexplained cardiac symptoms and the right exposure. Board add-on Right bundle branch block is a classic ECG clue.

Histology

PatternAssociated with
LymphocyticPathogens, mostly viral; drugs, radiation, immune disorders
EosinophilicParasites; hypersensitivity
Giant-cellAutoimmune (non-infectious); Board add-on often fulminant
GranulomatousSarcoidosis

Signs and symptoms

FormPicture
SubacuteNo specific symptoms — only an unexplained troponin rise or ECG changes
AcuteNew, unexplained heart failure, chest pain, arrhythmia, dyspnea or leg swelling in a young patient, developing over 3 months or less
ChronicOver 3 months; cardiomyopathy alternating with stability — can end as a dilated cardiomyopathy (Section 19)
FulminantSudden cardiac collapse, cardiogenic shock
  • Often asymptomatic. Common features: fever, chest pain, unexplained sinus tachycardia, dyspnea, heart failure, palpitations, syncope, sudden death; S3 or S4, heart block or a new bundle branch block, cardiomegaly.
  • Ask about a preceding viral prodrome — flu-like, upper respiratory or GI.
  • Gardner’s typical patient: an otherwise healthy young person with URI symptoms plus cardiac symptoms and a mild troponin rise.

Diagnosis

  • Troponin raised — troponin T lasts longer, troponin I is more cardiac-specific — and Board add-on it tends to stay at a plateau rather than rise and fall like an infarct. CRP and ESR up; BNP up.
  • ECG: ST elevation, tachy- or bradyarrhythmias. Echo: dilation of all four chambers, diffuse hypokinesis. Board add-on Cardiac MRI shows myocardial edema and patchy late enhancement.
  • Endomyocardial biopsy is definitive (histology, immunohistochemistry, viral PCR) but invasive — reserved for rapidly progressive heart failure. PCR can find bystander viruses.
  • Virus isolated from another site, or rising antibody titres, is only circumstantial.

Treatment

  • Mostly supportive: treat the heart failure and arrhythmias — diuretics, renin–angiotensin blockers, beta-blockers (Section 18), up to mechanical support and transplant.
  • Dr. Gardner’s single most important step: bed rest — “get them off their feet.” Board add-on No competitive sport for 3–6 months, because exertion during myocarditis risks sudden death.
  • Sometimes IVIG or interferon for infectious forms; specific antibacterial, antifungal or antiparasitic drugs when the agent is known. Antivirals have no proven efficacy.

Pericarditis: signs, ECG and organisms

The sac

A double wall: an outer fibrous layer that does not stretch, and an inner serous membrane (parietal and visceral layers) with 15–50 mL of fluid between. It keeps the heart in place, prevents over-filling, lubricates, and sometimes blocks the spread of infection from nearby organs.

Organisms and other causes

ClassAgents
Viruses (most common in the US)Historically in children: enteroviruses (Coxsackie, echovirus), influenza. Adults: parvovirus B19, CMV, EBV, HIV, SARS-CoV-2
Bacteria — “purulent pericarditis”S. aureus, streptococci (pneumococcus, viridans), Haemophilus; M. tuberculosis in endemic countries (but needs supporting findings, not just geography)
Fungi (immunocompromised)Candida, Aspergillus; rarely Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides
Parasites (rare)Toxoplasma, Entamoeba, Echinococcus
Non-infectiousPost-MI (early fibrinous at 2–3 days; Dressler after 2 weeks — Section 15), post-cardiac surgery, uremia / renal failure, malignancy, radiation, trauma, autoimmune (SLE, RA, scleroderma, rheumatic fever), drugs (phenytoin, rifampin)

What the fluid looks like (Gardner)

TypeLookCauses
SerousClear fluidConnective tissue disease: SLE, rheumatic fever, scleroderma
FibrinousClotted fibrin — “bread and butter”Post-MI and Dressler, post-surgery, Board add-on uremia
PurulentNeutrophilsInfection — TB, pyogenic bacteria
HemorrhagicBloodMalignancy, TB, after procedures
ConstrictiveA scarred, thick pericardiumThe end result of any of the above; restricts cardiac motion and mimics restrictive cardiomyopathy

The signs — the pain is the giveaway

  • Sharp, stabbing anterior chest pain, worse with coughing, inspiration and lying flat.
  • Better sitting up and leaning forward.
  • Radiates to the left trapezius ridge.
  • A pericardial friction rub — scratchy and squeaky, essentially found only in acute pericarditis (“that’s the rub”). It usually has three parts and is best heard at the left lower sternal border, leaning forward.
  • Acute onset, a course of about 3 weeks, and it can recur. A non-specific prodrome: low-grade fever, fatigue, cough, dyspnea, hiccups.

The ECG

  • Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. The ST elevation is everywhere, not confined to one coronary territory. Textbooks say it is concave (“saddle”), but the electrophysiologist has seen plenty that are not — lean on distribution, PR depression and the history.
  • Board add-on PR elevation in aVR, and no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR and V1), also favour pericarditis over a STEMI.
  • Four stages over weeks: (1) diffuse STE ± PR depression; (2) ST and PR normalise; (3) diffuse T-wave inversion with an isoelectric ST (weeks 2–4); (4) normal again (1–2 months).

Diagnosis — 2 or more of 4

  1. Typical sharp, pleuritic chest pain, better sitting up.
  2. A pericardial friction rub.
  3. ECG changes: widespread ST elevation or PR depression.
  4. A new or worse pericardial effusion on echo (not needed on its own).

Supporting tests: CBC, ESR and CRP; troponin to look for myocardial involvement; chest X-ray; TTE for effusion.

🎈

Myopericarditis

  • Pericarditis predominates, with some myocardial involvement (troponin up).
  • Ventricular function is normal.
💪

Perimyocarditis

  • Myocarditis predominates, with pericardial features.
  • Ventricular function is reduced.

Treatment

  • NSAIDs + colchicine (colchicine cuts recurrence). Glucocorticoids only if NSAIDs cannot be used. Board add-on After an MI, aspirin is the NSAID of choice.
  • Empiric parenteral antimicrobials if bacterial or fungal disease is suspected, with drainage of a purulent effusion.
  • Antivirals: efficacy not proven.

Effusion and tamponade

  • Fluid in the sac stops the heart expanding, so it cannot fill; cardiac output and blood pressure fall. How fast the fluid collects matters more than how much.
  • Tamponade — Beck triad: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds. Plus tachycardia, a narrow pulse pressure and pulsus paradoxus (an inspiratory systolic drop over 10 mm Hg). Board add-on Electrical alternans on the ECG (the heart swinging in the fluid).
  • Imaging: echo shows the effusion with right atrial and ventricular compression; a large effusion gives a “water-bottle” heart on chest X-ray.
  • Treatment: drain it — echo-guided pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid), or a surgical subxiphoid pericardial window, which removes a piece for pathology and usually does not recur.
  • Settings in the lectures: a uremic dialysis patient (McGrath), a child 3 weeks after VSD surgery (post-pericardiotomy syndrome), cancer (a bloody effusion), and post-MI free-wall rupture (Section 15).
🧠 Constrictive pericarditis Board add-on

The scarred end-stage of pericarditis (TB worldwide; prior surgery or radiation in the US). The stiff shell limits filling, so the picture is right-sided failure: high JVP, edema, ascites. Clues: Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration), a pericardial knock in early diastole, and pericardial calcification. It mimics restrictive cardiomyopathy (Section 19); treatment is pericardiectomy.

Q: A 30-year-old has sharp chest pain radiating to the left trapezius, worse lying flat and better leaning forward, a week after a cold. The ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Diagnosis, the feature that argues against a STEMI, and first-line treatment?

Answer

Acute (viral) pericarditis. The ST elevation is diffuse, not in one coronary territory, with PR depression and positional pleuritic pain. Treat with NSAIDs plus colchicine.

Q: A 28-year-old develops new heart failure two weeks after a febrile illness. Endomyocardial biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrates with myocyte necrosis. Which viruses are most often found in adults today, and which older answer shares a receptor with adenovirus?

Answer

Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 in current data. Coxsackie B is the classic older answer; it and adenovirus use the coxsackie–adenovirus receptor. Management is supportive, with no exertion.

Q: A hiker in Connecticut with a recent expanding rash presents with syncope and complete heart block. Diagnosis?

Answer

Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi) — about 10% of Lyme patients develop conduction disease.

Q: A child with a grey pharyngeal pseudomembrane dies a week later of an arrhythmia. What is the mechanism?

Answer

Diphtheria toxin myocarditis — historically the main cause of diphtheria deaths, more than airway obstruction.

Q: A dialysis patient has weeks of dyspnea, JVD, distant heart sounds, a narrow pulse pressure and a 20 mm Hg inspiratory drop in systolic pressure. Diagnosis, and two ways to treat it?

Answer

Pericardial tamponade from a uremic effusion (Beck triad plus pulsus paradoxus). Drain it: needle pericardiocentesis, or a surgical subxiphoid pericardial window.

Q: How do myopericarditis and perimyocarditis differ?

Answer

Myopericarditis: pericarditis dominates and ventricular function is normal. Perimyocarditis: myocarditis dominates and ventricular function is reduced.

Q: When a pathologist peels back the pericardium at autopsy, shaggy strands connect it to the heart. Name the pattern and two common causes. What would a bloody effusion suggest instead?

Answer

Fibrinous (“bread-and-butter”) pericarditis — after an MI (early, or Dressler) or cardiac surgery; also uremia. A hemorrhagic effusion suggests malignancy (or TB).

LO 5LO 6Source: Cardiac Pathology (Gardner) · Cardiac Cycle & Valve Hemodynamics (Qazi) · Cardiothoracic Surgery (McGrath)

Section 24 · Valves & Surgery

Valvular Heart Disease

Section 3 covers how each valve lesion sounds and what it does to the pressures. This section is the other half: what the diseased valve looks like, why it got that way, and what is done about it. Dr. Gardner’s two-line summary is the frame: the important valve diseases are on the left (it carries the cardiac output); aortic stenosis is a bicuspid or ageing valve and insufficiency an expanding root; mitral stenosis is rheumatic and insufficiency is myxomatous or from heart failure.

Abbreviations used in this section AS / AR (AI) aortic stenosis / regurgitation (insufficiency) · MS / MR mitral stenosis / regurgitation · MVP mitral valve prolapse · TR / TS tricuspid regurgitation / stenosis · PS / PR pulmonic stenosis / regurgitation · RHD rheumatic heart disease · ARF acute rheumatic fever · GAS group A streptococcus · LV / LA / RV / RA left ventricle / atrium, right ventricle / atrium · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · EF ejection fraction · AF atrial fibrillation · PBMC percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy · MVR mitral valve replacement · TAVR / SAVR transcatheter / surgical aortic valve replacement (Section 25) · TEE transesophageal echo · IDU injection drug use · DOAC direct oral anticoagulant · CV cardiovascular · GI gastrointestinal · JVP jugular venous pressure · AVR aortic valve replacement · AV atrioventricular · CT computed tomography

The valve plane, and why the left side matters

  • Two pumps in series: “How much of the cardiac output goes out the pulmonary artery?” 100%.
  • The atrioventricular valves (tricuspid, mitral) are complex — leaflets tethered by chordae to papillary muscles, with the ventricle itself part of the apparatus. The semilunar valves (pulmonic, aortic) are simple check valves. That is why the AV valves can far more often be repaired.
  • All four grow from the fibrous skeleton; the aortic and mitral valves touch (fibrous continuity).
  • Valves have no blood supply of their own and are immune-privileged — one reason replacements work so well (Gardner).
  • Failure modes: stenosis is a pressure load; regurgitation is a volume load (Section 17).

The four left-sided lesions: cause, pathology and treatment

LesionCausesWhat the valve and heart look likeTreatmentPicture
Aortic stenosisBicuspid valve (4th–6th decades) · calcific degeneration of a tricuspid valve (6th–7th decades and beyond) · rheumaticThick, calcified, fused, immobile cusps; concentric LVHNo drug slows it; replace it — TAVR or SAVR (Section 25)
Aortic regurgitationRoot: dilation (age, hypertension), Marfan, syphilitic aortitis, ankylosing spondylitis, dissection · Valve: endocarditis (the commonest in Dr. Qazi’s practice), bicuspid, rheumatic, myxomatousLeaflets that do not coapt; eccentric hypertrophy and dilation, eventually irreversible systolic failureSurgical AVR (± root) when severe with symptoms, EF under 50% or a big LV; TAVR contraindicated in pure AR
Mitral stenosisRheumatic heart disease — “most pure mitral stenosis is rheumatic”; rarely a too-tight earlier repairThick leaflets, fused commissures, short thick chordae: a “fish-mouth” orifice; a big left atrium, AF, LA thrombusBeta-blockers, diuretics, anticoagulation for AF; balloon commissurotomy; surgical commissurotomy or MVR
Mitral regurgitationPrimary: myxomatous MVP (the commonest US cause), endocarditis, rheumatic, chordal rupture · Secondary: dilated LV, ischemic papillary dysfunction or rupture, calcified ringMVP: long, floppy, myxomatous leaflets billowing into the LA; dilated LA and LVPrimary → repair; functional → replace (and treat the LV)

Pictures: Qazi lecture (aortic schematics); AMBOSS (fish-mouth mitral valve, board add-on); CV Pathophysiology (MVP).

Aortic stenosis and regurgitation

Aortic stenosis — the most common valve problem needing surgery

  • A bimodal disease. A bicuspid valve (1–2% of people — the commonest congenital valve problem in adults) presents in the 40s to 60s. A normal three-leaflet valve calcifies with age and presents in the 70s to 90s.
  • Pathology of calcific AS: micro-injury, scarring and calcification give thick, fused, immobile leaflets. Catherine Otto’s work found inflammatory cells and actual lamellar bone in the leaflets. Statins did not slow it.
  • A bicuspid valve always comes with an aortopathy, so screen for an ascending aortic aneurysm and coarctation (contrast CT of the chest). Dr. McGrath’s 53-year-old with a bicuspid valve had a 5.2 cm ascending aneurysm replaced with the valve.
  • Progression is “almost a log curve” — slow, then rapid. The LV compensates with concentric hypertrophy until it cannot.
  • Symptoms and why: dyspnea (diastolic dysfunction of a hugely hypertrophied LV), angina with clean coronaries (high LV pressure squeezes the subendocardium in diastole), exertional syncope (fixed output), and sudden death.
  • Once symptoms appear, about half the patients are dead within 2 years without replacement. Board add-on Classic survival: angina about 5 years, syncope 3, heart failure 2.
  • Board add-on Heyde syndrome: AS with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia, because shear stress across the valve cleaves von Willebrand factor.
  • Management: no medical therapy slows it, so monitor, then replace. Dr. Qazi intervenes once it is severe on echo; guidelines trigger on severe AS with any symptom or with an EF under 50%. Severe AS is preload-dependent: avoid nitrates and over-diuresis. Details of TAVR versus SAVR are in Section 25.

Aortic regurgitation

  • The leaflets fail to meet, because of the root or the valve. An aortic root aneurysm (Marfan) stretches the sinuses and pulls the cusps apart; a dissection can unzip a commissure; endocarditis destroys a leaflet.
  • Board add-on The commonest cause in resource-rich countries is a bicuspid valve or root dilation; rheumatic disease in resource-limited ones. Acute AR comes from dissection or endocarditis and presents as sudden pulmonary edema and shock.
  • Volume overload: the LV dilates and compensates for decades — some patients present with an EF of 10–20%.
  • Surgical triggers (slide 61): severe AR; moderate AR with decompensation; EF under 50%; end-systolic dimension over 55 mm or end-diastolic over 75 mm — “remember the sarcomere: overstretch kills.”
⚠️ “Valves gone wrong — a bad deal”: why valves are fixed early

Dr. McGrath’s upstream cascade: aortic regurgitation overloads the LV, which dilates; the mitral annulus dilates, giving mitral regurgitation; the LA overloads, giving pulmonary hypertension; the RV overloads and the tricuspid annulus dilates, giving tricuspid regurgitation; the RA dilates, and the patient ends with massive cardiomegaly, edema and organ failure. Fixed pulmonary hypertension and RV failure make surgery far harder, so valves are fixed earlier rather than later.

Mitral stenosis, regurgitation and prolapse

Mitral stenosis

  • Most common cause worldwide: rheumatic heart disease — everywhere in South Asia, where balloon valvuloplasty is bread-and-butter, but rare in the US. About 80% of rheumatic MS is in women, and pregnancy often unmasks it. Board add-on
  • Pathology: fused commissures and leaflets, thick short chordae, calcification — the “fish-mouth” valve. A latent period of 20–40 years after rheumatic fever.
  • Consequences: a big LA, AF and LA thrombus (stroke can be the first sign), pulmonary edema and hemoptysis, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure.
  • Severe when the valve area is ≤ 1.5 cm² (normal about 4).
  • Treatment:
    • Beta-blockers (or rate control) to lengthen diastole and filling time, and diuretics for congestion.
    • Anticoagulation for AF — Board add-on warfarin, not a DOAC, in rheumatic MS.
    • Percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy for severe symptomatic disease with a suitable valve — it “buys time to tune the patient up”.
    • Surgical commissurotomy or mitral valve replacement; a tissue valve in women of childbearing age to avoid warfarin, with a mechanical valve at a later redo.

Mitral regurgitation and prolapse

  • Myxomatous degeneration (MVP): long, floppy leaflets infiltrated with proteoglycans, billowing into the LA. Tension stretches the chordae, so it worsens; a ruptured chord gives a flail leaflet and acute heart failure — surgery before discharge. Associated with Marfan and Ehlers–Danlos; a not-uncommon cause of sudden death in young women (Gardner).
  • Most MVP does not cause significant MR or need surgery.
  • Secondary (functional) MR: the valve is normal but a dilated LV stretches the annulus and pulls on the papillary muscles, or an inferior infarct tethers the posterior leaflet (ischemic MR; Section 15 for rupture).
  • Pathophysiology: LA volume overload, LA dilation, AF, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure.
🔑 Repair or replace?
  • Organic (degenerative) MR: repair. Repair keeps the valve and its chordae and papillary muscles helping the LV, and a good repair lasts a lifetime. Dr. McGrath repairs over 95% of repairable valves — send patients to a surgeon with those odds.
  • Functional MR: replace. The LV keeps remodelling, so repairs fail at 1–3 years.

Rheumatic heart disease

Section 3 covers the rheumatic murmurs; here is the pathology Dr. Gardner wants.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis in a child or teenager, untreated.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac self-antigens — in about 3% of infections.
  3. Acute rheumatic fever: polyarthritis, pancarditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea. Board add-on “J♥NES”.
  4. Healing is fibrosis: chronic scarring of the valves, decades later — mitral stenosis.
  • Valves involved: mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonic. Rheumatic tricuspid or pulmonic disease almost never occurs without mitral disease. Board add-on
  • Histology: Aschoff bodies — clumps of T cells, plasma cells and macrophages; the activated macrophages with wavy “caterpillar” chromatin are Anitschkow cells Board add-on. Chronic valves: thick leaflets, fused commissures, short thick chordae.
  • Now rare in the West because strep throats are treated; common in low-income countries — Dr. McGrath’s Iranian partner operated on rheumatic mitral disease every year.

The right-sided valves

Right-sided valve disease is uncommon, and the lectures touch it mainly through endocarditis and surgery; the rest is Board add-on UWorld library material. The pattern mirrors the left side, with right heart failure instead of pulmonary edema.

LesionMain causesCluesManagement
Tricuspid regurgitationFunctional (secondary) is far commoner: RV dilation, most often from left heart failure or pulmonary hypertension. Primary: IDU endocarditis (common in Maine), carcinoid syndrome, pacemaker leads, rheumaticHolosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration; large v waves in the JVP; pulsatile liver, edema, ascitesTreat the cause and diurese. Surgery: always try repair first; if replacing, a tissue valve does better than mechanical in the tricuspid position (McGrath)
Tricuspid stenosisRheumatic, almost always with mitral stenosis; radiation; carcinoidRight heart failure with clear lungs; diastolic rumble that increases with inspiration; giant a wavesDiuretics; repair or replacement, often with mitral surgery
Pulmonic stenosisCongenital (Noonan syndrome; part of tetralogy of Fallot); carcinoid (with TR)Ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration; RV hypertrophy; does not calcify with ageBalloon valvuloplasty
Pulmonic regurgitationUsually iatrogenic — after repair of tetralogy of Fallot or valvuloplasty; pulmonary hypertension (mild)Early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border (Graham Steell murmur with pulmonary hypertension); RV volume overloadPulmonary valve replacement in adults with repaired tetralogy and RV dilation
🧠 Why carcinoid attacks the right side Board add-on

Serotonin from hepatic metastases of a carcinoid tumour reaches the right heart and lays down fibrous plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves, giving TR and pulmonic stenosis. The lungs break serotonin down, so the left-sided valves are spared — unless there is a right-to-left shunt or a bronchial primary.

Q: A 55-year-old has severe calcific aortic stenosis — “early” for age-related disease. What is the most likely underlying valve anatomy, and what two other aortic problems should you look for?

Answer

A congenitally bicuspid aortic valve, which calcifies decades earlier than a normal one. Every bicuspid valve has an aortopathy: screen for an ascending aortic aneurysm and coarctation.

Q: Why does severe aortic stenosis cause angina with normal coronary arteries, and why does the onset of symptoms matter so much?

Answer

Massive concentric hypertrophy and a very high LV pressure compress the subendocardium in diastole, when the coronaries fill, while the thick muscle needs more oxygen. Once angina, syncope or dyspnea appears, about half are dead within 2 years without valve replacement.

Q: A 35-year-old woman who grew up in India has an opening snap, a low diastolic rumble at the apex, atrial fibrillation and hemoptysis. What is the lesion, what does the valve look like, and what are the treatment steps?

Answer

Rheumatic mitral stenosis: thick leaflets, fused commissures and short chordae — a fish-mouth orifice. Treat with beta-blockers (longer filling time), diuretics, warfarin for the AF, and balloon commissurotomy if severe and the valve is suitable; otherwise surgery.

Q: A 54-year-old with a known mitral click develops weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea and a new MR murmur; TEE shows a torn chord to the posterior leaflet. A second patient with ischemic cardiomyopathy has severe MR with a normal-looking valve. Repair or replace, and why?

Answer

The first is organic (degenerative) MR — repair, which keeps the valve apparatus helping the LV and lasts a lifetime. The second is functional MR — replace (and treat the LV), because the ventricle keeps remodelling and repairs fail within 1–3 years.

Q: A 40-year-old with Marfan syndrome has severe aortic regurgitation with an end-systolic LV dimension of 58 mm and an EF of 48%. Is surgery indicated, and what operation?

Answer

Yes — an EF under 50% and an end-systolic dimension over 55 mm are both triggers (“overstretch kills”). He needs surgical aortic root and valve replacement; TAVR is contraindicated in pure AR with a dilated root.

Q: A patient with flushing, diarrhea and liver metastases develops edema, ascites and a holosystolic murmur that gets louder with inspiration. Which valves are involved, and why not the left side?

Answer

Carcinoid heart disease: fibrous plaques on the tricuspid (regurgitation) and pulmonic (stenosis) valves. The lungs inactivate serotonin, so the left-sided valves are spared.

Section 25 · Valves & Surgery

Aortic Valve Replacement

The aortic valve opens and closes about 80 times a minute for a lifetime, and aortic stenosis is the valve problem that most often ends in surgery. Two choices define every replacement: how it goes in (open surgery or a catheter) and what goes in (mechanical or tissue). Dr. McGrath’s approach to the second one is simple — explain the trade-off, then let the patient choose.

Abbreviations used in this section AVR aortic valve replacement · SAVR surgical AVR · TAVR (TAVI) transcatheter aortic valve replacement (implantation) · AS / AR (AI) aortic stenosis / regurgitation (insufficiency) · LV left ventricle · LVEF / EF (left ventricular) ejection fraction · LVH left ventricular hypertrophy · CAD coronary artery disease · CABG coronary artery bypass grafting · STS Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk score · CPB cardiopulmonary bypass · RCA right coronary artery · PVL paravalvular leak · INR international normalized ratio · DOAC / NOAC direct (non-vitamin-K) oral anticoagulant · AV atrioventricular · LDH lactate dehydrogenase · ViV valve-in-valve · AF atrial fibrillation · TEE transesophageal echo · GI gastrointestinal · PCI percutaneous coronary intervention · CT computed tomography · IV intravenous

Indications ★ HY

LesionReplace when
Aortic stenosisSevere AS with any symptom — angina, syncope, dyspnea or reduced exercise tolerance (about half die within 2 years once symptoms start) · severe AS with an EF under 50% · severe AS when another cardiac operation (such as CABG) is being done anyway Board add-on · Dr. Qazi’s practice: intervene once it is severe on echo, rather than wait for symptoms
Severe on echo Board add-onPeak jet ≥ 4 m/s, mean gradient ≥ 40 mm Hg, valve area ≤ 1.0 cm². Dr. McGrath’s case: mean 50, peak 95 mm Hg.
Aortic regurgitationSevere AR with symptoms · moderate AR with decompensation · EF under 50% · end-systolic dimension over 55 mm or end-diastolic over 75 mm (“overstretch kills”)
OtherEndocarditis destroying the valve (Section 22); a bicuspid valve with an ascending aneurysm needing replacement anyway; a failed earlier prosthesis
  • No medicine slows aortic stenosis, so the job is to monitor it and replace it at the right time.
  • The work-up: echo for the valve and LV; cardiac catheterisation is mandatory before surgical AVR, because about 50% have coronary disease that needs bypass at the same operation (CT coronary angiography can screen a young patient). Carotid Dopplers in those at risk, pulmonary function in heavy smokers, an STS risk score, and a team review for high-risk patients.

Surgical versus transcatheter replacement

🔪

SAVR — open

  • Sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, cold high-potassium cardioplegia to stop the heart in diastole, cut out the calcified valve, sew in a new one.
  • Low- and intermediate-risk, younger patients; a mechanical or tissue valve; the only option when the root or ascending aorta also needs replacing.
  • Low-risk mortality under 1%.
  • At least 5 days in hospital; back to normal life in 4–6 weeks while the sternum heals.
🎈

TAVR — catheter

  • Mostly transfemoral: a wire across the valve, then a balloon-mounted stented tissue valve inflated during rapid ventricular pacing, pushing the native leaflets aside. “Kind of like having a PCI.”
  • Originally for intermediate- to high-risk elderly patients (70s–90s); now extending to low risk. Dr. Qazi: now first-line for most AS.
  • Mortality about 2.5% even in high-risk patients; trace-to-mild paravalvular leaks are tolerated.
  • Mick Jagger was back on tour about 2 weeks after his.
⚠️ TAVR is contraindicated in pure aortic regurgitation

A TAVR valve anchors on a calcified annulus. Pure AR (and a dilated root) usually has too little calcium, so the valve would migrate. These patients need surgical valve (± root) replacement.

⚠️ TAVR durability — the slides conflict

Slide 58 lists “50% structural degeneration at 8 years.” Slide 59 and the spoken lecture say current-generation TAVR valves track like surgical tissue valves, with data out to about 9 years; the unknown is what happens after year 10. The 50% figure most likely describes early-generation valves. This uncertainty is one reason younger patients still lean toward SAVR.

ChooseWhen
Transfemoral TAVRElderly, frail or high surgical risk; calcified annulus; adequate femoral arteries; isolated AS
SAVRYounger; wants a mechanical valve; needs a root or ascending aorta replaced, or CABG, or another valve at the same time; pure AR; a bicuspid valve with aortopathy; poor femoral access

Mechanical versus bioprosthetic valves

MechanicalBioprosthetic (tissue)Picture
What it isModern: bileaflet pyrolytic carbon with a cloth sewing cuff. Older: tilting disc (“an anticoagulation nightmare”), Starr–Edwards ball-and-cagePorcine valve or bovine pericardium, usually on a stent; all TAVR valves are tissue

Q: An 84-year-old frail woman has severe calcific aortic stenosis, a high STS risk score and good femoral arteries. What is the best option?

Answer

Transfemoral TAVR — elderly, high risk, with a calcified annulus to anchor the valve.

Q: A 53-year-old with a known bicuspid valve passes out chasing his dog. Echo shows severe AS (mean gradient 50 mm Hg) and a 5.2 cm ascending aorta. What operation, and what must be done first?

Answer

Surgical AVR with ascending-aorta replacement — symptomatic severe AS plus a bicuspid aortopathy that TAVR cannot address. First, coronary catheterisation, because about half of AVR patients have coronary disease needing bypass at the same operation.

Q: A 45-year-old with a new bileaflet mechanical aortic valve asks to switch from warfarin to apixaban. What do you tell him, and what happens when he needs a colonoscopy?

Answer

No — mechanical valves need warfarin for life; DOACs are not safe with them. For the colonoscopy, warfarin is stopped and he is bridged with heparin.

Q: A 28-year-old woman who plans to have children needs her aortic valve replaced. Which prosthesis, and what is the trade-off?

Answer

A bioprosthetic (tissue) valve, which needs only aspirin, avoiding warfarin’s teratogenicity and bleeding in pregnancy. The trade-off is structural degeneration and a later redo operation or valve-in-valve TAVR.

Q: Two days after TAVR, a patient’s heart rate falls to 35 with complete heart block. Why, and what is the treatment?

Answer

The expanded valve frame compresses the conduction system just below the aortic annulus (the His bundle runs in the membranous septum there). Treat with a permanent pacemaker. Surgical AVR carries the same risk at about 3–4%.

Q: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve and a subtherapeutic INR presents with dyspnea, a new murmur and muffled prosthetic clicks. What is the likely complication? A different patient, years after a tissue AVR, has a new harsh systolic murmur. What is that?

Answer

The first is prosthetic valve thrombosis — inadequate anticoagulation of a mechanical valve; confirm on echo or CT and treat with fibrinolysis or surgery. The second is structural degeneration of the bioprosthesis (calcified, stenotic leaflets), treated with redo surgery or valve-in-valve TAVR.

Q: A 40-year-old with Marfan syndrome has severe pure aortic regurgitation and a dilated root. Why not TAVR?

Answer

A TAVR valve needs a calcified annulus to anchor; pure AR with a dilated root has none, so the valve would migrate. He needs surgical root and valve replacement.

Section 26 · Congenital Heart Disease

Congenital Heart Disease: Cyanotic Versus Acyanotic

Congenital heart disease is the most common birth defect — about 1 in 125 live births, “you are going to see it.” It forms in the first 8 weeks of gestation, and about 90% has no known cause. The pediatric cardiologist’s one-line physics is the key to every shunt: blood goes from high pressure to low. Sort each lesion by two questions — is the baby blue, and is lung blood flow up or down?

Abbreviations used in this section CHD congenital heart disease · VSD / ASD ventricular / atrial septal defect · AVSD atrioventricular septal defect · PDA patent ductus arteriosus · PFO patent foramen ovale · TOF tetralogy of Fallot · TGA transposition of the great arteries · TAPVR total anomalous pulmonary venous return · HLHS hypoplastic left heart syndrome · COA coarctation of the aorta · L→R / R→L left-to-right / right-to-left shunt · RV / LV / RA / LA right / left ventricle and atrium · RVH right ventricular hypertrophy · RVOT right ventricular outflow tract · PVR / SVR pulmonary / systemic vascular resistance · PGE₁ prostaglandin E1 · CXR chest X-ray · LLSB / LUSB left lower / upper sternal border · BT shunt Blalock–Taussig shunt · DVT deep vein thrombosis · SVT supraventricular tachycardia · AR aortic regurgitation · MVP mitral valve prolapse · TR tricuspid regurgitation · WPW Wolff–Parkinson–White · ECG electrocardiogram · AV atrioventricular · IV intravenous

Mechanisms: the fetal circulation and the first breath

  • In the fetus, gas exchange happens in the placenta. Oxygenated blood returns by the umbilical vein and ductus venosus to the right atrium.
  • About a third crosses the foramen ovale to the left atrium; most of the rest goes RV to pulmonary artery and crosses the ductus arteriosus to the aorta, bypassing the fluid-filled lungs.
  • At the first breath the lungs open, PVR falls and oxygen rises. The ductus closes functionally within about 24 hours; left-atrial pressure now exceeds right and pushes the foramen ovale flap shut (sealed by 6–12 months).
  • Any hole left open now shunts left to right, from the high-pressure side.
  • The septa form in early gestation: three septa divide the tube (atrial, ventricular, and the spiral septum splitting the truncus into aorta and pulmonary artery), and the endocardial cushions divide the AV canal. A step that goes wrong leaves a hole or swapped great arteries.

Acyanotic lesions: left-to-right shunts

Everything that reaches the body is oxygenated, so the baby is pink. The cost is extra pulmonary blood flow and volume overload: tachypnea, poor feeding, sweating with feeds, failure to thrive, heart failure — and, if untreated for years, pulmonary hypertension.

  • ASD types Board add-on: ostium secundum (about 80%, usually isolated), ostium primum (with other defects — Down syndrome), sinus venosus. A PFO is a failure of fusion, not a true ASD.
  • AV septal defect (endocardial cushion defect) is the lesion of Down syndrome.

Eisenmenger syndrome — when a left-to-right shunt reverses

  1. A long-standing left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA) floods the lungs.
  2. The pulmonary vessels remodel, and pulmonary hypertension becomes fixed.
  3. RV pressure climbs above LV pressure, and the shunt reverses to right-to-left.
  4. Late cyanosis, clubbing and polycythemia appear. At this point closing the defect no longer helps. Board add-on An uncorrected PDA gives differential cyanosis — blue toes, pink fingers — because the reversed shunt enters below the arm vessels.

Cyanotic lesions: the five T’s ★ HY

Deoxygenated blood reaches the systemic circulation. These babies are blue early, often in the first hours or days, and many depend on the ductus.

🧠 The 5 T’s Board add-on

1 — Truncus arteriosus (one vessel) · 2 — Transposition (two vessels switched) · 3 — Tricuspid atresia · 4 — Tetralogy of Fallot · 5 — Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (five words). The lecture’s list adds hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary atresia and Ebstein anomaly.

Tetralogy of Fallot in more depth

  • The narrow pulmonic outflow forces deoxygenated RV blood across the VSD into the overriding aorta — a right-to-left shunt.
  • Tet spell: crying, feeding or agitation lowers SVR (or raises PVR), worsening outflow obstruction and right-to-left shunting — blue lips and limbs, hyperpnea. Knee-to-chest or squatting raises SVR and pushes blood back to the lungs.
  • Repair is soon after birth or later in infancy, depending on how tight the pulmonary stenosis is. The first operation was the Blalock–Taussig shunt — subclavian artery to pulmonary artery — developed by Alfred Blalock, Helen Taussig and lab technician Vivien Thomas (the film Something the Lord Made).
  • Board add-on Caused by anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum; associated with 22q11 deletion.

Cyanotic features and the chest X-ray ★ HY

  • Central cyanosis — circumoral, tongue and lips — in a baby with clear, equal breath sounds. The lecture’s case: a saturation of 80% on 100% oxygen.
  • Board add-on The hyperoxia test: a lung problem improves on 100% oxygen; a cyanotic cardiac shunt does not.
  • Later signs of chronic cyanosis: clubbing, polycythemia (and its stroke and clotting risk), squatting in older children with tetralogy, and paradoxical emboli or brain abscess. Board add-on

Dr. Gardner’s point about the genetics: about 90% of congenital heart defects are still genetically unexplained, and the known genes are mostly transcription factors — probably shifting the timing of development of parts of the heart.

Presentations, complications and comorbidities

  • Reasons to refer to a pediatric cardiologist: a possibly structural murmur (any diastolic murmur, grade 3 or more, a thrill, harsh or holosystolic, an abnormal S2 or click, or one that does not change with position), exertional chest pain, a possible arrhythmia, recurrent syncope.
  • Large left-to-right shunts: tachypnea, poor feeding, sweating with feeds, failure to thrive, frequent respiratory infections, heart failure — and Eisenmenger syndrome if untreated.
  • Cyanotic lesions: blue at birth or within days; ductal-dependent lesions (HLHS, critical coarctation, transposition with an intact septum) crash into shock as the ductus closes — start PGE₁.
  • ASD and PFO: atrial arrhythmias and paradoxical embolism in adults.
  • Endocarditis risk with VSDs, bicuspid valves and repaired disease (Section 21).
  • Comorbidities come with the syndrome: DiGeorge (thymic aplasia and T-cell deficiency, hypocalcemia, cleft palate), Turner (horseshoe kidney, ovarian failure), Down (duodenal atresia, early Alzheimer disease, leukemia), Noonan (short stature, webbed neck) Board add-on.

Q: A newborn stays at 80% saturation on 100% oxygen, with clear lungs and a 3/6 systolic murmur. The CXR shows a boot-shaped heart. Name the four defects, and the one that decides how blue the baby is.

Answer

Tetralogy of Fallot: VSD, pulmonary (RVOT) stenosis, RVH and an overriding aorta. The degree of pulmonary stenosis sets how much blood shunts right to left.

Q: A 5-day-old who was well at discharge presents in shock with weak pulses everywhere. Echo shows a tiny left ventricle. What drug do you start immediately, and why?

Answer

Prostaglandin E1, to reopen the ductus arteriosus. In hypoplastic left heart syndrome the RV supplies the body through the ductus.

Q: A newborn with transposition of the great arteries and an intact ventricular septum turns deeply cyanotic on day 2. Why now?

Answer

The ductus arteriosus is closing. Without a VSD, the PDA (and the foramen ovale) was the only place the two parallel circulations could mix. Give PGE₁ and consider balloon atrial septostomy.

Q: A 40-year-old with a leg DVT suddenly has a stroke. A bubble study shows right-to-left passage of contrast at the atrial level. Mechanism? And what heart sound would a large ASD give?

Answer

Paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale or ASD: a venous clot crosses to the left atrium and enters the systemic circulation. A large ASD gives a fixed split S2 from RV volume overload.

Q: A 28-week preterm infant has a continuous murmur, bounding pulses and increasing respiratory difficulty. Lesion and drug? Which drug would you give instead if the baby’s circulation depended on that vessel?

Answer

A PDA, closed with IV indomethacin (or ibuprofen), which blocks prostaglandin synthesis. To keep a ductus open in a ductal-dependent lesion, give PGE₁.

Q: A 25-year-old who had an unrepaired VSD as a child now has cyanosis, clubbing and a hematocrit of 62%. What has happened, and can the VSD simply be closed now?

Answer

Eisenmenger syndrome: years of left-to-right flow caused fixed pulmonary hypertension, RV pressure rose above LV pressure and the shunt reversed. No — with fixed pulmonary hypertension, closing the defect does not help and is dangerous.

Q: Match each to its lesion: trisomy 21; 22q11 deletion; maternal lithium; Williams syndrome; congenital rubella; maternal diabetes.

Answer

Trisomy 21: AV septal defect. 22q11: truncus arteriosus and tetralogy. Lithium: Ebstein anomaly. Williams: supravalvular aortic stenosis. Rubella: PDA (and pulmonary artery stenosis). Maternal diabetes: transposition.

Section 27 · Congenital Heart Disease

Coarctation and the Newborn Murmur

The pediatric cardiologist’s plea for this topic was blunt: “Check femoral pulses on every newborn.” It takes diligence, and it is how coarctation is caught before the ductus closes. The second half of this section is the question every nursery raises: a newborn has a systolic murmur — how likely is it to be structural, and when does it need an echo?

Abbreviations used in this section COA coarctation of the aorta · BAV bicuspid aortic valve · PDA patent ductus arteriosus · PFO patent foramen ovale · VSD / ASD ventricular / atrial septal defect · TGA transposition of the great arteries · TOF tetralogy of Fallot · BP blood pressure · PGE₁ prostaglandin E1 · CHD congenital heart disease · CCHD critical congenital heart disease · SpO₂ pulse-oximetry oxygen saturation · CXR chest X-ray · ECG electrocardiogram · MRA / CTA magnetic resonance / CT angiography · WCC well-child check · LLSB / LUSB left lower / upper sternal border · TAPVR total anomalous pulmonary venous return · AV atrioventricular

Coarctation in the newborn: the exam findings ★ HY

🩺 The lecture’s case: a 6-hour-old with cool, mottled legs

A term boy with no risk factors. The nurse is worried: mildly fast breathing (40–50) and a fast heart rate (about 150), a murmur, and mottled, cool legs. Saturation 94% in arms and legs; glucose 60. A grade 2–3/6 systolic murmur radiating to the back; weak femoral pulses; arm pressures 25–30 mm Hg higher than leg pressures. The lower body gets oxygenated blood — just not enough of it.

FindingWhy
Weak or absent femoral pulses; Board add-on a brachio-femoral delayFlow beyond the narrowing is reduced and delayed
Arm BP higher than leg BP (a gradient of 20 mm Hg or more is significant)Pressure is normal or high before the narrowing and low beyond it. Take four-limb pressures
Systolic murmur radiating to the back (interscapular)Turbulent flow through the narrowed segment
Cool, mottled legs; tachypnea; tachycardiaPoor lower-body perfusion and early heart failure
Shock, acidosis, absent femorals on day 1–2 (critical coarctation)Board add-on The lower body was being fed by the ductus; as it closes, the legs and gut are starved
Differential saturation (feet lower than right hand) Board add-onDeoxygenated blood crossing an open ductus to the descending aorta — picked up by newborn pulse-oximetry screening
  • About 5% of congenital heart disease; boys more than girls, 2:1.
  • The narrowing is usually near where the ductus arteriosus inserts (juxtaductal).
  • Associations: Turner syndrome (25–30% have coarctation — “suspect Turner? Get an echo”) and a bicuspid aortic valve. Board add-on Berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis.
  • Diagnosis: echocardiography; angiography or MRA defines the anatomy.
  • Treatment depends on the pressure gradient: balloon angioplasty (catheter up from the femoral artery) or surgical resection and re-anastomosis. A critical, ductal-dependent coarctation needs PGE₁ first to reopen the ductus. Board add-on
🧠 Coarctation in the older child or adult Board add-on

A non-critical coarctation can go unnoticed until later: upper-body hypertension (a secondary cause in the young — Section 28), headaches, cold legs or claudication, a brachio-femoral delay, an interscapular murmur, and rib notching on CXR from enlarged intercostal collaterals. Complications: heart failure, aortic rupture or dissection, intracranial hemorrhage from berry aneurysms, and endocarditis.

The relative incidence of structural lesions

  • Congenital heart disease occurs in about 1 in 125 live births — the most common birth defect.
  • The lecture’s chart, in order: VSD (over 30%), then PDA, pulmonary stenosis, ASD, coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve, tetralogy of Fallot and transposition.
  • The lecturer’s update: with routine echo, many bicuspid aortic valves are now found by chance, so VSD and bicuspid aortic valve are about equally common in practice. (A bicuspid valve affects 1–2% of people, males twice as often.)

⚠️ Two incidence figures to read carefully

The lecture chart gives VSD at about 31% of congenital heart disease; Dr. Gardner’s table gives 42%. One pediatric slide says VSD occurs in “2 to 5% of births”; board sources give 2–5 per 1,000 births. Either way, VSD is the commonest.

The significant newborn systolic murmur and the predictive value of echo

What the lecture says

  • A systolic murmur in the nursery with an otherwise normal baby — pink, good saturation, good femoral and brachial pulses, clear lungs — can reasonably be watched: it might be a closing PDA or PFO.
  • But a murmur that persists or gets louder after the first weeks “shouldn’t be there by now” — refer. The lecture’s 4-month-old with a louder grade 2–3 murmur had a large VSD on echo.
  • The cardiologist’s work-up is a history, an exam, an ECG and an echo. Echo with colour Doppler is the definitive test — “the lighter the colour, the faster the flow.”
  • Features that make a murmur sound structural: any diastolic murmur, grade 3 or more or a thrill, harsh or holosystolic, an abnormal S2 or a click, loudness that does not change with position, and symptoms (poor growth, cyanosis, sweating with feeds).

What the predictive value means Board add-on

  • A murmur heard in the first days of life is common and often transitional (the closing ductus, a PFO, peripheral pulmonary flow). Even so, published newborn series find structural disease on echo in a substantial fraction — roughly a third to a half of newborns referred with a murmur, far more than for an older child’s murmur. The lecture gives no figure, so treat this range as approximate.
  • That is why a persistent or pathologic-sounding newborn murmur gets an echo rather than reassurance: the clinical exam alone misclassifies a meaningful share, and echo is close to definitive for structural disease.
  • The converse matters too: many critical lesions have no murmur at all (transposition, hypoplastic left heart, critical coarctation before the ductus closes). The absence of a murmur does not exclude serious disease, which is why every newborn has pulse-oximetry screening for critical CHD after 24 hours: right hand (pre-ductal) and a foot (post-ductal); a saturation under 95% in either, or a big difference between them, gets an echo.
Newborn murmurLikely meaningNext step

Persists or gets louder at follow-upPossibly structural (VSD, pulmonary stenosis)Refer; echo
Harsh, holosystolic, diastolic, thrill, click, or abnormal S2Structural until proven otherwiseEcho
Any murmur with poor feeding, tachypnea, cyanosis, weak femorals or a failed oximetry screenPossibly criticalUrgent echo; PGE₁ if ductal-dependent disease is suspected

Q: A newborn has weak femoral pulses and an arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg higher than the leg pressure. What is the diagnosis, and which syndrome should you think of in a girl?

Answer

Coarctation of the aorta. In a girl, think of Turner syndrome (45,X) — 25–30% have coarctation, and many have a bicuspid aortic valve.

Q: A 2-day-old boy who seemed well becomes pale, tachypneic and acidotic, with absent femoral pulses and a falling urine output. What is happening, and what is the first drug?

Answer

Critical coarctation presenting as the ductus closes — the lower body was being supplied through it. Start prostaglandin E1 to reopen the ductus, then repair.

Q: A 16-year-old has a blood pressure of 158/92 in the right arm, cold feet when running, and notching of the inferior rib margins on a chest X-ray. Diagnosis and the mechanism of the rib sign?

Answer

Coarctation of the aorta found late. Enlarged intercostal collateral arteries, carrying blood around the narrowing, erode the undersides of the ribs.

Q: A newborn has a soft systolic murmur on day 1 but is pink, feeding well, with normal pulses and saturation. At 4 months the murmur is louder (grade 2–3). What do you do, and what is the likely finding?

Answer

Watching on day 1 was reasonable (a closing PDA or PFO). A murmur that persists and gets louder at 4 months “shouldn’t be there by now”: refer for ECG and echo. The lecture’s case was a large VSD.

Q: Which congenital lesion is the most common, and why does the lecturer say the bicuspid aortic valve now rivals it?

Answer

The VSD (about 31–42% of congenital heart disease). With routine echocardiography, many bicuspid aortic valves (1–2% of people) are found by chance, so in practice the two are about equally common.

Q: A newborn passes the nursery exam with no murmur. Why is that not reassurance against critical heart disease, and what screening test closes the gap?

Answer

Many critical lesions — transposition, hypoplastic left heart, critical coarctation while the ductus is open — have no murmur. Pulse-oximetry screening after 24 hours (right hand and a foot) catches them: a saturation under 95% or a pre-/post-ductal difference prompts an echo.

Section 28 · Vessels

Hypertension: Subtypes, Secondary Causes and Resistance

Hypertension is “the silent killer”: it is invisible until it has damaged the heart, brain, kidney or eye. About 90–95% is primary (essential); the rest is secondary, and Dr. Segal’s case was built to teach when to go looking for it. His rule for the work-up: “don’t throw a net of labs and hope to catch the fish” — think through the history and exam, then order what the differential needs.

If systolic and diastolic fall in different categories, use the higher one. Average 2 or more readings on 2 or more occasions.

Measuring it properly

  • Seated with feet flat and back supported, after 5 minutes of rest (an exam table does not count); no caffeine, exercise or smoking for 30 minutes; empty bladder; arm supported at heart level; nobody talking; correct cuff; check both arms and use the higher.
  • A cuff over clothing can be off by 5–50 mm Hg. Crossed legs add 2–8; a small cuff 2–10; a full bladder, talking or an unsupported arm about 10 each.
  • Home and 24-hour ambulatory readings correlate better with outcomes and catch two phenotypes:
Out-of-office BP normalOut-of-office BP high
Office BP highWhite-coat hypertensionSustained hypertension
Office BP normalNormotensionMasked hypertension

Physiologic subtypes (Dr. Scully)

TypePatternWho
Cardiac (pump)High CO, normal SVRTends to be younger patients
VascularNormal CO, high SVR (endothelial and smooth muscle dysfunction, stiff arteries)Tends to be the ageing population; Board add-on isolated systolic hypertension of the elderly
Renal (volume)Sodium and water retention: high CO and high SVRSalt-sensitive patients; CKD
Neuroendocrine (secondary)Catecholamines (pheochromocytoma), aldosterone (primary aldosteronism), thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism)Treat the cause
  • Primary (essential) hypertension: many small genetic variants in BP control (such as sodium sensitivity), moderated by lifestyle — mostly sodium intake. One teaspoon of salt holds about 2,330 mg of sodium, the whole daily limit. High sodium causes oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction (less nitric oxide) and stiffens large arteries.
  • The baroreceptors reset to whatever pressure is held long enough — why the body defends the high pressure, and why follow-up after starting a drug is in 2–4 weeks.
  • Contexts that change the drug (Section 29): diabetes or CKD with albuminuria, heart failure, a recent MI, AF, pregnancy, osteoporosis or kidney stones, benign prostatic hyperplasia.

What chronic hypertension does

  • Vessels (Gardner): chronic endothelial injury lets plasma proteins pile up under the endothelium (hyaline arteriolosclerosis), smooth muscle proliferates, and arterioles can no longer relax — loss of end-organ autoregulation and, paradoxically, end-organ hypoxia. Malignant hypertension gives hyperplastic “onion-skin” arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis (Section 11).
  • Heart: higher afterload, concentric LVH, diastolic then systolic failure; accelerated coronary disease.
  • Brain: stroke and hemorrhage; cognitive decline. Kidney: nephrosclerosis. Eye: retinopathy (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, hemorrhages and exudates, papilledema). Aorta: aneurysm and dissection.
⚠️ The treatment trap

Because the arterioles are fixed-narrow and autoregulation has shifted, dropping blood pressure quickly to “normal” can under-perfuse the brain — common when elderly patients start drugs for the first time.

Secondary causes: labs and exam clues ★ HY

When to look — new or uncontrolled hypertension plus any of:

  • Drug-resistant or drug-induced hypertension
  • Abrupt onset, or onset before age 30
  • Worsening of previously controlled hypertension
  • Target-organ damage out of proportion to the degree of hypertension
  • Accelerated or malignant hypertension
  • New diastolic hypertension at 65 or older
  • Unprovoked or excessive hypokalemia

Dr. Segal’s 26-year-old with a pressure of 200/110 (120/80 a year before) ticked two boxes at once: onset under 30, and abrupt.

Primary aldosteronism1.4–10% · 6–23%Fatigue, weakness, polyuria and nocturia (hypokalemic nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), polydipsia; no edemaARRLow K, metabolic alkalosis, low renin, high ARR
Thyroid disease1–2% · 1–3%Hyper: tachycardia, AF, weight loss, heat intolerance. Hypo: weight gain, bradycardia, diastolic HTNTSHTSH, free T4
Cushing syndrome0.5% · < 1%Weight gain, striae, skin atrophy, osteopenia24-h urine cortisol, dexamethasone suppressionHigh cortisol, glucose, cholesterol; low K
Pheochromocytoma0.2–0.5% · < 1%Paroxysmal HTN with headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor — “spells”; mucosal fibromas (MEN 2)Plasma metanephrinesHigh metanephrines
Coarctation< 1%Arm–leg BP difference of 20/10 or more; weak or delayed femorals; interscapular murmur; rib notching (Section 27)EchoNot specific
  • Drugs and substances that raise BP: NSAIDs, decongestants (pseudoephedrine, phenylephrine), estrogen contraceptives, glucocorticoids, calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, tacrolimus), erythropoietin, VEGF and tyrosine-kinase inhibitors, antidepressants (SNRIs, MAO inhibitors), amphetamines, cocaine, caffeine, alcohol, licorice, herbal ephedra.
  • Other secondary causes (Gardner): pre-eclampsia (“probably the commonest secondary cause”), polycystic kidney disease, glomerulonephritis, renin-secreting tumours, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, acromegaly, polyarteritis nodosa, raised intracranial pressure.
🩺 The Cushing reflex

High systolic pressure with a normal diastolic and a bradycardia: think of an intracranial cause (raised ICP). The body raises systolic pressure to perfuse the brain; the baroreceptors answer with bradycardia. Board add-on The full Cushing triad adds irregular respirations.

Hypokalemia, renin and aldosterone — reading the pattern

Dr. Segal’s patient: Na⁺ 144, K⁺ 3.1, bicarbonate 29 — unprovoked hypokalemia with a metabolic alkalosis in a young person with abrupt, severe hypertension.

  • What aldosterone does: at the principal cell it binds the mineralocorticoid receptor and makes more ENaC (sodium in), ROMK (potassium out) and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; intercalated cells secrete hydrogen ion. Result: sodium retention, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis.
  • Cortisol can also bind the receptor; 11β-HSD2 protects it by converting cortisol to cortisone. Licorice blocks that enzyme.
ReninAldosteroneThink
LowHighPrimary aldosteronism — autonomous aldosterone
HighHighSecondary: renal artery stenosis, diuretics, a renin-secreting tumour
LowLowA non-aldosterone mineralocorticoid: Liddle syndrome, licorice (AME), Cushing, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (11β- or 17α-hydroxylase), a DOC-secreting tumour

Primary aldosteronism — “something you’re going to see on boards”

  • The most common curable endocrine cause of hypertension: about 5–14% in primary care and 36% of resistant hypertension. Hypokalemia is seen in only a minority — a normal potassium does not exclude it.
  • Subtypes: bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia about 60%, aldosterone-producing (Conn) adenoma about 30%, rarer familial and malignant forms.
  • Who to screen: resistant hypertension, hypokalemia, an adrenal nodule, AF, sleep apnea, early stroke in the family. The 2025 Endocrine Society says everyone with hypertension; the 2025 ACC/AHA says resistant hypertension regardless of potassium. Dr. Segal’s honest answer: “I don’t think so… that’s a little bit much” — he screens when patients start to look resistant.
  • The test: a morning, seated aldosterone-to-renin ratio on an unrestricted diet, after correcting the potassium (hypokalemia suppresses aldosterone). Positive is about ARR 30 or more with aldosterone 10 ng/dL or more. The ratio means something only when renin is suppressed and aldosterone is inappropriately high.
  • Drug interference: beta-blockers suppress renin (false positive); ACEi, ARBs and diuretics raise it (false negative). MRAs must be stopped for 4 weeks; control BP meanwhile with α-blockers, non-dihydropyridine CCBs or hydralazine.
  • Management: if the patient wants and can have surgery, adrenal CT plus adrenal venous sampling to lateralise (CT alone misclassifies). Unilateral: laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral: medical — sodium restriction, spironolactone (eplerenone if gynecomastia), then amiloride; titrate until renin is no longer suppressed.
  • Why it matters beyond the number: against matched essential hypertension, PA raises the odds of atrial fibrillation 3.5-fold, proteinuria 2.7, stroke 2.6, LVH 2.3 and heart failure 2.1. “It’s not something that you just let smolder.”
🎙️ From the recording: the man with the milk jug

A patient arrived holding a milk jug full of his urine to show how much he was passing.

The cause was not the blood pressure but hypokalemia (K⁺ 2.6–2.7) causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. He had a unilateral adenoma; after adrenal venous sampling and adrenalectomy his verdict was “I no longer have to carry a jug.”

Resistant hypertension

  • Definition: BP above goal despite 3 drugs of different classes at maximally tolerated doses, ideally including a diuretic — or controlled only on 4 or more.
  • Exclude pseudo-resistance first: poor technique (the cuff over clothing), white-coat effect (check home or ambulatory readings), non-adherence (the commonest reason; single pills and once-daily dosing help), and interfering drugs and substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, alcohol, stimulants, licorice, high salt).
  • Then look for a secondary cause — the biggest in resistant hypertension are sleep apnea (over 30%) and primary aldosteronism (6–23%).
  • Board add-on The usual fourth drug is spironolactone, which works even without proven aldosteronism.

Hypertensive urgency versus emergency

UrgencyEmergency
BP≥ 180/120≥ 180/120 (any level with acute damage)
Acute target-organ damageNone — headache, epistaxis, anxietyPresent: hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke or intracranial hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhages or papilledema, acute heart failure or pulmonary edema, MI, aortic dissection, acute kidney injury, microangiopathic hemolysis, eclampsia
WhereOutpatient or EDICU
Treatment Board add-onOral drugs; restart missed medicines; lower over hours to daysIV titratable drugs (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol, esmolol; nitroprusside). Lower MAP by no more than about 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100 over the next hours — except aortic dissection (SBP under 120 within 20 minutes, beta-blocker first) and severe pre-eclampsia
  • Malignant hypertension is a medical emergency: retinal hemorrhages, exudates and papilledema with acute kidney injury. The lecture’s classic patient was a man in his 30s to 40s; the kidney shows hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis. Modern drugs make it very treatable.
  • Common triggers: non-adherence, drugs (NSAIDs, cocaine, amphetamines, MAO inhibitor interactions), renal disease, pregnancy, pheochromocytoma, head injury.

Q: A 26-year-old with no history has a BP of 200/110 (120/80 a year ago), potassium 3.1 and bicarbonate 29. Which two features should make you look for a secondary cause, and what is the leading suspect?

Answer

Onset before 30 and abrupt onset (plus unprovoked hypokalemia). With hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, the leading suspect is primary aldosteronism: check an aldosterone-to-renin ratio after correcting the potassium.

Q: A patient on metoprolol has an ARR of 45 with aldosterone 8 ng/dL and renin 0.18 ng/mL/h. Is this primary aldosteronism?

Answer

Not established. The beta-blocker suppresses renin and inflates the ratio (a false positive), and aldosterone is not inappropriately high. The ARR counts only when renin is suppressed and aldosterone is non-suppressed.

Q: A 19-year-old with severe hypertension, potassium 2.9 and metabolic alkalosis has low renin and low aldosterone; his father had early hypertension. Amiloride normalises his BP. Diagnosis?

Answer

Liddle syndrome — a gain-of-function ENaC mutation: mineralocorticoid-like physiology without aldosterone, treated with an ENaC blocker.

Q: A 31-year-old woman with no atherosclerotic risk factors has new hypertension and an epigastric bruit. Renin and aldosterone are both high. Most likely cause and the classic angiogram?

Answer

Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery — renovascular (secondary) hypertension with secondary aldosteronism. The angiogram shows a “string of beads.”

Q: A patient with a posterior fossa tumour develops a BP of 190/80 and a heart rate of 48. Why?

Answer

The Cushing reflex from raised intracranial pressure: systolic pressure rises to perfuse the brain, and the baroreceptors respond with bradycardia.

Q: A patient’s BP is 168/100 on amlodipine, lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide at full doses. What must you check before calling this resistant hypertension, and what are the two commonest secondary causes to look for next?

Answer

Exclude pseudo-resistance: measurement technique, white-coat effect (home or ambulatory readings), adherence, and interfering substances (NSAIDs, decongestants, alcohol, salt). Then screen for obstructive sleep apnea and primary aldosteronism.

Q: Two patients have a BP of 210/124. One has a headache and nothing else; the other is confused with papilledema and a rising creatinine. Classify each and say how fast to lower the pressure.

Answer

The first is hypertensive urgency — oral drugs, lowered over hours to days. The second is a hypertensive emergency (encephalopathy, retinopathy, kidney injury) — ICU and IV drugs, lowering MAP by no more than about 25% in the first hour, because autoregulation has shifted and a sudden drop can cause cerebral ischemia.

Section 29 · Vessels

Hypertension Pharmacology and Electrolyte Adverse Events

Dr. Scully tests the pharmacology domain: for each drug, the name, indication, mechanism, adverse effects, contraindications and interactions. His warning for vignettes: “Pregnant” can be one word buried in the stem, and reading fast you will give an ACE inhibitor. The study-guide objective here is narrower and very testable — which drug does what to which electrolyte — and it sits at the end of this section as one table.

Abbreviations used in this section BP blood pressure · CO cardiac output · SVR systemic vascular resistance · ACE / ACEi angiotensin-converting enzyme / ACE inhibitor · ARB angiotensin II receptor blocker · AT II / AT1R angiotensin II / its type-1 receptor · RAAS / RASi renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system / its inhibitors · CCB calcium channel blocker · DHP dihydropyridine · HCTZ hydrochlorothiazide · NCC sodium–chloride cotransporter · NKCC2 sodium–potassium–2-chloride cotransporter · DCT distal convoluted tubule · TAL thick ascending limb · ENaC epithelial sodium channel · ROMK renal outer medullary potassium channel · MR / MRA mineralocorticoid receptor / its antagonist · AF atrial fibrillation · CKD chronic kidney disease · BPH benign prostatic hyperplasia · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · ACOG American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists · ER extended-release · SIADH syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone · QT QT interval (ventricular depolarisation plus repolarisation) · SGLT2 sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 · DASH Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension · NSAID non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug · ARNI angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor · AT1 angiotensin II type 1 receptor · MI myocardial infarction · AV atrioventricular · IV intravenous

First-line classes and compelling indications

Why one drug is often not enough

  • Lower BP with one drug and two compensations fire: the baroreceptor reflex raises sympathetic outflow (heart rate, contractility, vasoconstriction), and reduced renal perfusion raises renin, with sodium and water retention. Block one branch and the other can bring the pressure back — the rationale for two complementary drugs.
  • Lifestyle for everyone: weight loss (about 1 mm Hg per kg), DASH or Mediterranean diet, low sodium and more potassium, exercise, moderate alcohol, removing causes such as oral contraceptives and stimulants. Each gives about 1–10 mm Hg; together about 10–20.

Choosing initial therapy (2025 guideline)

StageAskThen
Stage 1 (130–139 / 80–89)ASCVD, heart failure, diabetes, CKD, age 65 or more, or 10-year risk ≥ 7.5%?Yes: one drug. No: lifestyle, recheck in 3–6 months
Stage 2 (140–180 / 90–120)Over 75, underweight or frail, or many drug intolerances?Yes: one drug. No: two drugs, ideally in one pill
Severe (> 180 / > 120)Acute target-organ damage?Yes: emergency care (Section 28). No: combination therapy
  • First-line classes: an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a dihydropyridine CCB, or a thiazide.
  • Preferred pair: dihydropyridine CCB + ACE inhibitor or ARB, in one pill for adherence. Three-drug pills are for stepping up, not for starting.
  • The risk calculator (PREVENT) now uses zip code and has removed race; race-agnostic prescribing raised control to about 80% and narrowed the racial gap from 6.3% to 2.8%. (ACE-inhibitor angioedema is still about 5× commoner in Black patients.)

Compelling indications — let the comorbidity choose

ComorbidityChooseWhy
Osteoporosis, calcium kidney stones with hypercalciuria, edemaThiazideRaises calcium reabsorption — less in the urine, more in bone
CKD with albuminuria, diabetesACE inhibitor or ARBRenal protection
Atrial fibrillationBeta-blocker or non-DHP CCB (not both)Rate control at the AV node
Recent MIBeta-blocker, ACEi or ARBSecondary prevention
Heart failureACEi or ARB (or ARNI), beta-blocker, MRA, diureticsMortality benefit (Section 18)
Orthostatic hypotensionDHP CCB, ACEi or ARBAvoid sympatholytics and diuretics
May become pregnantDHP CCBRAAS inhibitors are teratogenic
BPHα1 antagonist (prazosin)Relaxes prostate and vessels; otherwise not first-line

The drugs

ClassMechanismKey adverse effectsContraindications and interactions
ACE inhibitors (-pril: captopril, enalapril — a prodrug, lisinopril — excreted unchanged)Block ACE: no angiotensin II (less vasoconstriction and aldosterone) and bradykinin accumulates (ACE is kininase II)Hyperkalemia, dry cough, angioedema (can recur up to 2 years after stopping; intestinal angioedema), acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosisPregnancy (and planning it); history of angioedema; never with an ARB or aliskiren
ARBs (-sartan: losartan, valsartan)Competitive AT1 receptor antagonist; no bradykinin build-upHyperkalemia, hypotension, kidney injury; little coughPregnancy; with an ACEi; with aliskiren in diabetics
AliskirenDirect renin inhibitorHyperkalemiaNever with another RAAS drug; pregnancy
DHP CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine)Block L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle: lower SVRPeripheral edema (arteriolar dilation raises capillary pressure — diuretics do not fix it; adding an ACEi helps), reflex tachycardia (worst with nifedipine), flushing, headacheSafe in pregnancy; best partner for an ACEi or ARB
Non-DHP CCBs (verapamil — heart; diltiazem — both)Block cardiac and nodal L-type channelsBradycardia, AV block, constipation (verapamil)Never with a beta-blocker (IV verapamil can cause acute heart failure)

Beta-blockersLower heart rate, contractility and reninBradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm (non-selective), masking of hypoglycemiaNot first-line for uncomplicated hypertension; avoid atenolol in pregnancy; not with verapamil or diltiazem; not with clonidine
α1 antagonists (prazosin, doxazosin)Block arteriolar and venous α1First-dose orthostatic hypotensionUse for BPH; not with clonidine
Central α2 agonists (clonidine, methyldopa)Reduce central sympathetic outflowSedation, dry mouth; clonidine rebound hypertension if stopped suddenly Board add-onNot with another sympatholytic
HydralazineDirect arteriolar dilatorReflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus Board add-onAcute use in pregnancy
🧠 A dry cough predicts angioedema

Nearly every patient who develops ACE-inhibitor angioedema had the cough first. Counsel patients, and switch a persistent cough to an ARB, which keeps the renin–angiotensin benefit without bradykinin build-up. Early laryngeal signs are hoarseness and inspiratory stridor.

Combinations to avoid

  • ACEi + ARB, or either + aliskiren — stacked hyperkalemia, kidney injury, hypotension.
  • Beta-blocker + verapamil or diltiazem — additive nodal and myocardial depression.
  • Two sympatholytics (α1 antagonist + clonidine, beta-blocker + clonidine) — one branch hit twice, side effects stacked.
  • ACEi or ARB in anyone who may become pregnant.

Hypertension in pregnancy

✅

Use

  • Labetalol — β1/β2 + α1 block; the α1 block prevents reflex vasoconstriction, so placental flow is preserved (metoprolol would reduce it). Avoid in asthma.
  • Nifedipine ER (and amlodipine).
  • α-methyldopa — central α2 agonist; the longest safety record, less effective.
  • Hydralazine — acute use only.
⛔

Avoid

  • ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren — fetal kidney toxicity and low amniotic fluid (worst in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters; if she is already on one, switch — no need to panic).
  • Nitroprusside.
  • Spironolactone — anti-androgenic.
  • Atenolol — low birth weight.

ACOG: hypertension in pregnancy is ≥ 140/90 twice, 4 hours apart; severe range ≥ 160/110; chronic if before pregnancy or before 20 weeks.

Electrolyte disturbances by drug ★ HY

The key mechanism for almost every row: more sodium delivered to the principal cell is taken up through ENaC alone, leaving the lumen negative, so potassium (through ROMK) and hydrogen ion are secreted. Anything that blocks aldosterone, its receptor or ENaC does the opposite and keeps potassium and hydrogen ion in.

DrugK⁺Na⁺Ca²⁺Mg²⁺Acid–baseOtherWhy
Thiazides↓↓ (the commonest cause of drug-induced hyponatremia Board add-on)↑↓Metabolic alkalosis↑ uric acid, glucose, lipidsNCC block; lower cell sodium drives more basolateral Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange, so calcium is reabsorbed; distal sodium delivery wastes K⁺ and H⁺
Loop diuretics (furosemide)↓↓↓↓Metabolic alkalosis↑ uric acid; ototoxicityNKCC2 block removes the lumen-positive potential that drives Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ reabsorption between TAL cells. “Loops lose calcium”
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren↑———Mild acidosis↑ creatinineLess angiotensin II, less aldosterone, less ENaC-driven K⁺ secretion
Spironolactone, eplerenone↑↓ mild——Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosisGynecomastia (spironolactone)Receptor block: fewer sodium channels; K⁺ and H⁺ retained
Amiloride, triamterene↑———Metabolic acidosis—ENaC block removes the driving force for K⁺ and H⁺ secretion
Sacubitril/valsartan↑————HypotensionThe ARB component
Beta-blockers (non-selective) Board add-on↑ mild————Mask hypoglycemiaLess β2-driven K⁺ uptake into cells; less renin
SGLT2 inhibitors Board add-on————Euglycemic ketoacidosis (rare)Volume depletionNatriuresis and glucosuria
Acetazolamide Board add-on↓———Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis—Proximal bicarbonate loss
🔑 Preventing electrolyte adverse events
  • Check potassium and creatinine 1–2 weeks after starting or raising an ACEi, ARB, MRA or ENaC blocker, and after adding a diuretic.
  • Pair drugs whose potassium effects cancel — a thiazide with an ACEi or ARB; but potassium can still go either way, so monitor.
  • Never two RAAS blockers; avoid potassium supplements and NSAIDs with them; be careful in CKD.
  • Watch sodium in older women on thiazides; watch magnesium on loops, and remember low potassium or magnesium makes digoxin toxic and the QT long.
  • Board add-on The “hyperGLUC” thiazide hook: hyperGlycemia, hyperLipidemia, hyperUricemia, hyperCalcemia.

Q: A 60-year-old with a confirmed BP of 152/96, not frail, no drug intolerances. One drug or two, and which?

Answer

Stage 2, under 75, not frail: two drugs, ideally one pill — a dihydropyridine CCB plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (an ACEi or ARB plus a thiazide is also acceptable).

Q: A patient taking lisinopril and losartan (prescribed by different doctors) presents with weakness and peaked T waves. Mechanism?

Answer

Double RAAS blockade: less aldosterone, so less ENaC-driven potassium secretion — hyperkalemia. ACEi plus ARB is a combination to avoid.

Q: A hypertensive patient has recurrent calcium oxalate stones and osteopenia. Which antihypertensive helps all three, and how? What electrolyte changes will it cause?

Answer

A thiazide. NCC block lowers cell sodium in the distal tubule, driving more basolateral Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange and more calcium reabsorption. Expect low sodium, low potassium, metabolic alkalosis, high calcium and high uric acid.

Q: A patient on furosemide for heart failure has a potassium of 2.9, a magnesium of 1.3, a low calcium and a bicarbonate of 33. Explain each.

Answer

NKCC2 block removes the lumen-positive potential in the thick ascending limb, so calcium and magnesium are not reabsorbed between cells. Extra sodium reaching the principal cell is taken up through ENaC, leaving the lumen negative, so potassium and hydrogen ion are secreted — a hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

Q: Which first-line class most often causes ankle edema, and why does a diuretic not fix it well? Which CCB causes the most reflex tachycardia?

Answer

Dihydropyridine CCBs: arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure — it is not volume overload, so diuretics help little; adding an ACEi or ARB does. Nifedipine causes the most reflex tachycardia.

Q: A 27-year-old at 16 weeks of pregnancy has a BP of 160/114 on two readings. Classify it, name three drugs to use, and four to avoid.

Answer

Chronic hypertension (before 20 weeks), in the severe range. Use labetalol, nifedipine ER or α-methyldopa (hydralazine acutely). Avoid ACE inhibitors, ARBs and aliskiren, nitroprusside, spironolactone and atenolol. Watch for superimposed pre-eclampsia.

Q: A man on spironolactone for resistant hypertension develops tender breast enlargement and a potassium of 5.8. Explain both, and what would you switch to?

Answer

Spironolactone blocks androgen receptors (gynecomastia) and the mineralocorticoid receptor (less ENaC, so potassium is retained). Switch to eplerenone for the gynecomastia — but it still raises potassium, so reduce or stop other potassium-raising drugs and monitor.
