Section 30 · Vessels

Dyslipidemias: Types and Pathophysiology

Dr. Scully’s point in reviewing the dyslipidemias: much of the stigma is about diet, but lipid metabolism has many genetic determinants that lifestyle cannot fix, and many dyslipidemias are secondary to something else that can be treated. This section covers how lipoproteins move, the familial disorders the boards use, the secondary causes, and the diet. The drugs are in Section 31.

Abbreviations used in this section TG triglycerides · LDL / HDL / VLDL / IDL low-, high-, very-low-, intermediate-density lipoprotein · LDL-C LDL cholesterol · apo apolipoprotein · LPL lipoprotein lipase · HL hepatic lipase · LCAT lecithin–cholesterol acyltransferase · CETP cholesteryl ester transfer protein · ABCA1 ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 · FH familial hypercholesterolemia · AD / AR autosomal dominant / recessive · Lp(a) lipoprotein(a) · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · MI myocardial infarction · DASH Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension · PREDIMED the Mediterranean diet trial · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · PCSK9 proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 · CV cardiovascular

Lipoprotein metabolism

Lipids are insoluble, so they travel as lipoproteins: a core of triglyceride and cholesteryl ester inside a coat of phospholipid, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins.

ParticleMade byCarriesKey apolipoproteinsWhat it does
ChylomicronIntestineDietary TGB-48, C-II, EDelivers dietary fat to muscle and fat (LPL, activated by apoC-II, frees fatty acids); the remnant goes to the liver via apoE
VLDLLiverHepatic TGB-100, C-II, EDelivers liver-made TG to tissues; becomes IDL
IDLFrom VLDLTG and cholesterolB-100, EReturns to the liver or is trimmed by hepatic lipase into LDL
LDL — “lethal”From IDLCholesterolB-100 (binds the LDL receptor)Delivers cholesterol to tissues; cleared by the hepatic LDL receptor. Enters the injured intima and is oxidised — the raw material of the plaque (Section 11)
HDL — “healthy”Liver and intestineCholesterolA-I (activates LCAT)Reverse cholesterol transport from the tissues back to the liver; a reservoir of apoC and apoE

Table built from First Aid Board add-on; the lecture showed the AMBOSS transport figure below.

  • Why LDL matters most: the hepatic LDL receptor is the main exit for LDL from the blood. Anything that lowers liver cholesterol (statins) or protects the receptor (PCSK9 inhibitors) raises LDL-receptor numbers and lowers serum LDL.
  • PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor and sends it for degradation instead of recycling. People with loss-of-function PCSK9 mutations have low LDL and less cardiovascular disease — the genetic clue that produced a drug class.
  • Too much LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; macrophages eat it and become foam cells; plaques form and rupture, giving a site for thrombosis — why lipid drugs and antiplatelet drugs go together.

Describing the dyslipidemias

The primary dyslipidemias (slide 3 — “not something I want you to memorise”)

  • Hypercholesterolemia (high LDL): familial (LDL-receptor defects), familial defective apoB-100, polygenic.
  • Hypertriglyceridemia: familial; familial LPL deficiency; apoC-II deficiency.
  • Mixed: familial combined; dysbetalipoproteinemia; lysosomal acid lipase deficiency.
  • HDL disorders (rare): apoA-I, ABCA1 (Tangier disease), LCAT defects.

The familial dyslipidemias, board version ★ HY Board add-on

TypeInheritance and defectRaisedClinical picturePicture
I — hyperchylomicronemiaAR; LPL or apoC-II deficiencyChylomicrons, TGPancreatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, eruptive xanthomas, creamy serum; no extra atherosclerosis
II — familial hypercholesterolemiaAD; absent or defective LDL receptor, or defective apoB-100 (IIa: LDL; IIb: LDL and VLDL)LDLHeterozygotes (1 in 500): cholesterol about 300; homozygotes 700 or more, MI before 20. Tendon (Achilles) xanthomas, corneal arcus
III — dysbetalipoproteinemiaAR; apoE (“type thrEE”)Chylomicron and VLDL remnantsPremature atherosclerosis; palmar and tuberoeruptive xanthomas. Treated with a fibrate (lecture indication)
IV — hypertriglyceridemiaAD; hepatic overproduction of VLDLVLDL, TGTG over 1,000 can cause acute pancreatitis; linked to insulin resistance

Familial hypercholesterolemia at the bedside

  • Tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus before 45 are highly specific for FH; xanthelasma has low specificity (Dr. Watkins).
  • Any of these should prompt lipid testing, an FH clinical score and cascade screening of relatives. Eruptive xanthomas point instead to very high triglycerides.
  • Measure lipoprotein(a) once, especially with a family history of early disease.

Pathophysiology and the secondary causes

Treat the secondary cause and the lipids may follow — a full work-up can avoid lipid drugs altogether.

Raises triglyceridesRaises cholesterol
Diabetes (insulin resistance: more hepatic VLDL, less LPL activity)Hypothyroidism (fewer LDL receptors)
Chronic renal failureNephrotic syndrome (the liver over-makes lipoproteins as albumin is lost)
HypothyroidismAnorexia nervosa
Alcohol excessCholestasis and obstructive liver disease
Pregnancy, oral estrogen, lipodystrophyCorticosteroids
Antihypertensives: beta-blockers, diureticsProtease inhibitors
Glucocorticoids, protease inhibitors, stress, sepsis, acute hepatitis, SLE, glycogen storage diseaseAcute intermittent porphyria
  • Deciding to treat depends mostly on the patient’s calculated cardiovascular risk (PREVENT or pooled-cohort, Section 28), and matters most near the thresholds. Board add-on Statins regardless of risk score for clinical ASCVD, LDL 190 or more, and diabetes aged 40–75.
  • Which lipid, which drug (slide 6): high LDL — a statin; high TG — diet, omega-3 fatty acids, fibrates; low HDL — niacin (fibrates a little), though treating isolated low HDL is contested.

The dietary approach

  • Diet can lower total cholesterol by about 25%, depending on adherence and the genetic basis (Dr. Scully). Lifestyle will not be enough for everyone, so drugs are widely used.
  • The full diet evidence — the 2019 primary-prevention nutrition recommendations, the Mediterranean diet and PREDIMED (about 30% fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths), and DASH and sodium — is in Section 4. The points for lipids:
Lipid problemDiet
High LDLReplace saturated fat with mono- and polyunsaturated fat; avoid trans fats; more fibre (oats, legumes), nuts and plant sterols Board add-on; dietary cholesterol matters less than saturated fat — “eggs are fine” (Dr. Qazi)
High triglyceridesCut refined carbohydrate, sugar-sweetened drinks and alcohol; lose weight; more cold-water fish (omega-3); very high TG (familial chylomicronemia) needs a very low-fat diet Board add-on
Low HDLExercise, weight loss, stopping smoking
EveryoneMediterranean or DASH pattern: vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, whole grains, fish; olive oil for fat; little processed meat; plus 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week

Q: A patient with new hypercholesterolemia also has fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain. What should you check before starting a statin, and why?

Answer

Thyroid function. Hypothyroidism reduces LDL-receptor expression and is a secondary cause of hypercholesterolemia; treating it may correct the lipids.

Q: A 34-year-old has Achilles tendon thickening, corneal arcus and an LDL of 260. His father died of an MI at 42. Diagnosis, defect, inheritance — and what should happen to his relatives?

Answer

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type II): absent or defective LDL receptors (or apoB-100), autosomal dominant. Tendon xanthomas and arcus before 45 are highly specific. His first-degree relatives need cascade screening.

Q: A child has recurrent pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, hepatosplenomegaly and milky serum. Which lipoprotein is raised, what is the defect, and is atherosclerosis risk increased?

Answer

Type I hyperchylomicronemia — lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency, autosomal recessive. Chylomicrons and TG are raised. Atherosclerosis risk is not increased; the danger is pancreatitis. Treat with a very low-fat diet.

Q: Which two antihypertensive classes are listed as causes of secondary hypertriglyceridemia, and name two causes of secondary hypercholesterolemia?

Answer

Beta-blockers and diuretics. Secondary hypercholesterolemia: hypothyroidism and nephrotic syndrome (also cholestasis, anorexia, corticosteroids, protease inhibitors).

Q: How does a loss-of-function mutation in PCSK9 protect against heart disease?

Answer

PCSK9 normally sends the LDL receptor for degradation. Without it, receptors recycle to the hepatocyte surface, more LDL is cleared, serum LDL is lifelong low and cardiovascular disease is less common — the observation behind the PCSK9-inhibitor drugs.

Q: A patient with a triglyceride level of 480 and a normal LDL asks what to change in his diet. What do you advise?

Answer

Cut refined carbohydrate, sugary drinks and alcohol, lose weight, and eat more cold-water fish (omega-3s), within a Mediterranean-style diet; exercise. Look for secondary causes (diabetes, alcohol, hypothyroidism, drugs such as beta-blockers, thiazides and estrogen).

Section 31 · Vessels

Lipid-Lowering Drugs: Interactions and Adverse Events

Dr. Scully’s refresher worked three cases: a statin for high LDL, a fibrate for high triglycerides and low HDL after an infarct, and a PCSK9 inhibitor when nothing else reached goal. The study-guide objectives here are specific — drug–drug interactions and how to prevent adverse events — and they come down to one enzyme (CYP3A4), one protein-binding interaction (warfarin) and one combination (statin plus gemfibrozil).

Statins, ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, fibrates, niacin and the rest

Statins — first choice for high LDL

  1. A statin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
  2. Hepatocyte cholesterol falls, and the SREBP signal switches on.
  3. LDL-receptor expression rises on hepatocytes.
  4. LDL is pulled out of the serum to replace the cell’s stores.
StatinMetabolismIntensity
LovastatinCYP3A4Low–moderate
SimvastatinCYP3A4Moderate
AtorvastatinCYP3A4High
FluvastatinCYP2C9Low
PitavastatinCYP2C9 (limited)Moderate
PravastatinNon-CYP — fewer interactionsLow–moderate
RosuvastatinNon-CYP (minimal) — fewer interactionsHigh
  • The two high-intensity statins — atorvastatin and rosuvastatin — are for secondary prevention after an MI and for high-risk patients.
  • Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are the “special” non-CYP statins with fewer drug interactions.
  • Board add-on Potency hook: “Flo Loves Prague Since A Tour of Russia” — fluva < lova < prava < simva < atorva < rosuva.
  • Indications: hypercholesterolemia and mixed hyperlipidemia; used more broadly in practice (they lower TG and raise HDL a little).

The other classes

The step-up sequence

  1. Lifestyle and treat secondary causes (Section 30).
  2. A statin — high-intensity (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin) after an MI or with high risk.
  3. LDL still above goal: add ezetimibe (or, less often, a bile acid sequestrant).
  4. Still above goal on a maximal statin plus ezetimibe: a PCSK9 inhibitor. Patients normally must fail first-line drugs first; costs are falling.
  5. High TG or low HDL on a statin: omega-3s or a fibrate (fenofibrate if combining with a statin).

CombinationResultMechanismWhat to do
Statin (lova-, simva-, atorvastatin) + CYP3A4 inhibitor — clarithromycin, erythromycin, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, diltiazem and verapamil, grapefruit juice Board add-onMyopathy, rhabdomyolysisLess statin metabolism, higher levelsUse pravastatin or rosuvastatin (non-CYP), lower the dose, or pause the statin during a short antibiotic course
Statin + fibrateMore myopathy, myositis and rhabdomyolysisAdditive muscle toxicity; Board add-on gemfibrozil also blocks statin glucuronidation and raises levelsAvoid gemfibrozil; pair a statin with fenofibrate; watch for muscle pain

Preventing adverse events

  • Statin myopathy: it happens, but less often than first thought, and guidance now advises not front-loading counselling about it, because of the nocebo effect. Severe muscle pain with tea-coloured urine means rhabdomyolysis — stop the drug and work it up (CK, creatinine, urinalysis).
  • Board add-on Baseline lipids and LFTs; check CK only if symptoms; risk rises with age, hypothyroidism, kidney disease, high doses and interacting drugs. For intolerance: lower the dose, switch statin, alternate-day dosing, or add ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor.
  • Hepatotoxicity Board add-on: statins (and niacin, fibrates) can raise transaminases; avoid in active liver disease.
  • Niacin flushing Board add-on: take aspirin 30 minutes before, use extended-release, take with food and avoid hot drinks or alcohol at dose time.
  • Fibrate gallstones and myopathy: choose fenofibrate with a statin; avoid in kidney or liver failure.
  • Bile acid sequestrants: space other drugs; avoid if TG is over 300–500; supplement fat-soluble vitamins.
  • Pregnancy Board add-on: statins are avoided; stop before conception.

Q: How does inhibiting cholesterol synthesis lower serum LDL?

Answer

Lower hepatocyte cholesterol switches on more LDL-receptor expression, so the liver clears more LDL from the blood.

Q: A patient on simvastatin is prescribed clarithromycin and a week later has severe muscle pain and dark urine. What happened, and which two statins would have avoided it?

Answer

Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising simvastatin levels and causing rhabdomyolysis. Pravastatin and rosuvastatin are not CYP-metabolised.

Q: A patient on warfarin is started on gemfibrozil and develops bleeding gums with a high INR. Mechanism? And which fibrate is the safer partner for a statin?

Answer

Fibrates displace warfarin from plasma-protein binding sites, raising free warfarin. With a statin, fenofibrate is safer — gemfibrozil carries the higher rhabdomyolysis risk.

Q: Why does ezetimibe lower LDL well with a statin but poorly on its own?

Answer

Blocking absorption lowers intracellular cholesterol, so the liver up-regulates its own synthesis and LDL drifts back. The statin blocks that synthesis.

Q: A 61-year-old a year after a STEMI is on simvastatin and fish oil. HDL is 32, LDL 106, triglycerides 354. What class addresses the TG and HDL, and what else would you change?

Answer

A fibrate (PPAR-α activator) lowers TG and raises HDL — fenofibrate rather than gemfibrozil alongside a statin. After an MI he should also be on a high-intensity statin (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin); an LDL of 106 is above secondary-prevention goals.

Q: LDL is still above goal on maximal atorvastatin plus ezetimibe. What comes next, and how do the two injectable forms differ?

Answer

A PCSK9 inhibitor. The monoclonal antibodies bind circulating PCSK9; inclisiran is an siRNA that reduces PCSK9 production. Both let LDL receptors recycle. The main adverse effect is injection-site reactions.

Q: A patient on cholestyramine develops easy bruising and a prolonged INR, and his levothyroxine seems to have stopped working. Explain both, and how to prevent them.

Answer

Bile acid sequestrants cause fat-soluble vitamin (K) malabsorption, and they bind other drugs in the gut. Give other medicines 1 hour before or 4 hours after the resin, and supplement vitamin K.

Section 32 · Vessels

Aneurysms and Dissections

Dr. Gardner’s theme again: a small weakness in a high-pressure pipe, given decades, becomes a catastrophe. An aneurysm is the wall stretching outward; a dissection is the wall splitting from within. The vascular surgeon added two things he promised would be on the test — the aneurysm surveillance chart (“memorize that chart”) and what to do with type A versus type B dissection.

Abbreviations used in this section AAA abdominal aortic aneurysm · TAA thoracic aortic aneurysm · EVAR endovascular aneurysm repair · TEVAR thoracic endovascular aortic repair · CT / CTA computed tomography / CT angiography · US ultrasound · TEE transesophageal echo · MRA magnetic resonance angiography · IMA / SMA inferior / superior mesenteric artery · EDS Ehlers–Danlos syndrome · TGF-β transforming growth factor beta · MMP matrix metalloproteinase · SAH subarachnoid hemorrhage · MI myocardial infarction · AR aortic regurgitation · HTN hypertension · COPD chronic obstructive pulmonary disease · CSF cerebrospinal fluid · USPSTF US Preventive Services Task Force · SBP systolic blood pressure · HR heart rate · MAP mean arterial pressure · GI gastrointestinal · ICU intensive care unit · BP blood pressure · IV intravenous · PET positron emission tomography

Definitions, gross and microscopic features

TermDefinition
True aneurysm — saccularAn outpouching on one side of the wall; all three layers intact
True aneurysm — fusiformCircumferential dilation of a segment. An AAA is a dilation over 3 cm (or 1.5× normal) Board add-on
False aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm)The wall is breached (trauma, a catheter puncture, local disease); an extravascular hematoma is held in by adventitia and surrounding tissue — the layers themselves have not dilated
DissectionBlood enters through an intimal tear and tracks within the media, splitting the wall into a true and a false lumen behind an intimal flap

Why vessel walls give way

🧵

Weak material

  • Poor connective tissue: Marfan (fibrillin-1), vascular Ehlers–Danlos (collagen III), altered TGF-β signalling (Section 33).
🔥

Remodelling

  • Inflammation and matrix turnover: MMP activity, chronic plaque inflammation, hypertension lifting damaged endothelium.
🩸

Ischemia of the wall

  • Thick walls need their own blood supply, the vasa vasorum; narrow it and the media dies back.
🦠

Infection

  • Tertiary syphilis inflames and obliterates the vasa vasorum of the thoracic aorta; a mycotic aneurysm is an infected wall (often from endocarditis emboli).

Microscopic features Board add-on

  • Thoracic aneurysm and dissection: cystic medial degeneration — loss and fragmentation of elastic fibres and smooth muscle cells, with pools of mucoid (proteoglycan) ground substance in the media. Seen in Marfan, with hypertension and with age.
  • Abdominal aneurysm: transmural inflammation and extracellular-matrix degradation (MMPs), a thinned media, overlying atherosclerosis and often laminated mural thrombus.
  • Syphilitic aortitis: obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum with plasma cells, giving a wrinkled “tree-bark” intima.

Locations and pathogenesis

LocationKey factsMain causePicture
Abdominal aortic (AAA)The most common. Lower aorta, below the renal arteries, often into the iliac bifurcation. Risk: smoking (strongest), hypertension, age, male sex, family historyAtherosclerosis / degenerative
Thoracic aortic (TAA)Ascending, arch or descending; the ascending is strongly tied to Marfan; also hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, tertiary syphilis. Root dilation causes ARConnective tissue disease / cystic medial degeneration
Cerebral “berry”Branch points of the circle of Willis; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage. Board add-on Polycystic kidney disease, coarctation, EDSPrimarily congenital
Splenic arteryWomen, multiple pregnancies; a “double rupture” (into the lesser sac, then free); famous for rupturing in pregnancy. Repair if over 2 cm, symptomatic, or in a woman of child-bearing ageDegenerative, hormonal
PoplitealPrimarily men; a pulsatile mass behind the knee. It embolises or thromboses rather than rupturing. Repair if over 2 cm or symptomatic. Board add-on Bilateral in about half, and about a third have an AAAAtherosclerosis
VentricularA late complication of MI: a scarred, non-contractile wall bulging (Section 15)Post-infarct scar

Abdominal aortic aneurysm: screening and surgical thresholds ★ HY

  • Mostly asymptomatic — found as a pulsatile abdominal mass or by chance. Symptoms: abdominal or back pain, early satiety, hydronephrosis.
  • Rupture: severe back or abdominal pain, a pulsatile mass and shock. Board add-on Straight to the operating room if unstable.
  • Four complications: rupture, embolisation, dissection, fistulisation (aortoduodenal or aortoenteric).
  • Grows about 0.2–0.3 cm a year. Risk of rupture is raised by hypertension, COPD, female sex, smoking and steroids.
  • Screening: men 65–70 and those with a family history (slide). Board add-on USPSTF: a one-time ultrasound in men 65–75 who have ever smoked.
  • Imaging: an eggshell calcified rim on X-ray; ultrasound for screening and surveillance; CT with contrast is the gold standard.
Diameter (asymptomatic)Plan
< 4.5 cmUltrasound every 6 months
4.5–5.0 cmUltrasound every 3 months (chart: 3–6) — “you’re in the danger zone”
5.0–5.5 cmRepair if female, familial, proven rapid growth, a positive PET or high serum markers; otherwise follow every 3–6 months
> 5.5 cmRepair (open or endovascular) — rupture risk 3–15% (slide)
🔑 Indications for surgery

Symptomatic at any size · over 5.5 cm · growth of more than 5 mm in 6 months · an eccentric or saccular shape. A non-compliant patient who will not change their behaviour may be operated on sooner. And always: stop smoking.

Repair and its complications

  • EVAR needs suitable anatomy: an aortic neck over 15 mm long, an angle under 60°, big enough access arteries and calcification under 50% of the circumference. Fenestrated and branched grafts keep the renals and SMA open. Open repair is now mostly for those who cannot have a stent graft.
  • Complications: kidney injury, leg ischemia, ischemic colitis, spinal cord ischemia, sexual dysfunction, endograft migration or leak (endoleak — why EVAR needs lifelong imaging Board add-on).
  • The classic ICU question: the night after aortic repair, an unstable patient on norepinephrine passes bloody diarrhea in the first 12–24 hours — ischemic colitis of the sigmoid from lost IMA flow; confirm with sigmoidoscopy. At surgery, pulsatile back-bleeding from the cut IMA means good SMA collaterals (tie it); a weak trickle means the colon depends on it (re-implant).
  • Graft infection (dull pain, fever, a high white count): antibiotics, remove the graft, extra-anatomic bypass. Aortoenteric fistula: a known graft plus GI bleeding, often a small “herald bleed” first.

Dissection: classification and management ★ HY

What happens

  1. An intimal tear — on a diseased, hypertensive wall, or from blunt deceleration trauma.
  2. Blood tracks through the media, forward and sometimes back toward the aortic valve ring.
  3. Three bad endings (Gardner): breach of the adventitia with fatal hemorrhage; extension into the great vessels or coronary ostia, giving stroke or MI; or re-entry and a chronic “double-barrelled aorta”.
  • Rupture is actually rare; the usual harm is ischemia downstream as the flap cuts off branches — the renals, the gut, the legs, the brain. Dr. Ciraulo: “I think more lethal than atherosclerotic disease.”
  • Ascending dissections can also cause acute AR and tamponade.
  • Timing: acute under 2 weeks (complicated or uncomplicated); chronic over 2 weeks.

Who, and how it presents

  • Risks: hypertension (Board add-on the strongest risk factor), aortic wall disease (Marfan, EDS, Loeys–Dietz, Turner), bicuspid aortic valve, cocaine (“the most dramatic hypertensive crisis”), pregnancy, trauma.
  • Excruciating, tearing chest pain that moves to the back and downward as it propagates — “someone’s trying to rip my back apart”, against the infarct’s “elephant on my chest”.
  • Board add-on A pulse or BP difference of more than 20 mm Hg between the arms, a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray, a new AR murmur.
  • It can present as a stroke: Dr. McGrath’s 48-year-old security guard collapsed with right-sided weakness, and the stroke CT angiogram found a type A dissection occluding the left carotid.
  • “It’s not time to break out the manipulation box. That’s the time to get a CAT scan.”
DeBakeyExtentShareStanfordManagement
IStarts at the root, extends into the descending aorta60%A — involves the ascending aortaEmergent open surgical repair, whatever the hour (root ± valve; the arch with re-implanted head vessels; hypothermic circulatory arrest with cerebral perfusion)
IIAscending aorta only10–15%
IIIStarts distal to the left subclavian25–30%BMedical blood-pressure control; “if you control the hypertension, sometimes these dissections will heal.” Complications (malperfusion, rupture, expansion, uncontrollable pain or BP) — TEVAR

Diagnosis and medical management

  • CT angiography of the chest and abdomen; TEE when the patient is unstable Board add-on. Exclude dissection before giving anticoagulants or thrombolytics to a patient with chest pain.
  • Board add-on “Impulse control”: an IV beta-blocker first (esmolol, labetalol) to a heart rate of about 60 and SBP 100–120, before any vasodilator such as nitroprusside — a vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia, which raises the shear force (dP/dt) on the aortic wall. Opioids for pain.
  • Paraplegia after descending repair: the clamp cuts flow to the artery of Adamkiewicz, supplying the spinal cord. Prevention: shorter clamp times or aortic bypass, and a lumbar CSF drain to protect cord perfusion. (The recording placed the artery around T4–T8; it usually arises at T9–T12 Board add-on.)

Q: An asymptomatic 70-year-old man who smoked for 40 years has a 4.8 cm AAA on ultrasound. What is the plan?

Answer

Ultrasound surveillance every 3 months (the 4.5–5.0 cm band), plus risk-factor control — above all, stop smoking.

Q: A 68-year-old woman has a 5.2 cm AAA; her brother died of a ruptured aneurysm. Repair or watch?

Answer

Repair. In the 5.0–5.5 cm band, female sex and a familial aneurysm are on the chart’s list of reasons to operate.

Q: A hypertensive 60-year-old has sudden tearing pain between the shoulder blades. CTA shows a dissection starting just beyond the left subclavian artery and running to the iliacs. He is stable, with good pulses and kidney function. Classify and manage.

Answer

DeBakey III, Stanford B, uncomplicated — medical blood-pressure control: an IV beta-blocker first (heart rate about 60), then a vasodilator if needed, to an SBP of 100–120. TEVAR if it becomes complicated.

Q: A tall 25-year-old with long fingers and a dislocated lens has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back and a new diastolic murmur. Diagnosis, defective protein, and management?

Answer

A type A aortic dissection, with aortic regurgitation from root involvement, in Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1). Emergency surgery.

Q: Twenty hours after open AAA repair, a patient on norepinephrine passes bloody stool. Diagnosis, test, and what intraoperative finding should have prompted re-implanting the IMA?

Answer

Ischemic colitis of the sigmoid — sigmoidoscopy. The IMA should be re-implanted when its back-bleeding is weak (poor collaterals from the SMA); pulsatile back-bleeding means it can be tied.

Q: Which part of the aorta does tertiary syphilis affect, how, and what is the microscopic lesion of a Marfan thoracic aneurysm?

Answer

The thoracic (ascending) aorta — obliterative inflammation of the vasa vasorum starves the media (a “tree-bark” intima). Marfan aneurysms show cystic medial degeneration: fragmented elastic fibres and mucoid pools in the media.

Q: After repair of a descending thoracic aneurysm, a patient cannot move his legs. Mechanism and prevention?

Answer

Spinal cord ischemia from lost flow through the artery of Adamkiewicz during cross-clamping. Prevent it with short clamp times or aortic bypass, and a lumbar CSF drain.

Section 33 · Vessels

Connective Tissue Disorders of the Aorta

Dr. Gardner’s first reason why a vessel wall gives way is weak material: a faulty structural protein, or faulty signalling around it. Given decades of high-pressure flow, that weakness shows up as an aortic root aneurysm, a dissection or an arterial rupture — often in someone young. The lecture compared Marfan with vascular Ehlers–Danlos; Loeys–Dietz and Turner complete the board list.

Abbreviations used in this section EDS Ehlers–Danlos syndrome · vEDS vascular EDS · LDS Loeys–Dietz syndrome · FBN1 fibrillin-1 gene · COL3A1 collagen type III alpha-1 gene · TGF-β transforming growth factor beta · TGFBR1/2 TGF-β receptor genes · AD autosomal dominant · AR aortic regurgitation · MVP mitral valve prolapse · BAV bicuspid aortic valve · ARB angiotensin receptor blocker · MRA / CTA magnetic resonance / CT angiography · 45,X the Turner karyotype

Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz and Turner: gene to complication ★ HY

MarfanVascular EDS (type IV)Loeys–Dietz Board add-onTurner Board add-on
Gene / defectFBN1 — fibrillin-1 (scaffold for elastic fibres; excess TGF-β activity)COL3A1 — collagen III (α1 chain)TGFBR1/2 and other TGF-β pathway genes45,X
InheritanceADADADSporadic
Aortic root dilationVery common, progressive (root and ascending)Fairly commonCommon, aggressiveAscending dilation; with BAV

DissectionLifetime risk up to 30%; type A most commonSignificant; can be spontaneousDissects at smaller diametersIncreased, especially with BAV, coarctation or pregnancy

Body cluesTall, long limbs, arachnodactyly, upward lens dislocation, pectus, high-arched palate, joint laxity, pneumothoraxThin translucent skin with visible veins, easy bruising, characteristic face; less joint laxity than classic EDSBifid uvula or cleft palate, hypertelorism, arterial tortuosity, club footShort, webbed neck, broad chest, streak ovaries, horseshoe kidney

The Marfan and vascular EDS columns follow Dr. Gardner’s slide; the Loeys–Dietz and Turner columns are board add-ons.

Why the aorta fails

  • Fibrillin-1 builds the microfibrils that scaffold elastic fibres, and it normally sequesters TGF-β. In Marfan the elastic lamellae fragment and TGF-β signalling rises, giving cystic medial degeneration of the root (Section 32). Board add-on
  • Collagen III gives hollow organs and arteries their tensile strength; in vascular EDS medium arteries, bowel and uterus can rupture without warning.
  • The aortic root stretches, the cusps are pulled apart (aortic regurgitation), and the weak media dissects — usually type A.
  • A bicuspid aortic valve is itself an aortopathy: every patient needs the ascending aorta imaged (Section 24).

Management Board add-on

  • Regular imaging of the aortic root and ascending aorta (echo, then MRA or CTA), and screening of first-degree relatives.
  • Slow the dilation: a beta-blocker (less shear stress) and/or an ARB (losartan), which also damps TGF-β signalling.
  • Prophylactic aortic root replacement before it ruptures — in Marfan typically around a 5.0 cm root (earlier with rapid growth or a family history of dissection), and at smaller sizes in Loeys–Dietz. A valve-sparing root operation keeps the patient’s own valve.
  • Avoid contact sports and heavy isometric lifting; avoid fluoroquinolones Board add-on; plan pregnancy carefully (high dissection risk).
  • Vascular EDS: avoid invasive procedures where possible — even angiography can tear vessels.
  • Turner syndrome: “suspect Turner? Get an echo” for coarctation and BAV; image the aorta before and during any pregnancy.

Q: A tall 25-year-old with long fingers and an upward lens dislocation has a 4.9 cm aortic root and mitral valve prolapse. Diagnosis, gene, and how do you reduce his dissection risk?

Answer

Marfan syndrome, FBN1 (fibrillin-1), autosomal dominant. Serial root imaging, a beta-blocker and/or losartan, avoiding contact sports, and prophylactic root replacement at about 5.0 cm (sooner with rapid growth or a family history of dissection).

Q: A 28-year-old with thin translucent skin and easy bruising dies of a spontaneous splenic artery rupture. Her mother died of a ruptured colon at 35. Which gene, and what is unusual about the arterial risk compared with Marfan?

Answer

Vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome — COL3A1 (collagen III). Unlike Marfan, where the risk centres on the aortic root, vEDS carries a high risk of rupture of medium-sized arteries (and bowel and uterus), often without a preceding aneurysm.

Q: A child with hypertelorism, a bifid uvula and tortuous neck arteries has an aortic root of 4.2 cm. Diagnosis, pathway, and why the surgical threshold differs?

Answer

Loeys–Dietz syndrome — mutations in the TGF-β receptor pathway. It dissects at smaller diameters than Marfan, so the root is replaced earlier.

Q: A short 16-year-old girl with a webbed neck and primary amenorrhea has arm hypertension and weak femoral pulses. Which two cardiovascular lesions are most likely, and what later aortic risk follows?

Answer

Turner syndrome with coarctation and a bicuspid aortic valve. Both add to the risk of aortic dilation and dissection, especially in pregnancy.

Q: Why does Marfan syndrome cause aortic regurgitation, and why is mitral valve prolapse so common?

Answer

The dilating aortic root stretches the sinuses and pulls the aortic cusps apart, so they cannot coapt. The abnormal connective tissue also makes the mitral leaflets myxomatous and floppy — MVP in over 90%.

LO 86LO 87LO 88LO 89LO 90Source: Vascular Pathology (Gardner) · Vascular Surgery (Ciraulo) · Pediatric Cardiology

Section 34 · Vessels

Vasculitis

Dr. Gardner flagged this topic: “they tend to get tested.” Most vasculitides are rare, but they mimic other diseases, are devastating if untreated, and are mostly immune-driven and highly treatable if caught early — usually with steroids first. His practical advice: in the emergency department, just thinking of vasculitis and calling the right specialist is a win. The boards will still want the details, so sort by vessel size first.

Abbreviations used in this section GCA giant cell arteritis · PMR polymyalgia rheumatica · PAN polyarteritis nodosa · GPA granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener) · MPA microscopic polyangiitis · EGPA eosinophilic GPA (Churg–Strauss) · HSP Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) · ANCA anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody · c-ANCA / PR3 cytoplasmic pattern / proteinase 3 · p-ANCA / MPO perinuclear pattern / myeloperoxidase · GBM glomerular basement membrane · NETs neutrophil extracellular traps · ESR / CRP inflammatory markers · HBV / HCV hepatitis B / C virus · IVIG intravenous immunoglobulin · URI upper respiratory infection · SLE systemic lupus erythematosus · HLA human leukocyte antigen · DSA digital subtraction angiography · MI myocardial infarction · IgG immunoglobulin G · CT computed tomography · IL interleukin

Immunologic mechanisms

MechanismHow it injures the vesselExamples
Immune complexesAntigen–antibody complexes deposit in vessel walls and fix complement; neutrophils arrive and are blown apart (leukocytoclastic — “nuclear dust”)HSP / IgA vasculitis (IgA), cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (HCV), PAN with hepatitis B, SLE vasculitis, serum sickness
ANCA (pauci-immune — few deposits)Cytokine-primed neutrophils display PR3 or MPO; ANCA binds and activates them, with a positive feedback of neutrophil and complement activation; they release reactive oxygen species, proteases and NETs onto the endothelium; T cells and monocytes followGPA (c-ANCA/PR3), MPA (p-ANCA/MPO), EGPA (p-ANCA in about half)
Direct antibody against a vessel antigenAntibody binds a structural antigen in the wallAnti-GBM disease (Goodpasture: GBM and alveolar basement membrane); Board add-on anti-endothelial antibodies in Kawasaki disease
Cell-mediated (granulomatous)T cells and macrophages form granulomas with giant cells in the wall, fragmenting the elastic laminaGiant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis; granulomas also in GPA and EGPA
InfectionDirect invasion of the wall, or molecular mimicrySyphilitic aortitis, mycotic aneurysm, Board add-on rickettsiae; HBV-PAN and HCV-cryoglobulins (immune complex); Cogan syndrome (antibody to a reovirus peptide); Buerger (tobacco-driven autoimmunity)

Large, medium and small vessels ★ HY

🏛️

Large

  • Giant cell (temporal) arteritis
  • Takayasu arteritis
🧱

Medium

  • Polyarteritis nodosa
  • Kawasaki disease
  • Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)
🕸️

Small

  • ANCA: GPA, MPA, EGPA
  • Immune complex: IgA vasculitis (HSP), cryoglobulinemic, anti-GBM
  • Variable vessel: Behçet, Cogan

The comparison: presentation, labs and histology ★ HY

DiseaseWhoPresentationLabs and testsHistologyPicture
Giant cell (temporal) arteritisOver 50; the commonest vasculitisNew headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss; polymyalgia rheumatica (shoulder and hip stiffness); fever, fatigueHigh ESR and CRP Board add-on; temporal artery biopsyGranulomas, giant cells, fragmented internal elastic lamina; segmental (skip) lesions
Takayasu arteritis — “pulseless disease”Younger women, especially of Asian descent, under 40Arm or leg claudication, weak or absent pulses, unequal arm pressures, bruits, hypertension; fever, myalgia, weight lossHigh ESR; angiography (DSA or CT angiography): narrowed arch branchesGranulomatous inflammation; massively thickened aortic wall
Polyarteritis nodosaAdultsHypertension, abdominal pain, renal dysfunction, neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex Board add-on), livedo, nodules; spares the lungHepatitis B; ANCA-negative; angiogram: microaneurysms (“rosary”)Transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries; lesions of different ages
Kawasaki diseaseChildren under 5Fever 5 days or more + conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical node, strawberry tongue / cracked lips, swollen red hands and feet, then peeling fingertipsVery high platelets in weeks 2–4 (the case: 960K); urgent echoMedium-vessel (coronary) arteritis
Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans)Young male heavy smokersHand and foot claudication, Raynaud, ulcers and gangrene of the digits; normal proximal pulses, absent distal ones; migratory superficial thrombophlebitis Board add-onAngiogram: distal occlusions with corkscrew collateralsInflammatory thrombosis involving arteries and veins; organs spared
GPA (Wegener)AdultsUpper airway (chronic sinusitis, nosebleeds, saddle nose), lungs (nodules, cavities, hemorrhage) and kidneys (glomerulonephritis)c-ANCA (PR3) about 75%Necrotising granulomas plus small-vessel vasculitis
Microscopic polyangiitisAdults; often drug- or infection-associatedKidney and lung: glomerulonephritis, pulmonary capillaritis and hemorrhage, fever, weight loss; no upper airway, no granulomasp-ANCA (MPO) about 60%Necrotising small-vessel vasculitis without granulomas
EGPA (Churg–Strauss)Adults with asthmaAsthma, eosinophilia, allergic rhinitis, peripheral neuropathy (foot drop), rash; sometimes heart and kidneyp-ANCA about 45% (half are ANCA-negative); eosinophilsGranulomas with eosinophils
IgA vasculitis (HSP)Children after a URI; adults have worse kidney involvementTetrad: palpable purpura (buttocks and legs), arthritis, abdominal pain, glomerulonephritis; Board add-on intussusceptionNormal platelets; IgA deposits on biopsyLeukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA immune complexes
Cryoglobulinemic vasculitisHepatitis C, SjögrenPurpura, joint pain, neuropathy, kidney involvementCryoglobulins — antibodies that precipitate in the cold; low complement Board add-onImmune-complex small-vessel vasculitis
Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture)Often after a viral illnessGlomerulonephritis + pulmonary hemorrhage — needs rapid treatmentAnti-GBM antibodiesBoard add-on Linear IgG along the GBM
Behçet diseaseMiddle East, Turkey — HLA-B51 (500 per 100,000 there, 5 in the US)Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, skin lesions; arteries and veins of any size; aneurysms; renal failure—Neutrophils always present

Pictures: Gardner lecture and Robbins & Cotran Atlas; AMBOSS (Kawasaki illustration, ANCA immunofluorescence — board add-on); Ciraulo lecture (Buerger).

🧠 Memory hooks Board add-on

Kawasaki = “CRASH and burn”: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Adenopathy, Strawberry tongue, Hands and feet, plus burn = fever of 5 days or more. PAN = “Pulmonary-Avoiding, No ANCA”, with hepatitis B. c-ANCA fills the Cytoplasm; p-ANCA hugs the nucleus (Perinuclear).

The lecturer’s take: most of these are vanishingly rare — GCA and Takayasu are the relatively common ones, and Behçet in the right population. Pay attention to ethnicity when building a differential.

Life-threatening complications and management

DiseaseThe complication that kills or maimsManagement
Giant cell arteritisBlindness from ophthalmic artery involvement — irreversible; Board add-on stroke; later thoracic aortic aneurysmHigh-dose corticosteroids started the same day, before the biopsy result; then the biopsy. Board add-on Tocilizumab spares steroids
Takayasu arteritisArch-branch stenosis (stroke, arm ischemia), renal artery stenosis and hypertension, aortic regurgitation, aneurysmsCorticosteroids; consider revascularisation once quiescent
Kawasaki diseaseCoronary artery aneurysm (about 5%; 1% giant), thrombosis or later stenosis, MI and sudden death in children; myocarditis, pericarditis, valvulitisUrgent echo; IVIG + aspirin immediately (IVIG shrank existing aneurysms in the lecturer’s own research). Aspirin is the exception to the Reye rule. Antithrombotics for aneurysms
Polyarteritis nodosaRenal failure, mesenteric ischemia and bowel perforation, aneurysm rupture, MI, malignant hypertensionBoard add-on Corticosteroids ± cyclophosphamide; antivirals and plasma exchange for HBV-PAN
GPA and MPARapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and diffuse alveolar hemorrhageBoard add-on Corticosteroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange in severe disease
EGPAMyocarditis and heart failure (the main cause of death), neuropathyBoard add-on Corticosteroids; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5)
Anti-GBM diseasePulmonary hemorrhage plus kidney failureRapid treatment — Board add-on plasmapheresis, steroids, cyclophosphamide
IgA vasculitis (HSP)Nephritis (worse in adults), intussusceptionUsually self-limited in children; supportive; steroids for severe disease Board add-on
Buerger diseaseGangrene and amputationStop smoking — the only cure: “you don’t stop smoking, your hand’s coming off, pick one”
Behçet diseaseAneurysm rupture, venous thrombosis, uveitis and blindness, renal failure (the biggest single consequence per lecture)Board add-on Colchicine, steroids, immunosuppressants

Q: A 72-year-old woman has new temporal headaches, pain when chewing, and stiffness in her shoulders and hips. Her ESR is 95. What must be started today, and why?

Answer

High-dose corticosteroids for giant cell arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica — started before the temporal artery biopsy result, because ophthalmic artery involvement causes irreversible blindness.

Q: A 25-year-old Japanese woman has arm claudication, unequal arm blood pressures and an absent radial pulse. Diagnosis, vessels involved, and the confirming test?

Answer

Takayasu arteritis (“pulseless disease”) — granulomatous inflammation of the aortic arch and its major branches; confirm with angiography (CT angiography or DSA). Treat with corticosteroids.

Q: A 2-year-old has had fever for 8 days, red eyes, cracked lips, a neck node and a rash; platelets are 960K. What is the most important test, and the treatment?

Answer

Kawasaki disease. An urgent echocardiogram for coronary artery aneurysms, and IVIG plus aspirin immediately.

Q: A 45-year-old has chronic bloody sinusitis, cavitating lung nodules and red-cell casts in the urine. Which antibody, which histology, and which mechanism?

Answer

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: c-ANCA / anti-PR3; necrotising granulomas with small-vessel vasculitis in the upper airway, lung and kidney. The mechanism is ANCA activation of primed neutrophils (pauci-immune).

Q: A 50-year-old with chronic hepatitis B has hypertension, abdominal pain after meals, foot drop and a raised creatinine. His chest X-ray is clear and ANCA is negative. Diagnosis and the histology?

Answer

Polyarteritis nodosa — a medium-vessel, immune-complex vasculitis linked to hepatitis B, sparing the lung, ANCA-negative. Histology: transmural fibrinoid necrosis of medium arteries, with lesions of different ages.

Q: A 7-year-old, two weeks after a cold, has palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, knee pain, colicky abdominal pain and hematuria. What deposits in the vessel walls, and what is the mechanism?

Answer

IgA immune complexes — IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), a leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis: immune complexes deposit, fix complement and draw in neutrophils.

Q: An asthmatic adult develops foot drop, purpura and an eosinophil count of 20%. Diagnosis? And a 35-year-old two-pack-a-day smoker has a fingertip ulcer, normal radial pulses and corkscrew collaterals on a hand angiogram — diagnosis and treatment?

Answer

The first is eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg–Strauss) — often p-ANCA, about half ANCA-negative. The second is thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); the only treatment that works is complete smoking cessation.

Section 35 · Vessels

Peripheral Arterial Disease and Claudication

Dr. Segal’s case was a 70-year-old former smoker whose leg pain had been blamed on her back, her “arthritis” and finally her statin. It was peripheral arterial disease — common, under-recognised and deadly, because the legs are a window on the heart and brain. Two decisions run the topic: is the leg pain vascular or neurogenic, and is the limb threatened?

Abbreviations used in this section PAD peripheral arterial disease · ABI ankle–brachial index · TBI toe–brachial index · CLTI / CLI chronic limb-threatening / critical limb ischemia · ALI acute limb ischemia · AIOD aortoiliac occlusive disease · SFA superficial femoral artery · CFA common femoral artery · DP / PT dorsalis pedis / posterior tibial pulse · CTA / MRA / DSA CT angiography / MR angiography / digital subtraction angiography · SET supervised exercise therapy · SAPT / DAPT single / dual antiplatelet therapy · MACE / MALE major adverse cardiovascular / limb events · PDE3 phosphodiesterase-3 · tPA tissue plasminogen activator · PTFE polytetrafluoroethylene graft · AF atrial fibrillation · DM diabetes mellitus · HTN hypertension · CKD chronic kidney disease · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · ED erectile dysfunction · BKA / AKA below- / above-knee amputation · ACE angiotensin-converting enzyme · AAA abdominal aortic aneurysm · ARB angiotensin receptor blocker · LDL low-density lipoprotein · PCSK9 proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 · BP blood pressure · MI myocardial infarction · LV left ventricle · AV arteriovenous · IV intravenous

Vascular versus neurogenic claudication ★ HY

FeatureVascular (PAD)Neurogenic (lumbar spinal stenosis)
CharacterCramping, tightness, fatigueTingling, numbness, weakness, clumsiness; radiating
WhereButtock, hip, thigh, calf (by level of block); isolated foot pain is unusualButtock, hip, thigh; with back pain
TriggerExertion — a reproducible distanceStanding or walking; variable
ReliefStanding still, within minutesSitting or flexing forward — the “shopping-cart sign”; better walking uphill
Pulses and skinWeak pulses, low ABI, hair loss, shiny skin, cool feetNormal pulses and ABI; may have bladder or bowel symptoms, foot drop
🎙️ “Boards love this question”

Who feels better walking uphill?

The patient with neurogenic claudication — you lean forward going uphill, and lumbar flexion opens the canal; in extension the hypertrophic ligamentum flavum compresses the nerves. The same goes for leaning on a grocery cart.

⚠️ One slide row is backwards

One App Session 2 table gives pain dissipating in “30 minutes (vascular)” versus “1–3 minutes (neurogenic)”. The guideline and NEJM tables on the same slides say the opposite: vascular claudication settles within minutes of standing still; neurogenic pain is slow and needs sitting or flexion.

The rest of the leg-pain differential

  • An AAA in a smoker — the one “you don’t want to miss” (Section 32).
  • Hip or knee arthritis (aching at joints, slow relief); venous congestion (bursting pain, relieved by elevation); chronic compartment syndrome or popliteal entrapment in young athletes; vasculitis and Buerger disease in young smokers (Section 34).
  • “Is it the statin?” Never dismiss it, but most statin symptoms are nocebo: in an N-of-1 trial (SAMSON), symptoms on placebo were about 90% of those on the statin, and lowest with no tablets.

The exam and the ankle–brachial index

Who gets it

  • About 7% of US adults; rising steeply with age; men and women equally.
  • Smoking and diabetes, smoking and diabetes. Smoking raises the risk 2–3× (2–4× on one quiz slide), and it persists for about 30 years after quitting (“the Energizer Bunny of vascular disease”). Diabetes drives severe, limb-threatening and tibial disease. Hypertension accounts for about 40% of the risk; LDL matters, but less than for coronary disease.
  • Most PAD is silent or atypical: 20–50% asymptomatic, 40–50% atypical leg discomfort, only 10–30% classic claudication.

The clinical spectrum

SubsetWhat it looks likeOutlook
Intermittent claudicationExertional, reproducible muscle pain relieved by restUnder 5% progress to limb ischemia; major amputation about 1% a year — “the risk of losing the limb for just claudication is really nothing”
Chronic limb-threatening ischemia — “the unstable angina of PAD”Ischemic rest pain (forefoot, at night, worse lying flat, relieved by dangling the leg), ulcers, gangrene, for 2 weeks or moreAbout 30% major amputation and 25% death within a year, mostly cardiovascular
Acute limb ischemiaSudden hypoperfusion under 2 weeks — the six P’sAn emergency: “time = tissue”

The exam

  • BP in both arms (a difference over 10 mm Hg suggests subclavian disease); all pulses, symmetric or not; bruits (abdominal, femoral, carotid).
  • Skin: hair loss, shiny atrophic skin, thick nails, cool feet, ulcers (arterial ulcers are on the toes and pressure points, painful, punched-out Board add-on).
  • Elevation pallor and dependent rubor (the Buerger test): pale when raised, dusky red when hanging down. Rubor fades with elevation; cellulitis does not — the island patient’s “recurrent cellulitis” was CLTI.
  • Sensory and motor testing (10-g monofilament in diabetics).

The ankle–brachial index

ABI = the higher ankle pressure (DP or PT) on that side ÷ the higher of the two arm pressures.

ABIMeaning (2024 guideline)
≤ 0.90PAD (about 90% sensitive, 95% specific for a stenosis of 50% or more)
0.91–0.99Borderline — get an exercise ABI
1.00–1.40Normal — but with typical symptoms, still get an exercise ABI
> 1.40Non-compressible, calcified arteries (diabetes, CKD) — use the toe–brachial index (abnormal ≤ 0.70)
0.40 or lessRest pain and tissue-loss range
  • Segmental pressures: a drop of 20 mm Hg or more between adjacent levels localises the block. Doppler waveforms go from triphasic to biphasic to monophasic.
  • Imaging only if revascularisation is considered. CT angiography with runoff is the diagnostic study; an angiogram (DSA) is for procedures — “the way they trick you on exams is to say the hallmark for the diagnosis is an aortogram.” MRA is an alternative (gadolinium risk). Check creatinine before contrast.
  • The vascular patient is a coronary patient: assess cardiac status and duplex the carotids.

Aortoiliac occlusive disease

  • Atherosclerosis begins in the infrarenal aorta. Focal disease in young women who smoke with high cholesterol (the worst outcomes); diffuse multi-segment disease in older men with diabetes and hypertension.
  • Hallmark: diminished or absent femoral pulses. Buttock and thigh claudication; the resting ABI can be near-normal (get an exercise ABI).
  • Collaterals from the iliac, lumbar and internal mammary arteries keep the legs alive.
🔑 Leriche syndrome — “a great board question”

A triad: buttock and hip claudication, diminished or absent femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction — aortoiliac occlusion at the bifurcation. ED, especially in a younger man, is a vascular sign: “Don’t just write a prescription for Viagra.” Because the occlusion sits near the renal arteries, many also have kidney disease.

Revascularisation (aortoiliac)DetailsPatency
Angioplasty and stentDistal aorta and iliacs do well. Access-site risks: bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, dissection, distal embolisationExcellent at 5 years
Aortobifemoral bypassBifurcated Dacron or PTFE graft90% at 5 years, 75% at 10
Femoral–femoral bypassUnilateral iliac disease; the other femoral is the inflow75% at 5 years
Axillobifemoral bypassHigh-risk patients or an infected aortic field; extra-anatomic60–85% at 5 years — long grafts thrombose

Below the inguinal ligament: femoropopliteal (SFA) disease — strong femorals but weak popliteal and pedal pulses — is treated with stents, CFA endarterectomy, or bypass with the great saphenous vein (the preferred conduit; 70–90% five-year patency). Tibial disease (diabetes, dialysis) presents with ulcers and gangrene; for tissue loss, open bypass to a tibial or pedal target is the procedure of choice.

Acute limb ischemia

🚨 The six P’s — “probably the most important thing you’re gonna have”

Pain, Pallor, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Pulselessness, Poikilothermia (“perishingly cold”). Board add-on Sensory loss comes before motor loss; once the foot cannot move, the limb is immediately threatened.

  • Causes: embolism, mostly cardiac — left atrial thrombus in AF (“the biggest thing we have”), LV thrombus after MI, valve vegetations, atrial myxoma; also a popliteal aneurysm. Thrombosis in situ on a plaque, a hypercoagulable state, a dissection, or a failed bypass graft. Emboli lodge at bifurcations (Board add-on commonly the common femoral).
  • An acute occlusion is far worse than the same chronic one, because there is no time for collaterals.
  • Treatment: IV unfractionated heparin first — “always the first step” — and emergent vascular surgery. If motor and sensory function are intact there is time for catheter-directed thrombolysis or percutaneous thrombectomy; otherwise open Fogarty balloon embolectomy. Then find the source (echo, rhythm monitoring, long-term anticoagulation for AF).
  • Absolute contraindications to thrombolysis: stroke or brain surgery within 2 months, major surgery within 2 weeks, significant bleeding risk.
  • Reperfusion and compartment syndrome: after about 6–8 hours without flow the limb may not be salvageable; reperfusion free radicals make muscle swell inside its fascia. Signs: pain on passive stretch, a tense calf, numbness of the first web space (deep peroneal nerve). Treatment: fasciotomy.
  • Amputation when the limb cannot be saved (“life over limb”): a below-knee amputation costs 10–40% more energy to walk, above-knee 50–70% — a frail patient may not manage it.

Management: exercise, smoking cessation, drugs and revascularization

🎯 Supervised exercise first

A 65-year-old with progressive claudication on the golf course and an ABI of 0.7: the best initial management is supervised exercise therapy — not a stent, not a bypass, not pentoxifylline (no role), and certainly not a golf cart (“anti-osteopathic!”). Exercise grows collaterals, improves oxygen use and lowers inflammation.

ElementWhatWhy
Smoking cessationCounselling plus nicotine replacement, varenicline or bupropion (cytisine in Europe); the state quitline; Dr. Segal’s “which cigarette would you vote off the island?”The biggest lever: better survival and amputation-free survival
Supervised exerciseTreadmill walking to moderate–maximal claudication, 30–45 min, 3 or more times a week, for 12 weeks or more (Medicare-covered); structured home programmes also class 1Collaterals, symptom relief; first-line unless the limb is threatened
StatinHigh-intensity for everyone (the case’s simvastatin 20 was not enough); ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL stays 70 or morePAD is high-risk ASCVD
AntithromboticSymptomatic PAD: single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel) or low-dose aspirin + rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice dailyAspirin + low-dose rivaroxaban reduces both MACE and MALE (COMPASS, VOYAGER-PAD)
CilostazolPDE3 inhibitor: vasodilation plus less platelet aggregationThe only drug that improves walking distance (not survival). Boxed warning: contraindicated in heart failure of any severity
BP and diabetesACE inhibitor or ARB; glucose control; foot care; vaccinationsCardiovascular and limb protection
RevascularisationFor lifestyle-limiting claudication despite therapy, rest pain or tissue loss; endovascular or open depending on location, extent and riskLimb salvage and function
⚠️ A recording slip

Answering a student, the surgery recording says “the first line of treatment is going to be anticoagulation” for early claudication. The slides are right: antiplatelet therapy for claudication; IV heparin is the first step in acute limb ischemia.

Natural history — the heart is the bigger risk

  • Over 5 years: stable claudication in 70–80%, revascularisation 10–20%, critical limb ischemia only 1–2% — but MI or stroke about 20% and death 15–30%.
  • Polyvascular disease: one-year cardiovascular death, MI, stroke or hospitalisation rises from 5.3% (risk factors only) to 12.6%, 21.1% and 26.3% with one, two and three affected beds. “Atherosclerosis is a systemic illness” (Dr. Qazi) — and it almost never involves the arms.

Q: A 66-year-old smoker gets calf cramping after two blocks that goes away after 3 minutes standing still. A 70-year-old with chronic back pain gets burning, tingling leg pain standing at the sink, relieved by sitting and leaning forward. Label each, and say who feels better walking uphill.

Answer

The first is vascular claudication (exertional, reproducible, relieved by standing still). The second is neurogenic claudication from lumbar stenosis. The neurogenic patient feels better walking uphill — lumbar flexion opens the canal.

Q: Arm pressures are 136 and 140 mm Hg; the left ankle is 54. Calculate the left ABI. In a diabetic on dialysis, an ABI of 1.6 with absent pedal pulses — what does it mean, and what next?

Answer

54 ÷ 140 (the higher arm) = 0.39 — severe, in the critical-ischemia range. An ABI over 1.40 means non-compressible calcified arteries; use the toe–brachial index.

Q: A 58-year-old man has pain in both buttocks climbing a ladder, new erectile dysfunction and weak femoral pulses. Name the syndrome and the level of disease.

Answer

Leriche syndrome — aortoiliac occlusive disease at the aortic bifurcation.

Q: A 74-year-old with atrial fibrillation who stopped her apixaban has a sudden cold, pale, pulseless right leg; sensation is reduced but she can wiggle her toes. First drug, and the next step?

Answer

IV unfractionated heparin immediately, and emergent vascular surgery. With motor function intact there is time for catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy if no contraindication; otherwise Fogarty embolectomy. Then long-term anticoagulation for the AF.

Q: Six hours after a femoral embolectomy the calf is tense, passive dorsiflexion of the toes is excruciating and the first web space is numb. Diagnosis and treatment?

Answer

Compartment syndrome from reperfusion injury — emergency fasciotomy.

Q: A 65-year-old has progressive claudication on the golf course and an ABI of 0.7. What is the best initial management, and which drug addition most reduces cardiovascular and limb events?

Answer

Supervised exercise therapy with smoking cessation, a high-intensity statin and BP control. For events, low-dose aspirin plus rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily reduces both MACE and MALE. Cilostazol helps walking distance but not events, and is contraindicated in heart failure.

Q: A patient with claudication asks whether he is more likely to lose his leg or have a heart attack in the next 5 years.

Answer

A heart attack, stroke or death (about 20% MI or stroke and 15–30% death over 5 years) is far likelier than limb loss (critical limb ischemia 1–2%). Treat PAD as high-risk ASCVD.

LO 77Source: Vascular Surgery

Section 36 · Vessels

Mesenteric Ischemia

Dr. Ciraulo called it “probably one of the most lethal things in the world… because people don’t pay attention to it.” The story is an older patient with a poor appetite and vague belly pain who turns up with dead bowel. Take abdominal pain in elderly patients seriously — especially when they have atrial fibrillation.

Abbreviations used in this section SMA / IMA superior / inferior mesenteric artery · SMV superior mesenteric vein · AF atrial fibrillation · NOMI non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia · CTA CT angiography · AAA abdominal aortic aneurysm

The blood supply

  • Celiac (foregut), SMA (midgut), IMA (hindgut).
  • Two collateral highways: the pancreaticoduodenal arcade (celiac to SMA) and the marginal artery (SMA to IMA). They are why one slowly narrowing vessel is often silent, and why the surgeon checks IMA back-bleeding during AAA repair (Section 32).
  • Board add-on The watershed zones — the splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid — are where low-flow ischemic colitis shows up.

Acute versus chronic

TypeWho and whyTreatment
Embolus (most common)Atrial fibrillation; lodges in the SMA distal to the proximal jejunal branches, so the proximal jejunum is sparedEmbolectomy and lifelong anticoagulation — “if you have a thrombus once, your heart’s gonna have thrombus again”
Acute thrombosis (about 20%)On an atherosclerotic plaque at the origin of the SMA; often prior intestinal angina Board add-onAortomesenteric bypass
Non-occlusive (NOMI)Diffuse mesenteric vasospasm in low-flow states Board add-on — shock, heart failure, dialysis, vasopressors, digoxinBowel rest, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation; treat the cause
Mesenteric venous thrombosisSuperior mesenteric vein; Board add-on hypercoagulable statesAnticoagulation; surgery as needed
Bowel infarction (any cause)PeritonitisResect the dead bowel
Chronic mesenteric ischemia (“intestinal angina”)Middle-aged women, smokers with atherosclerosis; postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss (Board add-on “food fear”; usually two of the three vessels are narrowed)Revascularise — endovascular, or open bypass with vein or prosthetic graft — to prevent infarction. “Very treatable.”

Diagnosis and management ★ HY

🔑 Acute mesenteric ischemia in one line

An older patient with AF and severe abdominal pain out of proportion to a soft, benign-feeling abdomen Board add-on — get a CT angiogram now. Lactate, leukocytosis and peritonitis come late, when the bowel is already dying.

  • High index of suspicion first. Plain film: ileus, pneumatosis (late). Duplex can show SMA stenosis.
  • CTA is the diagnostic study — it shows the bowel and the vessels; the SMA clot “shows up really nicely, especially on the sagittal view.” A mesenteric angiogram is the gold standard and lets you treat at the same time.
  • “When in doubt, operate” — “better to have a negative laparotomy than to go in and see this.” At surgery: restore flow, resect what is dead, and often second-look the bowel Board add-on. About 100 cm of small bowel is needed to live without parenteral nutrition (recording).
  • Chronic disease: mesenteric duplex (about 80% sensitive and specific), then CTA as the test of choice; angiography with endovascular treatment.

Q: An 80-year-old with atrial fibrillation who is not anticoagulated has sudden severe periumbilical pain. She is writhing, but her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness. What is the diagnosis, the first imaging, and the definitive treatment?

Answer

Acute mesenteric ischemia from an SMA embolus (pain out of proportion to the exam). CT angiography, then embolectomy, resection of any dead bowel, and lifelong anticoagulation.

Q: A 60-year-old woman who smokes has had abdominal pain 30 minutes after every meal for months. She has lost 9 kg because she is afraid to eat. Diagnosis, best test and treatment?

Answer

Chronic mesenteric ischemia (intestinal angina). CTA, then revascularisation (endovascular or bypass) before the bowel infarcts.

Q: A patient in septic shock on high-dose norepinephrine develops abdominal pain and rising lactate. CTA shows patent mesenteric arteries. What is it, and how is it treated?

Answer

Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia — vasospasm from low flow and vasopressors. Bowel rest, antibiotics, fluid resuscitation and improving cardiac output; resect bowel only if it infarcts.

Supporting sectionSource: Cardiovascular Health in Women

Section 37 · Supporting Lecture

Cardiovascular Health in Women

No summative objective maps to Dr. Qazi’s lecture, so this is a short version. The message: heart disease is the leading killer of women. Women share every traditional risk factor with men, and they also carry female-specific risk enhancers from their reproductive history — menarche, pregnancy complications and menopause.

Abbreviations used in this section CVD cardiovascular disease · CHD coronary heart disease · MI myocardial infarction · SCAD spontaneous coronary artery dissection · MINOCA MI with non-obstructive coronary arteries · ASCVD atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease · MHT menopausal hormone therapy · WHI Women’s Health Initiative · HERS Heart and Estrogen/progestin Replacement Study · VTE venous thromboembolism · TIA transient ischemic attack · RR / HR relative risk / hazard ratio · LDL low-density lipoprotein · HDL high-density lipoprotein · BP blood pressure

How ischemia presents differently

Two myths, corrected

  • “Heart disease is a man’s disease.” CVD causes 1 in 3 deaths in US women, about one a minute; more than 60 million US women live with it.
  • “Heart attacks happen after menopause.” More than 10,000 US women under 45 have an MI each year, and under 65 a woman’s acute-MI mortality is almost twice a man’s.
  • Men have more CVD when young; the sexes are level at 60–79, and women overtake men at 80 and over.
  • Age counts as a coronary risk factor from over 50 in women (over 40 in men).

What looks different in women Board add-on

  • More often atypical or accompanying symptoms with MI — dyspnea, fatigue, nausea, jaw or back pain — and so later diagnosis and treatment.
  • Diabetes and smoking raise coronary risk proportionally more in women.
  • Causes that cluster in women: SCAD (young and peripartum women, fibromuscular dysplasia), Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (postmenopausal women after emotional stress; Section 19), MINOCA and coronary microvascular dysfunction.

Pregnancy-related cardiovascular conditions

Pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test. A woman who develops hypertension or diabetes under its load is showing a susceptibility that comes back later, so ask about pregnancy history in every woman.

  • Female-specific enhancers on the slides: age at menarche, postmenopausal status and pregnancy complications. Premenstrual syndrome is linked to later hypertension (HR 1.4; 3.3 for hypertension before 40).
  • Menarche: a U-shaped curve, lowest at 13; menarche at 10 or younger gives RR 1.27 for CHD, and late menarche (17 or older) also raises it.
  • Preeclampsia (hypertension and proteinuria, usually after 32 weeks; 2–8% of pregnancies) predicts heart failure, stroke, CHD and later hypertension. Gestational diabetes predicts type 2 diabetes; gestational hypertension and multiple gestation predict heart failure.
  • Pregnancy loss: miscarriage roughly 1.4× CHD; stillbirth HR 2.65 and more than three miscarriages HR 8.90 for later MI. Preterm delivery also raises later cardiovascular hospitalisation.
  • A 50-year cohort found the strongest predictors of CVD death were glycosuria (HR 4.2), early-onset preeclampsia (3.6) and pre-existing hypertension (3.5); combinations multiply risk. Obstetricians are many young women’s primary-care doctors — the chance to spot risk early.

Menopause and hormone therapy

  • ACC/AHA guidelines give postmenopausal status the same weight as male sex; early natural menopause (44 or younger) carries more CVD.
  • Estrogen helps the vessels (eNOS-driven vasodilation, angiogenesis, less fibrosis and oxidative stress). Its loss brings sympathetic activation and insulin-resistance features — higher BP, visceral fat, dyslipidemia (Board add-on higher LDL and triglycerides, lower HDL).
  • But menopause is not proven causal: in the alternative paradigm, risk is already climbing through the reproductive years and menopause only adjusts it.
  • WHI and HERS: hormone therapy did not reduce cardiovascular events and may have increased them — but those women were more than 10 years past menopause.
  • The timing hypothesis: MHT started within 10 years of menopause and before age 60 appears to cut CHD by about 50% and all-cause mortality by about 30%. Started late, it does nothing. ELITE: estradiol slowed carotid intima thickening only in women under 6 years post-menopause.
  • First, though, control the traditional risk factors: BP, cholesterol, diet, smoking, weight, and at least 30 minutes of exercise most days.

Q: A 38-year-old has had preeclampsia in two pregnancies and gestational diabetes in one. Why does this change her wellness visit?

Answer

These are female-specific ASCVD risk enhancers: preeclampsia predicts heart failure, CHD, stroke and hypertension, and gestational diabetes predicts type 2 diabetes. Screen her for hypertension, diabetes and lipids early, and treat her risk factors more aggressively.

Q: Why did WHI and HERS show no cardiovascular benefit from hormone therapy, and who might benefit?

Answer

Their participants were mostly more than 10 years past menopause. Under the timing hypothesis, MHT started within 10 years of menopause and before 60, in a woman at low cardiovascular risk, appears protective; late initiation is not.

Q: A 51-year-old, a year past menopause, has migraine with aura and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 6%. Which hormone-therapy traffic-light category is she in?

Answer

Yellow — caution (migraine with aura and a 10-year risk of 5–7.4%).

Part A · things to know

Where the sources disagree

  • Atrial kick: Dr. Qazi said 20–25% of output; Dr. Morganelli said about 10% of end-diastolic volume; the electrophysiologist said about 15% (Sections 1 and 9).
  • c wave timing: the recording placed it in rapid ejection; boards place it at the onset of systole (Section 1).
  • S4 timing: the recording said “before S2”; it is before S1 (Section 2).
  • Pulse pressure in aortic stenosis: the lecture said it varies; UWorld says narrow in severe disease (Section 3).
  • Renin and ADH directions: two slips in the physiology recording (Section 5).
Part B · things to know

Slips and judgement calls

  • Carotid body versus carotid sinus: the arrhythmia recording says the carotid body carries parasympathetic tone. Carotid massage works on the carotid sinus baroreceptors; the body is a chemoreceptor (Section 8).
  • Adenosine and cyclic AMP: the recording says adenosine works through an “uptick in cAMP.” The A1 receptor is Gi-coupled, so cyclic AMP falls and potassium efflux rises (Sections 8 and 10).
  • QT versus QRS: in the long-QT case the recording says “QRS” once where it means QT (Section 8).
  • Wellens’ morphology table was explicitly excluded by the lecturer (“I do not expect you to know this, nor would it be tested”), so Section 8 gives the four Brugada steps and stops there.
  • Delayed- versus rapid delayed-rectifier potassium subtypes were explicitly excluded by Dr. Scully, so Section 10 names IKr for dofetilide and does not go further.
  • No UWorld figures were used. Two useful ones from the lecture notes — the conduction-system drawing and the coronary dominance diagram — are UWorld images, so they were left out and the anatomy is given as text instead.
Part C · things to know

Where the sources disagree

  • Wavy fibres: the lecture slide puts them at ½–4 hours, First Aid at 0–4 hours, UWorld at 4–12 hours. All agree they are the first light-microscope change, on day 1 (Section 14).
  • Free-wall rupture timing: Dr. Gardner 3–7 days; Dr. Watkins two peaks (24 hours and 3–5 days); First Aid 5–14 days; UWorld up to 2 weeks (Section 15).
  • The papillary-rupture murmur: the case slide says holosystolic to the axilla; UWorld says often early systolic and silent in up to half (Section 15).
  • Ivabradine’s mechanism: one Application Session 1 slide gives ranolazine’s (late sodium current). Ivabradine blocks the funny current (Section 16).
  • The acute coronary syndrome bundle was left by Dr. Scully to the clinical lectures, so Section 16 builds it from Dr. Watkins’s case plus the UWorld library, with the library material tagged.
Part D · things to know

Slips and judgement calls

  • HFpEF and the ejection fraction: the physiology recording says “reduced ejection fraction” at the end of the HFpEF explanation; the slide is right that it is preserved (Section 17).
  • Vericiguat is called an sGC “inhibitor” on one slide; it is a stimulator (Section 18).
  • Intercalated cells: the recording says “beta”; hydrogen-ion secretion is by α-intercalated cells (Section 18).
  • “Most common cardiac tumour”: the lecturers mean primary; metastases are the most common overall (Section 20).
  • ARVC, takotsubo, rhabdomyoma and the echo features of each cardiomyopathy are thin in the lectures, so they are built from First Aid, the ECG II and Women’s Health notes and AMBOSS, and tagged.
Part E · things to know

Where the sources disagree

  • Endocarditis incidence: the lecture says about 1–3 per 100,000; the outline says 3–7 (Section 21).
  • Leukopenia: the lecturer said it is not usual; the outline lists it (Section 22).
  • MSSA duration: the handout’s “3–5 days” is almost certainly a typo for about 6 weeks (Section 22).
  • Bartonella: corrected in class to doxycycline plus rifampin, not gentamicin (Section 22).
  • The IDU valve: the board answer is tricuspid; the pediatric case showed a mitral vegetation (Section 21).
  • Antibiotic mechanisms, surgical indications and dental prophylaxis are not in the lecture; Section 22 gives the First Aid and AMBOSS versions, tagged.
Part F · things to know

Slips and judgement calls

  • TAVR durability: slide 58 says 50% degeneration at 8 years; slide 59 and the lecture say current valves track like surgical ones to about 9 years (Section 25).
  • The AS pulse: the surgery recording first calls it “water hammer” and then corrects itself — AS is pulsus parvus et tardus; water hammer is AR.
  • The AI murmur: one slide says crescendo–decrescendo diastolic to the axilla; the board version is early diastolic decrescendo at the left sternal border (Section 3).
  • Right-sided valves and TAVR complications beyond heart block and coronary obstruction come from the UWorld library, tagged. No calcific aortic stenosis gross photograph was available outside UWorld, so the Qazi schematic stands in.
Part G · partly covered

Objective 15: the echo predictive value

  • What is missing: the lecture gives the incidence chart and says a persistent newborn murmur needs echo, but it gives no figure for the predictive value of echo (or how often a newborn murmur is structural). Section 27 offers an approximate range from the literature, flagged as such. If the new study guide or a lecture slide gives a number, put it in Section 27 and mark objective 15 covered.
  • Incidence figures differ: VSD about 31% on the pediatric chart and 42% on Dr. Gardner’s table; one slide’s “2–5% of births” should read 2–5 per 1,000.
  • Recording slips in the pediatric lecture (the HLHS flow directions and which artery leaves which ventricle in transposition) are corrected in the source notes and in Section 26.
Part H · things to know

Where the sources disagree

  • How fast vascular claudication settles: one App Session 2 table gives 30 minutes for vascular and 1–3 minutes for neurogenic pain. The guideline tables on the same slides say the reverse: vascular pain settles within minutes of standing still (Section 35).
  • “Anticoagulation first” for claudication: a recording slip in the surgery lecture. Claudication gets antiplatelet therapy; IV heparin is the first step only in acute limb ischemia (Section 35).
  • Women’s cardiovascular health (Section 37) has no summative objective, so it is kept short, and the female-specific presentations (SCAD, Takotsubo, MINOCA) are board add-ons.
  • Pictures: UWorld figures for the renin–angiotensin system, diuretic sites, the thiazide–calcium link, pre-eclampsia and the lipid-drug sites were left out. Lecture slides and AMBOSS images stand in.
