Every abbreviation used above, expanded

Reference

Glossary and Abbreviations

If a short form appears anywhere in this file, its long form is here. Each section also carries its own abbreviation strip at the top.

The cardiac cycle and pressure–volume loops

a, c and v waves
The three atrial pressure waves: atrial contraction, the atrioventricular valve bulging back at the onset of systole, and atrial filling against the closed valve.
Afterload
The load the ventricle must overcome before it can eject — mainly aortic diastolic pressure.
Atrial kick
The last part of ventricular filling, supplied by atrial contraction. Lost in atrial fibrillation.
CO — cardiac output
Stroke volume times heart rate; about 4–5 L/min at rest. The cardiac index is cardiac output divided by body surface area.
Diastasis
The slow middle part of ventricular filling, between rapid filling and the atrial kick. The first part of diastole to disappear when the heart rate rises.
Dicrotic notch
The small dip on the aortic pressure tracing at aortic valve closure.
EDV / ESV — end-diastolic / end-systolic volume
How full the ventricle is just before it contracts, and what is left after it ejects.
EDPVR — end-diastolic pressure–volume relationship
The passive filling curve on a PV loop. Steeper means a stiffer, less compliant ventricle.
EF — ejection fraction
Stroke volume divided by EDV; normally 55–70%.
ESPVR — end-systolic pressure–volume relationship
The line joining the end-systolic corners of loops at different fillings. Its slope is contractility.
Isovolumetric (isovolumic)
A phase with all four valves closed, so volume stays constant while pressure rises (contraction) or falls (relaxation).
Preload
Stretch on the ventricle before it contracts, indexed by EDV or end-diastolic pressure.
PV loop — pressure–volume loop
Left ventricular pressure plotted against volume for one beat.
SV — stroke volume
EDV minus ESV; about 70 mL.
Wiggers diagram
Aortic, ventricular and atrial pressures, ventricular volume, the ECG and the heart sounds on one time axis.

Heart sounds and murmurs

A2 / P2
The aortic and pulmonic components of the second heart sound.
AR / AS — aortic regurgitation / stenosis
A leaking aortic valve (diastolic murmur, wide pulse pressure) / a narrowed one (systolic murmur, gradient across the valve).
Austin Flint murmur
An apical diastolic rumble in severe aortic regurgitation that mimics mitral stenosis.
Concentric / eccentric hypertrophy
A thick wall from pressure overload / a dilated chamber from volume overload.
HCM — hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
A thick septum that obstructs outflow; its murmur gets louder when the ventricle is smaller.
LBBB / RBBB — left / right bundle branch block
Delayed conduction down one bundle branch; LBBB can give paradoxical splitting, RBBB wide splitting.
MR / MS — mitral regurgitation / stenosis
A leaking mitral valve (tall v wave, holosystolic murmur) / a narrowed one (diastolic gradient, rumble and opening snap).
MVP — mitral valve prolapse
Floppy, myxomatous leaflets that billow into the atrium; midsystolic click and late systolic murmur.
Opening snap
The sound of a stiff mitral valve snapping open in early diastole; a shorter S2-to-snap interval means more severe stenosis.
Pulsus parvus et tardus
A weak, late-peaking pulse — severe aortic stenosis.
S1–S4
Atrioventricular valve closure · semilunar valve closure · early-diastolic volume sound · late-diastolic stiff-ventricle sound.
Valsalva maneuver
Forced expiration against a closed glottis; the strain phase lowers venous return and preload.

Exercise and prevention

ASCVD — atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
Coronary disease, stroke and peripheral artery disease caused by atherosclerosis.
CR — cardiac rehabilitation
A supervised secondary-prevention programme of exercise, education and risk-factor management. Phase II is 36 ECG-monitored sessions.
DASH — Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension
A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and low-fat dairy that lowers blood pressure, more so with less sodium.
FITT
Frequency, intensity, time and type — the parts of an exercise prescription.
HF-ACTION / REHAB-HF
The heart-failure exercise trials: HF-ACTION in reduced ejection fraction, REHAB-HF in frail older patients after an admission.
Heart-rate reserve
Peak heart rate minus resting heart rate.
MET — metabolic equivalent
The energy of resting metabolism, about 3.5 mL of oxygen per kg per minute.
PREDIMED
The Spanish trial showing that a Mediterranean diet with olive oil or nuts cut cardiovascular events by about 30%.
RPE — rating of perceived exertion
The Borg scale, 6–20; training is usually prescribed at 11–16.
VO₂max / VO₂peak
Oxygen uptake at maximal effort / at the point symptoms stop the test.

Receptors, signals and control of the circulation

ACE — angiotensin-converting enzyme
Converts angiotensin I to II and, as kininase II, breaks down bradykinin.
ADH — antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin)
Makes the collecting duct reabsorb water without sodium.
Bainbridge reflex
A rise in heart rate when the atria are stretched by extra volume.
CVP — central venous pressure
Pressure in the vena cava near the right atrium; the clinical stand-in for right atrial pressure.
Funny current (If)
The slow inward sodium current of pacemaker phase 4, switched on by hyperpolarization; its slope sets the heart rate.
Gq / Gi / Gs
The three G-protein pathways: Gq raises calcium through IP3, Gi lowers cAMP, Gs raises cAMP.
MAP — mean arterial pressure
The average arterial pressure over a cycle, about 90–95 mm Hg; equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance.
MLCK — myosin light-chain kinase
The enzyme that switches smooth muscle contraction on; PKA inhibits it.
Pmsf — mean systemic filling pressure
The pressure throughout the circulation when flow stops, about 7–8 mm Hg, set by the stressed volume.
PDE3 / PDE5 — phosphodiesterase 3 / 5
Enzymes that break down cAMP (blocked by milrinone and inamrinone) and cGMP (blocked by sildenafil).
RAAS — renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system
The kidney’s long-term pressure and volume defence.
Stressed / unstressed volume
Blood that stretches the vein walls and makes pressure / blood that fills them without making pressure.
TPR / SVR — total peripheral / systemic vascular resistance
The resistance of the whole systemic circulation, set mostly by arteriolar radius.

The ECG and arrhythmias

Aberrancy
A supraventricular beat conducted down the ventricles with a bundle-branch pattern, so it looks wide. The reason a wide tachycardia is not automatically ventricular.
ARVC — arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
An inherited disease in which the right ventricular wall is replaced by fibro-fatty tissue, predisposing to ventricular arrhythmia.
AV dissociation — atrioventricular dissociation
Atria and ventricles depolarizing on independent schedules. Seen in complete heart block and in ventricular tachycardia.
AVNRT — atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia
Re-entry between a slow and a fast pathway inside the atrioventricular node. The P wave hides in the QRS.
AVRT — atrioventricular re-entrant tachycardia
Re-entry using an accessory pathway as one limb. Orthodromic (down the node, up the pathway) is narrow; antidromic is wide.
Bazett’s formula
The corrected QT equals the measured QT divided by the square root of the R–R interval in seconds.
Brugada syndrome
An inherited sodium-channel disease of the right ventricular outflow tract, giving coved ST elevation in V1 and V2 and a risk of sudden death. Not the same as the Brugada algorithm for wide tachycardias.
Bundle of Kent
The accessory pathway of Wolff–Parkinson–White, connecting atrium to ventricle directly and bypassing the atrioventricular node.
Capture beat
A single narrow beat during a wide tachycardia, where a sinus impulse got through the node. Nearly diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia. A fusion beat is the hybrid version.
CHA₂DS₂-VASc / CHA₂DS₂-VA
The stroke-risk score in atrial fibrillation, with and without the point for female sex.
Cinchonism
Quinidine toxicity: reduced hearing, tinnitus, blurred vision and delirium. Named after the cinchona bark the drug comes from.
Concordance (precordial)
Every QRS from V1 to V6 pointing the same way. Negative concordance is virtually diagnostic of ventricular tachycardia.
CTI — cavotricuspid isthmus
The strip of right atrial tissue between the inferior vena cava and the tricuspid annulus. The circuit of typical flutter runs through it, and it is the ablation target.
Delta wave
The slurred upstroke of a pre-excited QRS, caused by early ventricular activation through an accessory pathway. It eats into the PR segment, so the PR is short.
EAD / DAD — early / delayed afterdepolarization
Triggered activity. Early ones occur during a prolonged repolarization and cause torsades; delayed ones occur after repolarization from calcium overload and cause ischemic and digoxin arrhythmias.
Early repolarization
J-point elevation from a larger transient outward potassium current in the epicardium than the endocardium. Usually a normal variant in young people.
Ebstein anomaly
A tricuspid valve displaced downward into the right ventricle. The congenital lesion most strongly associated with Wolff–Parkinson–White.
Electromechanical dissociation
Electrical activity with no effective contraction. The feared result of giving intravenous verapamil to a patient on a beta-blocker.
ERP — effective refractory period
The interval during which a cell cannot be re-excited. Lengthening it is how class III drugs stop re-entry.
Funny current (If)
The sodium-carried pacemaker current that produces the slow phase 4 drift. “Funny” because hyperpolarization, not depolarization, opens it.
Holiday heart
Atrial fibrillation precipitated by an alcohol binge.
Mobitz I (Wenckebach) / Mobitz II
The two forms of second-degree block. Mobitz I lengthens the PR until a beat drops and is benign; Mobitz II drops a beat with a constant PR and needs a pacemaker.
NAPA — N-acetylprocainamide
The active metabolite of procainamide, formed by hepatic acetylation and cleared by the kidney.
Northwest axis
An axis pointing up and to the right, so aVR is strikingly positive. A feature favouring ventricular tachycardia.
P mitrale / P pulmonale
A wide notched P wave of left atrial enlargement / a tall peaked P wave of right atrial enlargement.
Pre-excitation
Ventricular activation that begins through an accessory pathway before the atrioventricular node delivers the impulse. Gives a short PR and a delta wave.
P1 purinergic receptor
The adenosine receptor. Acting through Gi/o, it opens potassium channels and hyperpolarizes nodal tissue.
R-wave progression
The growth of the R wave from V1 to V6, with the transition where R equals S normally at V3 to V4.
Re-entry
A self-sustaining circuit between two pathways of different conduction speed and refractoriness. The commonest arrhythmia mechanism.
RVR — rapid ventricular response
Atrial fibrillation conducting fast to the ventricles.
Schwartz score
A diagnostic score for long QT syndrome combining the tracing, the clinical history and the family history. Four or more means high probability.
Sokolow–Lyon criterion
The S wave in V1 or V2 plus the R wave in V5 or V6 totalling 35 mm or more — the most sensitive voltage criterion for left ventricular hypertrophy.
Strain pattern
T-wave inversion and ST depression accompanying ventricular hypertrophy, easily mistaken for ischemia.
TdP — torsades de pointes
Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis, arising on a long QT. Treated acutely with intravenous magnesium.
Use-dependence
More drug block at faster heart rates, because the drug binds the open and inactivated channel states. A property of class I drugs.
WAP / MAT — wandering atrial pacemaker / multifocal atrial tachycardia
Three or more P-wave shapes with an irregular rhythm, below 100 beats per minute and at 100 or above respectively.
Xanthopsia
Yellow-green colour vision with halos around lights — a sign of digoxin toxicity.

Atherosclerosis and ischemic heart disease

ACS — acute coronary syndrome
Unstable angina, NSTEMI or STEMI: plaque rupture with thrombus.
ALDH2 — mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2
The enzyme that converts organic nitrates to nitric oxide. Polymorphisms common in East Asian populations blunt nitrate effect.
Arteriosclerosis / atherosclerosis
Any hardening of the arteries / the subset caused by intimal lipid plaques (atheromas).
BNP / NT-proBNP — B-type natriuretic peptide / its N-terminal fragment
Released in equal amounts from stretched ventricular myocytes. BNP is active and short-lived; NT-proBNP is inert, longer-lived and renally cleared.
CAC — coronary artery calcium score
A CT measure of calcified plaque; a score of zero makes obstructive disease much less likely.
CCTA — coronary computed tomography angiography
Anatomic, non-invasive imaging of the coronary lumen.
CK-MB — creatine kinase, MB fraction
An older cardiac marker that clears in 2–3 days, so it can show re-infarction.
Contraction band necrosis
Hypereosinophilic transverse bands in myocytes from calcium influx on reperfusion.
Coronary flow reserve
How much coronary flow can rise above rest. Falls from about 50% stenosis, whereas resting flow holds until about 80–90%.
Coronary steal
Diversion of flow away from an ischemic bed when a strong arteriolar dilator opens healthy beds.
Dressler syndrome
Autoimmune (post-cardiac injury) pericarditis weeks after an infarct.
Fatty streak
The earliest visible atherosclerotic lesion: collections of lipid-laden foam cells in the intima.
FMD — fibromuscular dysplasia
Segmental replacement of the arterial wall by connective tissue, giving a “string of beads” angiogram; classically the renal arteries of young women.
Foam cell
A macrophage (or smooth muscle cell) filled with oxidized LDL.
GRACE score
Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events: a risk score that helps time angiography in NSTE-ACS.
hs-cTn — high-sensitivity cardiac troponin
A troponin assay able to detect very small rises, allowing rule-in or rule-out at 0 and 1–3 hours.
Hyaline / hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis
Glassy pink arteriolar wall thickening (benign hypertension, diabetes) / concentric “onion-skin” layers (malignant hypertension).
Ivabradine
A blocker of the funny current (If) through HCN channels in the sinus node, slowing the heart rate.
MINOCA / INOCA
Myocardial infarction / ischemia with non-obstructive coronary arteries.
Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis
Calcification of the arterial media with an open lumen; usually asymptomatic.
Nitrate-free interval
A daily break from long-acting nitrates, usually overnight, to prevent tolerance.
NSTE-ACS
Non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome: unstable angina or NSTEMI.
PDE5 — phosphodiesterase-5
The enzyme that breaks down cGMP; inhibited by sildenafil and tadalafil.
PEA — pulseless electrical activity
An organised rhythm on the monitor with no pulse; after an infarct, think free-wall rupture with tamponade.
Pseudoaneurysm
A contained ventricular rupture walled only by pericardium and clot; high risk of rupture.
Ranolazine
Blocks the late sodium current in ischemic myocytes, lowering calcium overload and diastolic wall stress.
Type 1 / type 2 MI (primary / secondary)
Infarction from plaque rupture with thrombus / from a supply–demand mismatch such as sepsis or tachycardia.
Vasospastic (Prinzmetal, variant) angina
Rest angina from coronary spasm, with transient ST elevation.

Heart failure, cardiomyopathy and tumours

ACC/AHA stages A–D
At risk; structural disease without symptoms; symptomatic; refractory heart failure.
ARNI — angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor
Sacubitril/valsartan: blocks neprilysin (raising natriuretic peptides) and the AT1 receptor.
ARVC — arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Inherited fibro-fatty replacement of the right ventricle causing ventricular arrhythmias.
Braking phenomenon
Diuretic tolerance as the distal tubule hypertrophies and reabsorbs more sodium.
Carney complex
A familial syndrome of multiple myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation and endocrine tumours.
Concentric / eccentric hypertrophy
Thick wall with a normal cavity from pressure overload / dilated cavity from volume overload.
Forrester profiles
The bedside grid of congestion (wet or dry) against perfusion (warm or cold) in acute heart failure.
GDMT — guideline-directed medical therapy
The four mortality-reducing heart-failure drug classes, titrated to target doses.
H₂FPEF score
A 0–9 score of obesity, hypertension, AF, pulmonary hypertension, age and filling pressure estimating the probability of HFpEF.
Heart-failure cells
Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages in chronic left heart failure.
HFrEF / HFmrEF / HFpEF / HFimpEF
Heart failure with EF ≤ 40% / 41–49% / ≥ 50% / previously ≤ 40% and now above 40%.
HOCM — hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
HCM with outflow-tract obstruction from the septal bulge and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
MRA — mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
Spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone: block the aldosterone receptor.
Myofibre disarray
Hypertrophied myocytes in a haphazard, whorled pattern — the histology of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Neprilysin
A neutral endopeptidase that degrades natriuretic peptides, bradykinin and substance P.
Nutmeg liver
Mottled centrilobular congestion from right heart failure.
NYHA classes I–IV
Symptom classes from no limitation to symptoms at rest.
SAM — systolic anterior motion
The mitral leaflet pulled toward the septum in systole, obstructing the outflow tract in HOCM.
SGLT2i — sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor
Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin: natriuretic drugs that lower mortality in HFrEF and HFpEF.
Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
Stress-induced transient apical ballooning, typically in postmenopausal women.
Titin
The giant elastic sarcomere protein; a shift to its stiff N2B isoform contributes to HFpEF.
Vericiguat
A soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator used as an add-on in worsening HFrEF.

Infection and inflammation of the heart

Beck triad
Hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds — cardiac tamponade.
Biofilm
A matrix-embedded community of slow-growing bacteria on a surface, far more resistant to antibiotics; made by S. aureus and S. epidermidis.
CAR — coxsackie–adenovirus receptor
The myocyte receptor shared by Coxsackie B and adenovirus.
Chagas disease
Infection with Trypanosoma cruzi from the triatomine bug; decades later cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus and megacolon.
CoNS — coagulase-negative staphylococci
Chiefly S. epidermidis; the organism of prosthetic-valve and device endocarditis.
Constrictive pericarditis
A scarred, stiff pericardium limiting filling; Kussmaul sign and a pericardial knock.
Duke criteria (2023)
Major and minor criteria for endocarditis; definite with 2 major, 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor.
EMB — endomyocardial biopsy
A catheter biopsy of the right ventricular septum; the definitive test for myocarditis.
HACEK
Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella: slow-growing gram-negative endocarditis organisms.
Janeway lesions / Osler nodes
Painless embolic macules on palms and soles / painful immune-complex nodules on finger and toe pads.
Libman–Sacks endocarditis
Sterile flat vegetations on both sides of the valve leaflets in SLE.
Marantic (non-bacterial thrombotic) endocarditis
Sterile platelet–fibrin vegetations in advanced cancer or other hypercoagulable states.
Mycotic aneurysm
An arterial aneurysm caused by an infected (septic) embolus weakening the wall.
Myopericarditis / perimyocarditis
Pericarditis with myocardial involvement and normal function / myocarditis with pericardial features and reduced function.
Pericardial window
A surgical opening (usually subxiphoid) that drains a pericardial effusion into the abdomen or pleura.
Pulsus paradoxus
An inspiratory fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg; a sign of tamponade.
Roth spots
Retinal hemorrhages with pale centres, from immune complexes in endocarditis.
Septic pulmonary emboli
Infected fragments from right-sided vegetations lodging in the lungs, giving cavitating nodules.
Synergy
Greater killing by two drugs together than either alone — a cell-wall drug plus gentamicin for enterococci.
TTE / TOE
Transthoracic / transesophageal echocardiography (about 65% and 95% sensitive for vegetations).

Valves and valve surgery

Anitschkow cells / Aschoff bodies
Macrophages with wavy “caterpillar” chromatin / granulomatous foci of T cells, plasma cells and macrophages in rheumatic carditis.
Bioprosthetic valve
A tissue valve (porcine or bovine pericardium): aspirin only, but structural degeneration over 10–15 years.
Bicuspid aortic valve
A congenital two-cusp aortic valve in 1–2% of people; calcifies early and comes with an aortopathy.
Carcinoid heart disease
Serotonin-driven fibrous plaques on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves (TR and pulmonic stenosis).
Cardioplegia
A cold, high-potassium solution that stops the heart in diastole during surgery.
Heyde syndrome
Aortic stenosis with GI bleeding from angiodysplasia, through shear-induced loss of von Willebrand factor.
Myxomatous degeneration
Proteoglycan infiltration that makes valve leaflets long and floppy — the lesion of mitral valve prolapse.
Paravalvular leak
Regurgitation around, not through, a prosthetic valve; commonest after TAVR.
PBMC — percutaneous balloon mitral commissurotomy
A catheter balloon that splits fused commissures in rheumatic mitral stenosis.
SAVR / TAVR
Surgical (open, on bypass) / transcatheter (usually transfemoral) aortic valve replacement.
STS score
The Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk calculator for operative mortality.
Valve-in-valve
A transcatheter valve placed inside a failed bioprosthesis.

Congenital heart disease

AVSD — atrioventricular septal defect
An endocardial cushion defect involving both septa and the AV valves; the lesion of Down syndrome.
Blalock–Taussig shunt
A subclavian-to-pulmonary-artery connection that increases lung blood flow in cyanotic disease.
CCHD — critical congenital heart disease
Lesions needing intervention in the first weeks of life; screened for by newborn pulse oximetry.
Coarctation of the aorta
A juxtaductal narrowing of the aorta: arm pressure above leg pressure and weak femorals.
Ductal-dependent lesion
A defect in which systemic or pulmonary blood flow relies on an open ductus arteriosus.
Ebstein anomaly
Downward displacement of the tricuspid leaflets into the right ventricle; linked to maternal lithium.
Eisenmenger syndrome
Reversal of a long-standing left-to-right shunt after fixed pulmonary hypertension develops.
Endocardial cushions
Embryonic tissue that divides the atrioventricular canal and forms parts of the septa and AV valves.
Fixed split S2
A split second heart sound that does not vary with breathing — an ASD.
HLHS — hypoplastic left heart syndrome
A tiny left ventricle and left-sided valves; the RV supplies the body through the ductus.
Hyperoxia test
Giving 100% oxygen: lung disease improves the saturation, a cyanotic shunt does not.
Norwood, Glenn, Fontan
The three staged operations for single-ventricle hearts such as HLHS.
PGE₁ — prostaglandin E1
Keeps the ductus arteriosus open in ductal-dependent lesions.
TAPVR — total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Pulmonary veins draining to the right side of the heart.
Tet spell
A hypercyanotic episode in tetralogy of Fallot, relieved by knee-to-chest positioning or squatting.
TGA — transposition of the great arteries
The aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV; survival needs mixing.
TOF — tetralogy of Fallot
VSD, RV outflow stenosis, RV hypertrophy and an overriding aorta.

Vessels

AAA — abdominal aortic aneurysm
A focal aortic dilation over 3 cm, usually infrarenal and atherosclerotic; repaired at about 5.5 cm.
ABI — ankle–brachial index
The higher ankle pressure divided by the higher arm pressure; 0.90 or less is PAD, over 1.40 means calcified arteries.
Acute limb ischemia
Sudden loss of limb perfusion (under 2 weeks), usually an embolus; the six P’s.
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio
The screening test for primary aldosteronism, done after correcting the potassium.
ANCA — antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
c-ANCA (PR3) in granulomatosis with polyangiitis; p-ANCA (MPO) in microscopic polyangiitis and EGPA.
Cilostazol
A phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that improves walking distance in claudication; contraindicated in heart failure.
CLTI — chronic limb-threatening ischemia
Ischemic rest pain, ulcers or gangrene for 2 weeks or more; “the unstable angina of PAD.”
Compartment syndrome
Rising pressure inside a fascial compartment, here after reperfusion; pain on passive stretch; treated by fasciotomy.
Cystic medial degeneration
Loss of elastic fibres and smooth muscle with mucoid pools in the aortic media; Marfan and the dissecting aorta.
Dependent rubor
A dusky red foot when hanging down that blanches on elevation; advanced arterial insufficiency.
EVAR — endovascular aneurysm repair
A stent graft placed through the femoral arteries to exclude an aneurysm.
Familial hypercholesterolemia
An autosomal dominant LDL-receptor defect: very high LDL, tendon xanthomas, early coronary disease.
GCA — giant cell arteritis
Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis over 50: headache, jaw claudication, high ESR, risk of blindness.
Hypertensive emergency
Severe hypertension with acute organ damage; IV drugs, lowering MAP by no more than about 25% in the first hour.
Kawasaki disease
Medium-vessel vasculitis under 5: fever 5 days or more, conjunctivitis, rash, mucosal and extremity changes; coronary aneurysms.
Leriche syndrome
Aortoiliac occlusion: buttock claudication, absent femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction.
Mesenteric ischemia
Inadequate gut blood flow: acute (embolus, thrombosis, non-occlusive, venous) or chronic (intestinal angina).
NOMI — non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia
Mesenteric vasospasm in low-flow states or on vasopressors, with patent arteries.
Neurogenic claudication
Leg pain from lumbar spinal stenosis, brought on by standing and relieved by sitting or flexing.
PCSK9 inhibitor
A monoclonal antibody (evolocumab, alirocumab) that stops LDL-receptor degradation, so the liver clears more LDL.
Primary aldosteronism
Autonomous aldosterone excess (adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia): hypertension, low potassium, metabolic alkalosis.
Stanford type A / B
Dissection involving the ascending aorta (A, surgery) or only the descending aorta (B, medical therapy).
Takayasu arteritis
Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of young Asian women: weak arm pulses, unequal arm pressures.
TBI — toe–brachial index
Toe pressure over arm pressure, used when ankle arteries are calcified; 0.70 or less is abnormal.

🎯 Cardiology Summative — High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by part: the normal heart · the ECG and arrhythmias · ischemia · heart failure and the myocardium · infection and inflammation · valves and surgery · congenital heart disease · vessels.

The Normal Heart

Cardiac cycle & PV loops

  • Blood flows high → low pressure; a valve opens when the chamber before it is higher. LV > LA: mitral shuts (S1) · LV > aorta (~80): aortic opens · LV < aorta: aortic shuts (S2, dicrotic notch) · LV < LA: mitral opens.
  • Isovolumetric contraction and relaxation: all four valves closed, volume flat.
  • a = atrial contraction · c = AV valve bulging at the onset of systole · v = atrial filling. AF: no a wave, no kick, no S4.
  • Kick: Qazi 20–25% of output, Morganelli ~10% of EDV. Diastasis shortens first as HR rises.
  • Ao 120/80 · LV 120/8–10 · LA 8–10 · PA 25/10 · RV 25–30/4 · RA 0–4. SV ≈ 70 · EF 55–70% · CO 4–5 L/min · MAP 90–95.
  • Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, never tropomyosin. Cardiac = calcium-induced calcium release (L-type → RyR2). Heart works on the ascending limb → Starling.
  • Boards use PV loops, not Wiggers. Width = SV · ESPVR slope = contractility · EDPVR = stiffness.
  • ↑Afterload: taller + narrower (ESV ↑, SV ↓) · ↑preload: wider right · ↑contractility: steeper ESPVR, ESV ↓.
  • Acute MI, first seconds: lower Starling curve at a higher EDV.

Heart sounds

  • S1 = mitral + tricuspid close · S2 = aortic + pulmonic close. Normal valve opening is silent.
  • S3 right after S2 = volume overload (HFrEF, dilated cardiomyopathy, MR, AR); normal in the young · "Ken-tuck-y".
  • S4 just before S1 = kick into a stiff LV (hypertension, AS, LVH) · gone in AF · "Ten-nes-see". (Recording said "before S2" — slip.)
  • Split S2: physiologic wider on inspiration · wide = PS, RBBB · fixed = ASD · paradoxical = severe AS, LBBB.
  • Opening snap = MS (short S2–snap = severe) · midsystolic click = MVP (earlier on standing) · soft S2 = severe AS.

Murmurs & maneuvers

  • Systolic = AS or MR · diastolic = MS or AR. Stenosis = gradient · regurgitation = extra volume.
  • Thick wall = concentric (AS) · big chamber = eccentric (AR, MR). MS spares the LV.
  • MS: LA > LV in diastole · rumble + opening snap at apex · rheumatic · AF, LA clot, hemoptysis, pregnancy unmasks.
  • AS: LV ≫ aorta in systole (200/25 vs 110/70) · crescendo–decrescendo R 2nd ICS → carotids · parvus et tardus · LA always high · bicuspid (40–60) vs calcific (70+) · exercise intolerance first, then angina, syncope, HF · avoid nitrates.
  • MR: tall v wave · holosystolic apex → axilla · MVP = click + late systolic murmur · posteromedial papillary muscle after inferior MI.
  • AR: wide pulse pressure (160/60) · early diastolic decrescendo, LSB · water-hammer pulses · Austin Flint.
  • Standing/Valsalva (↓preload): HCM and MVP louder, others softer · squat/leg raise: opposite · handgrip (↑afterload): MR, AR, VSD louder; AS and HCM softer · inspiration: right-sided louder.
  • Innocent: soft (<3/6), midsystolic, positional. Diastolic is almost always pathologic.

Exercise, rehab & prevention

  • 75–90% of CAD from diet, inactivity, smoking. Exercise: ↑vagal/↓sympathetic, ↑HDL, ↑NO, ↓CRP, ↑ischemic threshold.
  • HRmax = 220 − age · 1 MET ≈ 3.5 mL O₂/kg/min · SV plateaus at ~50% VO₂max, then HR drives CO.
  • SBP ↑ 8–12 mm Hg per MET · DBP flat or ↓ (TPR falls).
  • Each 1 MET → 8–35% ↓ mortality (RR 0.87/MET). ≥150 min moderate or ≥75 min vigorous a week (class I).
  • Rehab phase II = 36 sessions, ~3/wk, ECG-monitored, 8–12 wk. Start 1–2 wk (PCI/MI) · 2–6 wk (CABG).
  • Class I: ACS <12 mo, CABG/PCI, stable angina, PAD · class IIa: chronic HF. Only 30–40% enrol; physician endorsement is the lever.
  • FITT: ≥3×/wk · 40–80% HR reserve, RPE 11–16 · 30–60 min · angina → ~10 beats below the ischemic threshold.
  • Mediterranean (PREDIMED, HR 0.70) = only diet with RCT event reduction · DASH + low sodium add · Na <2,400 mg (<1,500 better) · trans fats = class III harm.

Control of the circulation

  • α1 Gq vasoconstriction · α2 Gi brake · β1 Gs heart + renin · β2 Gs dilation · M2 Gi slows SA/AV · NN in all ganglia. Vessels: no parasympathetic supply.
  • Odd = Gq, even = Gi, betas are Gs. Smooth muscle: MLCK contracts; PKA (cAMP) and PKG (cGMP, NO) relax.
  • Pacemaker: phase 4 funny Na⁺ (slope = rate) · phase 0 Ca²⁺ · phase 3 K⁺. Myocyte: phase 0 Na⁺ · plateau Ca²⁺ vs K⁺ · phase 3 K⁺.
  • AV delay ~0.1 s · Purkinje fastest, AV node slowest · denervated HR ~100 · relative refractory period = arrhythmia window.
  • MAP = CO × TPR (MAP is the dependent variable). ACE = kininase II (bradykinin → cough).
  • Poiseuille: R ∝ 1/r⁴ (½ radius → 1/16 flow) · capillaries slowest · parallel lowers total R.
  • ~70% of blood in veins · Pmsf ~7–8 set by stressed volume · nitrate + sildenafil collapses it · Guyton crossing = steady state.
  • HF paradox: pressure systems beat the volume reflex → retention, dilutional hyponatremia (low urine Na⁺).
  • Phenylephrine → reflex bradycardia (atropine) · M2 block + NE → HR ↑ BP ↑ · dobutamine + PDE3i both ↑cAMP.
The ECG & Arrhythmias

Reading the ECG

  • Same order every time: rate → rhythm → axis → intervals (PR, QRS, QT) → chamber enlargement → ischemia → one sentence.
  • Rate = QRS on the strip × 6 (12-lead = 10 s; 6-s strip × 10). Tachy ≥100, brady <60.
  • Small box 40 ms · big box 200 ms · PR 120–200 · QRS <120 · QTc <450 M / <460 F, danger >500.
  • Sinus = 5 criteria: R–R regular, P–P regular, PR constant, a P for every QRS, P upright in II (biphasic in V1).
  • 5 irregular rhythms: AF (no P, irregularly irregular) · sinus arrhythmia (with breathing) · 2nd-degree AV block · WAP (≥3 P shapes, <100) · MAT (same, ≥100).
  • Flutter: sawtooth in II, III, aVF; fixed ratio (regular) or variable (irregular). Right atrium / cavotricuspid isthmus; AF = pulmonary veins / left atrium.
  • Axis from I and aVF: both up = normal · I up, aVF down = left · I down, aVF up = right. aVF isoelectric → use lead II.
  • Left axis: LVH, LBBB, LAFB, old inferior MI. Right axis: RVH, LPFB, old lateral MI.
  • RBBB has a normal axis — RBBB + right axis = RBBB + LPFB.

ECG Patterns of Disease

  • Atria: RAE = tall peaked P in II (>2.5 mm, "P pulmonale"), mostly positive V1 · LAE = wide notched P (>120 ms, "P mitrale"), mostly negative V1. RA makes the P taller, LA makes it wider.
  • LVH: left axis + R in aVL >11 mm (most specific) or S(V1/V2) + R(V5/V6) ≥35 mm (most sensitive). Strain = TWI/ST depression, mimics ischemia.
  • RVH: right axis + reversed R-wave progression (tall R in V1). Normal transition R=S at V3–V4.
  • LBBB: QRS ≥120, left axis, V1–V3 negative, broad notched R in I/aVL/V5–V6 · W in V1, M in V6 (WiLLiaM).
  • RBBB: QRS ≥120, normal axis, rSR′ rabbit ears V1–V2, slurred S in I/V5–V6 · M in V1, W in V6 (MaRRoW).
  • Fascicular block = normal QRS width, axis shift with no other cause. Bundle = wide QRS.
  • Territories: II, III, aVF = RCA (inferior) · V1–V3 anteroseptal, V4–V6 anterior = LAD · I, aVL, V5–V6 = LCx/diagonal. LCx has no direct leads → reciprocal change in V1–V3.
  • ST elevation = transmural = STEMI (≥1 mm, 2 contiguous leads) → open the artery now. ST depression = subendocardial = NSTEMI → stabilise, no emergent cath. Q waves = old, dead (normal only in III). TWI = non-specific.
  • Reciprocal ST depression confirms a STEMI. Evolution: hyperacute T → STE → Q + TWI. Posterior MI = ST depression + tall R + upright T in V1–V3.
  • Hyperkalemia: tall narrow peaked T, then everything widens. Hypokalemia: flat T + U wave → long-looking QT → torsades.
  • QT: eyeball test — T ends before halfway between R waves = normal. Lengtheners: dofetilide/sotalol, low K⁺/Mg²⁺, fluoroquinolones, antidepressants, antiemetics, antifungals, congenital LQTS.

Arrhythmias & Heart Block

  • Mechanisms: automaticity · triggered (EAD → long QT → torsades; DAD → ischemia, digoxin) · re-entry = most common. Slow path = short refractory; fast path = long refractory; a premature beat blocks the fast path, goes down slow, returns up fast.
  • AV block — measure P–P, R–R, PR. 1st: PR long but constant. Mobitz I: PR lengthens then drops; PR after the drop is shorter than before it; benign. Mobitz II: PR constant, sudden drop; pacemaker. 3rd: P and QRS both regular but dissociated.
  • P–P is constant in every AV block. If the Ps don't march, it isn't block.
  • 2:1 block: never two conducted Ps in a row → cannot subtype. Let the history decide; look for the P hidden in the T.
  • SVT is a category, not a diagnosis. Sinus tach = most common. AVNRT = down slow / up fast → atria and ventricles fire together → P hidden in the QRS.
  • Breaking SVT: unstable → sedate + synchronised cardioversion. Stable → vagal (carotid sinus 10–20 s) → adenosine 6 then 12 mg rapid push + flush → IV β-blocker/diltiazem/verapamil → cardioversion. Long term: EP study + ablation (class I).
  • Adenosine: half-life <5 s; flushing, chest pain, doom, brief asystole, bronchospasm. Avoid in heart transplant and WPW.
  • Carotid massage contraindications: recent MI; stroke/TIA <3 months; carotid occlusion; VT/VF history; prior bad reaction. Bruit = image first.
  • Typical flutter: negative sawtooth II, III, aVF; positive V1; counterclockwise around the tricuspid annulus via the cavotricuspid isthmus. Atria 250–300 → locks 2:1 at ~150. Adenosine unmasks, doesn't break it. CTI ablation; ~50% later get AF.
  • Wide + can't tell → treat as VT. Favours VT: AV dissociation (25–33%), capture/fusion beats (~5%, nearly diagnostic), negative precordial concordance (virtually diagnostic), northwest axis, QRS >140/160, slurred from the first millisecond. SVT + BBB has a fast initial deflection.
  • Brugada steps: no RS in any precordial lead → R-to-S >100 ms (onset of R to nadir of S) → AV dissociation → morphology. First yes = VT.
  • WPW: no adenosine, no CCB, no β-blocker, no vagal manoeuvres. Give procainamide, or sedate and cardiovert. Short PR + delta wave; pattern = no symptoms, syndrome = + arrhythmia. Ebstein anomaly is the associated lesion.
  • Congenital long QT: 1 in 5,000, autosomal dominant, mostly K⁺ channels, LQT1–3 = 85–90%. Syncope and sudden death. Acute torsades: IV magnesium.
  • Genetic syndromes: LQTS · short QT · WPW · Brugada (coved STE V1–V2, RV outflow tract) · ARVC (fibro-fatty RV) · HCM, the most common.

Atrial Fibrillation

  • Irregularly irregular, no P waves, no isoelectric baseline, usually narrow. No two "P waves" look the same.
  • Paroxysmal ≤7 days · persistent >7 days and needed intervention · long-standing persistent >12 months · permanent = jointly decided to stop trying.
  • Young: pulmonary-vein triggered, autonomic/genetic. Old: remodelled scarred "maze" — no complete cure by ablation.
  • Triggers: hypertension, coronary disease, valve disease, low K⁺/Mg²⁺, infection, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol ("holiday heart", #3 risk factor), PE, sympathomimetics, obesity, sleep apnea.
  • Most common symptoms = fatigue and shortness of breath, not palpitations (only ~50–60% feel those).
  • Steps: diagnose → how long? → anticoagulation score → rate control first → treat the cause.
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc: CHF 1 · HTN 1 · Age ≥75 = 2 · DM 1 · Stroke/TIA = 2 · Vascular 1 · Age 65–74 1 · female 1. ≥2 → anticoagulate (usually a DOAC). Female sex is a modifier and is dropped in CHA₂DS₂-VA.
  • Flutter is anticoagulated exactly like AF — same score, class 1 recommendation.
  • AFFIRM found rate and rhythm control equivalent; today rhythm control is favoured long term for symptomatic patients or reduced function. Rate control: β-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem. Rhythm control: class I or III.
  • Two dangers: stroke and heart failure. Losing the atrial kick costs ~15% of filling (physiology lecture says ~10% at rest); a persistently fast rate causes tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.

Antiarrhythmic Drugs

  • Rate = nodal tissue = classes II and IV. Rhythm = myocytes = classes I and III.
  • Phase 0 is Ca²⁺ in the node and Na⁺ in the myocyte; K⁺ repolarises both. Funny current (Na⁺) drifts phase 4 and is opened by hyperpolarisation.
  • I = fast Na⁺ block, ↓ phase 0 slope, wider QRS · II = β-block, flatter phase 4, longer PR · III = K⁺ block, longer phase 2–3 and ERP, longer QT · IV = L-type Ca²⁺ block, slower nodal phase 0, longer PR.
  • Phase 0 slowing: C > A > B. Repolarisation Goldilocks: IA prolongs, IB shortens, IC unchanged. IA therefore carries torsades risk, like class III.
  • Use-dependent block: class I binds open/inactivated channels, so faster rates and ischemic tissue get more block.
  • IA: quinidine (cinchonism: tinnitus, blurred vision, delirium; raises digoxin), procainamide (drug-induced lupus; drug of choice in WPW + AF; no digoxin interaction), disopyramide (most anticholinergic).
  • IB: lidocaine (IV, ventricular, CNS effects and seizures), mexiletine (oral). IB is Best post-MI; IC is Contraindicated.
  • IC: flecainide, propafenone — AF prevention in a structurally normal heart only. Widen the QRS, more with exertion. Always pair with an AV-nodal blocker or you get 1:1 flutter.
  • II: 1st gen non-selective propranolol (not in asthma) · 2nd gen β1-selective metoprolol, esmolol (very short half-life, unstable patients) · 3rd gen carvedilol/labetalol (+α1), nebivolol (NO). Propranolol for a long QT (no repolarisation effect); labetalol in pregnancy (α1 block protects placental perfusion). Lipophilic drugs → vivid nightmares.
  • III: ibutilide (IV, terminates only, TdP ~2%) · dofetilide (oral, terminates and maintains, no negative inotropy so OK with low EF, renally dosed) · sotalol (II + III). Started in hospital.
  • Amiodarone = all four classes. Toxicities: pulmonary fibrosis (baseline + annual PFTs), thyroid (37% iodine; TFTs), liver, neuropathy, corneal microdeposits, photosensitivity and blue-grey skin. Safe in HFrEF; low actual torsades risk.
  • IV: verapamil (heart) → diltiazem (both) → "-dipines" (vessels). IV verapamil + β-blocker = electromechanical dissociation, contraindicated. Verapamil → constipation; diltiazem → edema.
  • Adenosine: P1 receptor → Gi/o → opens K⁺ channels → hyperpolarises the node. 6 then 12 mg, hard push + flush. Doom, flushing, chest pain, bronchospasm up to 30 min in asthma. Theophylline and caffeine block it.
  • Digoxin: blocks Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na⁺ → NCX can't extrude Ca²⁺ → ↑ SR Ca²⁺ → ↑ contractility; plus ↑ vagal tone and slower AV conduction. Hypokalemia increases toxicity — check K⁺ first. Scooped "reverse check" ST depression, yellow-green halos, anorexia. Antidote: fix K⁺, digoxin immune Fab. Interactions: loop/thiazide diuretics, erythromycin (kills gut flora), quinidine, verapamil/diltiazem.
  • Atropine: muscarinic antagonist, crosses the blood–brain barrier. First-line for symptomatic bradycardia and AV block; catecholamines second. Toxidrome → physostigmine (crosses the BBB; pyridostigmine doesn't; pralidoxime is for organophosphates).
Atherosclerosis & Ischemia

Arteriosclerosis vs Atherosclerosis

  • Arteriosclerosis = any hardening (umbrella); atherosclerosis = the intimal-plaque subset.
  • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: glassy pink wall, benign HTN/diabetes → nephrosclerosis. Hyperplastic: "onion skin" ± fibrinoid necrosis, malignant HTN.
  • Mönckeberg: calcium in the media, lumen spared, asymptomatic, pipe-stem on X-ray. Intimal hyperplasia: after stents/grafts → restenosis. Don't confuse with FMD (string of beads, young women's renal arteries).
  • Injury response: SMCs cross the IEL into the intima, proliferate, lay down matrix → intimal thickening → stenosis. Turbulent flow at branch points.
  • Plaque: injury → LDL in, oxidised → monocyte → macrophage → foam cell (fatty streak) → platelets/PDGF → SMC migration (fibrofatty atheroma) → necrotic core, cholesterol clefts, calcium. All inside the intima.
  • Sites: abdominal aorta > coronaries > popliteal > carotid > circle of Willis.
  • Thin cap = vulnerable → rupture/hemorrhage → thrombosis → MI, sudden death. Thick cap/fibrocalcific = stable → critical stenosis → angina.
  • Risk: LDL (main driver), smoking (initial injury), HTN, diabetes (glycation), age, male, family history. Risk factors multiply.

Stable Angina vs ACS

  • Stable: fixed ≥70% stenosis, exertional, minutes, rest relieves, troponin normal. UA: rupture + non-occlusive clot, crescendo or rest, troponin normal. NSTEMI: partial occlusion, subendocardial, troponin ↑, ST↓/T inversion. STEMI: complete occlusion, transmural, ST↑ → Q waves.
  • Vasospastic: young, rest/night, transient ST↑, no plaque needed.
  • Flow reserve: stress flow falls at ~50% stenosis, rest flow at ~80–90%.
  • Type 1 (primary) = plaque rupture, younger men · Type 2 (secondary) = supply–demand (sepsis, tachycardia, anemia), older women · MINOCA 10–15%.
  • History: pressure, substernal, radiating, minutes, exertional, inducible ("can you make it happen?"). Women, diabetics, elderly atypical. NTG relief not diagnostic.
  • Testing: pre-test probability first. Exercise + readable ECG → ETT (± imaging); unreadable ECG → exercise imaging; can't exercise → pharmacologic stress or CCTA. Never stress-test active ischemia. Stress echo better in women.
  • Cath timing: STEMI door-to-balloon <90 min · NSTE-ACS very high risk (shock, refractory pain, arrhythmia) <2 h · high risk (troponin+) <24 h · intermediate <72 h.
  • ACS in the office: aspirin, NTG, O₂ if hypoxic, monitor, ambulance — never by car. Troponin = ED only.
  • Optimal medical therapy: antiplatelet + statin + ACEi/ARB + β-blocker (~13% vs ~20% 10-yr mortality).

Troponin & BNP

  • Troponin = myocytes dying. hs-cTn rises 1–3 h, peaks 12–24 h, elevated 7–10 d. Diagnose MI by rise and/or fall on serial values (repeat at 1–3 h). Height ∝ infarct size.
  • Specific for heart muscle, not for infarction: marathon, PE, myocarditis, chronic HF, sepsis, CKD (flat), takotsubo.
  • CK-MB back to normal in 2–3 d → re-infarction.
  • BNP = ventricular stretch. Pro-BNP → active BNP (32 aa, t½ ~20 min) + inert NT-proBNP (76 aa, t½ 1–2 h). Acts via cGMP: vasodilation, natriuresis, ↓ renin/aldosterone.
  • Rule-out: BNP ≤100, NT-proBNP ≤300. Rule-in: BNP >400; NT-proBNP >450 / 900 / 1,800 by age (<50 / 50–75 / >75).
  • Sacubitril ↑ BNP (neprilysin blocked) → follow NT-proBNP. CKD ↑ both (NT-proBNP more). Obesity falsely lowers both. Age ↑.

MI Histology Timeline

  • 0–½ h: EM only (reversible) · ½–4 h: wavy fibres at border · 4–12 h: early coagulative necrosis, edema · 12–24 h: dark mottling, pyknosis, hypereosinophilia, contraction bands, first neutrophils.
  • 1–3 d: yellow-tan centre; loss of nuclei/striations, neutrophils.
  • 3–7 d: hyperemic border, soft; macrophages → softest wall = rupture window.
  • 7–10 d: maximally yellow and soft, granulation at margins · 10–14 d: granulation tissue, new vessels, early collagen · 2–8 wk: grey-white scar · >2 mo: dense scar.
  • Wavy-fibre timing differs (lecture ½–4 h, First Aid 0–4 h, UWorld 4–12 h): first LM change, day 1.
  • Transmural = complete occlusion (STEMI); subendocardial = inner third, partial occlusion (NSTEMI).
  • Reperfusion injury: Ca²⁺ floods in → contraction band necrosis; free radicals; hemorrhagic infarct.

Post-MI Complications

  • 0–24 h: VF/VT (sudden death), bradycardia/AV block (RCA → SA 60%, AV 90%), acute HF, cardiogenic shock (≥40% LV).
  • 1–3 d: fibrinous pericarditis.
  • 3–14 d (soft wall): papillary rupture — inferior MI, posteromedial (PDA only), flash pulmonary edema, apical murmur to axilla (may be silent) · septal rupture — holosystolic LSB murmur + thrill, O₂ step-up RA→PA · free wall — anterior, elderly woman, first MI, tamponade, PEA, no murmur · pseudoaneurysm (pericardium + clot, operate).
  • Weeks–months: true aneurysm (persistent ST↑ + Q, dyskinetic, mural thrombus, VT), Dressler (>2 wk, autoimmune pericarditis), chronic HF.
  • RV infarct: hypotension + JVD + clear lungs → fluids, no nitrates.
  • Free-wall timing differs: lecture 3–7 d, Watkins 24 h + 3–5 d, First Aid 5–14 d.
  • Mortality ~30% year 1, then ~3%/yr. AKI in ~40% of CPR survivors.

Antianginal Drugs

  • Lower demand — the easy lever. Stable: SL NTG + β-blocker (best monotherapy, resting HR ~50) ± CCB/long nitrate → ranolazine. Vasospastic: SL NTG + CCB, no β-blocker (unopposed α).
  • Nitrates: ALDH2 → NO → sGC → cGMP → venodilation, ↓ preload. Headache, flushing, hypotension, reflex tachycardia. Tolerance → nitrate-free interval overnight. ISMN = high oral bioavailability. ALDH2 polymorphism (East Asian) → less effect.
  • PDE5 inhibitor + nitrate = refractory hypotension. Also avoid nitrates in RV infarct, HOCM, severe AS, hypotension.
  • DHP CCB: ↓ afterload, edema, reflex tachycardia. Verapamil/diltiazem: ↓ HR + contractility, AV block, constipation. β-blocker + IV verapamil contraindicated.
  • Ranolazine: blocks late Na⁺ current → less Ca²⁺ overload, ↓ diastolic wall stress; no HR/BP change; QT ↑, dizziness, constipation; women benefit more.
  • Ivabradine = funny current (If/HCN), not late Na⁺ (slide slip).
  • ACS bundle: aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant, NTG, β-blocker (not in shock/bradycardia/ADHF/cocaine), high-intensity statin, O₂ only if hypoxic, reperfusion.
Heart Failure & the Myocardium

HFrEF vs HFpEF

  • CHF ≈ 50% 5-year survival. Pressure overload → sarcomeres in parallel → concentric (HTN, AS). Volume overload → in series → eccentric (AR, MR, post-MI).
  • HFrEF (EF ≤40%): ↓ contractility, ESPVR flatter, ↑EDV/ESV, dilated, S3; younger man post-MI; CV death. HFpEF (EF ≥50%): ↓ compliance, steep EDPVR, ↓EDV at ↑EDP, EF preserved, S4; older woman, obesity, HTN, DM, CKD, AF; early endothelial dysfunction, stiff N2B titin.
  • Neurohumoral spiral: ↓ BP → sympathetic → β1 renin → AT II (↑ afterload) → aldosterone (↑ preload) → ↑ O₂ demand. Dilated chambers resist natriuretic peptide.
  • Left HF: dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, crackles, heart-failure cells. Right HF: ↑JVP, +HJR, edema, nutmeg liver → cardiac cirrhosis. Commonest cause of right HF = left HF.
  • High-output HF: AV fistula, thyrotoxicosis, anemia, wet beriberi (↑CO, ↓SVR). NYHA I–IV + ACC/AHA stage A–D.
  • Forrester: wet-warm commonest (diurese); wet-cold = cardiogenic shock (ICU, inotropes). Decongest preload first; no new β-blocker while decompensated.
  • Labs: CBC, CMP, TSH, A1c, iron, BNP/NT-proBNP; no office troponin. Echo diastolic grade 2 = ↑LA pressure. CXR Kerley B. H₂FPEF: heavy 2, HTN 1, AF 3, PASP 1, >60 1, E/e′ 1.
  • Cocaine + β1-selective blocker → unopposed α → ↑ afterload.

Heart Failure Drugs

  • Mortality ↓: ARNI (> ACEi > ARB), β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol), MRA, SGLT2i (also HFpEF); hydralazine + ISDN add-on (A-HeFT). Symptoms only: diuretics, digoxin, nitrates, inotropes, tolvaptan.
  • All four: HR 0.84 → 0.36; ~5 years longer life. Start low doses of all four in hospital, then titrate over 4–6 weeks.
  • Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin → ↑ natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, substance P. 36-h ACEi washout (angioedema). Hypotension, ↑K⁺, fetal toxicity. Follow NT-proBNP.
  • β-blocker only when compensated. Carvedilol adds α1 block (↓ afterload).
  • Spironolactone: ↑K⁺, gynecomastia (antiandrogen) → eplerenone. ACEi/ARNI + MRA → hyperkalemia.
  • SGLT2i: natriuresis, tubuloglomerular feedback → afferent constriction; Fournier gangrene, euglycemic DKA, genital infection.
  • Furosemide: NKCC2; ↓K/Na/Ca/Mg, hypokalemic alkalosis, ototoxicity; sulfa allergy → ethacrynic acid. Braking (DCT hypertrophy) → add thiazide.
  • Dobutamine = β1 (racemic, α cancels). Milrinone = PDE3. Norepinephrine → reflex bradycardia. Nitroprusside = spontaneous NO, arteries + veins, cyanide. Ivabradine = If. Vericiguat = sGC stimulator.
  • Starling: preload ↓ slides down the same curve; afterload ↓ or inotrope moves to a higher curve.

Cardiomyopathies

  • Dilated (EF <40%, systolic): genetic (TTN), alcohol, peripartum, myocarditis (Coxsackie B, Chagas), hemochromatosis, doxorubicin, sarcoid. Treat as HFrEF + ICD.
  • Hypertrophic (1 in 500, AD, sarcomere MYH7/MYBPC3): asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM, myofibre disarray; murmur ↑ Valsalva; appears in adolescence. #1 cause of sudden death in young athletes (~36%). Do less, β-blocker, septal myectomy/alcohol ablation, ICD; avoid diuretics, nitrates, vasodilators.
  • Restrictive: amyloid (low-voltage ECG, thick walls, apple-green birefringence), radiation, sarcoid, hemochromatosis, Löffler. Big atria. Mimic: constrictive pericarditis.
  • ARVC: fibro-fatty RV, VT, epsilon wave; ICD.
  • Takotsubo: postmenopausal woman, stressor, apical ballooning, clean coronaries.

Heart Tumors

  • Myxoma: most common primary (adults), left atrium, stalk at fossa ovalis; ball-valve positional syncope/dyspnea, emboli (TIA), IL-6 fevers/weight loss, tumour plop; stellate cells in myxoid stroma. Resect stalk + septal cuff → no recurrence (Carney complex can recur).
  • Rhabdomyoma: most common in children, ventricles, tuberous sclerosis, often regress.
  • Papillary fibroelastoma: mitral chordae, emboli.
  • Metastases: most common overall (~10% of autopsies); bloody pericardial effusion → tamponade; RCC up the IVC.
Infection & Inflammation

Endocarditis: Who and What

  • Acute: S. aureus, normal valve, fulminant, broad (MRSA) cover. Subacute: viridans strep, damaged valve, dental source. Now ~75% acute.
  • In-hospital mortality 15–20%, 1-year up to 40%; ~half need valve surgery.
  • Risk: >50 y, men, dental disease, structural disease (75%; MVP with MR now #1 over RHD), devices (23%), IDU, dialysis, diabetes.
  • Pathogenesis: endothelial injury → sterile platelet–fibrin nidus → bacteremia → colonisation → biofilm (~500× resistant, slow-growing bacteria).
  • Vegetation → seeding, valve destruction (perforation, ring abscess, block), septic emboli (stroke, mycotic aneurysm, spleen/kidney infarcts).
  • Left: mitral > aortic; systemic emboli. Right: tricuspid (~60% in IDU), S. aureus 70–80%, no murmur, septic pulmonary emboli; repair tricuspid first.
  • Organisms: S. aureus 31% (GPC, catalase+, coagulase+) · viridans 17% · S. epidermidis 11% = prosthetic valves · enterococci 11% (urinary catheters) · S. gallolyticus → colon cancer · HACEK · fungi (bulky, immunocompromised).
  • Culture-negative: antibiotics before cultures (commonest) · Coxiella (Q fever, phase I IgG >1:800) · Bartonella (cats, homeless). Libman–Sacks (SLE) and marantic = sterile.

Endocarditis: Diagnosis & Treatment

  • Fever 90%, new murmur 85% (MR, AR, TR). Splenomegaly, petechiae ~40%.
  • Emboli: Janeway (painless palms/soles), splinters, petechiae. Immune complex: Osler (painful pads — "Ouch"), Roth spots, GN, +RF (50–60%).
  • 3 blood-culture sets before antibiotics (low-level continuous bacteremia). TTE ~65% → TOE ~95%; CT for abscess; PET for prosthetics.
  • Duke 2023 definite: 2 major · 1 major + 3 minor · 5 minor. Possible: 1 + 1 or 3 minor. Majors: typical organism ×2 sets, vegetation/abscess/new regurgitation.
  • Bactericidal, 4–6 weeks. Empiric: vancomycin + cefepime/ceftriaxone. MSSA: nafcillin/oxacillin (~6 wk; handout "3–5 days" typo). MRSA & S. epidermidis: vanc + rifampin (biofilm). Viridans: PCN G or ceftriaxone 4 wk. Enterococci: ampicillin/PCN + gentamicin (synergy). HACEK: ceftriaxone. Bartonella: doxy + rifampin.
  • Mechanisms: β-lactams → PBPs; vancomycin → D-Ala-D-Ala; aminoglycosides → 30S; rifampin → RNA polymerase.
  • Surgery: HF from valve damage, abscess/heart block, persistent bacteremia, fungi/resistant organisms, large vegetation with emboli, prosthetic dehiscence.
  • Prophylaxis (amoxicillin) only for prosthetic valve, prior IE, certain CHD, transplant valvulopathy.

Myocarditis & Pericarditis

  • Myocarditis: young (20–50), viral prodrome then unexplained HF/chest pain/arrhythmia; troponin up (plateau). Viruses: parvo B19, HHV-6 now; Coxsackie B classic (CAR receptor with adenovirus). Diphtheria toxin; Lyme → heart block (~10%); Chagas (kissing bug, cardiomyopathy + megacolon/megaesophagus, now US-endemic); checkpoint inhibitors.
  • Histology: lymphocytic = viral · eosinophilic = parasite/hypersensitivity · giant-cell · granulomatous = sarcoid. EMB definitive. Treatment supportive, bed rest/no exertion, antivirals unproven.
  • Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic pain, better leaning forward, radiates to trapezius, friction rub, diffuse STE + PR depression (no territory). ≥2 of 4: pain, rub, ECG, effusion. NSAIDs + colchicine.
  • Causes: viral (Coxsackie, parvo, CMV), purulent (S. aureus, pneumococcus), TB, uremia, post-MI/Dressler, SLE/RA, cancer, radiation. Fluid types: serous · fibrinous ("bread and butter") · purulent · hemorrhagic (cancer) · constrictive.
  • ECG stages: STE/PR↓ → normal → diffuse TWI (wk 2–4) → normal.
  • Tamponade: Beck triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus + electrical alternans; water-bottle CXR; pericardiocentesis or subxiphoid window.
  • Constrictive: Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock; mimics restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Valves & Surgery

Valvular Heart Disease

  • Left side matters. Stenosis = pressure load (concentric); regurgitation = volume load (eccentric). AV valves can be repaired; semilunar valves usually replaced.
  • AS: bicuspid (40s–60s; screen for ascending aneurysm + coarctation) vs calcific (70s+; lamellar bone; statins don't help). Symptoms → ~50% dead in 2 yr. No drug slows it → replace. Heyde syndrome (vWF cleaved → GI bleed). Avoid nitrates.
  • AR: root (Marfan, syphilis, dissection, ankylosing spondylitis) or valve (endocarditis, bicuspid). Surgery: symptoms, EF <50%, ESD >55 mm. No TAVR in pure AR.
  • MS: rheumatic, fish-mouth fused commissures; AF + LA thrombus (warfarin). β-blocker, diuretic, balloon commissurotomy, MVR (tissue in young women).
  • MR: MVP (myxomatous) commonest US cause; functional from dilated LV or inferior MI. Organic → repair, functional → replace.
  • Upstream cascade AR → MR → pulmonary HTN → TR → right failure: fix valves early.
  • RHD: GAS M-protein mimicry (~3%), Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells; mitral > aortic > tricuspid > pulmonic.
  • Right side: TR mostly functional (left HF); IDU, carcinoid (TR + PS), leads. Tricuspid: repair first; tissue valve if replaced. PS congenital (Noonan) → balloon. PR after tetralogy repair.

Aortic Valve Replacement

  • Indications: severe AS + any symptom, severe AS + EF <50%, severe AS at other cardiac surgery (severe = ≥4 m/s, ≥40 mm Hg, ≤1.0 cm²). AR: symptoms, EF <50%, ESD >55 mm.
  • Cath before SAVR (~50% need CABG too). STS risk score.
  • SAVR: sternotomy + bypass + cardioplegia; younger, mechanical option, root/CABG at the same time; mortality <1% low risk; 4–6 weeks recovery.
  • TAVR: transfemoral, balloon valve during rapid pacing; elderly/high risk, now first-line for most AS; ~2.5% mortality; needs a calcified annulus → not for pure AR.
  • Mechanical: lasts forever, lifelong warfarin (no DOACs), heparin bridge. Tissue: aspirin only, wears out (~90% free of redo at 15 yr aortic) → valve-in-valve. Tissue for older patients and women planning pregnancy.
  • Complications: heart block → pacemaker (SAVR 3–4%, more with TAVR), RCA ostium obstruction, paravalvular leak (TAVR), stroke, vascular injury, valve thrombosis (mechanical, low INR), hemolysis (schistocytes), structural degeneration (tissue), prosthetic-valve endocarditis (S. epidermidis early).
Congenital Heart Disease

Congenital Heart Disease

  • 1 in 125 births, most common birth defect, first 8 weeks, ~90% unexplained. Blood goes high → low pressure; after the first breath PVR falls, so open holes shunt L→R.
  • Acyanotic (L→R, ↑ lung flow): VSD (commonest; holosystolic LLSB; small = louder; small ones close by 2 yr) · ASD (fixed split S2, AF, paradoxical embolism; Amplatzer) · PDA (machinery murmur, preterm, rubella; indomethacin closes, PGE₁ keeps open). Coarctation = obstruction.
  • Eisenmenger: long L→R shunt → fixed pulmonary HTN → R→L → late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia; too late to close.
  • Cyanotic — 5 T's: Truncus · Transposition · Tricuspid atresia · Tetralogy · TAPVR (+ HLHS, Ebstein).
  • TOF: VSD + RVOT stenosis + RVH + overriding aorta; stenosis sets cyanosis; tet spells (↓SVR) → knee-chest/squat (↑SVR); boot-shaped heart; BT shunt historically; 22q11.
  • TGA: aorta from RV; needs mixing; egg on a string; PGE₁ ± septostomy → arterial switch; maternal diabetes. HLHS: shock as ductus closes → PGE₁ → Norwood/Glenn/Fontan.
  • CXR: boot (TOF), egg on string (TGA), snowman (TAPVR), box (Ebstein), rib notching (coarct).
  • Syndromes: Down → AVSD · Turner → coarct + BAV · 22q11 → truncus, TOF · Williams → supravalvular AS · Noonan → PS · rubella → PDA · lithium → Ebstein · maternal diabetes → TGA · Marfan → MVP/root.

Coarctation & the Newborn Murmur

  • Check femorals on every newborn. Coarct: weak/delayed femorals, arm BP > leg (≥20 mm Hg), murmur to the back, cool mottled legs; juxtaductal; boys 2:1; Turner (25–30%), BAV.
  • Critical coarct is ductal-dependent → shock on day 1–2 → PGE₁, then balloon or resection by gradient. Late: arm HTN, rib notching, berry aneurysms.
  • Incidence: VSD > PDA > PS > ASD > coarct > BAV > TOF > TGA (lecture chart); BAV now ≈ VSD with routine echo.
  • Newborn murmur: well baby → watch (closing PDA/PFO); persists or louder → refer, ECG + echo (definitive). Diastolic, harsh, thrill, click, abnormal S2, symptoms → echo. Roughly a third to half of referred newborn murmurs are structural (approximate; not in lecture).
  • No murmur ≠ no disease: pulse-ox screening after 24 h (hand + foot), <95% or a difference → echo.
Vessels

Hypertension

  • Stage 1 130–139/80–89 · stage 2 ≥140/≥90 · severe >180/120. Measure right (cuff over clothing ±50 mm Hg); home/ambulatory → white-coat vs masked.
  • 90–95% essential (salt, genes). Pump (young, ↑CO) vs vascular (old, ↑SVR). Damage: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, LVH, stroke, nephrosclerosis, retinopathy; malignant = onion skin.
  • Look for secondary: resistant, abrupt, <30, TOD out of proportion, malignant, new diastolic ≥65, unprovoked ↓K⁺.
  • Causes: OSA (>30% of resistant) · PA (↓K, alkalosis, ↓renin, ↑ARR, no edema, polyuria) · renal artery stenosis (bruit, flash edema, ↑renin ↑aldo; FMD in young women) · renal parenchymal · thyroid · Cushing · pheo (spells, metanephrines) · coarct · pre-eclampsia · drugs (NSAIDs, decongestants, OCPs, steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, cocaine).
  • Renin/aldo: ↓/↑ PA · ↑/↑ secondary · ↓/↓ Liddle, licorice, Cushing, CAH.
  • PA: 60% bilateral hyperplasia (MRA) vs 30% adenoma (CT + AVS → adrenalectomy). ARR only valid with suppressed renin; stop MRA 4 wk; β-blocker false +.
  • Resistant = 3 drugs incl. diuretic. Exclude pseudo-resistance; add spironolactone.
  • Urgency (no TOD) → oral, slow. Emergency (TOD) → IV, ↓MAP ≤25% in hour 1 (dissection: SBP <120 fast). Cushing reflex: ↑SBP + bradycardia → raised ICP.

Antihypertensives & Electrolytes

  • First line: ACEi/ARB, DHP CCB, thiazide. Stage 2 <75 not frail → two drugs in one pill (DHP CCB + ACEi/ARB). Monotherapy is undone by baroreflex + renin.
  • Comorbidity picks: stones/osteoporosis → thiazide · CKD albuminuria → ACEi/ARB · AF → β-blocker or non-DHP CCB · pregnancy-possible → DHP CCB · BPH → α1 blocker.
  • ACEi: ↓AT II + ↑bradykinin → cough (predicts angioedema), angioedema, ↑K⁺; enalapril prodrug. ARB: no bradykinin. Avoid ACEi+ARB, β-blocker+verapamil/diltiazem, two sympatholytics, RAASi in pregnancy.
  • DHP CCB: edema (not fixed by diuretic), reflex tachycardia (nifedipine). Verapamil heart → diltiazem → dipines vessels.
  • Pregnancy: labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa (hydralazine acute). Avoid ACEi/ARB/aliskiren, nitroprusside, spironolactone, atenolol.
  • Electrolytes: thiazide ↓Na ↓K ↑Ca ↑urate ↑glucose, alkalosis · loop ↓K ↓Mg ↓Ca, alkalosis · ACEi/ARB/aliskiren ↑K · MRA ↑K + hyperchloremic acidosis (spironolactone gynecomastia) · amiloride ↑K + acidosis · acetazolamide ↓K + acidosis.
  • Mechanism: more distal Na⁺ → ENaC → lumen negative → K⁺ and H⁺ out. Block aldosterone/ENaC → K⁺ and H⁺ stay.

Dyslipidemias

  • Chylomicron (gut, B-48, dietary TG) · VLDL (liver, B-100, TG) → IDL → LDL (B-100, cholesterol, cleared by hepatic LDL receptor) · HDL (A-I, LCAT, reverse transport).
  • PCSK9 degrades LDL receptors; loss-of-function → low LDL, less CVD.
  • Type I (AR, LPL/apoC-II): chylomicrons, pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas, no ↑ atherosclerosis · Type II FH (AD, LDL receptor/apoB-100): LDL, tendon xanthomas, arcus <45, MI young · III (AR, apoE): remnants, palmar xanthomas · IV (AD, ↑VLDL): TG, pancreatitis.
  • Secondary ↑TG: diabetes, alcohol, CKD, estrogen, β-blockers, thiazides, steroids, HIV PIs. ↑Cholesterol: hypothyroidism, nephrotic, cholestasis, anorexia.
  • Diet ↓ cholesterol ~25%. ↑LDL: replace saturated fat, no trans fat, fibre. ↑TG: cut refined carbs, sugar, alcohol; fish. Mediterranean/DASH (Section 4).

Lipid Drugs

  • Statin → HMG-CoA reductase → ↑ LDL receptors. High intensity: atorva, rosuva (post-MI). Non-CYP: prava, rosuva. CYP3A4: lova, simva, atorva.
  • Ezetimibe (NPC1L1): add-on; weak alone (synthesis ↑). Sequestrants: GI, vit K deficiency, ↑TG, bind drugs. Fibrates (PPAR-α): ↓TG ↑HDL; myopathy, gallstones. Niacin: ↑HDL; flushing (aspirin), hyperglycemia, gout. Omega-3: ↓TG. PCSK9 mAb / inclisiran siRNA / oral: after max statin + ezetimibe.
  • DDIs: statin + CYP3A4 inhibitor (clarithromycin, azoles, PIs, grapefruit, diltiazem/verapamil) → rhabdo · statin + gemfibrozil → rhabdo (use fenofibrate) · fibrate + warfarin → protein-binding displacement, bleeding · sequestrant + other drugs → space doses.
  • Prevent: don't front-load myalgia counselling (nocebo); tea-coloured urine → CK; switch statin/dose; aspirin before niacin; no statins in pregnancy.

Aneurysms & Dissection

  • True (saccular / fusiform, all layers) · false (breach + hematoma) · dissection (intimal tear → blood in media → false lumen).
  • Causes: weak material (Marfan, EDS), remodelling (MMPs), vasa vasorum ischemia, infection (syphilis → thoracic, tree-bark; mycotic). Thoracic: cystic medial degeneration. AAA: transmural inflammation, mural thrombus.
  • AAA: commonest, infrarenal, smoking/age/male/family; rupture risk ↑ female, HTN, COPD, smoking. Screen men 65–75 who ever smoked (one US). CT gold standard.
  • Chart: <4.5 US q6mo · 4.5–5.0 q3mo · 5.0–5.5 repair if female, familial, rapid growth · >5.5 repair. Also symptomatic, >5 mm/6 mo, saccular.
  • EVAR (neck >15 mm) vs open. Post-op bloody diarrhea = ischemic colitis (IMA). Graft infection → remove graft. Aortoenteric fistula → herald bleed.
  • Splenic aneurysm ruptures in pregnancy (>2 cm repair). Popliteal: embolises, often bilateral + AAA.
  • Dissection: HTN, Marfan/EDS/LDS/Turner, BAV, cocaine, pregnancy; tearing pain to the back, arm BP difference, widened mediastinum; can present as stroke.
  • Stanford A (ascending; DeBakey I, II) → emergency surgery. Stanford B (distal to L subclavian; DeBakey III) → IV β-blocker first (HR ~60, SBP 100–120), then vasodilator; TEVAR if complicated. Adamkiewicz → paraplegia; CSF drain.

Connective Tissue Disorders

  • Marfan: FBN1 fibrillin-1, AD; root dilation → AR, type A dissection (lifetime up to 30%), MVP >90%; tall, arachnodactyly, upward lens dislocation, pectus.
  • Vascular EDS: COL3A1 collagen III, AD; rupture of medium arteries, bowel, uterus; thin translucent skin; avoid invasive procedures.
  • Loeys–Dietz: TGF-β receptor; tortuous arteries, bifid uvula, hypertelorism; dissects at smaller sizes → earlier surgery.
  • Turner (45,X): coarctation 25–30%, BAV, aortic dissection (esp. pregnancy).
  • Manage: serial imaging, β-blocker ± losartan, prophylactic root replacement (~5.0 cm Marfan, smaller in LDS), avoid contact sports, plan pregnancy.

Vasculitis

  • Mechanisms: immune complex (HSP-IgA, cryo-HCV, PAN-HBV, SLE) · ANCA pauci-immune (GPA PR3/c, MPA MPO/p, EGPA) · anti-GBM · cell-mediated granulomatous (GCA, Takayasu) · infection/mimicry (syphilis, Cogan, Buerger-tobacco).
  • Large: GCA (>50, headache, jaw claudication, PMR, ↑ESR, granulomas + fragmented IEL; steroids before biopsy — blindness) · Takayasu (young Asian women, pulseless, unequal arm BP, angiography, steroids).
  • Medium: PAN (HBV, ANCA−, spares lung, fibrinoid necrosis, renal/GI/nerve) · Kawasaki (<5, CRASH + fever ≥5 d, ↑platelets, coronary aneurysm → echo, IVIG + aspirin) · Buerger (young male smokers, distal ischemia, corkscrew collaterals, arteries + veins, stop smoking).
  • Small: GPA (sinus + lung + kidney, c-ANCA, granulomas) · MPA (lung + kidney, p-ANCA, no granulomas) · EGPA (asthma, eosinophils, neuropathy) · HSP (child after URI: purpura, arthritis, abdominal pain, GN) · cryo (HCV, cold) · anti-GBM (lung hemorrhage + GN).
  • Behçet: HLA-B51, Turkey/Middle East, oral + genital ulcers, uveitis. Leukocytoclastic = nuclear dust.
  • Severe ANCA disease: steroids + rituximab/cyclophosphamide ± plasma exchange.

Peripheral arterial disease

  • Vascular claudication: cramping calf, fixed distance, relieved by standing still in minutes, weak pulses · neurogenic: standing triggers it, relieved by sitting/flexing (shopping cart, better uphill), normal pulses.
  • Smoking (risk persists ~30 yr after quitting) + diabetes (limb-threatening, tibial). Most PAD is silent or atypical.
  • ABI = higher ankle ÷ higher arm: ≤0.90 PAD · 0.91–0.99 borderline · >1.40 calcified → toe–brachial index · ≤0.40 rest pain/tissue loss.
  • CTA diagnoses; angiogram is for procedures. Dependent rubor fades with elevation (cellulitis doesn't). Blue toe = look upstream.
  • Leriche: buttock claudication + absent femoral pulses + ED (aortoiliac).
  • Acute limb ischemia (6 P's, AF embolus): IV heparin first → lysis if motor/sensory intact, else Fogarty embolectomy; reperfusion compartment syndrome → fasciotomy.
  • Rx: supervised exercise (30–45 min, ≥3×/wk, ≥12 wk), quit smoking, high-intensity statin, SAPT or aspirin + rivaroxaban 2.5 bid (↓ MACE + MALE); cilostazol (PDE3) ↑ walking, contraindicated in HF. Revascularise for lifestyle-limiting symptoms, rest pain, tissue loss.
  • Claudication: limb loss rare (~1%/yr); MI/stroke/death far likelier.

Mesenteric ischemia

  • Elderly + AF + pain out of proportion to exam = SMA embolus (past the proximal jejunal branches) → CTA → embolectomy + lifelong anticoagulation.
  • Thrombosis (~20%, origin plaque) → aortomesenteric bypass · NOMI (low flow, pressors) → bowel rest, fluids, antibiotics · SMV thrombosis → anticoagulate · dead bowel → resect. "When in doubt, operate."
  • Chronic: middle-aged woman, postprandial pain, weight loss (food fear) → CTA → revascularise.
  • Collaterals: pancreaticoduodenal arcade (celiac–SMA), marginal artery (SMA–IMA); watershed = splenic flexure, rectosigmoid.
Supporting Lecture

Cardiovascular health in women

  • CVD = 1 in 3 deaths in US women; >10,000 MIs/yr under 45; under 65, MI mortality ~2× men's. Age is a risk factor from >50 (men >40).
  • Atypical symptoms; SCAD, Takotsubo, MINOCA, microvascular disease cluster in women.
  • Enhancers: menarche ≤10 (RR 1.27, U-shaped), preeclampsia, gestational HTN/diabetes, pregnancy loss, preterm birth; postmenopause weighted like male sex.
  • MHT: WHI/HERS no benefit (women >10 yr post-menopause); timing hypothesis — start <10 yr after menopause and <60 · avoid with ASCVD, VTE, breast cancer, 10-yr risk ≥7.5%.
